/en/course/2026/ARDM22PRA1.outcomes:
Learning outcomes
The concrete interpretation of the curriculum professional experience is different for each student, both in the character of the work or professional experience and in the order in which it is gained. Because of these differences in practical situations, the curriculum of professional experience does not consist of a detailed curriculum. The curriculum professional experience is a framework in terms of content, in the form of a matrix (see appendix 1 professional practice guide) with action levels and learning outcomes, linked to the competences. This matrix provides clarity
about the professional experiences, skills, knowledge and insights you are expected to gain while working in practice. It does not express an opinion on the way in which and the order in which this is done. To a large extent, each student can and must determine this for themselves, based on their own practical situation.
/en/course/2026/ARDM22PRA1.content:
Content
In the extracurricular curriculum, the accent is on the development of competences that are relevant to the practice of the profession of architect.  The central idea of the curriculum professional experience is that in the course of the four-year course, working at one or more architectural firms, you come into contact with all relevant aspects of the professional practice of an architect. The professional experience you are expected to gain relates to eight distinct domains, four of which focus on general competencies (attitude) and four on professional competencies.
Working method
During the academic year the student keeps a practical portfolio of what he/she has done and learned from it. The main purpose of the portfolio is to gain insight into the student's own development, because it presupposes that the choice of what the student does or does not document is related to the competencies, learning outcomes and action levels of the academic year in question.
Assessment
The assessment of the curriculum professional experience is competence oriented. The professional competencies of the Academy of Architecture are central to this. During the assessment it is mainly determined whether you have reached the desired level of competence, to be traced back to action levels and learning outcomes. As part of the professional experience curriculum, each student is assessed once per academic year. At the end of the academic year a summative assessment takes place.
Study load
Whole year / 28 EC.

/en/course/2026/AEA26FED.outcomes:
Methodisch handelen:
De student verkent de context van de cliënt en sluit daarbij aan door eigen ervaringskennis te delen met de cliënt. De student deelt deze kennis over de context en de eigen ervaringskennis met collega’s.
De student legt, aan collega's, uit wat herstelondersteunende activiteiten kunnen zijn.
De student legt de aandachtsgebieden uit in relatie tot inclusie en verbindt deze met de eigen ervaringskennis.

Professionele identiteit
Hierin kijken we naar de geschiedenis van het beroep, waar staat het beroep voor en welke rollen zijn er voor ervaringsdeskundigen. /en/course/2026/AMVB26OCSC2.outcomes:
You develop tools to develop curiosity and play in the young child and in yourself and how to maintain and apply them in your own (educational) practice.
You learn to observe and place your observations in context in order to recognize creative moments in preschoolers.
You will learn what the value of the process of play and discovery is for preschoolers and how it contributes to the development of their creativity.
You apply educational, creative and contextual knowledge in your designs and implementation.
You investigate what a learning environment can be for the young child and investigate what it demands of you.
You contribute by adopting an enthusiastic, curious and flexible attitude in which you adopt an enterprising attitude and are open to experiment.
You work together, share your results and learn how the joint results contribute to your own development.
/en/course/2026/AMVB26OCSC2.content:
What can you learn from, with and about preschoolers? What do art and creativity mean for the development of preschoolers? How do you, as a young adult, relate to the young child and what can you learn from the young child? How can you cultivate the curiosity that is already present, in preschoolers and in yourself?
You get to know the target group: toddlers in groups 1 and 2 of primary school. You will learn about the artistic development of young children and the role of art education in this. You are largely present in groups 1 and 2 of the primary school we work with; the Rietzee in Groningen.
Together with your fellow students, local teachers and experts, you map out how preschoolers express their curiosity, how you can stimulate their curiosity, and what obstacles there may be. Other questions you can ask are: what is the importance of play? How do preschoolers discover what is unknown to them? And what is the role of materials and how can you use materials with toddlers?
You first answer these questions by taking the time to observe children. You observe which artistic (creative) behavior young children show themselves, such as playing, exploring, trying out, experimenting.
Secondly, and partly at the same time, you explore the possibility of participation together with children. Is there room to join them? In interaction with the toddlers you play, explore and experiment together with the children.
Thirdly, you regularly speak with the teachers of the nursery groups. Guest speakers are also invited to tell you more about the world of young children. You have a contribution from your own experience as a young child.
Finally, you use all the information obtained through observation, participation and conversations to shape new opportunities in the field of play and art (e.g. activities) to awaken children's curiosity.
At Minerva you will also work with materials, try out, experiment and play with art. Collect your own work as a toddler! What do you learn from yourself as a child and from toddlers? Specialists are also invited here as guest lecturers. You expand your repertoire of actions and take that new knowledge and ideas back to primary school.
We discuss your experiences and questions through intervision sessions. Important concepts in this optional module (Off Course): playing, curiosity, the young child, creativity, unbiased viewing, participation, sensory learning.
You are in a Dutch context, at a primary school. The lessons at Minerva can be in English, at primary school the language is Dutch. No prior knowledge is necessary about art and children or education. The prerequisite is an open attitude.
The project culminates in a festival on the schoolyard of the primary school.

gezonde leefstijl te bevorderen.

Biedt, binnen de beschikbare beleidsmatige en financiële kaders, begeleiding bij het realiseren van een ondersteuningsaanbod, dat recht doet aan de wensen en behoeften van de cliënt en het cliëntsysteem.

Werkt preventief door vroegtijdige signalering van probleem veroorzakende en probleem versterkende factoren op het gebied van positieve gezondheid.

Leeruitkomst op niveau jaar 1: Student laat een ontwikkelingsgerichte attitude zien, toont inzicht in eigen functioneren, formuleert leerdoelen voor zichzelf en probeert nieuw gedrag uit.

Niveau
Basis (1)
Kiezen (2)
Inhoud
De module is gericht op het in kaart brengen van de wensen van één of meerdere cliënt(en) op het gebied van een gezonde leefstijl. Om te ervaren hoe ingewikkeld gedragsverandering kan zijn, verdiept de student zich in de eigen socialisatie en leefstijl om dit vervolgens met een cliënt te kunnen uitvoeren. De student bedenkt een plan om gezonde leefstijl te bevorderen passend bij de kenmerken van de doelgroep en maakt daarbij o.a. gebruik van digitale technologie. Kennis en vaardigheden staan in het teken van een gezonde leefstijl en het stimuleren daarvan. Er is aandacht voor instrumenten en methodieken die dit ondersteunen, zoals: psychologie, positieve gezondheid van Machteld Huber, netwerktaxatie en basisgespreksvaardigheden waaronder motiverende gespreksvoering.

/en/course/2026/SOXA26SI.outcomes:
1.
Versterken van de cliënt
Werkt vanuit een visie op volwaardig burgerschap aan het vergroten en in stand houden van de competenties van de cliënt en doet daarbij altijd een beroep op de eigen kracht van de cliënt en het cliëntsysteem. Stuurt aan op betrokkenheid en participatie en neemt alleen de regie over in situaties waar dat (tijdelijk) niet anders kan.
2. Benutten van de context
Versterkt de eigen kracht en zelfregie van de cliënt en het cliëntsysteem. Overziet het formele en informele netwerk en maakt hier binnen de beschikbare mogelijkheden, effectief gebruik van om maatschappelijke participatie te realiseren op de drie leefgebieden: wonen, werken/dagbesteding en zingeving.
6. Verantwoorden van handelen
Is aanspreekbaar op het eigen beroepsmatig handelen en de gevolgen daarvan voor het realiseren van de doelen van de cliënt. Kan daarbij te allen tijde verantwoording afleggen tegenover cliënten, hun wettelijk vertegenwoordigers, financiers, en andere betrokkenen.
Leeruitkomst op niveau jaar 1: Werkt aan aanspreekbaarheid op het eigen beroepsmatig handelen en de gevolgen daarvan voor het realiseren van de doelen van de cliënt. Kan gemaakte keuzes onderbouwen in gesprek met het cliënt(systeem), collega's en/of andere betrokkenen.
7. Professioneel samenwerken
Werkt samen binnen interdisciplinaire samenwerkingsverbanden en versterkt netwerken met als doel de sociaal maatschappelijke participatie van de cliënt en het cliëntsysteem te ondersteunen en te realiseren. Maakt verbinding door verantwoordelijkheden te delen, gebruik te maken van deskundigheid van anderen en eigen deskundigheid over te dragen.
12. Kritisch reflecteren
Reflecteert kritisch op eigen beroepsmatig handelen, leert van ervaringen en deelt deze met collega’s en partijen waarmee wordt samengewerkt.
Leeruitkomst op niveau jaar 1: De student reflecteert kritisch op het eigen professioneel handelen en kan zowel sterke punten als leerpunten van zichzelf benoemen.

Inhoud
In deze module gaat de cursist aan de slag met de methodiek Kwartiermaken op basis van het eerder geïnventariseerde beleid, de missie en visie en de methodiek van de eigen werkplek. De cursist bekijkt hierbij in hoeverre inclusie en inbedding in de maatschappij een rol spelen voor de eigen organisatie. Vervolgens wordt een interventie beschreven hoe inclusie bevorderd zou kunnen worden voor de cliënt(engroep). De volgende kennis en vaardigheden worden aangeboden: Wet-en regelgeving (Wmo, Wlz, etc.), sociologie (kwartiermaken en inclusie), muzisch-agogisch werken, herstelondersteunende zorg (HOZ), rehabilitatie, destigmatisering en empowerment.

3. Hanteren van de relatie
Bouwt vanuit oprechte betrokkenheid en een open en respectvolle houding een vertrouwensrelatie op en draagt er zorg voor dat de behoefte van de cliënt en/of het cliëntsysteem helder wordt. Zet communicatieve vaardigheden in om binnen deze relatie om te gaan met strijdige belangen.

Verheldert vragen en behoeften van de cliënt en het cliëntsysteem. Vertaalt dit zelfstandig binnen de cyclus van methodisch handelen en neemt het zelfbeschikkingsrecht van de cliënt en het cliëntsysteem als uitgangspunt.
5. Ontwerpen van programma’s
Stimuleert de cliënt en het cliëntsysteem om zelf oplossingen te bedenken die leiden tot de voor hen gewenste situatie. Biedt, binnen de beschikbare beleidsmatige en financiële kaders, begeleiding bij het realiseren van een ondersteuningsaanbod, dat recht doet aan de wensen en behoeften van de cliënt en het cliëntsysteem.
6. Verantwoorden van handelen
Is aanspreekbaar op het eigen beroepsmatig handelen en de gevolgen daarvan voor het realiseren van de doelen van de cliënt. Kan daarbij te allen tijde verantwoording afleggen tegenover cliënten, hun wettelijk vertegenwoordigers, financiers, en andere betrokkenen.
9. Signaleren en initiëren
Herkent signalen van crisissituaties en reageert adequaat hierop. Werkt preventief door vroegtijdige signalering van probleem veroorzakende en probleem versterkende factoren op het gebied van sociaal maatschappelijke participatie en brengt deze onder de aandacht bij betrokkenen en belanghebbenden waardoor zwaardere zorg voorkomen kan worden.

Inhoud
In deze module staan de thema’s netwerkgericht werken, ethiek, werken in en met een groep en kennis van (dubbele) diagnoses centraal. De module is gericht op het in kaart brengen van de wensen van één of meerdere cliënt(en) die voor hen belangrijk zijn. De cursist stelt samen met de cliënt en diens netwerk een plan op waarin doelen geformuleerd zijn die voor de cliënt bijdragen aan het hebben van een goed leven. Kennis en vaardigheden staan in het teken van het samenwerken met het netwerk, waaronder systemische gespreksvoering, groepsdynamica en omgaan met agressie. Er is aandacht voor theorieën die dit ondersteunen, zoals: ethiek, wet- en regelgeving, kennis van verslaving, co-morbiditeit en medische basiskennis.

/en/course/2026/BFVP23DNA.outcomes:
You correctly name and describe the sequential steps of replication, transcription, translation and repair processes of DNA at the molecular level.
You describe the regulation of gene expression from transcriptional to post-translational levels for prokaryotic and eukaryotic systems.
You recognise DNA technologies cloning, PCR, sequencing, DNA array, and can explain their application in practice
You explain the influence of evolutionary processes on the genome
You independently describe biological concepts based on English literature in a form that is understandable and appealing to a layperson
You summarise study texts meaningfully in appropriate textual or graphic form
You work in a team on a project in which you recognise, realistically prioritise, distribute, implement and evaluate tasks

/en/course/2026/BFVP23DNA.content: The module starts with an introduction in which various cases/topics are presented. You choose a topic from these, which is the common thread running through the course. Under the guidance of a lecturer, in small project groups you master the necessary biological and chemical theory on how hereditary information enables important biomolecules to work in a cell. There are weekly workshops on various biological topics and study skills needed to complete the group assignment. Together with fellow students (under the guidance of a lecturer), you make your own arrangements and a schedule to study and practise the material taught using given learning materials. Halfway through the module, you present your progress as a group to the rest of the class. During the course of this module, you will also work on developing a game or multimedia product that represents "the central dogma" of molecular biology: this may be a computer game, a board or card game, or a film or (stop-motion) animation, or a similar product. You will give feedback on each other's created products after having played or seen them.

/en/course/2026/BFVP22GENEN.outcomes:
You work in a team on a project in which you identify, define, prioritise, divide, implement and evaluate tasks.
Together with your working group, you present the results of a case studied by you to your fellow students and lecturers, and you actively participate in discussions following the presentations
You know the structure of different macromolecules (sugars, proteins, DNA/RNA and lipids) and you explain their function in a cell/organism
You can describe the different cellular compartments of a cell and relate their role to their structure
You understand the role of enzymes in the main metabolic pathways in a cell
You can explain a cell biological process in detail, including what goes wrong in disease
/en/course/2026/BFVP22GENEN.content:
You probably don't think about it every day, but at the molecular level, you are constantly falling apart. Fortunately, the damage is repaired as quickly as it occurs by all kinds of biochemical processes. But if one or more of these so-called metabolic processes become disrupted, not everything is repaired fully or properly anymore. In other words: you can get sick. The other way round is also possible. You can cure a disease (a disturbed biochemical process) with the right drugs (by intervening in that disturbed process). Or you can, for instance, adjust the bacterial and fungal growth in a young cheese so that it does not simply spoil, but turns into a delicious blue cheese.
Because bioinformaticians are often involved in this kind of research, in this module you will learn how the most important biochemical processes take place and what role they play within an organism.
Whether you have mastered the material enough to apply it in practice is assessed on the basis of a study of a biological process that you carry out in a group. You will look in detail at a cell biological process, what the consequences of a disruption are on a cellular/biochemical level, and also how and why this disruption affects the entire organism. You will present your study to the rest of the class and lecturers.
You carry out your study largely during the working lectures in which lecturers are available to ask any questions and help you carry out the study.
To do your studies, you need to know a thing or two about cellular and molecular biology. This material is offered in the form of working lectures, where exercises are also offered and discussed in groups. Although the lecturers will help you on your way during these contact moments, you will spend most of the time familiarising yourself with the material based on the literature provided. Of course, you can always ask your lecturers questions if something is unclear, and by asking questions, lecturers will check your understanding of the material.

/en/course/2026/BFVP24BIOCHBEELD.outcomes:
This module has the following learning outcomes:
You independently create simple programmes in which you correctly use libraries and functions, and self-written Python modules.
You can calculate with and understand simple mathematical formulas including logarithms and exponents.
You can visualise data with Python.
You can apply Regular Expressions, list comprehension and error handling in Python.
You have a basic knowledge of chemistry such that you can understand simple chemical structures and perform chemical reaction equations and calculations.
You understand the structure of a protein at different levels and visualise a self-chosen protein with the aim of understanding structure and function of this protein at different levels.
You know in which databases you can find substantive information about proteins and can use these databases to find the right information and data about the protein in your final product.
/en/course/2026/BFVP24BIOCHBEELD.content:
In this module, you will master the basics of mathematics and chemistry and start looking at how a protein works through a chemical lens. One way of visualisation is to make graphs in which you show biological data and start describing this data with appropriate mathematical formulas. You will write this visualisation in Python.
In addition, we are going to show you what proteins (enzymes) look like and where in the structure the reactions take place. You will create this visualisation using specific software that can visualise protein structures.
By visualising your protein, you can also find out whether a mutation in the gene coding for this protein can cause problems with its function.
Biologists produce a lot of data with their experiments on proteins. You will learn how to visualise and mathematically approach the data from simple experiments. Basic mathematics lessons are offered for this purpose. In this way, the basic chemistry you need in your education is also offered. Your maths and chemistry knowledge is tested by means of two written tests.
To create your visualisations, you need knowledge of Python, chemistry and mathematics. To help you master the Python skills, short seminars are offered, after which you make your own assignment on the explained material. You submit these assignments to your teacher, who evaluates them and discusses them with you. These assignments must be completed satisfactorily.
For this module, it is highly desirable to have followed these modules first: Module 1.1.2 - From DNA to protein and Module 1.1.3 - Molecular biology in code.

metadata.Name: Survival of the Fittest
metadata.Assessments: Survival of the Fittest - Other assessment

/en/course/2026/BFVP22SURVIVAL.outcomes:
This module has the following learning outcomes
You engage in professional discussions with fellow students about contemporary ethical issues in your field of work
You correctly name and describe the successive steps of mitosis and meiosis in a eukaryotic cell
You know the principles of evolutionary theory and can describe its connection to biodiversity.
You can describe a stable ecosystem and speculate on how it would respond to changes based on knowledge gained
You name the basic principles of epidemiology and the innate and acquired immune system
You can apply probability theory using Mendelian heritable traits
You can calculate for a Mendelian heritable trait, given the genotypes of the parents, the probability of the phenotypes of the offspring
You work in a team on a project in which you recognise, realistically prioritise, distribute, carry out and evaluate tasks
/en/course/2026/BFVP22SURVIVAL.content:
This module covers a number of biological topics, with the overarching theme of 'survival of the fittest'. Students also work on a case study, in which this theme plays a major role. In the introduction to the module, all theoretical topics are touched upon and groups of students choose one of the provided cases (or set one up themselves, in consultation with the lecturer).
Each week, a biological subtopic is covered, which has a link to the cases. The topics are introduced through a workshop. An individual assignment accompanies each topic. Each group of students is required to give an oral presentation once on their case study and how it relates to one of the subtopics. Another aspect of the case study is presented via a poster at the end of the quarter.
In addition, an introduction to the ethics at play in the bioinformatics field is given. For each case group, a forum discussion is prepared and held on an ethical aspect that plays a role in the chosen case.
In consultation with the lecturer, you will set milestones and work towards them in a targeted manner. You will do this using the agile methodology (scrum). Working with a ticketing system to distribute and prioritise partial problems is also part of this.
The knowledge of the first theoretical biology subject (from DNA to protein) is helpful background knowledge but not necessarily required to follow this subject.

metadata.Assessments: Backend - Other assessment Frontend - Other assessment

/en/course/2026/BFVP22TOOLBOX.outcomes:
This module has the following learning outcomes
- You correctly and efficiently use Object Oriented Programming in Python
- You create a website using a provided library
- You use common tooling to develop Python programmes; these include Debugger, Version Control, Unit Test and profiling.
- You work in teams on software, using agile methodologies
You independently install a bioinformatics application on your own system and can call it from another process
/en/course/2026/BFVP22TOOLBOX.content:
This is a large, 10 EC project in which you will work on researching and unlocking a technique/datatype common within bioinformatics.
Together with the class, you will research which techniques and associated data types are commonly used in the bioinformatics field. In a smaller group, you will choose a technique and investigate it further and make it accessible in a website made with Python. In this website, you not only present the background information, but also implement your chosen technique and visually display your results. That is, you choose and implement a suitable and appealing visualisation for the output of the chosen tool.
In the software design process, you apply object oriented programming concepts.
You make use of an interface (API) defined by the teachers, e.g. Flask, to develop the website.
To manage the code you write, you will use a version control system (git).
In consultation with the lecturer, you will set milestones and work towards them in a targeted manner. You will do this using the agile methodology (scrum). Working with a ticketing system to distribute and prioritise partial problems is also part of this.

metadata.Name: The Scientific Cycle
metadata.Assessments: Professional Product - Other assessment Science Communication - Other assessment

/en/course/2026/BFVP22CYCLUS.outcomes:
This module has the following learning outcomes:
You formulate testable, relevant and feasible research questions and translate these into expected outcomes (hypotheses).
You design a feasible experiment to answer a research question and record this in a protocol, taking into account reliability (e.g. proper checks), quality assurance and (privacy) legislation. You conduct this experiment according to protocol.
You assess the quality of the experiment, the reliability of the protocol and also of the data obtained. You log this verifiably and reproducibly.
Using relevant data visualisations and statistical techniques, you perform a data exploration on obtained or self-collected data using the R programming language.
You distinguish different sources of variation in your measured values and estimate their size using statistical methods.
You use your computer system efficiently -if relevant with git- to manage your research documents and data according to standards applicable in the field.
You give constructive feedback on scientific products of others.
You write a paper according to scientific standards using a template.
You evaluate your own performance and identify strengths and areas for development.
You select relevant sources and can transfer their essence to fellow students.
/en/course/2026/BFVP22CYCLUS.content:
As a bioinformatician, you often have to conduct research and you do so according to the scientific cycle. In this module, you will learn about this cycle with a research project of your own choice.
The scientific cycle always starts with a research question. A research question is never just any question: it has to meet a number of conditions, with aspects such as measurability.
In addition to formulating the research question, the scientific cycle has a whole number of other elements: drawing up hypotheses, studying what is already known, designing experiments, carrying out those experiments reproducibly, analysing and modelling obtained data, and, of course, answering the research question. Ultimately, this entire process needs to be written down in a way so that the scientific community has a chance to check, repeat or build on your work.
A very important aspect in all this is being able to estimate how much data you need, how good the data is and how good the method you use to answer the question is. Thus, there are some standard steps and 'checks' you need to do in a research study.
In short, how do you do scientific research? You will learn that in this module!
Professional duties represented
- Conduct research within the domain of Life Sciences
- Set up and manage a basic bioinformatics infrastructure

metadata.Name: Human Anatomy and Physiology: The Human Body under the Magnifying Glass
metadata.Assessments: Case study Anatomy - Other assessment Practical assignment Dissection and Hystology - Other assessment

/en/course/2026/LSVX23ANATOMIE.outcomes:
This module has the following learning outcomes:
You will describe the structure and function of the various organ systems in mammals, dissect a rat correctly and identify the organs in order to learn about the anatomy and physiology of mammals.
You will identify the various parts of a microscope and use a microscope to study tissues using the most important microscopic techniques.
You will produce overview and detailed drawings of histological specimens of the four different types of tissue and various organs in accordance with drawing guidelines, and present these in a portfolio organised by organ system.
You will collaborate effectively and document agreements in a verifiable manner in order to produce a multimedia group project on a case study that you have developed based on the anatomy, physiology and histology of the relevant organ systems, with a view to developing social, communication and information skills.
/en/course/2026/LSVX23ANATOMIE.content: In this module, you will be introduced to the anatomy, histology and physiology of the human body. You will do this in the laboratory through various practicals on anatomy and physiology. The practicals in the laboratory room are surrounded by scheduled seminars in which one organ system is dealt with from a case study and/or assignments. Histology preparations are also examined under the microscope and drawn. You process the drawings and completed assignments in an individual portfolio. At the end of the module, you and your fellow group members present a case study in which the anatomy, physiology and histology of the relevant organ systems are visualised and explained.

/en/course/2026/LSVX23OCTAVEMATL.outcomes:
This module has the following learning outcomes
You write scripts in Octave/MATLAB that use operations, flow control, standard functions, custom functions, file I/O and visualisation
You efficiently perform vectorised calculations by manipulating matrices as units
You simulate complex emergent behaviour based on a cellular automaton in Octave/MATLAB
You explain the formulations of diverse cellular automata in the context of biology, chemistry, physics, or computer science
You characterise the behaviour of a model or simulation by targeted experimentation with initial configurations and parameters
You collaborate effectively with fellow students from diverse natural science backgrounds
/en/course/2026/LSVX23OCTAVEMATL.content: You will be introduced to the MATLAB-compatible programming language (GNU) Octave for the purpose of performing simulations with data organised in multidimensional grids. First, based on available notebooks and online material, you will learn the basic syntax of the programming language with regard to operators, flow control and functions, and use single and compound data types such as vectors, matrices, and multidimensional arrays or cell arrays. With this knowledge, you implement some discrete models based on cellular automata, also using visualisations and file I/O. You discover that models based on deceptively simple basic rules can lead to highly complex emergent behaviour on a larger scale. Initially, you do this individually by implementing and exploring a "toy model", such as the well-known Conway's Game Of Life. Later, in small mixed groups, you also construct more relevant discrete natural science models with practical applications in biology, chemistry, physics, computer science, or possibly a proposal of your own. You will present final results in the form of an interactive digital demonstration set-up with accompanying documentation in the form of a wiki.

metadata.Name: Introduction Programming in Python
metadata.Assessments: Introductie Programmeren in Python - Other assessment

/en/course/2026/LSVX23PYTHON.outcomes:
You can translate a simple case study into a programme design and a set of functions to be implemented.
You write code using appropriate data types, flow control elements and functions. You make good use of documentation and help functionality. You use comprehensions and regular expressions where necessary.
You can debug and analyse your own code, using debugger and other techniques.
You can use the Python module system and create and deploy your own modules.
You understand the object-oriented nature of Python and can create and deploy a simple object-oriented design yourself.
/en/course/2026/LSVX23PYTHON.content:
In this module, you will be introduced to programming. We use the Python programming language because it is an easy and very versatile programming language.
All aspects of programming are covered: working with data from files, creating functions, performing explorations and writing stand-alone terminal programmes.
In the first 2 weeks, you learn all the theory and techniques. In the last week, you use these to develop your own programme for a final assignment. You think up this final assignment yourself, or choose one given by the teacher.

/en/course/2026/LSVX24COMMUNICAT.outcomes:
This module has the following learning outcomes:
You name the difference between perceiving and interpreting, explain how the individual frame of reference affects this and how this difference can be important in practice.
You name the basic conversation skills, explain how these skills can be applied in practice and actually apply these skills.
You distinguish the stages in the counseling process and influence this process effectively.
You name some important aspects of collaboration, explain how they can be applied in practice, and apply collaboration skills.
/en/course/2026/LSVX24COMMUNICAT.content:
In your future position, you will often need to communicate verbally with colleagues, clients and customers. Good oral communication skills of yours are critical to ensuring effective information transfer, strengthening cooperation, building trust and relationships, and conflict management.
This involves having the ability to convey thoughts, ideas, feelings and information in a clear and understandable way, while also listening carefully to what the other person has to say.
In this course, you will cover basic conversation skills (listening, summarizing, questioning, giving feedback). You also learn to distinguish the phases in the advisory process, to influence this process effectively and to deal with resistance. You will also identify the preconditions for effective cooperation, put together your 'dream team' and practice conflict management during the lectures.
Apart from addressing these topics on the basis of theory, there will be an interactive exchange on these topics based on the experiences of you and your fellow students, and plenty of attention will be paid to training conversation skills.

/en/course/2026/LSVX24CREATIEF.outcomes:
This module has the following learning outcomes:
You give effective and constructive feedback on others' work and incorporate feedback given into your own work.
You know the different narrative perspectives and basic writing techniques and apply them in your own work.
You write short stories in the genre prose.
/en/course/2026/LSVX24CREATIEF.content:
In this module we are going to give the creative muscles plenty of room! The central topic of this module is the short story. Through many exercises and assignments, we will explore different approaches to writing stories. We will explore a number of important concepts such as narrative perspective, “show, don't tell,” exposition, sensory writing and suspense.
Through much reading, discussion and listening to each other, you will learn to look critically at texts and sharpen your own work.
You will conclude the module with a final project, a short story.
Prior knowledge or experience is not required for this module, only the desire to learn to express yourself creatively in written word.
A nice bonus: your scientific writing and observation skills will definitely improve as well!

metadata.Name: Introduction to Industrial Biotechnology
metadata.Modes of delivery: Guest lecture Lecture Practical / Training Teaching method 1
metadata.Assessments: Posterpresentation - Other assessment Project - Other assessment

/en/course/2026/LSVX24INDUSTRBIO.outcomes:
This module has the following learning outcomes:
You explain the main concepts and applications of industrial biotechnology.
You identify and describe key biotechnology processes.
You identify the latest innovations and trends in industrial biotechnology and discuss their potential impact on the industry.
You explain the different types of bioreactors and their specific applications.
You explain the main techniques of downstream processing in biotechnological production processes.
You will carry out a small biotechnology project as a team.
You present and report research results effectively.
Translated with DeepL.com (free version)
/en/course/2026/LSVX24INDUSTRBIO.content:
In the transition to a sustainable society, many industrial processes are switching from fossil-based to biobased raw materials. This also increasingly offers the possibility of using microorganisms as catalysts in these (bio)conversions. This module introduces the concept of industrial biotechnology, which is also called white biotechnology. In industrial biotechnology, chemicals and materials are made with the help of microorganisms, or with enzymes produced by those microorganisms. An example is the production of bioplastics from biomass, but it also includes the enzymatic bioconversion of, for example, starch into biodegradable films, capsules or coatings. Aspects that (may) be covered in this elective module are: basic knowledge of industrial biotechnology; biotechnological processes; microorganisms and enzymes; bioreactors and equipment; downstream processing; ethical, environmental and safety aspects; innovations and trends in industrial biotechnology.
The industrial biotechnology module consists of the following 3 parts:
Introductory lectures (guest lectures) on the breadth of industrial biotechnology, linking to various regional biotech companies.
Company field trips to regional biotech companies.
Practicum in which specific fermentations are carried out or biochemical conversion with enzymes is studied.
The knowledge acquired during the lectures and the field trip is incorporated into an oral presentation.
The maximum number of students participating in this module is 24. For the company excursions, students are divided into groups of 4 persons. Students can register for a maximum of 2 company excursions. The companies considered are:
Sugar Union
Water purification Garmerwolde
Avebe
Kikkoman
Bax beer / Martinus
IQ Products
During the practical, the results are logged in Elabjournal. These results form the basis for a lab report on specific fermentations and enzymatic conversions.

metadata.Name: Infectious Diseases
metadata.Assessments: Infectieziekten portfolio - Other assessment Infectieziekten symposium - Other assessment

/en/course/2026/LSVX24INFECTIE.outcomes:
You will work effectively together to investigate a case study, outbreak or other problem in a group setting, applying knowledge about infectious diseases, transmission routes, resistance, surveillance, epidemiology, disease prevention and control strategies.
You investigate the effect of different (prevention) measures on the spread of infectious diseases using a disease compartment model.
You evaluate and use scientific literature and reliable internet sources to develop application assignments on infectious diseases.
You prepare a short self-reflection halfway through and at the end of the module to improve and evaluate your own actions.
/en/course/2026/LSVX24INFECTIE.content:
With increasing globalisation, rising population density and the effects of climate change, we are seeing a rise in the incidence of a large number of infectious diseases. In addition, the number of infections that are resistant to treatment with antibiotics or antiviral drugs is on the rise.
This elective module covers the epidemiological aspects of infectious diseases. You will learn more about the causes of outbreaks and the transmission of diseases, including factors such as the host, the pathogen and the environment. The module covers the surveillance and reporting of infectious diseases, prevention and treatment strategies, and the role of epidemiology in health policy. You will be introduced to the SIR model to predict and understand the spread of infectious diseases.
The module consists of introductory lectures, guest lectures and a series of seminars and assignments. You will compile both the assignments completed during the module and a short self-reflection into a portfolio (partial assessment 1). As a final assignment, you will work in a group to investigate a case study, outbreak or other problem and present your findings to your fellow students during a closing symposium (partial assessment 2).

/en/course/2026/LSVX24INLPSY.outcomes:
You demonstrate, through completed assignments, that you apply knowledge of the main theories in the science of psychology to everyday situations in your life. These completed assignments come together in a portfolio. The content of this portfolio is formatively reviewed by fellow students throughout the module and discussed during the seminars, and at the end of the module, a summative assessment of the complete portfolio is conducted by the instructor.
You creatively present a number of psychological theories from the course material to your fellow students, showing that you understand how psychological theories can be applied in practice.
/en/course/2026/LSVX24INLPSY.content:
Why do humans behave like they do? The module "Introduction to Psychology" aims to test your beliefs about human behavior against scientific insights based on theoretical explanations and empirical research. Ideas that are based on common sense or personal life experiences about behavior and psychological processes sometimes withstand, but often do not withstand, the test of scientific experimentation. At the same time, science cannot function without the use of common sense. It is often a source of inspiration for theory development and scientific research.
In this educational program, we will discuss a variety of psychological concepts and themes. We invite you to compare your own ideas with both older and more recent scientific insights. For each new topic, you will start by asking yourself what your common sense tells you, and what your intuition and personal experience suggest. Then, you will study the relevant topic in the textbook. Do you need to adjust your insights? Are your ideas confirmed? Do you discover important insights about the how, why, and purpose of our behaviors? What concepts or theories are behind these? What new questions arise?
In this way, using the textbook and your own knowledge and experience, you will conduct research. By the end of your investigation, you may have gained new insights and discarded old ideas that, upon further reflection, were incorrect or unhelpful. You will have learned psychological insights and concepts, and taken a step forward in developing a scientific professional attitude characterized by curiosity and critical (self-)examination.

metadata.Name: Climate Change and Saline Soils
metadata.Assessments: Climate Change and Saline Soils - Other assessment

/en/course/2026/LSVX24KLIMAAT.outcomes:
You present research data obtained from field measurements, lab analysis and an experimental setup clearly through a measurement letter report and a poster.
You interpret obtained research data on soil fertility and salinization in relation to plant growth.
You provide evidence-based advice on climate-adaptive measures against soil salinization and demonstrate how this advice contributes to the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).
You effectively reflect on collaboration with fellow students from other life sciences disciplines.
/en/course/2026/LSVX24KLIMAAT.content:
Longer periods of drought, more extreme rainfall, heat records: we experience the effects of climate change on a very regular basis. These changing weather conditions affect our Dutch soils. One of the consequences is that soils become saltier (salinization) and this has consequences for agriculture and nature.
In this elective module you will gain insight into soil hydrology and indicators of soil fertility, such as grain size, conductivity, nutrient concentrations and microbiome. In addition, you will gain knowledge about what climate change and salinization mean and their effects on plant growth and development. You will also think about climate-adaptive measures against salinization.
You will gain this knowledge during various (guest) lectures, an excursion and fieldwork during which soil samples will be taken and analyzed in the lab. The effects of salt on plant growth will be investigated in an experiment that you will conduct yourself.

/en/course/2026/LSVX24MEDICIJN.outcomes:
This module has the following learning outcomes:
You will explain the definition of a drug and describe key events and developments in the history of modern drug development.
You describe the application of bioinformatics tools in drug development and analysis and demonstrate how a drug works at the molecular level using a bioinformatics tool.
You describe acquired knowledge about various analytical techniques in the pharmaceutical industry and link methods to specific drugs using relevant literature.
You identify and name, based on the chemical structure and interactions with the target, the chemical characteristics of a drug, such as functional groups, pharmacophores, chiral centers, types of intermolecular interactions and hydrogen bond donors/acceptors. You assess whether the drug meets the Lipinski rule of five and determine whether it is a prodrug, including the type of prodrug.
You describe the pharmacokinetics of drugs, including absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion, and understand the pharmacodynamics of drugs, including action and side effects.
You will describe various types of in vitro screening used in the preclinical phase and explain in a simple manner the application of biological models in the testing of new drugs.
You present classically from an interdisciplinary joint and convincing manner the acquired knowledge and application of the specifically chosen drug, informing the audience jointly and each from each domain expertise about the genesis, application as well as all appropriate technically-relevant areas of knowledge of the drug.
/en/course/2026/LSVX24MEDICIJN.content:
What are drugs and how does one develop a drug?
Developing a drug is a long process in which much research must be done on the target of the drug, making a powerful drug, what the drug does to the body and what the body does to the drug. The analysis of the research data used and made is crucial in this development process. Thus, drug development is multidisciplinary research where biologists, chemists and bioinformaticians work together to create a new drug.
This module will introduce students to the basics of how a drug is developed, and how the various disciplines, taught within ILST, contribute to it. Different lecturers from different programs will give lectures explaining the contribution of the respective disciplines in drug development through concrete examples. The knowledge gained in the lecture is then directly applied in a partial assignment
For the assignment, multidisciplinary project groups are formed (i.e. consisting of students from different courses). The project groups must choose a drug, from a list of existing drugs compiled by the lecturers. The concepts taught must be applied to the chosen drug, and this will require some literature review. This must be done for each subject taught. The results of the subtasks will then be “compiled” into a final presentation in which the project groups present how the all disciplines were applied in the development of the drug.

metadata.Name: Preparing patients for surgery: diagnostics and care at Nij Smellinghe
metadata.Modes of delivery: Guest lecture Lecture Project-based learning Tutorial
metadata.Assessments: The patient is fit and prepared for surgery - Other assessment

/en/course/2026/LSVX25PATIENT.outcomes:
You will design an interprofessional treatment plan to optimally prepare the patient for surgery and improve their recovery. In doing so, you will take into account the applicable standards, POCT possibilities, ethical aspects, and current laws and regulations.
You share your knowledge of POCT and prehabilitation in a multidisciplinary team and, based on your own profession, identify your role in preparing the patient to be fit, taking into account the current principles within NijSmellinghe.
You determine interprofessionally what role POCT can play in the patient's health status within prehabilitation and incorporate this into the treatment plan.
You are able to critically analyze the process and product, reflect on your own contribution and the choices made by the group, and you can report this back to the client (Nij Smellinghe) by means of a presentation.
/en/course/2026/LSVX25PATIENT.content:
Surgery has a major impact on patients, and complications during and after the operation can further disrupt their lives. Previously, preparation for surgery consisted of explaining the procedure, mentioning possible complications, the length of the hospital stay, and providing guidelines for life after the operation. Patients waited passively for the surgery and were not encouraged to remain active. We now know that the risk of complications after surgery is lower and that patients recover more quickly when we actively prepare them and ensure they are as fit as possible going into surgery. This is an important aspect of prehabilitation. This is achieved through a prehabilitation program with a customized training and diet plan.
In order to measure the effect of prehabilitation, it is necessary to have as complete a picture as possible of the patient's mental and physical health status. The effect of prehabilitation can be measured using physical measurements, psychological tests, and analyses of the patient's body fluids before, during, and after the procedure using point-of-care technology (POCT). POCT allows rapid and accurate measurements and tests to be carried out close to the patient, both at home and in the hospital, by the patient themselves or by healthcare providers. A well-known example of POCT is the COVID-19 self-test, which allowed us to quickly test for COVID-19 at home.
The collection, interpretation, and analysis of data from the measurements is carried out by various disciplines, including nurses, physical therapists, nutritionists, diagnostic laboratory technicians, and imaging technicians, who work together interprofessionally to care for the patient so that a personalized prehabilitation plan can be created.
POCT, prehabilitation, and the patient are central to this elective module. Students from various health care programs will collaborate on a real patient case at Nij Smellinghe Hospital and will be supported by lectures and seminars at Hanze University of Applied Sciences.  During the meetings, students will come into contact with various (para)medical disciplines involved in prehabilitation. This will create close contact with medical professionals (including doctors and nurses), paramedics (analysts, physiotherapists, etc.) and the patients and their loved ones.
The course is held on Tuesday evenings from 5:30 p.m. to 8:30 p.m. and is also partly taught at Nij Smellinghe in Drachten. It is a parallel module; the elective module is taught throughout the entire fourth quarter.

metadata.Name: Healthy, Durable and Safe Food
metadata.Modes of delivery: Community of Learners Practical / Training Project-based learning Tutorial
metadata.Assessments: CoL en Practicum - Other assessment Theorie - Other assessment

/en/course/2026/LSVX25VOEDING.content: This module focuses on sustainable, safe and healthy food. We look at food from many angles: research in the field of nutrition, what is a healthy diet, how does our diet affect the planet, what are the safety issues regarding food and how do you deal with them, how does the environment affect food choices, the influence of the government on our food choices, global food issues, and the link between sport and nutrition. We do this by working in CoL groups on a self-chosen topic, to which a practical experiment is connected. In addition, seven inspiration lectures are given by experts from the field. The knowledge gained is presented in a personal report based on your own weekly menu and in a mini-symposium where you, as a CoL group, give a presentation on the knowledge gained and the practical experiment.

/en/course/2026/BFVH23NGS.outcomes:
This module has the following learning outcomes:
You know all the concepts of central dogma, the different types of macromolecules and enzymes, and you can describe the interrelationships between them
You can name different mechanisms of gene regulation, and predict the effects of various mutations on gene expression
You know the different genome structures and can detect, filter and annotate them in an NGS data set using appropriate tools and techniques.
You have a good understanding of the quality requirements of NGS data, depending on both the NGS technique used and the purpose. You can also apply the tools to provide insight into and improve this quality.
You know which tools and algorithms are available to map NGS reads against a reference genome and can justify which is the best for a given dataset and question.
You justify and present the choices made of steps performed to achieve a high-quality mapping.

/en/course/2026/BFVH23NGS.content:
In preparation for the genomics and transcriptomics project, we start with a comprehensive introduction to the required theory. This covers basic genetics (gene variation, gene regulation) for modern NGS techniques, the different forms of structural variation and the background of transcriptomics research. During this module, the various theoretical topics are practically implemented with small sub-tasks in the workflow manager Galaxy. Here the emphasis is on getting acquainted with the different types of NGS data and their associated techniques, performing a thorough quality control and mapping against a reference genome.
It is assumed that you are familiar with the central dogma as discussed in module 1.1.2: From DNA to Protein.

metadata.Name: Genomics & Transcriptomics
metadata.Assessments: Genomics - Other assessment Transcriptomics - Other assessment

/en/course/2026/BFVH23GENOMICS.outcomes:
This module has the following learning outcomes:
You design, implement, document and evaluate a genome analysis pipeline for determining variants within a workflow manager, such as Galaxy.
You design, implement, document and evaluate an expression analysis pipeline for determining and interpreting expression patterns.
You can use relevant tools and visualisations to assess whether an NGS data set is of sufficient quality and improve it if necessary.
You can apply statistical analysis to genomics and/or transcriptomics data in relation to phenotypes and external factors, and visually display and interpret the results.
You can use annotation to link biological knowledge to found results. For example, linking structural variants to disorders or using pathway and/or (gene-set) enrichment analysis to interpret the effects of a transcriptomics experiment.
You keep a logbook for all analyses in which the steps taken and results are recorded.
You present your research results in an attractive way and at the appropriate level to your fellow students.
/en/course/2026/BFVH23GENOMICS.content:
During this large 10 EC project, several facets of working on genome research are addressed. You search for a suitable - published, for instance available in the NCBI SRA - data set with which to complete both projects ('genomics' & 'transcriptomics'). During the genomics project, you look for variations between the data set found and a reference genome. An important aspect here is assessing the quality of the data (the 'raw reads') before setting up an analysis pipeline in a workflow manager. Found variants are annotated and interpreted for biological effect.
Furthermore, you need to have mastered some statistical concepts in order to be able to perform the necessary analyses for the transcriptomics project. For instance, we use statistical tests to determine which genes show significantly different patterns and enrichment analysis to link this group of genes to biological function. You will report extensively with visualisations to validate choices made and present the results.
To make your research reproducible, making a logbook is also part of this module. In this logbook, you keep track of the steps taken and the corresponding results.
To be able to perform statistical analyses, among other things, a basic level of programming in R is expected, as explained in module '1.4.1: The scientific cycle'. To work out (steps of) an analysis pipeline, terminal experience is required. Knowledge from module 2.1.1 is required to follow this module.

/en/course/2026/BFVH23DATADASH.outcomes:
This module has the following learning outcomes:
You design - expressly taking into account the purpose of the dataset - relevant (interactive) visualisations and tabulations for a given dataset, taking into account relevant statistical aspects.
You design and implement an efficient and relevant data backend for a data dashboard (from flat file to relational database, depending on the case).
You design a user-friendly data dashboard for a given data model. In doing so, you collect, prioritise and implement the client's requirements. You use a reactive dashboard platform, deliberately choosing between Shiny [R] or Panel [Python] and using any relevant libraries.
You collaborate in a development team to translate a client's requirements into product features.
You can pitch the final product to your client
You make a tested plan (and manual) for hosting the application once it is taken into production. You apply the FAIR principles here.

/en/course/2026/BFVH23DATADASH.content:
In this module, you work as a team to carry out an assignment provided by an "external" client. This could be the KCBBE (Hanze), the UMCG (e.g. clinical chemistry) or another client. You will enter into discussions with the client to find out what the purpose of the data dashboard is. Important questions to be answered include: Who are the users? What will the dashboard be used for? Which features are essential and which optional? How is the application going to be maintained and hosted. You then set to work designing and implementing the application. Here, you follow agile principles: short release cycles, a lot of contact with the client, intensive cooperation as a (scrum) team.
Of course, git version control is again an important aspect, as well as FAIR principles.
Alongside the main project, a sub-module runs where you learn the most important aspects of relational databases: design, implementation and querying/searching.
To follow this module successfully, knowledge of R or Python (depending on the chosen platform) and working in a terminal at a reasonable level is required. In addition, basic knowledge of web application architecture, html and css is highly desirable.

/en/course/2026/BFVH23IMMUNO.outcomes:
This module has the following learning outcomes
You study a component of the immune system and present this to an audience of your peers
You describe role and differentiation of different cell types in the human immune system and how B and T cells acquire their genetically unique receptors through gene rearrangement
You describe the mechanisms by which the innate and acquired immune system recognises and eliminates invaders
You visualise the behaviour of part of the innate or acquired immune system before and during an immune response
You use software to visualise protein/ligand interactions using an antibody-antigen pair.

/en/course/2026/BFVH23IMMUNO.content: In immunology, we take a closer look at the (human) immune system. During this module, we will learn about the many types of immune cells that keep us healthy, and the ways in which these cells work together to respond quickly to outside invaders. The differences between the innate and acquired immune system will be covered in detail, as well as how these cells learn what belongs and does not belong in the body. Some broader topics such as cell differentiation and protein-ligand binding are also covered in the context of cells in the immune system. At the end of the module, you will have worked out a case study with a project group in which you have visually represented part of the functioning of the immune system as information for your fellow students. There are also compulsory assignments covering the functioning and mechanisms of the immune system.

Given a microbial metagenomics dataset, you will delve into the techniques and experimental design used to obtain it. You can ask relevant questions to and have a meaningful discussion with your client about the design and implementation of the analysis pipeline.

/en/course/2026/BFVH23METAGEN.content:
In the metagenomics module, based on a research question about a metagenomic research dataset, you will build your own analysis pipeline to answer this question. You determine the steps in your pipeline together with your client and supervisor.
You will write up the results you find in a short publication. As a class, we will work in a research group in which active knowledge sharing through publication discussions and working meetings play a role.
At the end of the project, you present your project results in front of a wide audience.

metadata.Assessments: Casus - Other assessment Theorie - Written, organised by School

/en/course/2026/BFVH24MLEARNING.outcomes:
You are able to differentiate between different types of machine learning algorithms and are able to select a candidate algorithm given a dataset and research question
You perform a literature study on a given Machine Learning algorithm and can explain the model and its relevant hyperparameters to a group of peers
You explore, examine and prepare a dataset from the field of life sciences for use in Machine Learning
You implement and optimize various classification-algorithms in R and you evaluate and compare their performances
You document the process of selecting and processing data and developing a model and visualize the results in a notebook in a reproducable manner
You develop a notebook that can apply a developed machine learning model to classify new data
You critically discuss your methods and result in their biological context
/en/course/2026/BFVH24MLEARNING.content: In this module you will be introduced to the field of Machine Learning. Specifically, you will use ML classification on a data set of your choice. You will learn how to formulate a research question, and explore and prepare your data accordingly, learning what algorithm to put to the task, and what can go awry if an unsuitable algorithm is chosen. You will train your model to find patterns in the data, allowing it to make predictions when presented with new data. You will also learn how to judge these predictions accordingly, judging different models on their accuracy. You will also learn how to document your process and share it with colleagues. The module will be concluded with a Machine Learning competition, where you will work in small teams on the same dataset to see which team can build the most accurate model.

/en/course/2026/BFVH24JAVA.outcomes:
This module has the following learning outcomes:
You develop Java software for the bioinformatics domain, using the standards of this language (syntax elements, naming, code style, Javadoc, latest APIs, etc)
You apply object-oriented development principles such as inheritance, encapsulation, abstraction and polymorphism correctly at novice level and explain them to fellow students. In doing so, you use UML to design and communicate class diagrams.
You develop a (JUnit) test suite for relevant methods from your production code, loosely following Test-Driven Development (TDD) principles.
You develop robust bioinformatics Linux-style command-line applications, correctly using command-line argument parsing, error handling and logging.
You design demonstrably efficient algorithms and data structures to solve computational problems. You use profiler tooling, among other things.
/en/course/2026/BFVH24JAVA.content:
In this module, you will design and build Java applications using libraries and frameworks from the Java ecosystem. These applications will be command-line applications that accept and process command-line arguments according to Unix standards.
We will use the principles of Object Oriented Design and Test-Driven Development (TDD) in this module.
In small excursions, we will be introduced to Extreme Programming and division of roles Test Developer and Production Developer, and Designer versus Developer.
This module assumes you can already program well, and have a basic idea of what object-oriented programming entails, via Python or otherwise. Sound knowledge of git and version control is also assumed. The modules from the bioinformatics curriculum 1.1.3, 1.3.2, and 2.2.1 provide good preparation for this.
The module has two parts; a 3 ECTS part, assessed via a computer test in exam mode (i.e. no internet access) and a 7 ECTS part which is assessed with a project portfolio.

metadata.Name: Algorithms and Datastructures
metadata.Assessments: Algoritmen en Datastructuren - Computer, organised by School

/en/course/2026/BFVH24ALGODATA.outcomes:
This module has the following learning outcomes:
You analyse the time or memory complexity of an algorithm.
You use data sorting and searching algorithms appropriate to the data structure in which the data is stored.
You use linear data structures such as arrays, stacks and queues and/or the various forms of (linked) lists to solve problems efficiently.
You use (binary) trees and/or other graphs to solve problems efficiently.
You use maps and/or dictionaries to solve problems efficiently.
You use recursion to solve problems efficiently.
/en/course/2026/BFVH24ALGODATA.content:
In this module, you will learn to think about a programme on a deeper level than the code; you will realise that it is not necessarily about the fact that a programme works, but also how it works. In doing so, we will look at the underlying algorithms and data structures that you can use when creating a programme. You will learn how to prove that a particular algorithm works or is faster than another algorithm.
We start by analysing and implementing algorithms and data structures for search and sorting problems; in doing so, we address how to analyse the performance of these algorithms, both experimentally and mathematically. Then, among other things, we take a closer look at problems that require a tree or digraph structure. Here you can think, for example, of finding the shortest route from A to B, a hierarchy in a classification or finding the best move in a game.
You will also work practically with these algorithms: you will implement them to solve concrete problems. You will also apply scientific sources to supplement and deepen your knowledge of these topics.

/en/course/2026/BFVH24BIOCANCER.outcomes:
This module has the following learning outcomes:
You describe the cell cycle and its regulation in eukaryotes, and you predict the consequences of changes in (the regulation of) the cell cycle for the cell, tissue and organism as a whole.
You recognise different types of DNA changes, give possible causes for them and speculate on their possible effects at protein and cell level.
You know various types of biological markers and use them to make informed statements about the presence of tumour cells.
You delve into the pathology of tumour tissue, and understand the operation and function of various (radiological) techniques.
You use your biological knowledge to explain various forms of cancer, and speculate about points of leverage for possible treatment.
You deepen your topic appropriately within the biology of cancer and present it in a relevant way to an audience of your peers.
/en/course/2026/BFVH24BIOCANCER.content:
This module discusses various aspects of cancer biology. Briefly, causes, pathology, analytical techniques used and possible treatments are covered. This module builds on module 2.1.1 NGS and Genetics and module 2.2.2 Immunology. This module includes lecture/work, and will look at different tissue types in a lab practical. During the module, you will work on the theory yourself, which will be tested individually.
In addition, each student (alone or in pairs) will give a short theoretical lecture on a topic relevant to this module. To implement the theory directly, you will work on a case (a chosen type of cancer) in each pair. This module is designed in conjunction with module 3.2.2, where the theory covered in this module can be used for understanding the biological background of the projects.

metadata.Name: Modelling Cancer
metadata.Assessments: Casus Modelleren - Other assessment Verdiepend Model - Other assessment

/en/course/2026/BFVH24MODELLEREN.outcomes:
You process and analyse oncology data from a variety of data sources, using quantitative models commonly used in the field.
You critically evaluate and interpret outcomes of data analysis and draw biologically relevant conclusions based on these findings.
You search and study relevant literature on modelling techniques and express their operation using appropriate terminology.
You select available software to realise and evaluate models or, if necessary, develop this software yourself to a certain extent.
You present methods used and results found in oral and written form in a way that is understandable to a fellow student.
You assess analysis logs of fellow students for comprehensibility and reproducibility and provide them with constructive comments.
/en/course/2026/BFVH24MODELLEREN.content:
As a bioinformatician, you often work in the context of scientific or applied research. Your work then not only consists of applying techniques you already know, but you also continuously master new methods and develop your own tools to apply them.
This module consists of a ‘carousel’ with a number (~4) of introductory cancer cases, each lasting over a week. In alternating pairs, you will be introduced to methods that are often new and more advanced for you to perform an analysis on a question. Cases may vary according to availability and need, or may respond to current events, but can include, for example: dynamic models (e.g. differential equations, molecular dynamics); predictive models (hidden-markov models, convolutional neural networks, generative text); descriptive models (structural equation models, non-linear regression); statistical models (non-parametric statistics, Bayesian statistics); etcetera.
Halfway through the module, you formulate your own individual problem that allows you to either deepen the methods of analysis from a given case study, or explore another advanced modelling technique on your own. You independently study literature with information on the method in question, you evaluate software for usability or write your own routines in a programming language of your choice, and you gather relevant oncological data from available sources or partially generate them yourself in the form of a simulation.
Finally, you provide a biological interpretation of your outcomes and present them in the form of a scientific poster, preceded by a pitch.
In particular, this module builds on topics offered in the modules below:
Module 1.4.1 ‘The scientific cycle’
Module 2.1.2 ‘Genomics & Transcriptomics’
Module 2.3.2 ‘Machine Learning with Class(es)’
Module 2.4.1 ‘*Omics’
In terms of biological context, the content of this module links to the following parallel module:
Module 3.2.1 ‘Biology of Cancer’

/en/course/2026/BFVH25STAGE.outcomes:
During the internship period, students will further develop the knowledge, skills and competences required for the professional working environment. In consultation with the professional field, the domain has drawn up a competence-oriented profile for the Bachelor of Applied Science.
The internship has several objectives:
•    The internship is an introduction to the future professional environment. The emphasis during the internship period is on orientation: you should gain insight into the purpose, function and functioning of the various departments within the organisation. It is also instructive during this internship to experience
what it means to work routinely and according to a fixed schedule.
•    Learning and applying the desired professional attitude, profession-specific skills and knowledge in preparation for working in the professional field.
•    Acquiring the relevant competences at the appropriate level.
/en/course/2026/BFVH25STAGE.content:
In order to prepare students for professional practice, the programme includes an internship period. The aim of this internship period is to prepare students for the professional environment. The emphasis of the internship is on learning to function in the professional field by carrying out an internship assignment. Students do their internship at an organisation that offers internships, such as a company, university, research institute, etc. The internship period consists of the second half of year 3 or the first half of year 4. The period consists exclusively of the internship assignment of 30 EC. In special cases, a different period is possible in consultation with the mentor and internship coordinator.
For information about the internship, the Brightspace course “Internship and graduation” is available. OnStage is used as a tracking and administration system. The link to OnStage can be found here: https://OnStage.xebic.com.
The 20-week internship period is structured as follows: weeks 1-2, writing the Plan of Approach; weeks 2-18, carrying out the internship project; weeks 17-20, completing the portfolio, including a written and oral presentation of the internship project. Halfway through the internship period, a Midterm Review is planned with the student, internship supervisor and contact lecturer.
The internship period is assessed on the final competences and levels as described for the bioinformatics programme. Students must demonstrate that they meet these competences by submitting a portfolio with fixed and free components. During the internship period, return days are organised to help students with their portfolios.
The competencies that must be mastered by the student are:
1.    Research (O; 3); the student translates a problem into a research strategy and carries out the research.
2.    Experimentation (E; 3); the student sets up experiments under supervision, carries them out independently and systematically, and obtains reproducible and reliable results.
3.    Management (M; 2); the student assesses their own work or that of others against procedures described in relevant management systems.
4.    Advising (A; 2); the student contributes to solving a technical problem for the client. Independently provides advice in a non-complex situation.
5.    Instructing (I; 1); The student passes on their own knowledge and skills to colleagues on request (by demonstrating and explaining).
6.    Project-based working (P; 2); The student works on a project within a limited open project framework.
7.    Self-management (Z; 2); The student reflects on their own performance and development.
The above competencies have different levels, which can be described using the following keywords as a measure of behaviour:
Level 1: executing, on instruction
Level 2: solving, analysing
Level 3: integrating, developing, transferring knowledge and skills
(application of knowledge and skills in new situations)
Level 4: generating knowledge
For each competency, the level that must be achieved at that moment is indicated.

/en/course/2026/BFVH25AFSTUDEREN.outcomes:
During the graduation period, students will further develop the knowledge, skills and competences required for the professional working environment.
The graduation project has several objectives:
Acquiring and demonstrating the competences required at the final level of your programme;
Contributing to a current theme in the professional field through research;
Gaining experience in the professional field;
Gaining insight into your own professional competence development, areas for improvement and interests.

Competency      Level (I-IV)

Management       II

/en/course/2026/BFVH25AFSTUDEREN.content:
The graduation project is the final component of the programme. You will independently carry out a graduation project at a company, hospital, university or research institute. You will work under the supervision of a company supervisor. The graduation project consists of a research project in which you will demonstrate the final competencies associated with the programme. The graduation project is carried out in the second half of year 4. In consultation with the mentor and internship coordinator, a different period is possible. This period consists exclusively of the graduation project of 30 EC.
For information about the internship and graduation, the Brightspace course “Internship and Graduation” is available. OnStage is used as a tracking and administration system. https://OnStage.xebic.com.
The graduation project lasts 20 weeks and is structured as follows: weeks 1-2, writing the Plan of Approach; weeks 2-18, carrying out the graduation project; weeks 17-20, completing the portfolio and defending the graduation project. Halfway through the period, a Midterm Review is planned with the student, internship supervisor and contact lecturer.
The graduation project is assessed on the final competences and levels as described for the bioinformatics programme. Students must demonstrate that they meet these competences by submitting a portfolio with fixed and free components. Together with an oral defence, the portfolio is assessed by two examiners for a final assessment.
The competencies that must be mastered by the student are:
1.    Research (O; 3); the student translates a problem into a research strategy and carries out the research.
2.    Experimentation (E; 3); the student sets up experiments under supervision, carries them out independently and systematically, and obtains reproducible and reliable results.
3.    Management (M; 2); the student assesses their own work or that of others against procedures described in relevant management systems.
4.    Advising (A; 2); the student contributes to solving a technical problem for the client. Independently provides advice in a non-complex situation.
5.    Instructing (I; 1); The student passes on his or her own knowledge and skills to employees on request (by demonstrating and explaining).
6.    Project-based working (P; 2); The student works on a project within a limited open project framework.
7.    Self-management (Z; 2); The student reflects on their own performance and development.
The above competencies have different levels, which can be described using the following keywords as a measure of behaviour:
Level 1: executing, on instruction
Level 2: solving, analysing
Level 3: integrating, developing, transferring knowledge and skills
(application of knowledge and skills in new situations)
Level 4: generating knowledge
For each competency, the level that must be achieved at that moment is indicated.
