/en/course/2026/BVVH24KVEI.outcomes: The students is able to analyze and identify anomalies in existing infrastructures. The student applies digital tools/innovations to conduct inspections and evaluates them by writing a research report based on scientific standards.
/en/course/2026/BVVH24KVEI.content:
Addressing issues of wall cracks due to earthquakes and foundation settlements linked to climate change requires us to look back at recent events. Quick and reliable decisions are crucial, and to achieve that, we need more information, improved skills, and better predictions. This can only happen with the help of more knowledgeable people and advanced technology - better skilled students and the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI).
Building on what we already know about detecting cracks, it's important to gather more data and work on more projects. This isn't just good for our research department; it's a win-win situation for the students and the community. We can break down the process into three steps: Understanding the theory, gaining practical skills, and conducting our inspections.
In the theory phase, students will learn the essential knowledge needed for inspections and research methods. We'll also provide hands-on skills training, including using tools, coding, and research techniques. This prepares students to carry out their inspections on smaller building projects, mainly focusing on housing in the city of Groningen. The idea is to empower students to understand and address structural issues while making a positive impact in their local community.

/en/course/2026/BVVH25ADCOMP.content: This module focuses on various architectural drawing and presentation techniques. These techniques are explored through visual research into the spatial properties and proportions of geometric forms and patterns in architecture. The emphasis is placed on both manual and digital presentations (2D and 3D), models, diagrams, symbols, and imagery (photography). These techniques are then applied in research into the ordering and composition of space and mass, in relation to architectural design and a set of fundamental architectural principles.

/en/course/2026/BVVH25ADDET.content: The creative design process in architecture is a constant interaction between the design of the whole and its parts. It is the relationship between concept (the idea) and the technique and the material (the detail). Analysis of the precedents contributes to a better understanding of the strong integration of technical engineering and architecture. Furthermore, the frame of reference of the student will be expanded.

/en/course/2026/BVVH25ADSTR.content:
To explicate the creative design process and to create awareness of the designing way of thinking is the focus of the module Strategic Architectural Design.
The design qualities, characterized by being able to simultaneously analyze and solve within the various domains of the built environment, enables students to work in the broader context and deal with a wide range of relevant issues within the built environment. The expertise about the built environment combined with the ability to visualize concepts, allows students to embed their interest in culture and society in creative solutions. Furthermore, they learn to give advice to various parties involved in the initialization phase of the building process

/en/course/2026/BVVH25ADCAN.content: In this module, the focus is on exploring and analyzing iconic buildings, movements and styles from the architectural canon. Students develop a systematic understanding of the evolution of architecture over the centuries, and translate this insight into analyses, essays and presentations. Through inquiry-based learning, the relationship between style characteristics, time context and design principles is critically examined.

/en/course/2026/BVVH26URVD.outcomes:
Project 2
V&D_1) The student can analyse and integrate trends and developments based on research, and translate these into substantiated scenarios and a future-oriented, user-centered vision for an area. [Initiate, Design, Research]
V&D_2) The student can formulate and evaluate a substantiated strategy based on developed scenarios and a vision, in which choices and positions are justified and stakeholders and feasibility are taken into account. [Initiate, Research]
V&D_3) The student can translate a strategy into a concrete and integrated spatial design that incorporates future-proofing, liveability, and usability, and communicate this design clearly and purposefully to both professionals and a broader audience. [Design, Communicate]
V&D_4) The student can evaluate design choices and outcomes based on evidence in terms of alignment with user needs and future-proofing, and formulate improvements and next steps accordingly. [Design]
V&D_5) The student collaborates constructively, takes (shared) responsibility for process (contributing to knowledge development, opinion-forming, and decision-making) and outcomes, and uses (familiar) methods to develop supported products based on consensus within a complex practical context and under coaching supervision. [Communicate]
Portfolio 2
V&D_6) The student can recognise and apply various theoretical and practice-based methods within Research through Design, and systematically analyse relevant issues. [Research]
V&D_7) The student can translate research results into concepts and visualisations through a substantiated and annotated portfolio with alternative and improved design proposals. [Research]
V&D_8) The student can critically analyse and evaluate research results, design choices, and societal issues, and take and substantiate a well-founded position on these in dialogue with other professionals. [Research, Professionalise]
V&D_9) The student can systematically reflect on their own learning process, performance, and decision-making, and formulate substantiated improvements and next steps based on this. [Professionalise]
/en/course/2026/BVVH26URVD.content:
Vision & Design
This course is divided in Project 2 and Portfolio 2.
Project 2
:
In this phase, you take the lead in shaping future-oriented solutions for complex spatial challenges. You explore trends and developments and transform them into well-founded scenarios and a compelling, user-centered vision.
Building on this, you design and refine a strategy that considers stakeholders and feasibility, and translate it into a concrete, integrated spatial design focused on future-proofing, liveability, and usability.
You critically evaluate your design choices and continuously improve your work. Throughout the process, you collaborate actively, take ownership of both process and outcomes, and work together to create strong, well-supported solutions.
Portfolio 2:
In this phase, you deepen your expertise by learning through design. You tackle complex, real-world challenges and learn how to apply both theoretical and practice-based methods to analyse them in a structured way.
You turn research into action by developing concepts and visualisations, which you present in a portfolio with alternative and improved design proposals. Along the way, you sharpen your critical thinking by evaluating research, design choices, and societal issues, and by confidently taking and defending your position in dialogue with professionals.
At the same time, you focus on your own development: you reflect on your learning process, performance, and decision-making, and use these insights to take purposeful next steps.

/en/course/2026/BVVH26URSSR.outcomes:
Project 1
S&SR_1) The student can analyse the spatial, social, and economic characteristics of an area and identify the key problems and opportunities in the current situation. [Initiate]
S&SR_2) The student can map and analyse relevant stakeholders and their needs, and identify the key problems and opportunities in the current situation. [Initiate, Communicate]
S&SR_3) The student can analyse problems in an area and determine the urgency and priority of different issues based on substantiated criteria. [Initiate]
S&SR_4) The student can analyse and evaluate the consequences of not intervening for different target groups and functions within the area. [Initiate, Research]
S&SR_5) The student collaborates constructively, takes (shared) responsibility for process and outcomes, and uses (familiar) methods to develop supported products based on consensus, within a complex but familiar practical context and under coaching supervision. [Communicate]
Portfolio 1
S&SR_6) The student can analyse their own ambitions and development needs within the context of the field, relate these to personal qualities and roles within a team, and translate them into personal learning goals. [Professionalise]
S&SR_7) The student can compare and integrate their own work with that of others to develop interdisciplinary insights and evaluate the value of different perspectives. [Professionalise]
S&SR_8) The student can critically reflect on their own performance and values and formulate targeted improvement actions based on this. [Professionalise]
/en/course/2026/BVVH26URSSR.content:
Minor Urban Regeneration
Urban Regeneration is about renewing and improving existing urban areas, with the aim of strengthening livability, the local economy, and spatial quality. During this minor, you will work on a specific area facing challenges related to livability, future resilience, and the needs of its users. Your goal is to give this area a new impulse and make it more resilient to future developments.
After a short introduction period, during which you get to know your fellow students and complete a first urban regeneration exercise, you will start working on the central question:
How do we design and organise a future-proof built environment that meets the needs of its users?
By the end of this minor, you will be able to answer this question independently.
Social & Spatial Research
This course is divided in Project 1 and Portfolio 1.
Project 1
:
In this phase, you will learn how to analyse an area and engage with residents and users, examining a case study from both spatial and social perspectives. You analyse spatial, social, and economic characteristics, map stakeholders and their interests, and clearly identify the core problem. By working with designs, concepts, visualisations, and interviews, you develop the ability to systematically analyse and evaluate issues and to justify your decisions. You also assess the consequences of (not) intervening.
Throughout the process, you collaborate constructively, take responsibility for both process and outcomes, and work together to develop supported solutions under coaching supervision.
You are supported through (guest) lectures, tutorials, design sessions, fieldwork, and excursions.
Portfolio 1:
In this phase, you actively work on your professional development. You explore your ambitions and development needs and translate them into concrete learning goals. You critically reflect on your own actions, values, and role within a team, and use this to support your growth.
In addition, you learn to compare your own work with that of others and connect different perspectives. This helps you develop interdisciplinary insights and better understand and utilise the value of diverse viewpoints.

/en/course/2026/BVVH26URPCD.outcomes: PCD_1) The student can analyse and critically evaluate their own actions and achieved results in relation to the initial plan and the Urban Regeneration context, and substantiate their own learning and development process based on this.
/en/course/2026/BVVH26URPCD.content:
Personal Contextual Development
In this course, you have the freedom to shape your own learning path. You can choose to conduct an individual research project, take a course, or for instance participate in a short, intensive international programme, provided it connects to the context of Urban Regeneration.
At the start, you define your approach in a personal plan. After completing the course, you reflect critically on your approach, development, and results in relation to this plan, gaining clear insight into your progress and growth.

/en/course/2026/CCVP23CHEMICUS.outcomes:
You portray the study and profession of a chemist and chemical technologist (portfolio and group poster) (PI = Professional Identity).
You work safely in a lab room and are aware of safety rules and collection of chemical waste (multiple-choice test and practical).
You carry out a project in a group (PI = Professional Identity) according to the scientific method.
You make a scientific poster in a group and give, receive and process feedback. (PV = Personal Skills & SoCoVa).
You perform a simple synthesis with a group and analyse the composition, purity and work on the following aspects: product analysis, mass/energy balance, cost price calculation and process sustainability (Practicum and poster).
You gain insight into sustainability in society and in the chemical field.
You find your way within Hanze University, the digital learning environment and get to know your mentor and fellow students through introductory activities and joint mentor lessons, and you take responsibility for your study progress and reflect on it through a personal mentor conversation (PO = personal development).

/en/course/2026/CCVP23CHEMICUS.content: During the introductory course the chemist and the chemical technologist, you get a picture of the profession of a chemist and a chemical technologist. So you will learn all kinds of things about the work you can do after completing your studies in Chemistry or Chemical Engineering here at Hanze University. Thus, you will discover that Chemistry is a subject with various components, such as making (synthesising) substances in a laboratory, analysing a made substance and calculating the efficiency of making a substance in different ways. These are all components that you will perform or experience yourself in project groups during this introductory course.  Therefore, you will also be taught how to cooperate well with others. Collaboration will also play a role later on during your profession. Finally, we will look at how you, as a chemist or chemical technologist, can make an important contribution to chemical product development and sustainability. In short: in this introductory course, you will find out that chemistry is fun, that you can become good at it, earn money and make an important contribution to society!

/en/course/2026/CCVP25EVENWICHT.outcomes:
You predict the location of chemical equilibria of acids and bases in water based on strength of the acids and bases involved (Ka, Kb, Kw).
You apply acid-base theory according to Brønsted-Lowry to acid-base calculations for single and polyvalent acids, bases and salts (pH, pKa, Ka, Kb, pKb, BOE table, common ion, dissociation percentage)
You calculate the pH of buffer systems under specified conditions (using Henderson-Hasselbach formula).
You perform acid-base titrations and determine the location of equilibrium (Kn, acid-base titration).
You predict the occurrence of precipitation reactions using the solubility and ion product (Ksp and IP) and the influence of additional ions, pH and of complex ions on the solubility of ions, and you quantify them (Kf) (common ion).
You apply theoretical knowledge about chemical equilibria in an independent, safe and responsible way while performing a simple experiment and communicate about this via a logbook and/or result form according to the applicable guidelines.

/en/course/2026/CTVP23STROMING.outcomes:
The Process Technology 1 curriculum component covers the following components of the Chemical Engineering BOKS:
Knowledge:
Physical transport phenomena: Transport of gases and liquids through pipes
Skills:
Research skills and systematic problem approach

This module has the following learning outcomes:
You calculate and describe flow velocities and pressure differences based on Bernoulli's Law.
You describe and calculate with a given volume flow rate the pressure drop of a piping system (and vice versa). The calculations are set up according to the system where Reynolds number, friction factor and pressure drop are calculated sequentially. The method follows the approach for design of piping systems in practical situations (engineering office).
You describe the viscosity behavior of Newtonian, pseudoplastic and dilatant fluids and use this knowledge to create viscograms/rheograms.
You reflect on your performance and professional development.

/en/course/2026/CTVP23STROMING.content:
Fluid dynamics is about the flow behaviour of fluids.
To design a pipe network, the resistance encountered by the flow is very important. It largely determines the required pumping capacity. The resistance depends on the viscosity of the liquid, the flow velocity and the resistance of fittings in the pipe.
You learn to calculate the flow speed and the magnitude of the resistances and you gain insight into the flow behaviour of viscous fluids. The sedimentation rate of small particles in a fluid is also discussed.
Besides calculation, measuring flow behaviour is also important. You are therefore introduced to the operation of viscometers, pressure gauges and flow meters.

Knowledge:

This module has the following learning outcomes:
You apply concepts from descriptive statistics, then interpret these concepts and visualize them in writing in the chemical-technological context.

/en/course/2026/CTVP23STATIST1.content: In this module, various statistical analysis techniques are introduced to determine and interpret the significance and effect strength of differences between experimentally measured means and/or proportions. Attention is also paid to visualising experimental data. The analyses and visualisations are performed in Excel. During the practical course, students work in pairs to set up, carry out and elaborate their own research. The results are presented with a poster.

/en/course/2026/CTVP23PROCES2.outcomes:
The Process Technology 2 curriculum component covers the following components of the Chemical Engineering BOKS:
Knowledge:
Thermodynamics: chemical thermodynamics (equilibria, enthalpy)
Statistics and mathematics: differential equations (numerical solving), data processing and data analysis (non-linear regression)
Process modelling: simulating and modelling reaction mechanisms and growth curves
Reactor science: kinetics (reaction mechanisms, catalysis, enzyme kinetics)
Materials science: material properties (plastics)
Chemistry: chemical equilibrium, basic polymer chemistry, basic biochemistry
Skills:
ICT skills: use and deployment of state-of-the-art digital tools/software (Excel, Mathcad, Minitab)
Social and communication skills: reporting and presenting
General laboratory skills and chemical analysis methods: laboratory-scale experimentation
Working safely in laboratory and industrial environments
This module has the following learning outcomes:
You describe the growth of microorganisms (prokaryotes) using the Gompertz equation and logistic growth.
You describe the location and shift of chemical equilibria based on calculated values of Kc and Kp and on the Chantelier-Van t'Hoff principle.
You calculate the reaction enthalpy of a reaction based on formation enthalpies of the substances in the reaction equation.
You communicate in writing according to the given guidelines (logbook instruction, template report, poster instruction) in Dutch about a simple(er) experiment/professional task.
You execute in a safe way an experiment in a chemical laboratory and write a reflection on the obtained results.
You reflect on your functioning and professional development.

/en/course/2026/CTVP23PROCES2.content:
The basis of many chemical-technological processes is the chemical reaction. This module focuses on chemical equilibrium (Kc, Kp), reaction enthalpy, and reaction rate (kinetics). Kinetics are discussed for simple reactions, also for sequential reactions (polymers) and, in the case of low temperature, the use of a catalyst.
An introduction to biochemistry is also covered (DNA, RNA, fats, sugar, proteins, ADP/ATP) with the connection of catalysts in bacteria in the form of enzymes. Growth of bacteria/yeasts (Gompertz, logistic) is covered along with fitting growth data to models (Minitab) and calculating growth models (ODEs with Mathcad). Reaction kinetics using enzymes (Michaelis-Menten) is discussed.

/en/course/2026/CTVH24APPARAT2.outcomes:
This module has the following learning outcomes:
You perform the engineering of gas cleaning systems based on filtration and electrostatic separation.
You perform the engineering of settling tanks and centrifuges for liquid-solid separation.
You master essential concepts in solid-state processing, namely: 1.) segregation 2.) particle size distribution and 3.) flowability. In doing so, you perform experiments to analyse the flow from a silo and measure the mixing of solids. You relate the obtained experimental results to the concepts of segregation, particle size distribution and flowability.
You perform mixing experiments to determine mixing power and time for three impellers with and without baffles (turbine, propeller, blade agitator), calculating the power NP and comparing it with literature.
You experiment with two hydrocyclones and can measure the separation efficiency.
/en/course/2026/CTVH24APPARAT2.content:
The aim of the module is competence development in the field of engineering process equipment for mixing, gas-solid separation and liquid-solid separation. Development in this area is based on a theory module combined with performance of experiments on a semi-technical scale. The aim of the experiments is to establish links between theory and practice and application of the results of the experiments for production-scale equipment design.
The module is part of the Process Equipment Learning Line. The module is the continuation of Process Equipment 1 in study year 1.

metadata.Name: Heat Transfer
metadata.Assessments: Heat Transfer Practice - Other assessment Heat Transfer Theory - Written, organised by STAD examinations

/en/course/2026/CTVH24WARMTE.outcomes:
This module has the following learning outcomes:
You use the quantities of specific heat, specific mass, volume flow, mass flow, temperature difference and heat flow correctly in heat transfer calculations.
You calculate for a given heat transfer situation the overall heat transfer coefficient and total heat flow for conduction, conduction in combination with convection and radiation.
You carry out the design of heat exchangers for application in the process and food industry, applying the principles of heat transfer by conduction, convection and radiation, including time-dependent behaviour.
You determine at pilot scale the heat flow and overall heat transfer coefficient for heat transfer in a plate heat exchanger, a concentric tube heat exchanger and a shell and tube heat exchanger, and understand the concepts of entrainment and counter flow to perform the experiments at the required conditions.
You apply numerical methods in solving heat transfer problems in complex situations.
/en/course/2026/CTVH24WARMTE.content: The subject of heat transfer concerns the qualitative understanding of the concepts of heat flow and heat transfer. Quantitatively, the subject deals with the concepts: heat transfer by conduction and convection and a combination of these. It quantitatively discusses heat transfer by radiation for simple geometry. It covers the calculation of heat transfer determining quantities: heat flow, overall heat transfer coefficient, and partial heat transfer coefficient.

/en/course/2026/CTVH24STATIS2.outcomes:
This module has the following learning outcomes:
You perform linear and non-linear regression (ordinary and multiple) for a given or experimentally obtained dataset, interpret the data and apply model selection.
You use simultaneous Design of Experiment (DoE) methods to optimise factors for a given process, choosing the right design and using regression and model selection (Surface Response Method) to locate the optimum.
You use univariate and multivariate sequential optimisation methods (Binary, Fibonacci, Simplex and modified Simplex) for optimisation of factors for a given process, and use them to localise the optimum.
You select the appropriate techniques and methods in a screening phase and in a detailed optimisation phase.
You use matrix algebra as part of optimisation of process parameters and can use it to determine the quality of an experimental design.
/en/course/2026/CTVH24STATIS2.content: As a chemical technologist, you will often be involved in improving and optimising a production process. To give well-founded advice, you will often do a number of experiments. This module covers various optimisation techniques, with the aim of obtaining as much relevant information as possible with as few experiments as possible. Simultaneous (Design of Experiment, Surface Response Method) and sequential methods (Binary, Fibonacci, Simplex and Modified Simplex) approaches are discussed and applied to practical problems. Assessment is by means of a computer-based examination using Excel, Mathcad and Wolframalpha.

/en/course/2026/CTVH24ORGCHEMIE.outcomes:
This module has the following learning outcomes:
You assign the systematic name to simple alkanes, alkenes, carboxylic acids, alcohols, esters, ethers and amines and draw the correct structural formula from a provided name.
You identify a nucleophile and an electrophile and explain the course of an electrophile addition reaction and draw its mechanism.
You apply the acquired theoretical knowledge and translate it into an approach for simple organic synthesis with correct use of the reprocessing techniques provided.
You perform simple organic synthesis in a safe and responsible manner, work up the reaction mixture and apply relevant analytical techniques such as NMR & IR.
/en/course/2026/CTVH24ORGCHEMIE.content:
In this module, you will work on organic chemistry. You will learn the naming of organic molecules, type(s) of reactions and be introduced to reaction mechanisms. You apply this acquired theoretical knowledge to a number of organic chemical reactions in the lab where you synthesise your own substances.
Practical work is assessed by logbooks, measurement reports and practical competences. Theory is taught through instructional lectures and tested through a written examination.

/en/course/2026/CTVH24PROCESREG.outcomes:
This module has the following learning outcomes:
You can describe the components of a control loop and perform calculations on a control loop.
You can describe the operation of a control valve and an inverter and perform calculations on them.
You recognize basic characteristics of a process. You can determine the characteristics of a process/system and use these to set a controller.
You can describe the operation of different sensors (flow, temperature, pressure, level, quality) and select these sensors.
You can describe the operation of an On-Off controller and a P/PI/PID controller and apply these in a process.
You can recognise and/or apply the control aspects (codes and symbols) on a P&ID (Piping & Instrumentation Diagram).
You inform yourself through the internship information and participation in the activities during the Career Week about the internship possibilities in the Chemical Engineering programme and you can apply for an internship in the Netherlands or abroad at the company or institution of your choice.
/en/course/2026/CTVH24PROCESREG.content:
The subject of process control covers the techniques needed to obtain a good and stable regulated process or system.
The following topics are covered during various lectures:
Basic concepts of process control and the control loop
Corrective body: control valve and speed-controlled motor
Basic systems and process characteristics (process characterisation)
On-off controller and P/PI/PID controller
Control loop gain factors
Sensors
Piping & Instrumentation Diagram (P&ID)
In the practical session, the knowledge acquired is applied by characterising a process and using it to set the various controllers. The controllers and their settings are analysed and evaluated.

metadata.Name: Thermodynamics
metadata.Assessments: Phase Theory - Computer, organised by STAD examinations Thermodynamics Theory - Written, organised by STAD examinations

/en/course/2026/CTVH24THERMO.outcomes:
This module has the following learning outcomes:
- You can perform bubble point, dew point and flash calculations of ideal and non-ideal mixtures based on VLE and Antoine equations.
- You can apply different activity models (such as the 1- and 2-parameter Margules model) in equilibrium calculations, and determine appropriate model parameters from experimental data.
- You can both interpret phase diagrams of binary mixtures (including liquid-liquid de-mixing, and azeotropes with the effect on distillation) and calculate models.
- You describe and use concepts such as energy, heat, work, enthalpy, entropy, free energy and chemical potential in a chemical or chemical-technological context, and calculate the change in these quantities in processes involving changes in pressure, temperature, volume and/or phase state.
- You describe realistic chemical reactions in terms of free energy, enthalpy and entropy, and you predict the location of chemical equilibrium as a function of output composition, pressure and temperature, using tabulated values of the formation enthalpy and absolute entropy.
/en/course/2026/CTVH24THERMO.content:
This module provides an in-depth understanding of chemical thermodynamics and phase theory, crucial concepts for a chemical technologist. Calculations of the vapour pressure liquid-gas equilibrium of systems are the basis for modelling distillation processes.
Specifically, the module covers topics such as reaction heat, chemical work, Gibbs free energy and the location of chemical equilibria, with a strong focus on their application in chemical reactions. In addition, aspects from the process industry are covered, such as mixing and the compression and expansion of gases.

metadata.Name: Process Simulation & Modelling 1
metadata.Assessments: Processimulatie & Modelleren 1 Practicum - Other assessment Processimulatie & Modelleren 1 Theorie - Computer, organised by STAD examinations

/en/course/2026/CTVH24PROCESSIM1.outcomes:
This module has the following learning outcomes
- You can roughly dimension a stripper and a distillation column using existing correlations (Fenske, Gilliland-Eduljee), applying dish efficiency.
- You can apply the Lewis-Sorel method for sizing a flash vessel, a stripper and a distillation column for ideal and non-ideal binary mixtures.
- You can apply the McGabe-Thiele method for sizing a stripper and a distillation column for ideal and non-ideal mixtures.
- You can set up a model in the simulation programme Aspen Plus® and compare and evaluate experimental and model results with models in Excel.
- You can interpret research results using models and you can summarise, structure and interpret them in relation to the problem definition.
/en/course/2026/CTVH24PROCESSIM1.content:
In the chemical and petrochemical industries, distillation is the most common separation technique. Distillation is a process in which a liquid or vapour mixture consisting of two or more components is separated into component fractions of a desired purity by supplying and removing heat.
Distillation is based on the fact that the vapour of a boiling mixture will generally be richer in the component(s) with the lower boiling points. This means that when this vapour is cooled and condensed, this condensate will contain more of the volatile components. As a result, the original mixture will contain more of the less volatile components.
This module covers various elementary aspects of distillation, such as gas-liquid and liquid-liquid equilibrium, saturated vapour pressure, dew point and bubble point of binary and ternary mixtures, and flash calculations. In addition, various models for liquid-vapour and liquid-liquid equilibria are covered.
These models can be applied in Excel and in Aspen plus to predict the properties of different component mixtures.

metadata.Name: Circular Polymers
metadata.Assessments: Polymeerchemie - Written, organised by STAD examinations Project Circulaire Polymeren - Other assessment

/en/course/2026/CCVH24CIRCUPOLYM.outcomes:
With your (interdisciplinary and/or international) project group, you will go through the empirical cycle for a research project on the synthesis of a polymer, effectively collaborating, formulating an objective, searching and using scientific literature, choosing and justifying an approach for the research project, performing the experiments, collecting and interpreting the research data, and formulating a conclusion, final discussion and recommendations.
You choose a strategy for the chemical synthesis and/or recycling of a polyester from literature you have found or provided yourself, select relevant analytical methods and translate them into a practical approach, which you then implement in the laboratory.
With a proactive, open attitude, you ensure a pleasant and successful course of the project, meet agreements, communicate about progress, identify any bottlenecks and make them negotiable.
You report on your project through work meetings, logbooks and a group final interview (assessment).
You describe the basic principles of polymer synthesis, analysis and properties, and explain the relationship between the chemical and physical structure of polymers and their properties.
You study in groups a chosen polymer, and present the application of the basic principles to the chosen polymer during the theory lessons.
You know various aspects of intercultural communication and cooperation, and apply these during seminars, (online) group meetings, and reflect on your contribution to this by means of an individual report.
/en/course/2026/CCVH24CIRCUPOLYM.content:
In the Circular Polymers module, you will learn about the basic principles of Polymer Chemistry in the theory part (2 EC). You also apply some of these basic principles to a polymer of your own choice, about which you make a presentation in a group in one of the classes (“Adopt a Polymer!”). The theory part concludes with a written exam.
In the practical and project part, you perform a polymer synthesis (PLA or another polymer) on the basis of provided literature, in which you, in an interdisciplinary and/or internationally oriented project group, make your own proposal for a variation in the synthesis, to investigate its effect on the properties of the polymer.
Furthermore, you will immerse yourself in a project group on the circular application of polymers: you will choose an approach for the depolymerization of a polymer, select a number of variables and analysis techniques, after which you will search for the right conditions to rebuild the monomers into the same (or even a higher-quality!) polymer. You then implement the chosen approach for this yourself in the lab.
You will be assessed for your project work on your active participation, and the project will be concluded with a final substantive interview (group assessment).

metadata.Name: Reactor Engineering 1
metadata.Assessments: Reactorkunde 1 Practicum - Other assessment Reactorkunde 1 Theorie - Written, organised by STAD examinations

/en/course/2026/CTVH24REACTOR1.outcomes:
This module has the following learning outcomes:
You apply the concepts of reaction order and reaction rate constant to arrive at a mathematical description of the reaction rates of reactions with different reaction orders in the interval [0 - 2].
You apply the mathematical description of the concepts of reaction selectivity and yield to arrive at numerical values.
You establish for the three model reactors a mathematical model for the conversion of a reactant for reactions with reaction orders in the interval [0-2] and you solve them numerically.
You determine the kinetics of a reaction (order and reaction rate constant) based on experiments in a batch reactor.
You perform engineering from a CSTR based on kinetics measured in a batch reactor.
/en/course/2026/CTVH24REACTOR1.content: The aim of the module is competence development on the kinetics of reactions and its effect on the design of the three model reactors: batch, CSTR and plugflow. The module is part of the Reactor Science Curriculum. This module is the foundation required for successful completion of the Reactor Science 2 module in the third year of study.

/en/course/2026/CTVH24FABRONTW.outcomes:
This module has the following learning outcomes:
You perform an organic synthesis experiment safely and make the required product specifying purity and reaction efficiency.
You apply process technology concepts such as reactor science and separation technology to scale-up the laboratory synthesis to production scale.
You work with document versions to ensure optimal cooperation within the project group according to plan and content.
You cooperate professionally within a group, process feedback, reflect on your functioning and professional development and evaluate the group process.
/en/course/2026/CTVH24FABRONTW.content:
In the factory design module, you will scale up a synthesis from lab scale to factory scale in project form. You perform the synthesis yourself in the lab as a starting point for the factory design. Later, you will perform the synthesis again to verify and/or optimise choices within your factory design. The project days are full days in which you, as a project group, have to deliver a large number of documents per project day, with the content getting more and more detailed as the block progresses. The documents are provided with feedback by the lecturer after each project day. At the end of the project, you compile all documents into a report.
The content of the project uses knowledge from previous subjects.

metadata.Name: Food Technology
metadata.Assessments: Levensmiddelentechnologie Practicum - Other assessment Levensmiddelentechnologie Theorie - Written, organised by STAD examinations

/en/course/2026/CTVH24LEVENSMDL.outcomes:
This module has the following learning outcomes:
You define and describe colloids and master the basic concepts of colloid chemistry.
You describe different methods used for making colloid systems and for determining the particle size of colloids.
You describe and calculate the various forces (gravity, heat movement and intermolecular forces) acting in colloidal systems.
You describe and calculate the influence of surfactants on the properties of a solution.
You describe the industrial processes concerning food technology safety and hygiene (CIP, HACCP, HazOp).
You perform a lab/pilot experiment in a safe and accurate way and reflect on the results obtained.
/en/course/2026/CTVH24LEVENSMDL.content:
In this module, we will look at so-called colloidal systems within food technology: heterogeneous mixtures containing particles between 1 nanometre and 1 micrometre in size. These include emulsions, suspensions, sols, foams and the like. Colloids play and important role in everyday life and are found in creams, sauces, paints, cosmetics, gelatine, milk and many other products. We are going to look at 3 forces acting on colloid particles, namely gravity, heat motion (Brownian motion) and intermolecular forces acting on the boundary surfaces. The interplay of these forces creates the unique properties of colloids. In this module, you will also learn how to influence these forces in the technology of colloidal systems and how to make measurements on colloids. The theory (3 EC) will be tested with a written digital exam.
Besides theory, the practical part (2 EC) will focus on the quality and safety of industrial processes such as membrane technology, Cleaning in Place (CIP), food safety (HAACP) and Hazard & Operability analysis (HazOp).

/en/course/2026/CTVH26STAGE.outcomes:
During the placement period, the student will further develop the knowledge, skills and competences required for the professional workplace. In consultation with the professional sector, the department has drawn up a competence-based profile for the Bachelor of Applied Science.
The competencies and the levels at which the student is assessed are:
Research (Oz: 2): The student makes a significant contribution to a proposed research strategy and carries out the research.
Experimentation (E; 2): The student selects a protocol/approach, adapts it where necessary, carries it out and obtains reproducible and reliable results.
Development (Ow: 2): The student develops or improves by selecting or adapting an approach.
Management (B: 1): The student acts within the given frameworks and procedures described in relevant management systems.
Advising (A: 1): The student examines the client’s problems and/or requirements in depth. Contributes to a recommendation in accordance with a prescribed methodology.
Instructing (I: 1): The student, under supervision, passes on knowledge and skills to colleagues.
Project-based working (P: 1): The student works on a project within a defined project framework.
Self-management (Z: 2): The student reflects on their own performance and development.
The above competencies have different levels, which can be described using the following keywords as a measure of behaviour:
Level 1: executing, on instruction
Level 2: solving, analysing
Level 3: integrating, developing, transferring knowledge and skills
(applying knowledge and skills in new situations)
Level 4: generating knowledge
For each competence, the level that must be met at that point in time is indicated.
The work placement has several objectives:
The work placement serves as an introduction to your future professional environment. The focus during the placement period is on orientation: you need to gain an understanding of the purpose and functioning of the various departments within the organisation. It is also instructive during this placement to experience what it means to work routinely and on a regular basis.
Learning and applying the required professional attitude, job-specific skills and knowledge in preparation for working in the professional field.
Acquiring competencies at the appropriate level.
/en/course/2026/CTVH26STAGE.content:
To prepare students for professional practice, the programme includes a work placement period. The aim of this work placement is to prepare students for the professional environment. The focus of the work placement is on learning to function in the professional field by carrying out a work placement assignment or assignments. Students carry out an internship assignment at an organisation offering placements, such as a company, institution or research institute. In the curriculum, the internship period covers terms 1 and 2 of the third year of study. The internship carries a weighting of 30 ECTS credits in the curriculum.
For information about the placement, the Brightspace course ‘Placement and Graduation’ is available. OnStage is used as a monitoring and administration system. The link to OnStage can be found here:
https://OnStage.xebic.com
.
The 20-week internship period is structured as follows: weeks 1–4, drafting and discussing the Action Plan. Weeks 8–9, an interim evaluation is scheduled with the student, company supervisor and contact lecturer. Weeks 18–20: completion of the portfolio, including a written report and poster presentation.
The placement period is assessed against the competences and levels as described for the Chemical Technology programme. Students must demonstrate that they meet these competences by submitting a portfolio comprising set and optional components and by giving a poster presentation. During the placement period, a feedback session is organised to help students get started with their portfolio.

metadata.Name: Separation Technology 1
metadata.Assessments: Separation Technology 1 - Practical - Other assessment Separation Technology 1 - Theory - Written, organised by STAD examinations

/en/course/2026/CTVH26SCHEIDTCH1.outcomes:
The Separation Technology 1 module covers the following components of the BOKS Chemical Technology curriculum:
Knowledge:
Unit operations: separation techniques: Filtration and gas absorption
Skills:
Experimenting with pilot-scale separation techniques
Working safely in laboratory and industrial environments
Research skills and systematic problem-solving
This module has the following learning outcomes:
You describe the gas absorption process mathematically using the overall mass balance and the concepts of mass transfer coefficient (Kg·a), transfer unit (N) and Height Equivalent to a Theoretical Plate (HETP).
You describe the filtration process mathematically for the situation of filtration at constant pressure and filtration with a constant filtrate flow rate.
You carry out a gas absorption experiment on a semi-technical scale and use the concepts of flooding and overall transfer coefficient to describe the experimental results.
You will carry out batch filtration experiments on a semi-technical scale and use the results to determine the numerical values of the cake resistance coefficient a and the cloth resistance b.
The aim of the module is to develop competence in the field of separation technology. The module forms part of the Separation Technology learning pathway, alongside the modules Process Simulation and Modelling 1 and 2, and Separation Technology 2.

metadata.Name: Chemical Reactor Engineering 2
metadata.Assessments: Residence Time Distribution & Modeling Reactors - Computer, organised by STAD examinations Thermal Effects Reactors - Written, organised by STAD examinations

/en/course/2026/CTVH26REACTOR2.outcomes:
This module has the following learning outcomes:
You process, analyse and interpret the results of tracer studies in terms of residence time distribution functions.
You model real reactors based on the residence time distribution functions and use the model to predict the conversion in real reactors using the Excel software programme.
You diagnose potential problems in reactors using the obtained residence time distribution.
You determine the conditions for optimal production of the desired product in parallel and sequential reactions in ideal batch, tank and tubular reactors, where appropriate using the VisSim simulation package.
You calculate mole and energy balances for flow reactors, isothermal and non-isothermal continuously stirred tank reactors and plug flow reactors, where appropriate using a simulation package such as VisSim.
You determine the steady-state conditions for non-isothermal continuously stirred tank reactors and analyse ‘runaway’ effects.
/en/course/2026/CTVH26REACTOR2.content:
In the first part of the Reactor Engineering 2 module, ‘Residence Time Distribution & Reactor Modelling’, you will examine residence time distribution in ideal and non-ideal (real-world) reaction systems. You will learn to model real-world reactors and use these models to calculate conversion. The insights gained can also be used to identify reactor problems (reactor diagnosis). The following topics are covered in the first part:
fractional and cumulative residence time distribution functions E and F
average residence time, variation and skewness
macro and micro mixing; mixing models
modelling of non-ideal reactors
zero-parameter model: segregation and maximum mixedness
one-parameter model: tanks-in-series model
In the second part, Thermal Effects in Reactors, you will draw up an energy balance. You will use this to account for the temperature effects within the reactor on the progress of the reaction.
The content of Reactor Engineering 2 builds on the material covered in module 2.3.2, Reactor Engineering 1.
The Reactor Engineering 2 module covers the following components of the BOKS Chemical Technology curriculum:
Knowledge:
Model reactors (batch, CSTR, plug flow) and non-ideal reactors
Kinetics: order, temperature dependence of the reaction rate constant, reversible reactions, parallel reactions, consecutive reactions, reaction selectivity, reaction yield.
Simulation & modelling
Mass & energy balances
Skills:
Use and application of simulation software and Excel

metadata.Name: Materials Science & Electrolysis
metadata.Assessments: Materials Science & Electrolysis - Practical - Other assessment Materials Science & Electrolysis - Theory - Written, organised by STAD examinations

/en/course/2026/CTVH26MATELEKTRO.outcomes:
This module has the following learning outcomes:
•    You select construction materials based on the process conditions.
•    You interpret forms of corrosion in terms of electrochemical processes and translate these into corrosion cells.
•    You apply various corrosion prevention techniques.
•    You understand electrolysis and fuel cell processes and perform calculations relating to them.
•    You carry out experiments on a semi-technical scale using a bench-scale electrolyser and fuel cell and use the results to analyse these processes.
•    You carry out corrosion experiments and analyse the results obtained.
/en/course/2026/CTVH26MATELEKTRO.content:
The Materials Science & Electrolysis module covers the following areas of the BOKS Chemical Technology curriculum:
Knowledge:
•    Materials science: material properties (metals, plastics, metal corrosion) and applications of materials
•    Chemistry: electrochemistry (redox reactions)
Skills:
•    Experimenting with bench-scale electrolysers and fuel cells
•    Working safely in laboratory and industrial environments
•    Research skills and systematic problem-solving
The Materials Science & Electrolysis module covers construction materials (metals, plastics) used in industry and addresses electrochemical processes, including corrosion, electrolysis and fuel cells.

metadata.Name: Separation Technology 2
metadata.Assessments: Separation Technology 2 - Practical - Other assessment Separation Technology 2 - Theory - Written, organised by STAD examinations

/en/course/2026/CTVH26SCHEIDTCH2.outcomes:
The Separation Technology 2 module covers the following components of the BOKS Chemical Technology curriculum:
Knowledge:
Unit operations: separation techniques: Drying and Extraction
Skills:
Experimenting with pilot-scale separation techniques
Working safely in laboratory and industrial environments
Research skills and systematic problem-solving
This module has the following learning outcomes:
You describe the extraction process mathematically and graphically for single-stage, cross-flow and counter-flow extraction.
You calculate and/or determine relevant physical properties of air from the psychrometric chart.
You describe the drying process mathematically for drying under constant drying conditions.
You will conduct a semi-technical scale experiment using a bench-scale cooling tower and use a mass-energy balance and the psychrometric chart to describe the experimental results.
You will conduct a semi-technical scale drying experiment using a bench-scale dryer and use the results to describe and predict the drying process.
The aim of the module is to develop competence in the field of separation technology. The module forms part of the Separation Technology learning pathway, alongside the modules Process Simulation and Modelling 1 & 2 and Separation Technology 1.

metadata.Name: Process Data Analysis
metadata.Assessments: Process Data Analysis - Theory - Other assessment

/en/course/2026/CTVH26PROCESDATA.outcomes:
The module has the following learning outcomes:
You will import data from various sources (such as CSV, TXT and Excel files) into both Excel and Minitab, and select the appropriate methods and functions for different data formats and structures.
You will clean data in preparation for analysis in both Excel and Minitab, by applying techniques to identify and handle missing values, outliers, inconsistencies and duplicates.
You will apply and interpret various advanced data analysis functions in Excel and/or Minitab, including: ANOVA analyses (1-way, 2-way), time series analyses (correlation, correlation functions, principal component analysis), linear and non-linear regression (including model selection and interpolation) and categorical data analysis (1-way and 2-way chi-squared analyses, logistic regression).
You create effective and clear data visualisations in both Excel and Minitab (such as scatter plots, bar charts, line charts, pie charts and box plots) to communicate patterns, trends and relationships in data.
You will use and interpret methods and indices focused on statistical process control (Shewhart charts, process capability indices) in both Excel and Minitab.
The Process Data Analysis module covers the following components of the BOKS Chemical Technology:
Knowledge:
data processing and data analysis
process control
Skills:
Use and application of data analysis and processing software
/en/course/2026/CTVH26PROCESDATA.content:
Making process facilities more energy-efficient requires the identification, adjustment and monitoring of key process parameters. This module covers the collection and cleaning of large volumes of process data, followed by the application of advanced statistical methods such as multivariate data analysis, e.g. multivariate regression, Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and Analysis of Variance (ANOVA). In addition, attention is given to visualising large amounts of data in a clear and effective manner. Finally, an introduction to Statistical Process Control (SPC) is provided. The lessons make use of the Excel and Minitab programmes. Students are required to bring their own laptop to the lessons.
This module forms part of the statistics learning pathway and builds on the previous statistics modules.

/en/course/2026/CTVH26PROCESSIM2.outcomes:
This module has the following learning outcomes
You will model a process in the Aspen Plus® simulation programme and compare and evaluate experimental and model results.
You will interpret and organise research results using models with a view to addressing the problem.
You will work professionally in a group on a case study and present the findings clearly.
/en/course/2026/CTVH26PROCESSIM2.content:
Process Simulation & Modelling 2 builds on the fundamental knowledge acquired in Process Simulation & Modelling 1. Whereas the first part focused on phase equilibria and distillation, this module focuses on the modelling, simulation and optimisation of chemical reactors and integrated process plants using Aspen Plus.
This module covers various types of chemical reactors, such as batch reactors, continuously stirred tank reactors (CSTRs) and plug flow reactors (PFRs). The module covers reaction kinetics, stoichiometry, energy and mass balances, and the influence of process conditions and reactor design on conversion, selectivity and yield.
In addition, students learn to construct complete chemical processes by linking reactors to separation and auxiliary processes, such as distillation, heat exchangers and recycle streams. Attention is paid to flowsheet design, the selection of thermodynamic models, convergence behaviour and the interpretation of simulation results.
Finally, Aspen Plus is used as a tool for process analysis and optimisation. Students learn how process parameters can be systematically varied to improve energy consumption, raw material consumption and product quality, and how simulations can be used to support design and decision-making in the chemical industry.
In the Chemport Challenge, students are paired with second-year Chemistry students and linked to a company, where they have one working week to develop a consultancy case. These are then presented to the companies.
The Process Simulation & Modelling 2 module covers the following components of the BOKS Chemical Technology:
Knowledge:
Unit Operations
Reactors
Heat exchangers
Thermodynamics
Chemical thermodynamics
Process engineering
Process design
Process modelling
Simulation and modelling
Optimisation
Skills
Research skills and systematic problem-solving
ICT skills
Use of Aspen Plus
Interpersonal and communication skills

- You perform a simple organic synthesis in a safe and responsible way, work up the reaction mixture and apply relevant analytical techniques. You report on this according to the applicable guidelines and give an attractive and structured presentation on this for fellow students and teachers

/en/course/2026/CHVP23ELEKTROCHM.outcomes:
This module has the following learning outcomes:
- You formulate the principles of electrochemistry, set up (complex) semi-reactions and explain the occurrence or non-occurrence of redox reactions in acidic, basic or neutral environments.
- You understand the composition and operation of Galvanic cells and calculate cell voltages using the Nernst equation. You apply this to batteries and fuel cells.
- You perform equilibrium calculations on redox, precipitation and complex formation reactions.
- You explain the influence of poorly soluble salts, complex ions and buffers on electrode potentials and determine the respective K, K and K from measured cell voltages.
- You work on a project on solar cell concepts and principles, such as representing, naming and calculating solar cell components.
- You apply theoretical knowledge about electrochemistry in an independent, safe and responsible way while carrying out a simple experiment and communicate about this via a logbook and/or results form according to the applicable guidelines.
- You reflect on the study progress and study experience by means of a portfolio and a final personal interview with the mentor and make a planning for the next school year. (PI = personal identity; PD = personal development).

/en/course/2026/CHVP23ELEKTROCHM.content:
This module focuses on several applications of electrochemistry. We start by refreshing high school knowledge: what is a reductor and oxidiser and when does a redox reaction occur? Then you learn to derive half-reactions for complex oxidisers and reductors. We discuss in detail Galvanic cells and their practical application: batteries and fuel cells. Using Nernst's law, you learn to calculate the voltage given by a battery.
In the second half of this module, we continue calculating saturated solutions (Ksp) and solution containing a complexion (Kf) and we calculate the acid dissociation constant (Ka) using electrochemical reactions. Theory will also cover the solar cell project.
In practicals, you apply theory with the performance of basic electrochemical experiments, the construction of a galvanic cell and a solar cell project.
For professional identity, you will write a portfolio and conduct a final interview with your tutor.
It is desirable to have taken the modules Chemical Calculus, Chemical Equilibria and Chemical Bonding.

metadata.Name: Organic Chemistry 1
metadata.Assessments: Organische Chemie 1 Theory - Written, organised by STAD examinations Practicum incl. opwerkingstechnieken - Other assessment

/en/course/2026/CHVH24ORGCHEMIE1.outcomes:
You describe the role of chemicals mentioned in prescriptions/procedures for organic chemical reactions, and divide the prescription into the following phases: 1) build setup, 2) combine chemicals, 3) start reaction, 4) course reaction, 5) end reaction, 6) reprocessing/purification.
You recognize reprocessing techniques in regulations for organic chemical reactions and explain the application.
You draw relevant resonance structures and apply this knowledge to reaction mechanisms.
You recognize aromatic structures and can draw a simple electrophilic aromatic substitution (including reaction mechanism).
You can draw a simple substitution reaction (including reaction mechanism) according to a Sn1 and Sn2 mechanism.
You can draw a simple elimination reaction (including reaction mechanism) according to an E1 and E2 mechanism.
You perform simple organic synthesis in a safe and responsible manner, work up the reaction mixture, apply relevant analytical techniques and report on this according to the applicable guidelines.
/en/course/2026/CHVH24ORGCHEMIE1.content:
In this module you will learn what resonance is and how to draw different resonance structures of molecules. Using resonance, you can make statements about the reactivity of these molecules. This will therefore recur in all further organic chemistry modules. In addition, attention is paid to substitution and elimination reactions. You will learn the distinction between different mechanisms in relation to the order of the reactions. The competition between these two types of reactions and its cause are also discussed.
You will apply the theory from the first three lectures (reprocessing techniques) in practice.
Practical work is assessed by logbooks, practical competencies and a report. Theory is taught through instructional lectures and tested through a written exam.

metadata.Name: Spectrometry
metadata.Assessments: Spectrometrie Practicum - Other assessment Spectrometrie Theorie - Written, organised by STAD examinations

/en/course/2026/CHVH24SPECTRO.outcomes:
You apply Lambert-Beer's law in practical and in theoretical cases and name the limitations and/or deviations from Lambert-Beer's law.
You describe the absorption process of electromagnetic radiation in molecules and atoms in UV/VIS, Fluorescence and atomic spectrometry.
You name and describe the components of spectroscopic devices.
You calculate various quantitative analyses and name the advantages and disadvantages of the various analyses.
You apply the acquired theoretical knowledge about spectrometry in an independent, safe and responsible way during the performance of an experiment and communicate about this with a result form, presentation and/or logbook according to the applicable guidelines.
/en/course/2026/CHVH24SPECTRO.content:
In this module, we further explore spectrometric quantitative methods and extend the techniques in theory and practice. The techniques covered are UV-VIS, Fluorescence and atomic spectrometry. The basis is the Jablonski diagram and construction of equipment.
From here we delve into various limitations and deviations of the methods. In addition, various quantitative analyses that can be used in spectrometry are covered, as well as other analytical detection methods. Examples include one-point calibration, calibration line, internal standard, standard addition and two-component analysis (for spectrometry only).
Two experiments will be conducted during the practical days: LC experiment with UV detection at a one-point calibration and the analysis of a calibration line with the UV-VIS spectrometer. In the latter experiment, several parameters of the UV-VIS are also optimized.

metadata.Name: Statistics for Analytical Chemistry 2
metadata.Assessments: Dataverwerking - Other assessment Statistiek voor Analytische Chemie Theorie - Computer, organised by STAD examinations

/en/course/2026/CHVH24STATISTIEK.outcomes:
You perform regression analysis, for both external standard method and standard addition method, and apply Goodness of Fit and Lack of Fit tests to assess the accuracy of regression models.
You can during regression analysis: calculate detection limits, interpolate values with consideration of reliability, identify and remove outliers, recognize weighted regression, and apply method comparison.
You perform statistical process control and interpret the results of the Shewhart and Cusum maps, basic validation.
You apply, depending on the experimental design, different ANOVA methods (2-way, blocking, fixed- and random-factors, latin square) and interpret the results.
You calculate with software with fractions, powers, roots, logarithms and you solve algebraic equations.
You solve systems of equations analytically and numerically using Excel, MathCad and WolframAlpha.
You apply the acquired theoretical knowledge about chromatography and statistics in an independent and safe manner while performing an experiment, and communicate about it with an assignments applying correct data processing using software according to the applicable guidelines.
/en/course/2026/CHVH24STATISTIEK.content: Statistics for Analytical Chemistry 2 focuses on statistics and data processing. The data processing section provides a multifaceted approach to essential concepts and tools. It covers various aspects including basic mathematics, numerical mathematics with MathCad, Excel and WolframAlpha, chemical arithmetic, graph design, text formatting and reporting in Word.  In addition, this module also provides in-depth knowledge of linear regression analysis, analysis of variance and the use of control charts. You will learn to construct the best-fit regression equation. In addition, you learn to interpolate and interpret the reliability of a obtained value. You gain knowledge about detection limits, outliers and other applications of regression models.

metadata.Name: Organic Chemistry 2
metadata.Assessments: Organische Chemie 2 Theory - Written, organised by STAD examinations Practicum Organische Chemie 2 - Other assessment

/en/course/2026/CHVH24ORGCHEMIE2.outcomes:
You explain and apply various reactions involving aldehydes and ketones, carboxylic acids, nitriles and esters in syntheses.
You recognize and apply carbonyl α-substitutions and condensations, including the mechanisms of these reactions.
You name the boundary conditions of nucleophilic acyl substitution reactions and draw the reaction mechanisms.
You perform organic syntheses in a safe and responsible manner, work up the reaction mixture, apply relevant analytical techniques and report on them according to applicable guidelines.
/en/course/2026/CHVH24ORGCHEMIE2.content:
This module focuses on the carbonyl group. In the first part, we are introduced to various carboxylic acid derivatives, in particular acid chlorides, anhydrides, esters, amides as well as carboxylic acids themselves. In this part you will learn the relationships between these derivatives and how they can be converted into each other. The second part concerns the reactivity of aldehydes and ketones. The nucleophilic acyl substitution reaction is the focus here. Attention is also paid to condensation reactions and substitution reactions at the α-position relative to the carbonyl group.
Practical work includes the synthesis of fluorenone and a PTC (Phase Transfer Catalysis) oxidation of an alkene, and is assessed through logbooks, practical competencies and a report. Theory is taught by instructional lectures and tested by written examination.

metadata.Name: Spectroscopic Techniques
metadata.Assessments: Spectroscopische Technieken Practicum - Other assessment Spectroscopische Technieken Theorie - Written, organised by STAD examinations

/en/course/2026/CHVH24SPECTECH.outcomes:
You know the basic principles and application of the spectroscopic techniques Infrared Spectroscopy (IR), Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) and Mass Spectrometry (MS).
You recognize and describe the construction of the apparatus associated with the spectroscopic techniques IR, NMR and MS.
You interpret IR and 1H NMR spectra of simple organic compounds using tables of IR frequencies, NMR chemical shift values and 1H coupling patterns.
You independently perform a GC-MS experiment, preprocessing the sample and identifying the substances present, quantifying with calibration measurements, and after data processing and statistical analysis, reporting the results of your experiment according to applicable guidelines.
You will apply the knowledge gained on spectroscopic techniques by independently performing IR and NMR measurements and interpreting the measured spectra, in order to determine the structure and purity of supplied and/or self-synthesized compounds, and report the results according to the applicable guidelines.
/en/course/2026/CHVH24SPECTECH.content:
In this module, we cover three spectroscopic techniques that are essential for identifying and analyzing organic compounds. These techniques are mass spectrometry (MS), infrared spectroscopy (IR) and nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy.
You will learn the basics of the equipment used in these analyses, and how to determine the structure of an organic compound from a spectrum. You will do these structure analyses using MS, IR and NMR spectra from the literature, sometimes combining the information from different spectra to arrive at your answer.
The module also contains a practical part, where you will work with the equipment yourself. You will gain more insight into the possibilities offered by MS, in combination with GC, to identify and quantitatively measure substances. You will also perform a synthesis in which you will use NMR and IR to determine for yourself exactly what substance you have made, and what its purity is.

metadata.Name: Physical Chemistry 2
metadata.Assessments: Reactiekinetiek - Computer, organised by STAD examinations Thermodynamica - Written, organised by STAD examinations

/en/course/2026/CHVH24FYSCHEMIE2.outcomes:
You set up rate equations and use them to determine order and rate constant from experimental data.
You use various theoretical models to predict reaction rates, and calculate the effect of temperature and a catalyst on reaction rates.
You apply the theoretical knowledge gained about reaction kinetics in an independent, safe and responsible manner while conducting an experiment, and communicate about it with a log/results sheet according to the applicable guidelines.
You describe and use concepts such as energy, heat, work, enthalpy, entropy, free energy and chemical potential in a chemical or chemical-technological context, and calculate the change in these quantities in processes involving changes in pressure, temperature, volume and/or phase state.
You describe realistic chemical reactions in terms of free energy, enthalpy and entropy, and you predict the location of chemical equilibrium as a function of output composition, pressure and temperature, using tabulated values of the formation enthalpy and absolute entropy.
/en/course/2026/CHVH24FYSCHEMIE2.content:
This module provides an in-depth understanding of chemical thermodynamics and reaction kinetics, crucial concepts for a chemist in his daily work. You will learn the methods to calculate the location of chemical equilibria and gain insight into the (im)possibilities to influence this equilibrium. You will also learn how quickly this equilibrium is reached.
Specifically, the module covers topics such as reaction heat, chemical work, Gibbs free energy and the location of chemical equilibria, with a strong focus on their application in chemical reactions. In addition, aspects of the process industry are covered, such as mixing and the compression and expansion of gases.
The section on reaction kinetics provides an introduction to the kinetics of chemical reactions, allowing you to develop a complete understanding of both the thermodynamic and kinetic aspects of chemical processes.

metadata.Name: Chromatography and Potentiometry
metadata.Assessments: Chromatografie en Potentiometrie Practicum - Other assessment Chromatografie en Potentiometrie Theorie - Written, organised by STAD examinations

/en/course/2026/CHVH24CHROMATPOT.outcomes:
You describe and apply the van Deemter equation in theoretical cases and name the deviations in chromatograms.
You describe the application and operation of different types of chromatography.
You recommend changes in parameters to optimize chromatograms and methods, including calculation of pH (buffers) and eluent composition.
You name and describe different types of indication and reference electrodes and can explain/name the deviations in potentiometry.
You apply Nernst's law and the Nernst-like equation appropriate to the different types of electrodes in potentiometric issues.
You apply the acquired theoretical knowledge about chromatography in an independent, safe and responsible way while performing an experiment, and communicate about this with a logbook according to the applicable guidelines.
/en/course/2026/CHVH24CHROMATPOT.content:
In this module, we further explore chromatographic methods and deepen the techniques in theory and practice. The techniques covered are: GC, LC, HIC, SEC and IC.
The basics are the different separation principles, the van Deemter equation and equipment construction. The focus during this module is more on optimizing chromatograms so that as much separation as possible takes place in the shortest possible analysis time.
In Potentiometry (quantitative electrochemistry) we cover the different reference and indicator electrodes. Calculations on various issues using the Nernst and Nerstian equations are also performed.
During the practical days, one experiment will be performed: LC experiment with UV detection with a calibration line. In the method, statistical testing is applied and quantified in various ways.

metadata.Name: Biochemistry 2
metadata.Assessments: Biochemie 2 Practicum incl. Chemport - Other assessment Biochemie 2 Theorie - Computer, organised by STAD examinations

/en/course/2026/CHVH24BIOCHEMIE2.outcomes:
You draw the structure of carbohydrates and can identify and describe it.
You determine by calculation of the oxidation number whether a given reaction is an oxidation or reduction reaction and describe its implications.
You determine the Michaelis-Menten constants of an enzyme by incorporating enzyme kinetics data into a Lineweaver-Burk plot.
You describe, recognize and apply the concept of enzyme coupling in biochemical reactions.
You reproduce the net reactions of glycolysis, citric acid cycle, oxidative phosphorylation and beta-oxidation explain them.
You separate and identify proteins using SDS-page in a biochemistry laboratory.
You reflect through a portfolio on the study choices, you make, regarding your professional identity.
/en/course/2026/CHVH24BIOCHEMIE2.content:
Module biochemistry 2 focuses on metabolism in the human cell. We will proverbially open the “hood of the cell” and discover how the cell is able to convert fuel molecules into usable energy. This will cover the various metabolic pathways such as glycolysis and citric acid cycle. The emphasis here is on understanding these pathways and less on memorizing reactions. Theory also covers the structure of carbohydrates and basic enzyme kinetics.  The theory (3 EC) is tested using a written digital exam. The module also includes a practical of 2 days in which a mixture of proteins is separated using SDS-page.
During the academic year you work on your professional identity using a portfolio. Within Professional identity, preparation for upcoming study choices and career choices is central, through attending lectures, information sessions and the interns' poster presentations, among other things. This is reflected upon using related assignments in the portfolio.

metadata.Name: Chemometrics
metadata.Assessments: Chemometrie 1 Practicum - Other assessment Chemometrie 1 Theorie - Computer, organised by STAD examinations

/en/course/2026/CHVH24CHEMOMETR1.outcomes:
You apply univariate and multivariate sequential optimization and interpret the results, using the following search methods: Binary, Fibonacci and (modified) Simplex.
You can do matrix arithmetic (scalar product, matrix product, determinant, inverse, transposed).
You numerically determine maxima and minima of functions within optimization and discuss the results found in relation to chemical and experimental significance.
You perform univariate and multivariate simultaneous optimization and interpret the results, including through application of Response Surface Methodology (with screening and detail designs, such as factorial and Central Composite designs)
You can perform and interpret appropriate analysis of variance (ANOVA) based on the experimental design
You apply the acquired theoretical knowledge about spectrometry, potentiometry and optimization in an independent, safe and responsible way during the execution of an experiment, and communicate about this with a logbook and/or results form according to the applicable guidelines.
/en/course/2026/CHVH24CHEMOMETR1.content:
Chemometrics is the application of statistical and mathematical methods and techniques in chemistry. It is used to obtain and process measurement data for optimization, calibration, interpretation of data, etc. The focus of this module is on optimization. You will learn to collect chemical information, measurement data, in a structured way and thus efficiently find out the influence of variables and an optimum of a chemical experiment. For example, you can increase the yield of a reaction. From the beginning you will learn how to use factorial design, you will learn to apply matrix arithmetic so that you can solve regression problems and calculate the influence of variables.
In practice, you will use the knowledge gained in spectrometry, potentiometry and experimental design in experiments in which you apply these techniques. The processing of the experiment requires an elaboration using an ANOVA and an interpretation of the results.

metadata.Name: Colloid Chemistry
metadata.Assessments: Chemometrie 1 Practicum - Other assessment Chemometrie 1 Theorie - Written, organised by STAD examinations

/en/course/2026/CHVH24COLLOIDCHM.outcomes:
You define and describe colloids and master the basic concepts of colloid chemistry.
You describe various methods used for making colloid systems and for determining the particle size of colloids.
You describe and calculate the various forces (gravity, heat movement and intermolecular forces) operating in colloidal systems.
You describe and calculate the influence of surfactants on the properties of a solution.
You apply the knowledge gained about making and measuring colloidal systems in a practical situation and report the results according to the applicable guidelines.
You determine the surface tension and critical micelle concentration of various liquids in a chemical laboratory and report the results according to the applicable guidelines.
Within a project group of fellow students, you give advice to a company based on a current sustainability issue (Chemport Challenge).
/en/course/2026/CHVH24COLLOIDCHM.content:
In this module we are going to look at so-called colloidal systems: heterogeneous mixtures containing particles between 1 nanometer and 1 micrometer in size. These include emulsions, suspensions, sols, foams and the like. Colloids play and major role in everyday life and are found in creams, sauces, paints, cosmetics, gelatin, milk and many other products. We are going to look at 3 forces acting on colloid particles, namely gravity, heat motion (Brownian motion) and the intermolecular forces acting on the interfaces. The interplay of these forces creates the unique properties of colloids. In this module you will also learn how to influence these forces in the technology of colloidal systems and how to make measurements on colloids. Theory (3 EC) is tested with a written digital exam. The module also includes 2 days of practicals (2 EC) in which surface tension, critical micelle concentration and emulsions will be discussed.
In addition, the Chemport Challenge also takes place in this module. During the Chemport Challenge you will visit chemical companies at Chemiepark Delfzijl and Eemshaven to see what chemistry looks like in practice and on an industrial scale. You will then be explained a current problem (challenge) by one of the companies and, together with fellow students in a project group, you will make a recommendation on this to the company.
