/en/course/2026/CHVH26STAGE.outcomes:
The learning outcomes you are working towards are the programme-level learning outcomes. These can also be found on the Hanze website.
You will carry out practice-oriented research independently, translating a given problem into a research strategy and conducting the research, thereby contributing to the resolution of a current and/or socially relevant issue within the field of Applied Science.
Under supervision, you will design experiments, carry them out independently and systematically, and generate reproducible and reliable results that can be used to answer a practice-oriented research question within the Applied Science domain.
You operate within the framework of a management system, ensuring that your own work complies with applicable procedures and contributes to safeguarding quality, safety and compliance with legislation and regulations within an organisation in the Applied Science domain.
You gain a thorough understanding of the client’s problems and/or requirements and describe the context, enabling you to contribute to proposing a possible course of action within the field of Applied Science.
Upon request, you share your own knowledge and skills with others within the field of Applied Science, enabling them to gain a basic understanding of the use of relevant methods, equipment and tasks.
You will work in a structured and systematic manner with others on a project within a limited, open project framework in the field of Applied Science.
/en/course/2026/CHVH26STAGE.content:
To prepare you for professional practice, the course includes a work placement. The aim of this work placement is to familiarise you with the professional working environment. The emphasis of the work placement is on learning to function in the professional field by carrying out a work placement assignment. You will undertake your work placement at a host organisation, such as a company, hospital, university, research institute, etc. You will work under the supervision of a workplace supervisor. The placement is worth 30 EC, during which you will work on an assignment that aligns with the programme profile and the final-year competencies.
For information on graduation, the Brightspace course ‘Stage’ is available. OnStage is used as the administration system.
The placement lasts 20 weeks. You will start by drawing up a plan of action, carry out the work, and conclude the placement with a portfolio and a poster presentation. The portfolio comprises set and optional components, through which you demonstrate your competences. Halfway through the placement period, an interim evaluation will be scheduled with you, your placement supervisor and your contact lecturer.
During the placement period, review sessions are organised to assist you with the placement process, the portfolio and the poster presentation.

/en/course/2026/CHVH26AFSTUDEREN.outcomes:
The learning outcomes you are working towards are the programme-level learning outcomes. These can also be found on the Hanze website.
You will carry out practice-oriented research independently, translating a given problem into a research strategy and conducting the research, thereby contributing to the resolution of a current and/or socially relevant issue within the field of Applied Science.
Under supervision, you will design experiments, carry them out independently and systematically, and generate reproducible and reliable results that can be used to answer a practice-oriented research question within the Applied Science domain.

You work in a structured and systematic manner with others on a project within a limited, open project framework in the field of Applied Science.
/en/course/2026/CHVH26AFSTUDEREN.content:
You will carry out your final-year research project independently at a company, hospital, university or research institute. You will work under the supervision of a company supervisor. The final-year project is worth 30 EC. The organisation where the final-year project is carried out must offer you the opportunity to work on a project that aligns with the programme profile of your course and through which you can demonstrate the competencies required at the final level of your programme.
For information about the final-year project, the Brightspace course ‘Final-Year Project’ is available. OnStage is used as the administrative system.
The graduation period lasts 20 weeks. You will begin by drafting a project plan, carry out the research, and conclude the project with a portfolio, a presentation and a defence. The portfolio comprises both set and optional components, through which you demonstrate your competences. Halfway through the graduation period, an interim review will be scheduled with you, your graduation supervisor and your contact lecturer.

/en/course/2026/CMVB18STG.outcomes:
Learning Outcomes
You will work on various CMD competencies and their associated learning outcomes. The learning outcomes associated with competencies EFGHI are mandatory. You choose two additional learning outcomes from the ABCD competencies.
Learning outcomes from which you may choose two, fitting your internship (ABCD)
A) You map the user context during the design process of the multimedia products you design during the internship. In doing so, you involve end users and other stakeholders throughout the process.
B) You translate the wishes of end users and other stakeholders into creative concepts for (interactive) multimedia products and justify the choices made.
C) You develop various concepts into interactive prototypes and (partial) products for the internship organization. In doing so, you use your knowledge of interaction, storytelling, user experience, behavioral change, and multimedia interface design.
C) You consider the support base and future implementation by the organization when designing and realizing your (interactive) multimedia products and justify the choices made.
D) You validate and refine the design of the products you work on during the internship. You do this by evaluating usability and user experience quality with users through various evaluation methods and techniques.
Mandatory learning outcomes (EFGHI)
E) You follow the research process during the internship in a methodical and traceable manner, making justified choices from a broad range of research methods and techniques.
F) You demonstrate that you can plan, execute, monitor, and manage independently.
G) You demonstrate that you can connect different roles and disciplines within the internship organization while working in a team and seek expert help when needed.
H) You reflect on your learning process and intended CMD competencies during the internship period using a personal development portfolio.
I) You demonstrate an entrepreneurial and proactive attitude through which you can identify opportunities for the internship organization and translate creative innovative ideas into feasible market concepts.
/en/course/2026/CMVB18STG.content:
The internship is an external learning situation in which you work on the CMD competencies (domain competencies and the professional competencies). You do this within the context of a professional organisation and under the guidance of an experienced CMD professional.
During the internship, the student participates in the day-to-day running of the internship organisation.
You are going to:
Broaden and deepen CMD skills and knowledge
Learn to apply this knowledge and skills in practice
Learn how a professional organization works
Learn to set goals, reflect on them and develop yourself
The duration of the internship is approximately 100 working days (including Internship Event: internship return day). The starting point is a full working week based on the policies of the internship organisation.
Assignment
During the internship you will work on various assignments that together make up the development portfolio. As evidence for the different competencies, you add products that you have worked on during the internship. At the end of the internship, the internship teacher visits the internship organization. Halfway through the internship there is a mandatory Internship Event where the student has to give a presentation of his/her internship

/en/course/2026/CMVB24AFS.outcomes:
A) You can identify and understand the context of the problem, user's desire, client's objective, stakeholders' interests, and technology's capabilities.
B) You come up with ideas and develop concepts for (interactive) products, services, and experiences. This involves finding new ways to meet user requirements, client objectives and other interests.
C) You are able to shape concepts and make them concrete in prototypes. You can fit your design into applicable standards and the company's product portfolio.
D) You are able to repeatedly test results arising during different stages of the design process for their value and importance for the user/client's requirements.
E) You are a confident designer who can switch smoothly in the design process, who conducts thorough research and uses the outcomes to improve design.
F) You are enterprising and organisationally sensitive. You see opportunities and realise them. You organise yourself and others and include everyone in the innovation process.
G) You involve others from the team, users and other stakeholders in the design. Also from other disciplines. You understand relationships and make sure everyone feels comfortable in the process.
H) You work from a personal commitment to society and from a drive to improve it. You know where you stand and how you can develop.
/en/course/2026/CMVB24AFS.content:
Content
During graduation you show that you have mastered all the competencies of CMD at the final level. That is why you go through the design cycle as usual and you iterate from a problem (or opportunity or issue) up to and including an evaluated prototype. You prepare a graduation portfolio that consists of various components such as a prototype, a design process report, the evidence from the various phases of the design cycle and a reflection report (for a complete overview of the portfolio components, see the graduation manual).
You can only start your graduation with a graduation assignment approved by the graduation coordinator. You will be coached in the search for that assignment and the preparation of the application form. This takes place during the Introduction Week Year 4 (start of the first semester), the Graduation Bootcamp (during period 1) and the Kick Start Graduation (first week of the graduation semester). During the Kick Start Graduation you make a roadmap with a time planning. You will also formulate some learning goals.
During your graduation, you will be supervised by your graduation supervisor and receive structured feedback based on agreements. The graduation supervisor will be assigned to you by the graduation coordinator.
Assignment
You will design and develop an interactive media experience, documenting your design process in a portfolio. This will demonstrate that you have mastered the final competencies of CMD. You will find the assignment yourself in the professional field, taking into account the criteria set out in the graduation manual.
You choose the logical starting point in the design cycle: do you start with a problem, an existing product or prototype, or do you start with an initial prototype and iterate further? During the final interview (exam), you demonstrate your final design and process using the portfolio and prototype.

/en/course/2026/GTVP21PDP.outcomes:
Course independant learning outcomes
LOL A Level 1. The student actively participates in the team, engaging with team members in ways that facilitate their contributions and proactively cooperating to complete needed tasks.
LOL B Level 1. The student identifies own and others' assumptions under guidance to address a simple, structured problem.
LOL C Level 1. The student infers, indicates, and can ideate concepts relevant to the problem context.
LOL D Level 1. The student demonstrates understanding of relevant technological solutions and can create simple prototypes under guidance.
LOL E Level 1. The student can choose appropriate technical solutions to complex problems, constructs these solutions and can alter and differentiate these using identified improvements.
LOL F Level 1. The student is able to name their own strengths, can formulate simple learning goals and takes action to fulfil them.
/en/course/2026/GTVP21PDP.content:

/en/course/2026/GTVP21PPF.content:
Conten
t
Playful Pasts and Futures is a course that historicises games and confronts students with the questions like “Why do we study games?”. Students will learn how play is a form of learning and how we use games to explore the possibilities of new technology. The course touches on the history of the internet, technology and games and the ethics connected to it.
Essential to understanding interactive systems and their possibilities is to be able to see the elements of which a system consists and how they relate to the experience the system intends to deliver. For budding new technologies these elements might be clear, but the experiences they could deliver are still being explored. A fundamental part of exploring these experiences is to find goals and interactions for new technology that stimulates familiarization and sparks engaging interaction.
By being able to assess and identify the core tenets of interactive systems, the student is challenged to reassess their own relation to the interactive systems they know. In turn, this understanding opens the student up for identifying new interactions or applying old interactions in novel ways; and enables the student to assess the current interactive digital media industries and identify new opportunities to act on. The course is assessed by a poster presentation and a written report.

/en/course/2026/GTVP24PPP.content:
“Making a game in a team to develop yourself!”
In Project 3D Prototyping and Production, students will concept, develop, and produce a digital game as a solution to a chosen design challenge. Students will use evaluation and 3D game development tools to create a finished 3D solution to their design challenge. The finished solution will be evaluated with the target audience to ensure it meets the initial project brief and will be iterated upon, based on the findings of the evaluations.
Design Brief
Games and playful design can be used to address real social challenges, from small scale ('how to get more people to use this service?') to large scale (‘how to change people's behaviour around water usage?’) and everything in between. The theme for this block revolves around three 'Spaces': nature spaces, public spaces, and cultural spaces. The student will create, develop, and evaluate a 3D entertainment game to address one of the cases around these spaces.
Design Constraints
the game must be made using 3D tools (think Unity, Blender)
the game concept must address the project briefing.
the game concept must be evaluated with the users of the given space (think Research).
the game must exist in finished prototype form, suitable to be deployed in the relevant channel.
In solving the design brief, student teams are supported by project coaches, and a series of workshops and learning streams, including 3D Creative Media; 3D Game Programming; Game Design Tools; and Research.
Students are expected to put in the necessary hours in ideation and effort to have a tested, iterated, and finished prototype of their game, and to have tested their game with both fellow students and end-users.
Assessment
The course is assessed via a demonstration, in which the working prototype is shown to teachers and fellow students; by a development portfolio, assembled over the duration of the course, in which the student provides evidence of what they have done and what they have learned; and a Criterium Based Interview (CBI) were students are interviewed about the contents of the development portfolio.

/en/course/2026/GTVP21VOU.content:
The student will be offered several cases of products that can benefit from an improved user interface and user experience. They select one case to focus on and analyse the current UI and UX. During workshops general principles of UI and UX will be discussed. Students will work with methods (tools) of front-end prototyping that enable them to redesign the product of their case based on their just acquired insights.
UI and UX principles will be offered in the slides and by referencing general available sources online. As a book on UX design, human factors, and usability the book ‘The Gamer’s Brain’, by Celia Hodent will be used. This book is written for multimedia professionals in the creative media and game technology industry to better understand what UX is, its importance, how to improve games (or other multimedia products), and in what way UX can be integrated in in their production pipeline in different phases of production.
The workshops on UI design will use an industry standard prototyping tool. The student will learn to create low-fidelity prototypes to test new setups and how to iterate on them towards a high-fidelity prototype for testing more fleshed-out ideas. Having developed a high-fidelity prototype, students will conduct a short evaluation to find out whether their redesign has achieved its design goal. As a closure for the course the student will digitally hand in their prototypes and a report outlining their design rationale.

This course functions as a 'mirror capstone' of year 1. Students will create a showcase portfolio to present themselves to the industry and they will make the first steps in expanding their network by collecting feedback on their portfolio. In addition, students will develop the skill to pitch their value in a concise format to a Company Supervisor (Instructor) of their desired Internship Company.
The course is assessed via a hand-in of a showcase portfolio and a presentation.

/en/course/2026/GTVB22NTE.content:
Students will work in groups to create a game using a chosen technology from a selection provided. Students will explore that technology through the development of their game, uncovering the ethical, technical and artistic limits of their chosen technology. Building on Playful Pasts and Futures in Year 1, students will use games as a tool to map the contours and possibilities of their chosen technology, discovering and creating new uses for their technology. Students will engage with game engines, 3D modelling tools, theories of technology and ethical questions in their project.
Students work individually to create a development portfolio in which they submit evidence of their attainment of the competencies of the course, using as evidence the work they have done during the time of the project, including process, prototype and work done outside the project.
Design Brief  One of the main uses of games is as a tool to explore the possible uses of new technologies. In this course, students are challenged to make a game for 30 years in the future: what will that game look like, how will it play, who will play it? What is the next hit game for VR? What is the next technology to be mainstream in gaming? In attempting to address this design brief, students will address the question of ‘what is a game’ and will attempt to position themselves in this future.
Design Constraints
• The game must be made in Unity.
• The game must use one of the selected technologies.
• The game must have a visual style appropriate to the technology.
• The game must be playable at the demonstration.
• The game cannot have shooting.
In solving the design brief, student teams are supported by project coaches, and a series of workshops related to VR Development and Futures Literacy;
Students are expected to put in the necessary hours and effort to have a tested concept and a working prototype of their game.
The course is assessed via a demonstration, in which the working prototype is shown to teachers and fellow students; and by a development portfolio, assembled over the duration of the course, in which the student provides evidence of what they have done and what they have learned.
The entry requirement to this project is having passed GTVP24PPP in the CMGT first year programme.

/en/course/2026/GTVB22NTA.content:
In New Technology Adaptation, students will work in teams to build a solution to specific problem of a real client using mobile technology. Students will work following an Agile process to develop, iterate and test a solution to the client’s design brief. In making their solutions, students will address the extent to which the solution meets the needs of the target audience and the appropriateness of the technological solution.
Design Brief
The design brief for the assignment will be provided by the client.
Design Constraints
• The solution must be made in the technology preferred by the client.
• Feedback on the proposed solution must be gathered from the client prior to the final demonstration.
• The solution must be justified based on appropriate user experience research and must be playable at the demonstration.
• The visual style must be appropriate to the needs of the target audience.
In solving the design brief, student teams are supported by project coaches, and a series of workshops related to Mobile Development and UX.
Students are expected to put in the necessary hours and effort to have a tested concept and a working prototype of their game, and to have tested their game with the target audience.
The course is assessed via a demonstration, in which the working prototype is shown to teachers and fellow students; and by a development portfolio, assembled over the duration of the course, in which the student provides evidence of what they have done and what they have learned.

/en/course/2026/GTVB22GL.content:
During Gamelab, you will form start-up groups and work in partnership with fellow students and professionals to build a concept, pitch your solution and develop it in order to convince the judges of its potential. The goal of GameLab is that you have a product that can be published on one of the major platforms upon completion (eg, Steam, AppStore, Itch.io, etc)
In a series of workshops, coaching sessions and presentations you will proceed through a series of gates in which your concept and business case will be assessed by professionals. During the course of the project the professionals will have the ability to not accept various ideas as potential products. This means only the best ideas get to progress to the point of publishing.
You will develop according to the latest software engineering methods using production specifications determined by your team, the experts and coaches. By critically assessing your budget, role requirements, technology and concept you will guide your development team towards the release of your product.
As a professional individual you will provide your team the needed hours and effort to complete the development of the products. This means in most cases you will put in lots of hours to develop the needed assets and code.
During this course you will receive coaching from professionals on art, design, audience research, user experience and development. But it is your task to ensure you have access to the required information to succeed.
In a final demonstration to the judges and fellow students you will show the potential of your product. This includes the actual working product, but also an insight on your production process. You will provide evidence of and reflection on the work you have done in a development portfolio, and will defend that portfolio in an individual competency based interview.
The course is assessed via a demonstration, in which the working prototype is shown to teachers and fellow students; and by a development portfolio, assembled over the duration of the course, in which the student provides evidence of what they have done and what they have learned.
The entry requirement to this project is having passed GTVP24PPP in the CMGT first year programme.

As a designer you will come up with an innovative and creative game concept that will show off your skills as a future professional. In a written game design document you will showcase your design with a focus on level design. You will then develop a level of your game in an industry tool to showcase your skills.

They have to work in UE for this course. This focus track will cover a range of relevant topics, for example: workflow adjustments from Unity to UE; Blueprint scripting; Quixel; using UE tools to create environments; working with a group to finish a prototype.
At the end of this course, students will deliver a professional product made using blueprints and/or C++.

/en/course/2026/GTVB24ELAN.content:
For this elective, students will focus on creating a portfolio ready animation(s). These could have any kind of application ranging from, but not limited to: short films, music videos, advertisements or an animated website.
Go wild and use the LED screen in the Spacelab to record a video doing a dance off against your own animated avatar! Use your work from Narrative Design and bring your story world to life! Take your creature from Creature Design and animate it for a gripping cutscene.
The goal for students is to comprehend the principles of animation such as sense of weight, timing and style, how to apply them to their chosen concept and explore animation techniques (eg, 2D, 3D, Claymation etc) used in different industries.
By completing practical exercises in class like creating small animations, students build up the foundation to make their concept come to life. Additionally, they’ll be collecting supporting material for their design process on a week-by-week basis.
Students will then storyboard and plan their workflow, determining the appropriate techniques and technologies required to create a portfolio worthy piece.
Students are free to experiment, think outside of the box and pursue a topic and technique they are passionate about. This freedom extends both to the nature of the project
and the
makeup of the creative team. Students can decide to work as an individual, in pairs or in a team. If more people work on a project, then more will be possible, yet more will be expected in terms of complexity and scope.
A proposal will be discussed to realistically match the timeframe and expected workload.
The final product will be a rendered animation that is expected to have a coherent concept, theme, style and purpose.

/en/course/2026/GTVB22ELAI.content:
The field of AI is evolving rapidly, while simultaneously revolutionizing the field of Creative Media & Game Technology. New developments such as art and level generation, deep reinforcement learning for automatic AI behavior training, and automatic upscaling of old textures have large impacts on the industry.
You will need to research, understand, apply and expand these technologies, in order to show you can adapt to any new technologies that might come your way in the near or far future.
Over the course of this elective, we will address various topics from classical AI technologies such as search trees and state machines to modern AI technologies such as neural networks and large language models. The explanations of the functionality 'under the hood' helps demystify the often black box nature of AI systems.
For this course we expect at least some familiarity with programming, in order for you to develop your own prototype. There is no programming language/framework requirement.

/en/course/2026/GTVB22ELSG.content:
With a growing interest in the world for "Games to Grow", "Edugames" and other initiatives, the field of Serious Gaming is growing, and there is a need for well-thought-out games which teach technical and critical thinking skills developed by professionals. This Elective will dive into how "Learning Mechanics" translate to "Game Mechanics" and how games can be designed and facilitated with the purpose of solving local problems for a student-defined audience.
By experiencing and analyzing various Serious Games, students will comprehend the effectiveness and utility of games as solutions for complex problems. Through research and testing, students will define a problem statement for a self-chosen target audience. They will then test a prototype to determine its effectiveness and analyze the results. To complete the serious game cycle, students will create a facilitation manual that accompanies their serious game.
Assignment
The student works on an assignment from a real-world client. They make a Serious Game Solution prototype and accompanying Facilitation Manual.
The Prototype needs to be based on research on and understanding of the target audience for the case. It also needs to be tested and experienced by the target audience and client as well as addressing the problem statement.
The Facilitation Manual follows the CMGT dresscode and is easy to comprehend. It needs to include the learning goals for the target audience and explains how the Serious Game Solution helps achieve those goals. The Facilitation Manual also has explanatory notes on the development of the game and explains how the game needs to be set up and played / experienced. It describes the roles and tasks of the facilitator before, during and after the Serious Game experience.
Objective:
The student will research, prototype, and test a serious game solution to a problem for a specific target audience. The student will write a Facilitation manual and prototype.
Description of the Assessment task
During the course, the student learns the process for designing a serious game solution to a self-chosen problem. The student conducts research into the problem, defines learning goals which are used to inform the design requirements of the Serious Game solution. The design requirements inform the game mechanics used in the serious game. The student hands in a Serious Game prototype and accompanying Facilitation Manual. In it, they explain how the prototype is run AND how to maximise results during the reflection exercise afterwards.
The student hands in a Serious Game Prototype and the accompanying Facilitation Manual through blackboard. This prototype can be either digital or physical. The Facilitation Manual needs to be delivered in PDF format.

/en/course/2026/GTVB22ELUR.content:
This Unreal elective covers a range of relevant topics to achieve the end-goal: having polished feature(s) in a product. The topics include visual and functional aspects required for your feature. This course is designed for people with no prior knowledge and for those who do have some Unreal knowledge. You can decide on the feature(s) that you want, but your feature should be at the expected polished level at the end of the period. You can decide your own feature or choose to collaborate with others to create a product with multiple features. You are responsible for your work, and your feature should be able to function without the help of others (no dependencies).
You should have a polished feature at the end of the period.

/en/course/2026/GTVB22ELND.outcomes:
Learning Outcomes
This Elective has five Course Learning Outcomes.
Course Learning Outcomes
LO1:The student will be able to apply theory to their design by using a narrative design canvas
LO2:The student will be able to illustrate connections between experience, interaction, and narrative by using a narrative design canvas
LO3:The student will be able to model connections between mechanics and narrative as expressive play by using a narrative design canvas
LO4:The student will be able to illustrate how key design elements go beyond the narrative design canvas by using a representation
LO5:The student will be able to construct a representation demonstrating key features of the interactive experience
/en/course/2026/GTVB22ELND.content: In this Narrative Design elective, individual students will work on a Narrative Design Canvas and a representation of their own work combining game mechanics and narrative into an interactive experience. To do this, students will be mentored along this process through workshop-style courses that focus on building specific connections and narrative considerations. Students will be challenged with examples of works with diverse storytelling, theme, interesting characters, plot conflicts, world-building, and other narrative design elements.

/en/course/2026/GTVB23ELPA.outcomes:
Learning Outcomes
This course has five Programme Learning Outcomes.
Programme Learning Outcomes
LOL B Level 2 - The student considers contextual factors in the implementation of their solutions.
LOL B Level 2 - The student can make use of relevant visualisation techniques.
LOL C Level 2 - The student compares and selects appropriate technical solutions to satisfy complex problems.
LOL C Level 2 - The student can experiment with innovative concepts to address complex or complicated situations.
LOL D Level 2 - The student can construct technical solutions informed by relevant knowledge and theories.
/en/course/2026/GTVB23ELPA.content:
Procedural generation using algorithms is an effective way of using available computing power to create unique assets, levels, worlds or even universes. This elective focuses on teaching students about the different methods of procedural generation available, how to use these methods and how these methods can help in creating unique experiences.
The student will learn to set up their own use-case and implement specific learning goals. Starting with the exploration of the application and boundaries of a technique and the relevant software. First by replicating examples of procedural techniques and later applying different techniques in their own use-case. The solution to the use-case will be achieved by weighing the pros and cons of possible solutions and making the right design choices. These design choices are showcased in a presentation.
The student will build a product that consists of multiple procedural generation methodologies (noise, scatter, parametric etc). The specific product can be a scene that is procedurally generated or a tool that can be used to create new procedural created assets (city builder etc.). The assessment product will be a showreel video of the product suitable for the professional portfolio.

Learning Outcomes

LOL D Level 2 - The student elaborates digital prototypes using appropriate methods and techniques
LOL C Level 2 - The student can experiment with innovative concepts to address complex or complicated situations.
LOL A Level 2 - The student acts and performs within a team, valuing the team’s diversity and facilitating contributions of team members.
/en/course/2026/GTVB23ELRO.content:
The Robotics elective is designed to provide students with an opportunity to explore the world of robotics and its applications. Through guided project work, students collaborate in teams to build robots that can express different emotions and interactions with users. Throughout the elective, students not only gain a solid foundation in the basics of electronics, Arduino programming, basic sensors, and automation in both software and hardware design but also in social interactions, empathy and how emotions can be detected and shown.
The first few weeks of the course focus on fundamental electronics and Arduino programming, while the latter weeks explore more advanced topics such as social interaction, empathy, and behaviour. Students are encouraged to take on specialized roles within their teams, while still learning the basics of electronics, power systems, basic sensors, Arduino programming, visual detection, and more.
Assessment of each student’s progress and understanding is based on a group report that describes the build process and outlines how each group member contributed to the final product. In addition, each student participates in an individual interview to assess their intrinsic understanding of the fundamental topics covered in the course. The minimum requirement for each student is to design and implement a functional contribution to the robot in each of the following areas: electronics, Arduino coding, and mechanical design/construction and how these can show and influence the state of the robot.
By the end of the course, students should be able to apply their newly acquired skills and knowledge to create a functional robot that can express different emotions and interact with users. Students who wish to pursue more advanced topics in robotics can continue their studies in machine learning, advanced AI, more advanced sensor systems, or industry-standard development platforms. The Robotics elective offers an exciting opportunity for students to develop their creativity, problem-solving skills, and critical thinking abilities, all while having fun building robots.

/en/course/2026/GTVB23ELRP.content:
To test (parts of) a game, you need people to experience your ideas. In the Rapid Prototyping elective you will build the skills and confidence to quickly develop representative, playable prototypes. Prototypes that you can use to test out your ideas.
The best way to learn is to do, so you will be creating prototypes based on provided themes and from any perspective you want, be it artist, designer or programmer. For each prototype you have two weeks, so imagine the joy and excitement of a Game Jam but feeling less groggy!
The course is set up as such that there is a lot of opportunity to generate ideas and for feedback on what you have created. At the end, you pick your best of three prototypes and iterate upon it adding an additional, provided theme.

/en/course/2026/GTVB23ELGA.outcomes:
Learning Outcomes
This Elective has five Course independent learning outcomes
Course independent learning outcomes
LOL B Level 2 - Analyse a video/game to determine/select the best fitting audio design
LOL D Level 2 - Implement complex real-time sound effects and mixing that use parameter changes (e.g. Dynamic music systems, audio ducking and or use of side chain), environmental sound)
LOL D Level 2 - Select, record and edit high quality sounds effects
LOL E Level 2 - Effective use of (stereo) mixing and audio effects like EQ, compression, reverb and delay enhancing the overall sounds quality
LOL A Level 2 - Follow best practices for file organization, naming conventions and version control
/en/course/2026/GTVB23ELGA.content:
A mere few seconds of playing your preferred game without sound will make you appreciate how critical audio is in creating an engaging experience. This elective focuses on the production of sound effects, ambient audio and voice recording using a Digital Audio Workstation (DAW).
In this course, students will master audio manipulation by utilizing a DAW to implement audio theory, recording methods, microphones, sound effects, mixing, and integrating audio into a game engine. The assessment for this class is showcasing audio for a game or trailer, complete with sound effects, ambient audio, (looped) music and voice over, which demonstrates the practical application of the audio theory taught in this course.

Monetization and marketing strategy is constructed appropriately for the target audience

Based on course material and outside research, student has designed monetization and marketing models appropriate to the chosen platform

/en/course/2026/GTVB23ELMM.content:
The goal of this assessment is for students to create an investor-ready pitch deck (with appendix), for a product they designed previously or are in the process of designing.

/en/course/2026/GTVB23ELSG2.outcomes:
Learning outcomes
For this elective level 2 students have to write 5 personal learning outcomes that adapt to their level, development needs and the CMGT competencies. The learning outcomes have to be approved by the lecturer of the course.
/en/course/2026/GTVB23ELSG2.content:
With a growing interest in the world for "Games to Grow", "Edugames" and other initiatives, the field of Serious Gaming is growing, and there is a need for well thought out games which teach technical and critical thinking skills developed by professionals. This Elective will dive into how "Learning Mechanics" translate to "Game Mechanics" and how games can be designed and facilitated with the purpose of solving local problems for a student-defined audience.
By experiencing and analyzing various Serious Games, students will comprehend the effectiveness and utility of games as solutions for complex problems. Through research and testing, students will define a problem statement for a self-chosen target audience. They will then test a prototype to determine its effectiveness and analyze the results. To complete the serious game cycle, students will create a facilitation manual that accompanies their serious game.
Assignment:
The student works on an assignment from a real-world client. They make a Serious Game Solution prototype and accompanying Facilitation Manual.
The Prototype needs to be based on research on and understanding of the target audience for the case. It also needs to be tested and experienced by the target audience and client as well as addressing the problem statement.
The Facilitation Manual follows the CMGT dresscode and is easy to comprehend. It needs to include the learning goals for the target audience and explains how the Serious Game Solution helps achieve those goals. The Facilitation Manual also has explanatory notes on the development of the game and explains how the game needs to be set up and played / experienced. It describes the roles and tasks of the facilitator before, during and after the Serious Game experience.
Objective:
The student will research, prototype, and test a serious game solution to a problem for a specific target audience.

/en/course/2026/GTVB23ELUR2.content:
Choosing the Unreal elective a subsequent time requires you to formulate five of your own learning goals. The lecturers must approve your learning goals in order for you to be able to use them. You must base your learning goals on the CMGT competencies (on level 2) to create a digital product
The entry requirement for this elective is that the student has passed level 1 of the elective.

/en/course/2026/GTVB23ELAI2.outcomes:
Learning Outcomes
For this elective level 2 students have to write 5 personal learning outcomes that adapt to their level, development needs and the CMGT LOLs. The learning outcomes have to be approved by the lecturer of the course.
/en/course/2026/GTVB23ELAI2.content:
The field of AI is evolving rapidly, while simultaneously revolutionizing the field of Creative Media & Game Technology. New developments such as art and level generation, deep reinforcement learning for automatic AI behavior training, and automatic upscaling of old textures have large impacts on the industry.
You will need to research, understand, apply and expand these technologies, in order to show you can adapt to any new technologies that might come your way in the near or far future.
Over the course of this elective, we will address various topics from classical AI technologies such as search trees and state machines to modern AI technologies such as neural networks and large language models. The explanations of the functionality 'under the hood' helps demystify the often black box nature of AI systems.
For this course we expect at least some familiarity with programming, in order for you to develop your own prototype. There is no programming language/framework requirement.
The entry requirement for this elective is that the student has passed level 1 of the elective.

/en/course/2026/GTVB23ELCD2.outcomes:
Learning Outcomes

/en/course/2026/GTVB23ELCD2.content:
Content
Students will be creating a game ready character or creature from concept to 3D model. The model will have to convince that the students thought about the “why”, by creating a backstory that matches the visual characteristics, for example, physical abilities, use of colour etc. Why does my creature/character have this shape or colour? If it is an Aquatic creature, how does this influence its looks, its skin, its movements etc. This elective go through all the steps starting with brainstorming, visual research, concept-art, followed by modelling/sculpting, retopology, textures and hair/fur.
The entry requirement for this elective is that the student has passed level 1 of the elective.

/en/course/2026/GTVB24ELAN2.content:
For this elective, students will focus on creating a portfolio ready animation(s). These could have any kind of application ranging from, but not limited to: short films, music videos, advertisements or an animated website.
Go wild and use the LED screen in the Spacelab to record a video doing a dance off against your own animated avatar! Use your work from Narrative Design and bring your story world to life! Take your creature from Creature Design and animate it for a gripping cutscene.
The goal for students is to comprehend the principles of animation such as sense of weight, timing and style, how to apply them to their chosen concept and explore animation techniques (eg, 2D, 3D, Claymation etc) used in different industries.
By completing practical exercises in class like creating small animations, students build up the foundation to make their concept come to life. Additionally, they’ll be collecting supporting material for their design process on a week-by-week basis.
Students will then storyboard and plan their workflow, determining the appropriate techniques and technologies required to create a portfolio worthy piece.
Students are free to experiment, think outside of the box and pursue a topic and technique they are passionate about. This freedom extends both to the nature of the project and the makeup of the creative team. Students can decide to work as an individual, in pairs or in a team. If more people work on a project, then more will be possible, yet more will be expected in terms of complexity and scope.
A proposal will be discussed to realistically match the timeframe and expected workload.
The final product will be a rendered animation that is expected to have a coherent concept, theme, style and purpose.
The entry requirement for this elective is that the student has passed level 1 of the elective.

/en/course/2026/GTVB24ELGA3.content:
Game Sound. A mere few seconds of playing your preferred game without sound will make you appreciate how critical audio is in creating an engaging experience. This elective focuses on the production of sound effects, ambient audio, music and voice recording using a Digital Audio Workstation (DAW).
In this course, students will master audio manipulation by utilizing a DAW to implement audio theory, recording methods, microphones, sound effects, mixing, and integrating audio into a game engine. The assessment  for this class is showcasing audio for a game or trailer, complete with sound effects, ambient audio, (looped) music and voice over, which demonstrates the practical application of the audio theory taught in this course.
The entry requirement for this elective is that the student has passed level 2 of the elective.

The goal of this assessment is for students to create an investor-ready pitch deck (with appendix), for a game they designed previously or are in the process of designing.
Pitch Deck: Your solution for monetizing and marketing your game
Appendix: The research you did, what you point to when an investor asks you a question.
What monetization models didn't work and why? What marketing strategies were not appropriate? Why not? Together, these elements of the pitch deck prepare the student for professionally pitching their game to a publisher.
The entry requirement for this elective is that the student has passed level 2 of the elective.

/en/course/2026/GTVB24ELPA3.content:
Procedural generation using algorithms is an effective way of using available computing power to create unique assets, levels, worlds or even universes. This elective focuses on teaching students about the different methods of procedural generation available, how to use these methods and how these methods can help in creating unique experiences.
The student will learn to set up their own use-case and implement specific learning goals. Starting with the exploration of the application and boundaries of a technique and the relevant software. First by replicating examples of procedural techniques and later applying different techniques in their own use-case. The solution to the use-case will be achieved by weighing the pros and cons of possible solutions and making the right design choices. These design choices are showcased in a presentation.
The student will build a product that consists of multiple procedural generation methodologies (noise, scatter, parametric etc). The specific product can be a scene that is procedurally generated or a tool that can be used to create new procedural created assets (city builder etc.). The assessment product will be a showreel video of the product suitable for the professional portfolio.
The entry requirement for this elective is that the student has passed level 2 of the elective.

/en/course/2026/GTVB24ELRO3.content:
The Robotics elective is designed to provide students with an opportunity to explore the world of robotics and its applications. Through guided project work, students collaborate in teams to build robots that can express different emotions and interactions with users. Throughout the elective, students not only gain a solid foundation in the basics of electronics, Arduino programming, basic sensors, and automation in both software and hardware design but also in social interactions, empathy and how emotions can be detected and shown.
The first few weeks of the course focus on fundamental electronics and Arduino programming, while the latter weeks explore more advanced topics such as social interaction, empathy, and behaviour. Students are encouraged to take on specialized roles within their teams, while still learning the basics of electronics, power systems, basic sensors, Arduino programming, visual detection, and more.
Assessment of each student’s progress and understanding is based on a group report that describes the build process and outlines how each group member contributed to the final product. In addition, each student participates in an individual interview to assess their intrinsic understanding of the fundamental topics covered in the course. The minimum requirement for each student is to design and implement a functional contribution to the robot in each of the following areas: electronics, Arduino coding, and mechanical design/construction and how these can show and influence the state of the robot.
By the end of the course, students should be able to apply their newly acquired skills and knowledge to create a functional robot that can express different emotions and interact with users. Students who wish to pursue more advanced topics in robotics can continue their studies in machine learning, advanced AI, more advanced sensor systems, or industry-standard development platforms. The Robotics elective offers an exciting opportunity for students to develop their creativity, problem-solving skills, and critical thinking abilities, all while having fun building robots.
The entry requirement for this elective is that the student has passed level 2 of the elective.

/en/course/2026/GTVB24ELRP3.content:
To test (parts of) a game, you need people to experience your ideas. In the Rapid Prototyping elective you will build the skills and confidence to quickly develop representative, playable prototypes. Prototypes that you can use to test out your ideas.
The best way to learn is to do, so you will be creating prototypes based on provided themes and from any perspective you want, be it artist, designer or programmer. For each prototype you have two weeks, so imagine the joy and excitement of a Game Jam but feeling less groggy!
The course is set up as such that there is a lot of opportunity to generate ideas and for feedback on what you have created. At the end, you pick your best of three prototypes and iterate upon it adding an additional, provided theme.
The entry requirement for this elective is that the student has passed level 2 of the elective.

/en/course/2026/GTVB24ELSG3.content:
With a growing interest in the world for "Games to Grow", "Edugames" and other initiatives, the field of Serious Gaming is growing, and there is a need for well thought out games which teach technical and critical thinking skills developed by professionals. This Elective will dive into how "Learning Mechanics" translate to "Game Mechanics" and how games can be designed and facilitated with the purpose of solving local problems for a student-defined audience.
By experiencing and analyzing various Serious Games, students will comprehend the effectiveness and utility of games as solutions for complex problems. Through research and testing, students will define a problem statement for a self-chosen target audience. They will then test a prototype to determine its effectiveness and analyze the results. To complete the serious game cycle, students will create a facilitation manual that accompanies their serious game.
Assignment:
The student works on an assignment from a real-world client. They make a Serious Game Solution prototype and accompanying Facilitation Manual.
The Prototype needs to be based on research on and understanding of the target audience for the case. It also needs to be tested and experienced by the target audience and client as well as addressing the problem statement.
The Facilitation Manual follows the CMGT dresscode and is easy to comprehend. It needs to include the learning goals for the target audience and explains how the Serious Game Solution helps achieve those goals. The Facilitation Manual also has explanatory notes on the development of the game and explains how the game needs to be set up and played / experienced. It describes the roles and tasks of the facilitator before, during and after the Serious Game experience.
Objective:
The student will research, prototype, and test a serious game solution to a problem for a specific target audience.
The entry requirement for this elective is that the student has passed level 2 of the elective.

/en/course/2026/GTVB23INT.content:
The internship is an external learning situation in which you work on the CMGT competencies.
During a period of 20 calendar weeks, you will work at a company of your choice, provided you work with professionals with CMGT related skills you can learn from. During that time, your schedule mirrors that of a company employee. This means that you follow the same daily hours as the company you work at, observe the same company rules, enjoy the same holidays, and exhibit the same professional behavior. It is a challenging but often rewarding period where you will discover much about both the field and your professional self.
The internship has three main goals:
You can apply the theory, knowledge and skills learned in programme to professional practices in the real world.
You understand the tension between theoretical concepts and practical applications outside of the CMGT classrooms.
You observe and learn about yourself as a future professional.
To reflect this, credits are not awarded for merely experiencing the outside world and fulfilling your job, but for the learning that takes place in this period. This is why you will create a development portfolio in which you will not only collect evidence of CMGT-related activities (like for example concepting, designing, developing, programming, or testing) but will also reflect on these activities to display your learning process.

/en/course/2026/GTVB24IWP.content:
Introduction
The IWP (Innovation workplace project) is a project that focuses on bringing students together one last time before graduation, to work on an open challenge related to games, play, playful design, or new technology.  The student will answer a question, opportunity, and/or design challenge in the context of innovation, interactivity, and technology. The project implies a design-oriented research cycle using the double diamond model and the foundation will be formed by input from the client, researchers, target audience, coaches, and experts. The aim is to involve the stakeholders, work within a team, and be open to getting to know new contexts and domains while exploring and learning to understand other roles and interests.
In addition, students need to look and find a client for their graduation project and timely prepare everything that is needed. A graduation boot camp will be held during week 6.
What to expect?
Experiment, explore, conceptualize, prototype, and evaluate coming up with a product/solution while developing a professional, inquisitive, and enterprising attitude!
Deal with an open challenge related to games, play, playful design, or new technology in the context of innovation, interactivity, and technology.
Be ready to explore and immerse in a new or unknown context!
Work with a client, a coach, and a team assigned to you.
Cocreate and involve others: students, researchers, clients, stakeholders, experts, and users.
Professionalism. Communication, planning, deliverables, etc. You are in charge, define priorities and timely communicate to the company and stakeholders in every part of the process.
Orientation and preparation for the graduation assignment.
Shaping the future. Many possibilities could unfold from the student–company relationship, including becoming partners of the company/client.
Use the double diamond model to plan and deliver.
The deliverables are not set by us, are set up by you based on the above.
Freedom to make this project your own process, take your own decisions and assume responsibility.
Discover, explore, and of course have fun again while coming up with a solution/prototype.
The assignment will be delivered in the form of a development portfolio.
The journey
To start defining the professional world you need to start being part of that world; work with clients, involve stakeholders, and prepare for graduation. The IWP focus is to prepare you in this journey, being a project focused on explore, cocreate and deliver, while being a preparation for the graduation assignment.
How?
Teamwork
Planning
Using the double diamond model
Coaching sessions
Cocreation
Showing progress and professionalism
Finding a client for your graduation project and submitting the documentation needed (Block 1, Week 6)
Delivering a Portfolio
Define your path!
Year 4 is about defining your professional world. The IWP is an opportunity to start doing it, defining your journey means using everything you have learned! This time, you are in charge, you need to work on that proposal considering the double diamond model, the goal of the project, time frame, etc. What research do you need? When will you deliver the first prototype? Testing? Iterations? Delivery? Value capturing? Roadmap? And for sure, more questions will come depending on the project.

/en/course/2026/GTVB24GRA.outcomes:
LOL A: Organising and Managing. The CMGT professional is able to plan, manage and communicate process-based projects as part of a team.
LOL B: Contextualising and Framing. The CMGT professional is able to research the boundaries, scope, and requirements of a problem prior to exploring solutions.
LOL C: Exploring and Ideating. The CMGT professional is able to experiment with digital tools and ideate possible solution directions, in order to address a problem statement or design brief.
LOL D: Executing and Implementing. The CMGT professional is able to construct appropriate solutions, using relevant methodologies.
LOL E: Futures Innovating. The CMGT professional can deliver solutions that account for wider social ramifications, the needs of the client the requirements from research, taking ethical and intercultural values into account.
LOL F: Self-Fashioning. The CMGT professional builds connections, manages their own development, formulates learning goals, takes responsibility for their own learning process, and how they relate to the world.
/en/course/2026/GTVB24GRA.content:
The final graduation capstone is a test of the junior professional's competences, demonstrating the student's ability to independently and meaningfully contribute to the resolution of a concrete problem in the area of creative media and game technologies. The graduation project is the last major test prior to graduation, functioning as the capstone of the CMGT programme.
The graduating student works full time for one semester (20 weeks) on a complex assignment in a professional situation within the CMGT domain, following a method and producing a final product demonstrating that the graduating student has attained all competencies of the CMGT programme.
During graduation, the student displays all parts of the T-shaped professional – the breadth of their learning and skills; how they apply this to a wider context; the depth of their own specialisation and learning path, and how tey have reached the end-level of all the CMGT competences.
The graduation capstone is assessed by a submitted portfolio and a final product, both assessed at a Final Demonstration. Both the portfolio and the product must be submitted prior to the Final Demonstration. By successfully completing the graduation capstone, the student demonstrates that they are ready to enter the working field in their capacity as a junior professional.
Admission to the graduation capstone is determined by the requirements listed in the CMGT Teaching and Assessment Regulations (TER), and upon approval of the graduation assignment by the CMGT Graduation Committee. Students will be coached in the search for their graduation assignment at the beginning of Year 4, during the Graduation Bootcamp (during period 1). During the graduation, students will participate in a Community of Learners with up to six other students, all of whom have been assigned the same graduation supervisor.

/en/course/2026/LNVA26DA9.content:
Dance domain:
in this domain, mastery of the dance technical domain components is central. The Dance Technology domain is divided into a core and a basic part, where technical mastery is achieved in the basic part and in the core part a bridge is built between the technique, the different dance styles and the professional field.
Base
Ballet
Ballet is the foundation on which all other dance techniques build. This also includes the section on toe points.
Modern dance
Modern Dance serves as the foundation for pop theatre musical dance technique, but is also a dance technique in its own right. Modern dance is combined with creative development. Creative development aims to teach students to develop creative works, including the design of choreographies.
Jazz Dance
Jazz Dance serves as the foundation for pop theatre musical dance, but is also a dance technique in its own right.
Acrodance
Acrodance helps to optimise physical development and acrobatic skills. Acrodance supports various dance techniques.
Training Classes
Training classes are offered in period E during rehearsals for Project Integration. In the training classes, the basic techniques are maintained.
Dance Analysis
Dance Analysis is linked to the core subjects in the Dance Domain. Dance Analysis encompasses the theory and analysis of the techniques.
Core
Dance Trends
Hip-hop is an independent dance technique based on non-academic dance forms. This area is constantly subject to innovations, trends and change.
Pop, Theatre and Musical Dance
In this area, different dance styles come together and a bridge is built between the various techniques. Students also learn to develop creative works, including the design of choreographies.
Theatre Latin Standard Dance
Theatre Latin Standard Dance is a component of ballroom dancing and a collective term for various dances that originated from traditional non-academic dance forms. These dance forms have been standardised into independent dance techniques since the beginning of the 20th century.
Tap Dance
Tap dance serves as the basis for Musical Theatre Technique and Dance Technique, but is also an independent technique. Tap dance is a dance form in which rhythmic sounds are produced with the feet.

Musical Theatre Domain
: this domain focuses on mastering the technical aspects of musical theatre. The Musical Theatre domain is divided into a core and a foundation component, with technical skills being acquired in the foundation component and the core component serving to bridge the gap between technique, the various forms of musical theatre and the professional field.
Base
Voice coaching
Voice coaching supports the domain components Acting, Ensemble Singing, Musical Theatre and Vocal Technique.
Vocal Technique
Vocal Technique serves as the foundation for all programme components involving singing, but is also a standalone discipline.
Core
Acting
Acting serves as the foundation for the Musical Theatre programme component, but is also a standalone programme component in the form of Musical Acting.
Ensemble Singing
Ensemble Singing serves as the basis for the subject area Musical Theatre, but is also an independent subject area. The core objective is polyphony. This subject area is linked to the subject area Musical History and will, where possible, put musical history into practice.
Musical Theatre
In Musical Theatre, existing musicals, and in particular dance and ensemble singing pieces, form the teaching and learning material. Musical Theatre is the core module of the Musical Theatre domain.
Vocal Interpretation
Vocal Interpretation is a separate component of Vocal Technique, in which textual interpretation is central.

Musical Theatre Domain:
this domain focuses on mastering the technical aspects of musical theatre. The Musical Theatre domain is divided into a core and a foundation section, with technical proficiency being acquired in the foundation section and the core section bridging the gap between technology, the various forms of musical theatre and the Flex domain: the practical and theoretical components of this domain aim to give students the opportunity to design a personalised learning pathway. During the Intensive Weeks, students can shape this pathway themselves through optional modules. In Year 9Ad, a student may take modules from the Higher Professional Education (HBO) Bachelor’s programme in Dance Teaching within this domain, thereby gaining an introduction to the practice of teaching.
Flex module
Through flex modules, students have the opportunity to deepen or broaden their knowledge. There are two options to choose from: flex module(s) focused on education, or flex module(s) focused on performance. Education flex modules are a prerequisite for admission to the Plus de Deux programme (dual degree).
Intensive
An intensive takes place during a week free of regular timetabled classes. During an intensive, students are immersed in a specific aspect of Dance (creation) and/or
Musical Theatre (creation). In a short period of time, students develop the skills associated with this aspect.
Martha’s International Programme (MIP)
Through this module, students gain an understanding of the international performing arts sector. This is achieved through a range of activities, including intensive courses, exchange programmes and a study trip. By taking part in these activities, students learn to work with international choreographers and collaborate with students from partner institutions.

Knowledge domain:
in this domain, knowledge of the theoretical and historical background of (performing) art is acquired.
Base
Personal Development (PD)
I
n PD, the student is guided, in collaboration with other students or individually, in his study career, during projects and exchange programs.
Human and Movement Sciences only in step 9Ad
Human and Movement Science includes a basic knowledge of anatomy, physiology and pathology of the musculoskeletal system and subject-specific first aid skills.
History of the Musical
The history of the musical places the musical in a historical context.
Music Theory
Music theory addresses the theoretical aspects of music and includes being able to read notes and intervals.
Solfège
Solfège involves learning to identify notes and intervals by ear and to read them, and is taught in a series of modules. Students must first pass Module 1 at Level 9Ad before progressing to Module 2, and so on. In total, there are four modules that must be passed.
Core
Theatre Theory
Theatre Theory places the theory of dance, visual arts, musical theatre, dramaturgy (the study of dramatic art) and music in a (historical) context, thereby laying the foundations for an understanding of developments in the contemporary cultural landscape. Students learn to conduct artistic research within and across these disciplines.
Research Paper AD
The student learns to conduct research under the guidance of the Research Paper AD teacher.

Integration domain
: in this domain, students are introduced to their future professional field. Students gain practical experience through stage-based work placements and cross-domain projects at a level appropriate to the stage of their studies.
Performing Knowledge/IWP
Within this component of the domain, the theory and history of musical theatre are put into practice. The emphasis here is on establishing links between Education, Research and the Professional Field; Innovation Workshop (IWP). In Performing Knowledge, students integrate theory with practice through research, bringing this together into an innovative whole.
Projects
ArtCore
: Within the ArtCore Project, students work with their coach to create a presentation or Performing Arts project based on a theme, gaining experience in entrepreneurship and creation.
Project ADEP
: The Project ADEP is a final exam component linked to Project ArtCore.
Project “I”
: Project “I” takes place early in Year 9Ad and has an exploratory and collaborative objective.
Integration Project
: In the Integration Project, a theatre production is staged under the guidance of various choreographers and directors, integrating different disciplines into a coherent whole.
Theatre Work Placements
Theatre Work Placements offer opportunities for performing artists to gain stage and professional experience, partly independently and partly under supervision.
Institute Repertoire
In the Repertoire module, students learn and rehearse repertoire from LMIPA or the performing arts sector.

/en/course/2026/DAVP26DA9.content:
Dance domain
: this domain focuses on mastering the technical components of dance. The Dance Technique domain is divided into a core and a foundation section, with technical mastery being acquired in the foundation section and the core section serving to bridge the gap between technique, the various dance styles and the professional field.
Base
Ballet
Ballet forms the foundation upon which all other dance techniques are built. This also includes the element of pointe work (Ballet Pointe)
Modern Dance
Modern dance technique serves as the foundation for PopTheatreMusicalDance technique, but is also a dance technique in its own right. Modern dance is combined with creative development. Creative development aims to teach students to develop creative works, including the design of choreographies.
Jazz Dance
Jazz Dance serves as the foundation for PopTheatreMusicalDance technique, but is also a standalone dance technique.
Acrodance
Acrodance helps to optimise physical development and acrobatic skills and supports the various dance techniques.
Fusion
In Level 11Ba and Level 12Ba, the Fusion module forms part of the basic dance technique domain. Fusion combines two or more dance styles, each with its own stylistic characteristics. The module trains stylistic sensitivity, as well as freedom in handling and combining stylistic characteristics.
Training sessions
Training sessions are offered in period E during rehearsals for Project Integration. These sessions focus on maintaining basic techniques.
Core
Dance Trends
Dance Trends is a separate module and an independent dance technique based on non-academic dance forms. This module is constantly subject to innovation, trends and change.
PopTheatreMusicalDance (PTMD)
In this module, different dance styles come together and a bridge is built between the various techniques. Here too, students learn to develop creative works, including the design of choreographies.
Theatre Latin Standard Dance (TLSD)
Theatre Latin Standard Dance is a component of ballroom dancing and a collective term for various dances that have evolved from traditional non-academic dance forms. Since the early twentieth century, these dance forms have been standardised into independent dance techniques.
Rhythm/Tap
Tap dance serves as the basis for PTMD, but is also an independent technique. Tap dance is a dance form in which rhythmic sounds are produced with the feet.

Vocal Technique

Core

Ensemble Singing

Musical Theatre

Vocal Interpretation
Vocal Interpretation is a separate component of Vocal Technique, with a focus on textual interpretation.

/en/course/2026/DAVP26FL9.content:
Flexible module:
the modules in this area are designed to enable students to create their own personalised learning pathway. During the Intensive Weeks, students can design this pathway themselves by selecting optional modules. In Year 9Ba, it is possible to choose modules from the Higher Professional Education (HBO) Bachelor’s programme in Dance Teaching, enabling students to pursue the Bachelor’s in Dance and the Bachelor’s in Dance Teaching simultaneously from Year 10Ba onwards via the Plus de Deux pathway.
Intensive
An intensive takes place during a week without a timetable. During an intensive, students are immersed in a specific component of Dance (creation) and/or
Musical Theatre (creation). In a short period of time, the student develops the skills associated with this component.
Flex module
Through flex modules, students have the opportunity to deepen or broaden their knowledge. There are two options to choose from: flex module(s) focused on education, or flex module(s) focused on performance. Education flex modules are a prerequisite for admission to the Plus de Deux programme (dual degree).
Flexible learning space
The flexible learning space gives students the opportunity to explore a subject in greater depth or to broaden their horizons. In years 11 and 12, students can propose how this space should be organised as part of a personal plan. Guidance on drafting the Personal Plan is provided within Personal Development (PD). Through a personal plan, students themselves give direction to the ‘Flexible Space’ component by defining goals that address a personal, artistic, achievable and assessable need for their own development, in response to the question: ‘What do I need as an artist to improve?’
In Year 9, Year 10 and Year 11, the Personal Plan serves as a guideline setting out how the Flexible Space is to be utilised. In Year 12, there is also an assessment and reflection by the student on the achievement of these goals.
Martha’s International Programme (MIP)
Through this programme component, students gain an understanding of the international performing arts sector. This is achieved through, amongst other things, intensive courses, exchanges and a study trip. By participating in these activities, students learn to work with international choreographers and collaborate with students from partner institutions. Each academic year, students participate in one international component. See 2.3.3 for a more detailed description and the applicable procedures.
The international components consist of Innovation Workshops, in which students learn and work alongside students from partner institutions, choreographers from the professional field, and lecturers from their own programme and/or partner institutions.
Skills
Within the Skills module, students in years 11Ba and 12Ba have the opportunity to further deepen and broaden their knowledge individually within their chosen professional field. The hours are organised on an individual basis. Within this module, students also receive coaching in putting together their individual Skills Exam. This exam is described in the Higher Professional Education Dance Examination Specification.
For a more detailed description of the options, see 2.3.2 of this OER.
DIZO production
In Year 11Ba, students create their own performance as a class. They are jointly responsible for artistic, production and organisational decisions. DIZO production is part of the Examination Programme.
