: this domain focuses on mastering the technical aspects of musical theatre. The Musical Theatre domain is divided into a core and a foundation component, with technical proficiency being acquired in the foundation component and the core component serving to bridge the gap between technique, the various forms of musical theatre and the professional field.
Base
Voice coaching
Voice coaching supports Acting, Ensemble Singing, Musical Theatre and Vocal Technique.
Vocal Technique
Vocal Technique serves as the foundation for all domain components involving singing, but is also a standalone discipline.
Core
Acting
Acting serves as the foundation for the Musical Theatre module, but is also an independent module in the form of Musical Acting. Acting is linked to Dramaturgy, in which students develop their understanding of the dramatic arts and theoretical preparation for acting.
Ensemble Singing
Ensemble Singing serves as the basis for the Musical Theatre module, but is also a standalone module. The core objective is polyphony.
Musical Theatre
Musical Theatre brings together the elements of dance, singing and acting. In Musical Theatre, existing musicals, and in particular the dance and ensemble singing pieces, form the teaching and learning material.
Vocal Interpretation
Vocal Interpretation is a separate component of Vocal Technique, with a focus on textual interpretation.

/en/course/2026/DAVB26FL11.outcomes:
Artistic
You are able to give meaning to creative processes and performing arts productions within professional practice, based on your own artistic vision.
Technical
You apply a broad range of technical skills and knowledge in a professional manner both within and outside the educational context.
Inquisitive and reflective
You adopt an inquisitive approach and use insights to improve your own practice, placing your own actions within a social context.
Environmentally focused
You work independently and responsibly, encourage collaboration across disciplines and cultures, and contribute to national and international projects.
/en/course/2026/DAVB26FL11.content:
Flexible module:
the modules in this area are designed to enable students to create their own personalised learning pathway. During the Intensive Weeks, students can design this pathway themselves by selecting optional modules. In Year 9Ba, it is possible to choose modules from the Higher Professional Education (HBO) Bachelor’s programme in Dance Teaching, enabling students to pursue the Bachelor’s in Dance and the Bachelor’s in Dance Teaching simultaneously from Year 10Ba onwards via the Plus de Deux pathway.
Intensive
An intensive takes place during a week without a timetable. During an intensive, students are immersed in a specific component of Dance (creation) and/or
Musical Theatre (creation). In a short period of time, the student develops the skills associated with this component.
Flex module
Through flex modules, students have the opportunity to deepen or broaden their knowledge. There are two options to choose from: flex module(s) focused on education, or flex module(s) focused on performance. Education flex modules are a prerequisite for admission to the Plus de Deux programme (dual degree).
Flexible learning space
The flexible learning space gives students the opportunity to explore a subject in greater depth or to broaden their horizons. In years 11 and 12, students can propose how this space should be organised as part of a personal plan. Guidance on drafting the Personal Plan is provided within Personal Development (PD). Through a personal plan, students themselves give direction to the ‘Flexible Space’ component by defining goals that address a personal, artistic, achievable and assessable need for their own development, in response to the question: ‘What do I need as an artist to improve?’
In Year 9, Year 10 and Year 11, the Personal Plan serves as a guideline setting out how the Flexible Space is to be utilised. In Year 12, there is also an assessment and reflection by the student on the achievement of these goals.
Martha’s International Programme (MIP)
Through this programme component, students gain an understanding of the international performing arts sector. This is achieved through, amongst other things, intensive courses, exchanges and a study trip. By participating in these activities, students learn to work with international choreographers and collaborate with students from partner institutions. Each academic year, students participate in one international component. See 2.3.3 for a more detailed description and the applicable procedures.
The international components consist of Innovation Workshops, in which students learn and work alongside students from partner institutions, choreographers from the professional field, and lecturers from their own programme and/or partner institutions.
Skills
Within the Skills module, students in years 11Ba and 12Ba have the opportunity to further deepen and broaden their knowledge individually within their chosen professional field. The hours are organised on an individual basis. Within this module, students also receive coaching in putting together their individual Skills Exam. This exam is described in the Higher Professional Education Dance Examination Specification.
For a more detailed description of the options, see 2.3.2 of this OER.
DIZO production
In Year 11Ba, students create their own performance as a class. They are jointly responsible for artistic, production and organisational decisions. DIZO production is part of the Examination Programme.

/en/course/2026/DAVB26KE11.content:
Knowledge domain
: in this domain, students acquire knowledge of the theoretical and historical background of the performing arts.
Base
Personal Development (PD)
In PD, students receive guidance – either in collaboration with other students or individually – throughout their academic career, during projects and exchange programmes.
Human and Movement Sciences (MBK)  exclusively in year 9Ba
Human and Movement Sciences comprises a basic knowledge of the anatomy, physiology and pathology of the musculoskeletal and vocal systems, as well as subject-specific first aid skills.
Music Theory / Solfège
Music Theory explores the theoretical aspects of music and covers the ability to read notes and intervals.
Solfège involves learning to distinguish notes and intervals by ear and being able to read them, and is taught in various modules, whereby students must first have passed module one in level 9Ba in order to progress to module two, and so on. In total, there are four modules that must be passed.
WOOD
In the Entrepreneurship, Organisation and Digital (WOOD) programme, students are introduced to disciplines relevant to the professional field and supportive of their careers.
Core
Theatre Theory
Theatre Theory places the theory of dance, visual arts, musical theatre, dramaturgy (the study of dramatic art) and music within a (historical) perspective, thereby laying the foundations for an understanding of developments in the contemporary cultural landscape. Students learn to conduct artistic research within and across these disciplines.
Professional practice / artistic research
In these professional practice modules, students learn research methods, both in group and individual contexts, and carry out a number of research projects.

/en/course/2026/DAVB26IN11.content:
Integration domain
: in this domain, students are introduced to their future professional field. Students gain practical experience through stage-based work placements and cross-domain projects at a level appropriate to the stage of their studies.
Performing Knowledge/IWP
Within this component of the domain, the theory and history of musical theatre are put into practice. The emphasis here is on establishing links between Education, Research and the Professional Field; Innovation Workshop (IWP). In Performing Knowledge, students integrate theory with practice through research, bringing this together into an innovative whole, including within an international context.
Projects
ArtCore: Within the ArtCore Project, students work with their coach to create a presentation or Performing Arts project based on a theme, in order to gain experience in entrepreneurship and creation.
Project “I”: Project “I” takes place early in Year 9Ba and has an exploratory and collaborative objective.
Project DIZO (Dance, Inspiration, Singing & Entrepreneurship): Project DIZO is a final exam component. It comprises a dance, singing and acting programme produced entirely by the exam candidates.
Integration Project: In the Integration Project, a theatre production is staged under the guidance of various choreographers and directors, integrating different disciplines into a coherent whole.
Theatre Work Placements
Theatre Work Placements offer opportunities for performing artists to gain stage and professional experience, partly independently and partly under supervision.
Repertoire
In the Repertoire module, students learn and rehearse pieces from LMIPA’s repertoire or from the performing arts sector.

/en/course/2026/DAVB26DA12.content:
Dance domain
: this domain focuses on mastering the technical components of dance. The Dance Technique domain is divided into a core and a foundation section, with technical mastery being acquired in the foundation section and the core section serving to bridge the gap between technique, the various dance styles and the professional field.
Base
Ballet
Ballet forms the foundation upon which all other dance techniques are built. This also includes the element of pointe work (Ballet Pointe)
Modern Dance
Modern dance technique serves as the foundation for PopTheatreMusicalDance technique, but is also a dance technique in its own right. Modern dance is combined with creative development. Creative development aims to teach students to develop creative works, including the design of choreographies.
Jazz Dance
Jazz Dance serves as the foundation for PopTheatreMusicalDance technique, but is also a standalone dance technique.
Acrodance
Acrodance helps to optimise physical development and acrobatic skills and supports the various dance techniques.
Fusion
In Level 11Ba and Level 12Ba, the Fusion module forms part of the basic dance technique domain. Fusion combines two or more dance styles, each with its own stylistic characteristics. The module trains stylistic sensitivity, as well as freedom in handling and combining stylistic characteristics.
Training sessions
Training sessions are offered in period E during rehearsals for Project Integration. These sessions focus on maintaining basic techniques.
Core
Dance Trends
Dance Trends is a separate module and an independent dance technique based on non-academic dance forms. This module is constantly subject to innovation, trends and change.
PopTheatreMusicalDance (PTMD)
In this module, different dance styles come together and a bridge is built between the various techniques. Here too, students learn to develop creative works, including the design of choreographies.
Theatre Latin Standard Dance (TLSD)
Theatre Latin Standard Dance is a component of ballroom dancing and a collective term for various dances that have evolved from traditional non-academic dance forms. Since the early twentieth century, these dance forms have been standardised into independent dance techniques.
Rhythm/Tap
Tap dance serves as the basis for PTMD, but is also an independent technique. Tap dance is a dance form in which rhythmic sounds are produced with the feet.

Rhythm/Tap

In years 11 and 12, students can propose how this space should be organised as part of a personal plan. Guidance on drafting the Personal Plan is provided within Personal Development (PD). Through this programme component, students gain an understanding of the international performing arts sector. This is achieved through, amongst other things, intensive courses, exchanges and a study trip. By participating in these activities, students learn to work with international choreographers and collaborate with students from partner institutions. Each academic year, students participate in one international component. See 2.3.3 for a more detailed description and the applicable procedures.
The international components consist of Innovation Workshops, in which students learn and work alongside students from partner institutions, choreographers from the professional field, and lecturers from their own programme and/or partner institutions.
Skills
Within the Skills module, students in years 11Ba and 12Ba have the opportunity to further deepen and broaden their knowledge individually within their chosen professional field. The hours are organised on an individual basis. Within this module, students also receive coaching in putting together their individual Skills Exam. This exam is described in the Higher Professional Education Dance Examination Specification.
For a more detailed description of the options, see 2.3.2 of this OER.
DIZO production
In Year 11Ba, students create their own performance as a class. They are jointly responsible for artistic, production and organisational decisions. DIZO production is part of the Examination Programme.

Musical History

MeDi

Applied Theory

Dance Domain
: this domain focuses on mastering the technical components of dance.
The Dance Technique domain is divided into a core and a foundation section, with technical mastery being acquired in the foundation section and the core section serving as a bridge between technique, the various dance styles and the professional field.
Base
Ballet
Ballet forms the foundation upon which all other dance techniques are built. This also includes the element of pointe work (Ballet Pointe).
Modern Dance
Modern Dance technique serves as the basis for PopTheatreMusicalDance technique, but is also a standalone dance technique. Modern dance is combined with creative development. Creative development aims to teach students to develop creative products, including the design of choreographies.
Jazz Dance
Jazz Dance serves as the basis for PopTheatreMusicalDance technique, but is also a standalone dance technique.
Dance Analysis is linked to the core subjects in the Dance domain. Dance Analysis encompasses the theory and analysis of techniques.
Acrodance
Acrodance helps to optimise physical development and acrobatic skills and supports the various dance techniques.
Training sessions
Training sessions are offered in period E during rehearsals for Project Integration. The basic techniques are maintained in the training sessions.
Core
Dance Trends
Dance Trends is a separate module and an independent dance technique based on non-academic dance forms. This module is constantly subject to innovation, trends and change.
Pop Theatre Musical Dance (PTMD)
In this module, the various dance styles come together and a bridge is built between the different techniques. Here too, students learn to develop creative works, including the design of choreographies.
Theatre Latin Standard Dance (TLSD)
Theatre Latin Standard Dance is a component of ballroom dancing and a collective term for various dances that have evolved from traditional non-academic dance forms. Since the early twentieth century, these dance forms have been standardised into independent dance techniques.
Rhythm/Tap
Tap dance serves as the basis for PTMD, but is also an independent technique. Tap dance is a dance form in which rhythmic sounds are produced with the feet.

/en/course/2026/LDVB26MT10.outcomes:
Artistic practice
You are able to create artistic processes and products within the context of the course.
Community-focused practice
You identify and explore social issues and, in collaboration with fellow students, design art education materials based on these.
/en/course/2026/LDVB26MT10.content:
Musical Theatre domain:
this domain focuses on mastering the technical aspects of musical theatre. The Musical Theatre domain is divided into a core and a foundation component, with technical skills being acquired in the foundation component, whilst the core component bridges the gap between technique, the creation of various forms of musical theatre, and the professional field.
Core
Acting
Acting serves as the basis for the Musical Theatre domain component, but is also an independent domain component in the form of Musical Acting. Within this domain component, students learn teaching skills relating to acting.
Ensemble Singing
Ensemble Singing serves as the foundation for the Musical Theatre module, but is also a standalone module. The core objective is polyphony.
Musical Theatre
Musical Theatre brings together the elements of dance, singing and acting. In Musical Theatre, existing musicals, and in particular the dance and ensemble singing pieces, form the teaching and learning material.

/en/course/2026/LDVB26FL10.outcomes:
Artistic practice
You are able to create artistic processes and products within the context of the course.
Community-focused practice
You identify and explore social issues and, in collaboration with fellow students, design art education materials based on these.
/en/course/2026/LDVB26FL10.content:
Flex Domain
The components of this domain are designed to give students the opportunity to shape a personal learning pathway. During the Intensive Weeks, students can design this pathway themselves by selecting elective packages. In level 9Ba, it is possible to choose domain components from the Higher Professional Education Bachelor Programme in Dance Education, allowing students to create the possibility to follow the Bachelor of Dance and the Bachelor of Dance Education simultaneously from level 10Ba onward through the
Plus de Deux
track.
Intensive
An intensive takes place during a schedule-free week. In an intensive, students are immersed in a specific aspect of Dance (making) and/or Music Theatre (making). Within a short period of time, the student develops the skills associated with this component.
Flex Module / Flex Education
Through flex modules, students have the opportunity to deepen or broaden their learning. They can choose between two variants: flex modules focused on education or flex modules focused on performance. Flex modules in education are a requirement for admission to the
Plus de Deux
programme (double degree). In level 11, students may choose to specialize in Piano or Solfège, among other options.
Flexible Space
Through the Flexible Space, students have the opportunity to deepen or broaden their learning. In levels 11 and 12, students can propose how this space will be structured within a personal plan. Guidance in writing the Personal Plan is provided within Personal Development (PD). Through a personal plan, the student determines the direction of the Flexible Space domain component by formulating goals that reflect a personal, artistic, feasible, and assessable need for development, answering the question: “What do I need as an artist to improve?”
In levels 9Ba, 10Ba, and 11Ba, the Personal Plan serves as a guiding document in which the structure of the Flexible Space is recorded. In level 12Ba, the student is also assessed and reflects on the achievement of the goals.
Marthas International Program (MIP)
Through this domain component, students become acquainted with the international professional field of the Performing Arts. This takes place through intensives, exchanges, and a study trip. By participating, students learn to work with international choreographers and collaborate with students from partner institutions. Each academic year, the student participates in one international component. See section 2.3.3 for further description and applicable procedures.
The international components involve Innovation Labs, in which students collaborate with students from partner institutions, choreographers from the professional field, and teachers from their own programme and/or partner institutions.
(MeDi) Skills
Within the Skills component, students in levels 11Ba and 12Ba have the opportunity to further deepen and broaden their individual focus within their chosen professional field. The hours are arranged individually. This domain component is linked to MeDi Skills. The student selects a MeDi Skills package and learns the methodology and skills needed to further develop teaching within the chosen discipline.

/en/course/2026/LDVB26KE10.outcomes:
Artistic practice
You are able to create artistic processes and products within the context of the course.
Pedagogical and didactic practice
You apply pedagogical and didactic knowledge and skills under the supervision of the tutor within the context of the course.
Environment-oriented practice
You identify and explore social and societal themes and, in collaboration with fellow students, design art education materials based on these.
Inquisitive practice
You question and reflect on art education practice.
/en/course/2026/LDVB26KE10.content:
Knowledge Domain:
In this domain, the student explores the theoretical background of educational practice and becomes acquainted with the pedagogical, didactic, and methodological aspects of dance arts education. In addition, this domain covers the theoretical foundations of the performing arts.
Base
Personal Development (PD)
In PD, students receive guidance—either collaboratively with peers or individually—regarding their personal development, study trajectory, projects, exchange programmes, and internships.
Base Theatre
Musical History
Musical History places the musical within a historical context.
Theatre Theory
Theatre Theory situates the theories of dance, visual arts, musical theatre, dramaturgy (the study of dramatic art), and music within a (historical) perspective, forming the basis for understanding developments in today’s cultural landscape. Students learn to conduct artistic research within and across these disciplines.
Performing Knowledge Research
In the artistic research course, students learn to use methods for conducting research and analysing art. This course builds a bridge between Theatre Theory and Performing Knowledge.
Arts Education
Arts Education focuses on researching the educational system, the core objectives and examination requirements for the subjects CKV and General Arts, and on designing and teaching a lesson series within the upper levels of secondary education.
(Core) Education
MeDi
MeDi covers the theoretical foundations of teaching and includes the independent development and implementation of lesson plans, learning plans, and curricula. In levels 9Ba and 10Ba, a distinction is made between Dance and Music Theatre classes.
Psychology
Psychology covers the basic principles of (developmental) psychology.
Educational Science
Educational Science is the discipline that describes, understands, and explains learning, teaching, and development within education.
Dance Analysis
This domain component covers the theory and analysis of ballet, jazz, and PTMD technique.
Human Movement Sciences (MBK)
Human Movement Sciences includes basic knowledge of anatomy, physiology, and pathology of the movement and vocal apparatus, as well as discipline-specific first aid skills.
Music Theory / Solfège
Music Theory addresses the theoretical aspects of music and includes learning to read notes and intervals. Solfège focuses on learning to distinguish and read notes and intervals by ear and is taught in several modules. Students must first complete module one in level 9Ba before progressing to module two, and so on. In total, four modules must be completed.
Professional Field Research
This domain component focuses on developing research skills and knowledge of research methods.
Applied Theory
In this component, various theoretical subjects are applied within educational practice.

/en/course/2026/LDVB26IN10.outcomes:
Artistic practice
You are able to create artistic processes and products within the context of the course.
Pedagogical and didactic practice
You apply pedagogical and didactic knowledge and skills under the supervision of the tutor within the context of the course.
Environment-oriented practice
You identify and explore social and societal themes and, in collaboration with fellow students, design art education materials based on these.
Inquisitive practice
You question and reflect on art education practice.
/en/course/2026/LDVB26IN10.content:
Integration Domain
: in this domain, the student attends lessons and learns to teach independently. In this way, their awareness of both teaching practice and lesson structure is increased. Students also become acquainted with their future professional field. They gain practical experience through internships at a level appropriate to their stage of study.
Base Theatre
Performing Knowledge/IWP
In this domain component, the theory and history of music theatre are put into practice. The focus lies on creating connections between Education, Research and the Professional Field; Innovation Workplace (IWP). In Performing Knowledge, students integrate theory through research with practice and develop this into an innovative whole, also in an international context.
Cultural Educational Practice (CEP)
CEP offers the opportunity to put arts-educational teaching materials into practice within primary, secondary and general education. The projects operate at the intersection of the target group’s culture, the arts, and current social themes. Within CEP, the knowledge and skills acquired in the subjects Management, Organisation and Entrepreneurship and Cultural Educational Project Theory are applied in an integrated manner.
EXCEP/Arts Education Practice
Project EXCEP is an examination component in which the competencies related to translating theory into practice are assessed, as well as the artistic and creative components of the programme. “Creative and educational design”, “problem-solving skills” and “leadership and initiative” are key competencies within this project. Candidates take on the roles of designer, performer and teacher.
Theatre Practice/Integration
Project Theatre practice internships and the Integration Project offer opportunities to gain stage and professional field experience as a performing artist, partly independently and partly under supervision.
Core Education
MeDi Practice (Performing Education)
Out-of-School Educational practice focuses on out-of-school internships. Students gain experience teaching various target groups in PTMD and Ballet, modern, ADMV, TLSD, DAZ, singing, hip-hop or tap.
MeDi Practice (Performing Education)
In-School Educational practice focuses on in-school internships. Students gain experience teaching various target groups within the school environment.
Projects
CREACORE
This is a Performing Arts project in which students, guided by their coach and working from a theme, create a presentation or Performing Arts project within an educational setting, gaining experience in entrepreneurship and creation.
Project MT
In the MT education project, students acquire the skills to adapt an existing piece for a specific target group. Existing musical repertoire is studied and transformed into teaching material for primary and secondary school pupils. Research is conducted into the essence of the material and the didactic possibilities for conveying it.
Project “We”
Project “We” takes place early in level 9Ba and has an orienting and collaborative purpose.
Integration Project
In the Integration Project, a theatre production is created under the guidance of various choreographers and directors, integrating different domains into a coherent whole.
Project CEP
CEP offers the opportunity to put arts-educational teaching materials into practice within primary, secondary and general education. The projects operate at the intersection of the target group’s culture, the arts, and current social themes.

Artistic practice
You will develop a personal artistic vision, from which, under the guidance of a tutor, you will facilitate artistic processes and create artworks in practice.
Context-based practice
You will collaborate with professionals in the field to develop meaningful art education initiatives based on current social and societal themes.

In PD, students receive guidance—either collaboratively with peers or individually—regarding their personal development, study trajectory, projects, exchange programmes, and internships.
Base Theatre
Musical History
Musical History places the musical within a historical context.
Theatre Theory
Theatre Theory situates the theories of dance, visual arts, musical theatre, dramaturgy (the study of dramatic art), and music within a (historical) perspective, forming the basis for understanding developments in today’s cultural landscape. Students learn to conduct artistic research within and across these disciplines.
Performing Knowledge Research
In the artistic research course, students learn to use methods for conducting research and analysing art. This course builds a bridge between Theatre Theory and Performing Knowledge.
Arts Education
Arts Education focuses on researching the educational system, the core objectives and examination requirements for the subjects CKV and General Arts, and on designing and teaching a lesson series within the upper levels of secondary education.
(Core) Education
MeDi
MeDi covers the theoretical foundations of teaching and includes the independent development and implementation of lesson plans, learning plans, and curricula. In levels 9Ba and 10Ba, a distinction is made between Dance and Music Theatre classes.
Psychology
Psychology covers the basic principles of (developmental) psychology.
Educational Science
Educational Science is the discipline that describes, understands, and explains learning, teaching, and development within education.
Dance Analysis
This domain component covers the theory and analysis of ballet, jazz, and PTMD technique.
Human Movement Sciences (MBK)
Human Movement Sciences includes basic knowledge of anatomy, physiology, and pathology of the movement and vocal apparatus, as well as discipline-specific first aid skills.
Music Theory / Solfège
Music Theory addresses the theoretical aspects of music and includes learning to read notes and intervals. Solfège focuses on learning to distinguish and read notes and intervals by ear and is taught in several modules. Students must first complete module one in level 9Ba before progressing to module two, and so on. In total, four modules must be completed.
Professional Field Research
This domain component focuses on developing research skills and knowledge of research methods.
Applied Theory
In this component, various theoretical subjects are applied within educational practice.

/en/course/2026/LDVB26IN12.outcomes:
Artistic practice
You develop a coherent artistic vision from which you guide artistic processes and create works.
Pedagogical and didactic practice
You design and create meaningful learning environments, in consultation with those involved, based on a coherent artistic and pedagogical vision.
Environment-oriented practice
You facilitate meaningful art education interactions, establishing a connection with social and societal issues.
Inquiry-based practice
You adopt an inquiry-based approach, focused on developing and improving your professional practice in art education.
/en/course/2026/LDVB26IN12.content:
Integration Domain
: in this domain, the student attends lessons and learns to teach independently. In this way, their awareness of both teaching practice and lesson structure is increased. Students also become acquainted with their future professional field. They gain practical experience through internships at a level appropriate to their stage of study.
Base Theatre
Performing Knowledge/IWP
In this domain component, the theory and history of music theatre are put into practice. The focus lies on creating connections between Education, Research and the Professional Field; Innovation Workplace (IWP). In Performing Knowledge, students integrate theory through research with practice and develop this into an innovative whole, also in an international context.
Cultural Educational Practice (CEP)
CEP offers the opportunity to put arts-educational teaching materials into practice within primary, secondary and general education. The projects operate at the intersection of the target group’s culture, the arts, and current social themes. Within CEP, the knowledge and skills acquired in the subjects Management, Organisation and Entrepreneurship and Cultural Educational Project Theory are applied in an integrated manner.
EXCEP/Arts Education Practice
Project EXCEP is an examination component in which the competencies related to translating theory into practice are assessed, as well as the artistic and creative components of the programme. “Creative and educational design”, “problem-solving skills” and “leadership and initiative” are key competencies within this project. Candidates take on the roles of designer, performer and teacher.
Theatre Practice/Integration
Project Theatre practice internships and the Integration Project offer opportunities to gain stage and professional field experience as a performing artist, partly independently and partly under supervision.
Core Education
MeDi Practice (Performing Education)
Out-of-School Educational practice focuses on out-of-school internships. Students gain experience teaching various target groups in PTMD and Ballet, modern, ADMV, TLSD, DAZ, singing, hip-hop or tap.
MeDi Practice (Performing Education)
In-School Educational practice focuses on in-school internships. Students gain experience teaching various target groups within the school environment.
Projects
CREACORE
This is a Performing Arts project in which students, guided by their coach and working from a theme, create a presentation or Performing Arts project within an educational setting, gaining experience in entrepreneurship and creation.
Project MT
In the MT education project, students acquire the skills to adapt an existing piece for a specific target group. Existing musical repertoire is studied and transformed into teaching material for primary and secondary school pupils. Research is conducted into the essence of the material and the didactic possibilities for conveying it.
Project “We”
Project “We” takes place early in level 9Ba and has an orienting and collaborative purpose.
Integration Project
In the Integration Project, a theatre production is created under the guidance of various choreographers and directors, integrating different domains into a coherent whole.
Project CEP
CEP offers the opportunity to put arts-educational teaching materials into practice within primary, secondary and general education. The projects operate at the intersection of the target group’s culture, the arts, and current social themes.

/en/course/2026/DDVP26DA9.outcomes:
Artistic practice
Under the guidance of tutors and practitioners, you can develop artistic processes and create artistic works.
Context-oriented practice
You identify social and societal themes and incorporate them into collaborative projects with fellow students within the context of the programme.
/en/course/2026/DDVP26DA9.content:
Dance Domain
: this domain focuses on mastering the technical components of dance.
The Dance Technique domain is divided into a core and a foundation section, with technical mastery being acquired in the foundation section and the core section serving as a bridge between technique, the various dance styles and the professional field.
Base
Ballet
Ballet forms the foundation upon which all other dance techniques are built. This also includes the element of pointe work (Ballet Pointe).
Modern Dance
Modern Dance technique serves as the basis for PopTheatreMusicalDance technique, but is also a standalone dance technique. Modern dance is combined with creative development. Creative development aims to teach students to develop creative products, including the design of choreographies.
Jazz Dance
Jazz Dance serves as the basis for PopTheatreMusicalDance technique, but is also a standalone dance technique.
Dance Analysis is linked to the core subjects in the Dance domain. Dance Analysis encompasses the theory and analysis of techniques.
Acrodance
Acrodance helps to optimise physical development and acrobatic skills and supports the various dance techniques.
Training sessions
Training sessions are offered in period E during rehearsals for Project Integration. The basic techniques are maintained in the training sessions.
Core
Dance Trends
Dance Trends is a separate module and an independent dance technique based on non-academic dance forms. This module is constantly subject to innovation, trends and change.
Pop Theatre Musical Dance (PTMD)
In this module, the various dance styles come together and a bridge is built between the different techniques. Here too, students learn to develop creative works, including the design of choreographies.
Theatre Latin Standard Dance (TLSD)
Theatre Latin Standard Dance is a component of ballroom dancing and a collective term for various dances that have evolved from traditional non-academic dance forms. Since the early twentieth century, these dance forms have been standardised into independent dance techniques.
Rhythm/Tap
Tap dance serves as the basis for PTMD, but is also an independent technique. Tap dance is a dance form in which rhythmic sounds are produced with the feet.

/en/course/2026/DDVP26MT9.outcomes:
Artistic practice
Under the guidance of tutors and practitioners, you can develop artistic processes and create artistic works.
Context-oriented practice
You identify social and societal themes and incorporate them into collaborative projects with fellow students within the context of the programme.
/en/course/2026/DDVP26MT9.content:
Musical Theatre domain:
this domain focuses on mastering the technical aspects of musical theatre. The Musical Theatre domain is divided into a core and a foundation component, with technical skills being acquired in the foundation component, whilst the core component bridges the gap between technique, the creation of various forms of musical theatre, and the professional field.
Core
Acting
Acting serves as the basis for the Musical Theatre domain component, but is also an independent domain component in the form of Musical Acting. Within this domain component, students learn teaching skills relating to acting.
Ensemble Singing
Ensemble Singing serves as the foundation for the Musical Theatre module, but is also a standalone module. The core objective is polyphony.
Musical Theatre
Musical Theatre brings together the elements of dance, singing and acting. In Musical Theatre, existing musicals, and in particular the dance and ensemble singing pieces, form the teaching and learning material.

/en/course/2026/DDVP26FL9.outcomes:
Artistic practice
Under the guidance of tutors and practitioners, you can develop artistic processes and create artistic works.
Context-oriented practice
You identify social and societal themes and incorporate them into collaborative projects with fellow students within the context of the programme.
/en/course/2026/DDVP26FL9.content:
Flex Domain
The components of this domain are designed to give students the opportunity to shape a personal learning pathway. During the Intensive Weeks, students can design this pathway themselves by selecting elective packages. In level 9Ba, it is possible to choose domain components from the Higher Professional Education Bachelor Programme in Dance Education, allowing students to create the possibility to follow the Bachelor of Dance and the Bachelor of Dance Education simultaneously from level 10Ba onward through the
Plus de Deux
track.
Intensive
An intensive takes place during a schedule-free week. In an intensive, students are immersed in a specific aspect of Dance (making) and/or Music Theatre (making). Within a short period of time, the student develops the skills associated with this component.
Flex Module / Flex Education
Through flex modules, students have the opportunity to deepen or broaden their learning. They can choose between two variants: flex modules focused on education or flex modules focused on performance. Flex modules in education are a requirement for admission to the
Plus de Deux
programme (double degree). In level 11, students may choose to specialize in Piano or Solfège, among other options.
Flexible Space
Through the Flexible Space, students have the opportunity to deepen or broaden their learning. In levels 11 and 12, students can propose how this space will be structured within a personal plan. Guidance in writing the Personal Plan is provided within Personal Development (PD). Through a personal plan, the student determines the direction of the Flexible Space domain component by formulating goals that reflect a personal, artistic, feasible, and assessable need for development, answering the question: “What do I need as an artist to improve?”
In levels 9Ba, 10Ba, and 11Ba, the Personal Plan serves as a guiding document in which the structure of the Flexible Space is recorded. In level 12Ba, the student is also assessed and reflects on the achievement of the goals.
Marthas International Program (MIP)
Through this domain component, students become acquainted with the international professional field of the Performing Arts. This takes place through intensives, exchanges, and a study trip. By participating, students learn to work with international choreographers and collaborate with students from partner institutions. Each academic year, the student participates in one international component. See section 2.3.3 for further description and applicable procedures.
The international components involve Innovation Labs, in which students collaborate with students from partner institutions, choreographers from the professional field, and teachers from their own programme and/or partner institutions.
(MeDi) Skills
Within the Skills component, students in levels 11Ba and 12Ba have the opportunity to further deepen and broaden their individual focus within their chosen professional field. The hours are arranged individually. This domain component is linked to MeDi Skills. The student selects a MeDi Skills package and learns the methodology and skills needed to further develop teaching within the chosen discipline.

Pedagogical and didactic practice
You recognise and analyse a foundation of pedagogical and didactic knowledge and skills in professional practice.
Environment-oriented practice
You recognise social and societal themes and incorporate these into collaborative projects with fellow students within the context of the programme.
Inquisitive practice
You question and reflect on art education practice.

Rhythm/Tap

Core

Ensemble Singing

Musical Theatre

Plus de Deux
track.
Intensive
An intensive takes place during a schedule-free week. In an intensive, students are immersed in a specific aspect of Dance (making) and/or Music Theatre (making). Within a short period of time, the student develops the skills associated with this component.
Flex Module / Flex Education
Through flex modules, students have the opportunity to deepen or broaden their learning. They can choose between two variants: flex modules focused on education or flex modules focused on performance. Flex modules in education are a requirement for admission to the
Plus de Deux
programme (double degree). In level 11, students may choose to specialize in Piano or Solfège, among other options.
Flexible Space
Through the Flexible Space, students have the opportunity to deepen or broaden their learning. In levels 11 and 12, students can propose how this space will be structured within a personal plan. Guidance in writing the Personal Plan is provided within Personal Development (PD). In levels 9Ba, 10Ba, and 11Ba, the Personal Plan serves as a guiding document in which the structure of the Flexible Space is recorded. In level 12Ba, the student is also assessed and reflects on the achievement of the goals.

By participating, students learn to work with international choreographers and collaborate with students from partner institutions. Each academic year, the student participates in one international component. See section 2.3.3 for further description and applicable procedures.
The international components involve Innovation Labs, in which students collaborate with students from partner institutions, choreographers from the professional field, and teachers from their own programme and/or partner institutions.
(MeDi) Skills

The hours are arranged individually. This domain component is linked to MeDi Skills. The student selects a MeDi Skills package and learns the methodology and skills needed to further develop teaching within the chosen discipline.

/en/course/2026/DDVB26KE11.outcomes:
Artistic practice
You will develop a personal artistic vision, from which, under the guidance of a tutor, you will facilitate artistic processes and create works in practice.
Pedagogical and didactic practice
You will design and create meaningful learning environments within educational practice, based on pedagogical and didactic principles.
Environment-oriented practice
You will collaborate with professionals in the field to develop meaningful art education interactions based on current social and societal themes.
Inquiry-based practice

/en/course/2026/DDVB26KE11.content:
Knowledge Domain:
In this domain, the student explores the theoretical background of educational practice and becomes acquainted with the pedagogical, didactic, and methodological aspects of dance arts education. In addition, this domain covers the theoretical foundations of the performing arts.
Base
Personal Development (PD)
In PD, students receive guidance—either collaboratively with peers or individually—regarding their personal development, study trajectory, projects, exchange programmes, and internships.
Base Theatre
Musical History
Musical History places the musical within a historical context.
Theatre Theory
Theatre Theory situates the theories of dance, visual arts, musical theatre, dramaturgy (the study of dramatic art), and music within a (historical) perspective, forming the basis for understanding developments in today’s cultural landscape. Students learn to conduct artistic research within and across these disciplines.
Performing Knowledge Research
In the artistic research course, students learn to use methods for conducting research and analysing art. This course builds a bridge between Theatre Theory and Performing Knowledge.
Arts Education
Arts Education focuses on researching the educational system, the core objectives and examination requirements for the subjects CKV and General Arts, and on designing and teaching a lesson series within the upper levels of secondary education.
(Core) Education
MeDi
MeDi covers the theoretical foundations of teaching and includes the independent development and implementation of lesson plans, learning plans, and curricula. In levels 9Ba and 10Ba, a distinction is made between Dance and Music Theatre classes.
Psychology
Psychology covers the basic principles of (developmental) psychology.
Educational Science
Educational Science is the discipline that describes, understands, and explains learning, teaching, and development within education.
Dance Analysis
This domain component covers the theory and analysis of ballet, jazz, and PTMD technique.
Human Movement Sciences (MBK)
Human Movement Sciences includes basic knowledge of anatomy, physiology, and pathology of the movement and vocal apparatus, as well as discipline-specific first aid skills.
Music Theory / Solfège
Music Theory addresses the theoretical aspects of music and includes learning to read notes and intervals. Solfège focuses on learning to distinguish and read notes and intervals by ear and is taught in several modules. Students must first complete module one in level 9Ba before progressing to module two, and so on. In total, four modules must be completed.
Professional Field Research
This domain component focuses on developing research skills and knowledge of research methods.
Applied Theory
In this component, various theoretical subjects are applied within educational practice.

/en/course/2026/DDVB26IN11.outcomes:
Artistic practice
You will develop a personal artistic vision, from which, under the guidance of a tutor, you will facilitate artistic processes and create works in practice.
Pedagogical and didactic practice
You will design and create meaningful learning environments within educational practice, based on pedagogical and didactic principles.
Environment-oriented practice
You will collaborate with professionals in the field to develop meaningful art education interactions based on current social and societal themes.
Inquiry-based practice
You will adopt an inquiry-based approach and use insights to improve your own art education practice.
/en/course/2026/DDVB26IN11.content:
Integration Domain
: in this domain, the student attends lessons and learns to teach independently. In this way, their awareness of both teaching practice and lesson structure is increased. Students also become acquainted with their future professional field. They gain practical experience through internships at a level appropriate to their stage of study.
Base Theatre
Performing Knowledge/IWP
In this domain component, the theory and history of music theatre are put into practice. The focus lies on creating connections between Education, Research and the Professional Field; Innovation Workplace (IWP). In Performing Knowledge, students integrate theory through research with practice and develop this into an innovative whole, also in an international context.
Cultural Educational Practice (CEP)
CEP offers the opportunity to put arts-educational teaching materials into practice within primary, secondary and general education. The projects operate at the intersection of the target group’s culture, the arts, and current social themes. Within CEP, the knowledge and skills acquired in the subjects Management, Organisation and Entrepreneurship and Cultural Educational Project Theory are applied in an integrated manner.
EXCEP/Arts Education Practice
Project EXCEP is an examination component in which the competencies related to translating theory into practice are assessed, as well as the artistic and creative components of the programme. “Creative and educational design”, “problem-solving skills” and “leadership and initiative” are key competencies within this project. Candidates take on the roles of designer, performer and teacher.
Theatre Practice/Integration
Project Theatre practice internships and the Integration Project offer opportunities to gain stage and professional field experience as a performing artist, partly independently and partly under supervision.
Core Education
MeDi Practice (Performing Education)
Out-of-School Educational practice focuses on out-of-school internships. Students gain experience teaching various target groups in PTMD and Ballet, modern, ADMV, TLSD, DAZ, singing, hip-hop or tap.
MeDi Practice (Performing Education)
In-School Educational practice focuses on in-school internships. Students gain experience teaching various target groups within the school environment.
Projects
CREACORE
This is a Performing Arts project in which students, guided by their coach and working from a theme, create a presentation or Performing Arts project within an educational setting, gaining experience in entrepreneurship and creation.
Project MT
In the MT education project, students acquire the skills to adapt an existing piece for a specific target group. Existing musical repertoire is studied and transformed into teaching material for primary and secondary school pupils. Research is conducted into the essence of the material and the didactic possibilities for conveying it.
Project “We”
Project “We” takes place early in level 9Ba and has an orienting and collaborative purpose.
Integration Project
In the Integration Project, a theatre production is created under the guidance of various choreographers and directors, integrating different domains into a coherent whole.
Project CEP
CEP offers the opportunity to put arts-educational teaching materials into practice within primary, secondary and general education. The projects operate at the intersection of the target group’s culture, the arts, and current social themes.

/en/course/2026/VGVP25SLGI1.outcomes:
Level Orientation (semester 1-2): The student shows insight into the nature of the profession and the tasks, and sensitivity and potential for the continued acquisition of the competences.
1. ARTISTIC CREATION
The student can initiate a visual work process and create work in which practice-oriented research has a place. With the work and with a working method, the student creates meaning.
The student uses intuition and imagination during the work and making process. In the work, a story, meaning, way of thinking or intervening becomes manifest, and a voice of its own. The student has a strong understanding of the workings and sensory experiences that the work evokes.
Dealing with the not-knowing, the unexpected, is inherently linked to the practice of the artist or designer. The student is able to allow and use doubt and uncertainty in erratic work processes. By dealing with risks in the work, the student develops self-confidence to work as an artist/designer in a dynamic world.
The student works experimentally and inquisitively. While thinking, observing, doing, making, changing, processing, the student develops (artistic) methods and strategies in his own way and can show them. With the help of the students own working method, the student can create alternative solution options, scenarios, images and stories. The student can continue to develop his or her own work and working method, in a dynamic work area.
/en/course/2026/VGVP25SLGI1.content:
You work on the design dilemma your tutors formulated based on the competences of this course, and the content written below.
You discover how to make good choices in your design process and thus arrive at your own concepts and solutions in medium and form (Studio).
Next to that, making and experimenting you work on your designs, developing your own handwriting as designer; the workshops play an important role in this (Lab). Next to that, making and experimenting you work on your designs, developing your own handwriting as designer; workshops play an important role in this (Lab).
The design dilemma you work on also gives a first insight into our general description of Graphic & Interaction Design: visual storytelling through narrative structures using analogue and digital media in which images and typography are both important.

/en/course/2026/VGVP25PDTGI1.outcomes:
Level Orientation (semester 1-2): The student shows insight into the nature of the profession and the tasks, and sensitivity and potential for the continued acquisition of the competences.
2. RESEARCH AND REFLECTION
The student is able to critically and from multiple perspectives consider their own work and working method and that of others. This allows the student to deepen their own design or artistry, make it more layered and position.
The student has a curious, inquisitive, and entrepreneurial attitude towards other perspectives, work practices, and ways of thinking. By sharing findings with fellow students and with the professional field, the student also questions their own ways of thinking, working methods, work and positioning.
3. CONNECTING WITH THE ENVIRONMENT
The student takes position as an artist/designer, both in terms of content and relation, in the (international) contexts in which they work.
The student seeks connections with the environment in the students own way for the benefit of the work and the work process, as a method of artistic research.
The student can allow perspectives of others into the work and work process and is touched and inspired by them. These can be, for example, current developments in society, activities of fellow makers or sources from the past.
Artists/designers work in relation to and together with others. Collaboration, exchange and communication are crucial in the work process. The student actively seeks connections with others in order to advance their work. The student has insight into various forms of (collective) partnerships, both within and outside their own field.
In collaborations, the student can make an appropriate contribution and make their own voice heard, and deal inclusively with the different roles, relationships, motivations, responsibilities, interests, voices and specific qualities.
/en/course/2026/VGVP25PDTGI1.content:
The learning line professional development consists of two courses of the Theory and Student Guidance.
Theory 3 EC
You discover the contexts and concepts of current design practices linked to this semester’s majors and design dilemma.
Each of the three periods has a specific theoretical skill emphasized:
Period 1 > finding sources
Period 2 > understanding sources
Period 3 > sharing what you found out
Student Guidance 2EC
This course provides you with essential support in academic and professional development. How do you study at Minerva? Are you in the right place?
Your personal study coach will discuss your study progress, the challenges you face in the design program, and your course choices for the 4th period. The student coach can also guide you in selecting a major and electives for your second year to align with your learning goals.
This module includes mentorship, study support, and offering emotional well-being resources. You receive personalized guidance to navigate challenges, enhance your artistic growth, and prepare for professional opportunities by exploring the working field.

The student can discuss the intuitively created or conscious choices and relate them to the work, the audience, the environment or the larger context.

In addition, the student relates to the world with work and working methods, in which ecological, technological, social and economic issues and transitions play a role.
/en/course/2026/VGVB25SSD1.content:
You work on the design dilemma your tutor formulated based on the competences of this course, and the content written below.
Studio: You conduct design research based on (fictional) design dilemmas. Here you discover how to make good choices in your design process and thus arrive at your own concepts and solutions in medium and form.
Theme sem 3: In this semester on
People and Community Building
, community building is explored through social and urban research on a specific location, translating findings into the transformation of an existing building. Interaction between the building, its users and the area get special attention.
Parallel to this, you also design a new architectural structure on a smaller scale, giving attention to space-mass, sculpting solids, materiality and spatial quality in a tiny house.
You work together on getting to know the basic skills and insights of spatial design, like construction traits, phases in the design process and setting up well-structured and communicative architectural drawings.
Within the bandwidth of scale levels ranging from S to XL, in this semester you switch between both M and L.

You work on the design dilemma your tutor formulated based on the competences of this course, and the content written below.
Lab: Making and experimenting, you work on your designs, developing your own handwriting as designer; the workshops play an important role in this.
Theme sem 4: This semester
Purpose and Tectonic Experience
are central subjects. Tectonic experience is omnipresent in projects in which we build physical things. The concept of tectonics is about the expressiveness of a building, where it is important that there is an interplay between structure, façade, material, staging, facilities and the expressiveness of it. Construction, art, experience and functionality can potentially be fused together. Experience refers to the senses of the users: What does a design communicate? Does this fit your goal? How can you emphasize? Can it work in different scale levels?
Within the bandwidth of scale levels ranging from S to XL, in this semester you switch between both S and M.

You work on the design dilemma your tutor formulated based on the competences of this course, and the content written below.
Studio: You conduct design research based on (fictional) design dilemmas. Here you discover how to make good choices in your design process and thus arrive at your own concepts and solutions in medium and form.
Theme sem 5: In this semester on
Place and Layering
, you can choose on what scale level you wish to design: S, M, L and/or XL. Working more independently, with increasing insights into your own qualities while dealing with a more complex dilemma, is part of the challenge. Added to what you learned before, you work with experience, materiality, scale, light, sight, routing, composition, and so on.
You're trying to work towards your own position within the field of Spatial Design, interpreting and translating personal fascinations and inspirations. Observing, analysing and responding to the physical context is one of the main objectives. Visualizing your ideas and position in a compelling and authentic manner is another.

/en/course/2026/AMVB26PLIN1.outcomes:
Level Deepening (semester 3-7): The student shows insight into the importance of design and theoretical research and experiment for the acquisition of knowledge and skills and succeeds in giving shape to this.
3. CONNECTING WITH THE ENVIRONMENT
The student takes position as an artist/designer, both in terms of content and relation, in the (international) contexts in which he works.
The student's positioning is well-considered and is embodied in the work and working method. To this end, the student conducted research.
The student can make the value of this positioning clear in the context in which the student works. The student is able to deal with changing circumstances and different approaches to making and designing art in a resilient and agile way by being open to and acquiring new knowledge, insights and skills.
Artists/designers work in relation to and together with others. Collaboration, exchange and communication are crucial in the work process. The student actively seeks connections with others in order to advance their work. The student has insight into various forms of (collective) partnerships, both within and outside their own field.
In collaborations, the student can make an appropriate contribution and make their own voice heard, and deal inclusively with the different roles, relationships, motivations, responsibilities, interests, voices and specific qualities.
The student develops an understanding of the role that artists/designers can have in simple, interdependent systems. The student investigates one's own role as a maker in work and production processes and the implications of this for people, the environment and
society. In this way, the student sharpens the awareness that one's own work and work process are part of a larger, also international, whole: society, nature, history. In addition, the student relates to the world with work and working methods, in which ecological, technological, social and economic issues and transitions play a role.
4. WORKING IN A PRACTICE
The student is able to create conditions for his or her own work practice, in line with his/her own positioning. To this end, the student is able to organize and communicate with others.
In order to be able to work as an artist and designer in practice, the student organizes a suitable working environment. The student knows how to facilitate their own work processes and can create a safe working environment. The student deals with the physical and social working conditions in an agile way and adjusts the conditions of the working environment where necessary.
It takes self-confidence and courage to create the right working conditions, to claim time and artistic freedom, to negotiate finances, to be enterprising and to be enterprising, and to take a role in collaborations. The student has insight into this and develops confidence in their own positioning, qualities and ambitions.
It also requires empathy, inventiveness and imagination to see possibilities and opportunities in the field and to face them. The student takes initiatives to find work, for example by initiating and acquiring assignments and projects, but also by working together, exchanging knowledge and developing new forms of working practices.
/en/course/2026/AMVB26PLIN1.content:
Switchboard refers to a switching point in the study. You made preparations in semester 5 and formulated a learning question that is central for the choice you make in semester 6.
You can then choose from one of the options to go out into the world and encounter an aspect of the professional field. This gives you the space to develop a stronger profile. You have a switch board coach that guides you.
You can choose from various options: internship, Major of choice, exchange, minor, research project at a research center within the Hanze, Out There and H.A.L. This course description is about internship. The other descriptions can be found elsewhere in this document.
Internship
During an internship (in the Netherlands or abroad), you find out how the knowledge and skills you’ve acquired during your studies measure up to the requirements of professional practice.
NB More information and enrolment options can be found on Brightspace.

/en/course/2026/AMVB25PLHAL1.outcomes:
Level Deepening (semester 3-7):
The student demonstrates an understanding of the importance of art/design and theoretical research and experimentation for acquiring knowledge and skills and succeeds in shaping this.
Exploratory research (Artistic Creation & Researching and Reflecting)
The student independently conducts artistic research, where intuition, experimentation, and practice-based inquiry come together.
The student formulates and deepens a research question through an iterative working process.
The student develops artistic methodologies and alternative scenarios.
Interdisciplinary collaboration (Connecting with the Environment & Working in Practice)
The student collaborates with various disciplines and external parties, where knowledge exchange leads to new perspectives.
The student integrates external input and societal developments into the working process.
The student moves flexibly between different working methods and perspectives.
Reflective and experimental learning (Researching and Reflecting & Artistic Creation)
The student experiments with research methods and uses uncertainty as an artistic strength.
The student critically reflects on their own process and artistic choices.
The student connects reflection with artistic output.
Self-Direction and equality in Learning (Working in Practice & Connecting with the Environment)
The student takes initiative and shows ownership of their own learning process.
The student actively contributes to collective knowledge development.
The student consciously positions themselves within relevant fields and societal contexts.
Communication and presentation (Working in Practice & Connecting with the Environment)
The student explores and experiments with presentation forms and communication.
The student presents work and research in a meaningful way.
The student tailors communication strategies to the audience, medium, and context.
Conceptual exploration (Artistic Creation & Researching and Reflecting)
The student explores the influence of concept and context on artistic research.
The student experiments with thematic frameworks such as Choreography of a Fall and Poetics of Place.
The student integrates physical, digital, and social concepts into the working process.
Critical awareness and societal relevance (Connecting with the Environment & Researching and Reflecting)
The student connects artistic research to societal issues.
The student investigates the impact of art on knowledge production and collective imagination.
The student makes ethical choices in materials, technology, and themes.
/en/course/2026/AMVB25PLHAL1.content:
H.A.L. is an experimental platform for artistic research in semester 6, where students pioneer within an interdisciplinary community. In collaboration with the Research Center, technical specialists, and teachers, H.A.L. provides a dynamic learning environment centered on experimentation and dialogue. The project culminates in a collective presentation with an external partner.
H.A.L. is a free space for creation and research, without fixed hierarchies. Students explore the edges of their discipline and step outside their comfort zones. The starting point is a personal research question, which evolves within a Community of Learners and may develop into a shared inquiry.  Within H.A.L., there is no predefined (visual) language for the experiences students seek to explore. Teachers and students enter this process as equals, inspired by thinkers like Agamben and Rancière. The project is about discovering new research methods and open-ended explorations. H.A.L. fosters critical exchange between disciplines and cultures, offering space for both individual and collective imagination. It is an adventure where students, through making and reflecting, explore unknown territories and create new insights.

metadata.Language: Dutch, with parts in English, English

/en/course/2026/AMVB25PLOT1.outcomes:
Level Deepening (semester 3-7): The student shows insight into the importance of design and theoretical research and experiment for the acquisition of knowledge and skills and succeeds in giving shape to this.
Interdisciplinary artistic research (Artistic Creation & Research and Reflection)
The student develops and initiates an interdisciplinary artistic process based on biographies and personal stories. This process employs various media, materials, and techniques, with a focus on research into sensory perception and experience. The student combines intuition and experimentation, seeing the unexpected and uncertain moments as valuable elements of the process, and creates work that offers meaning and new perspectives.
Collaboration and social engagement (Connecting with the Environment & Working in Practice)
The student collaborates with students from various disciplines at both the Minerva Academy and the Prins Claus Conservatorium. This collaboration fosters a rich exchange of knowledge, perspectives, and skills that enhances the work process. The student reflects on the role of art in society and incorporates societal issues and personal stories into their work, giving the artistic output broader social and ecological significance.
Reflection and experimentation in the work process (Research and Reflection & Artistic Creation)
The student uses reflection and experimentation as central elements in the work process. The project enables the student to experiment with various research methods and artistic approaches, utilizing uncertainties and the unknown to create new forms of artistic expression. The student critically reflects on the process of creating work, the importance of biographies, and translating personal experiences into shared art forms.
Positioning as a maker (Connecting with the Environment & Working in Practice)
The student develops a conscious artistic positioning within the context of the Out There project. This involves situating themselves within the broader societal and artistic context, researching the impact of their work on society. The student develops their own voice and meaning in the work process by positioning themselves relative to the world and other participants, while acknowledging the ethical responsibility of their work.
Communication and participation in the artistic discourse (Working in Practice & Connecting with the Environment)
The student investigates and experiments with different forms of presentation and communication, both within the context of the Out There project and towards a wider audience. Emphasis is placed on connecting the work with its environment through communication strategies that consider the perspectives of both participants and the audience. The student adjusts communication strategies based on the specific contexts and themes addressed within the project.
Sensory and Conceptual exploration (Artistic Creation & Research and Reflection)
The student investigates the influence of sensory experience and space on the perception of reality in the Out There project. Experiments with different senses, such as sound, color, space, and movement, help the student forge a deeper connection between personal experiences and shared artistic output. This experimental approach allows the student to redefine conceptual frameworks and create work that integrates various sensory experiences.
Social relevance and ethical awareness (Connecting with the Environment & Research and Reflection)
The student links the artistic experience and work process to important societal and ecological issues by connecting their personal experiences and stories to broader social and cultural themes. The student critically reflects on the ethical dimensions of the project, such as the impact of art on collective imagination and the responsibility it entails. The work carries deeper social relevance and is presented with an awareness of its potential influence on both the creator and society.
/en/course/2026/AMVB25PLOT1.content:
Out There
is a transdisciplinary project between students from the Minerva Academy and the Prins Claus Conservatoire. It focuses on the multiple sensory ways in which people experience reality. In Out There, biographies (stories) serve as the foundation for encounters between participants and various art disciplines. The project provides a platform for rethinking art disciplines and the roles within them, while encouraging the exploration of new possibilities for collaboration and creation. Participants are challenged to share their perspectives and work together to develop artworks that reflect the rich complexity of human experience. The result of this process is a story that will eventually be shared with the world, as a try-out of the collective creations and discoveries. Out There emphasizes collaboration between art forms, with the ambition of achieving unexpected results and highlighting the value of diversity in the creative process.

As part of an increasingly independent artistic process, the student purposefully engages with material, form, intuition, reflection, and contemplation, and investigates the qualities and possibilities of different materials, techniques and technologies, showing a gradual awareness of how these shape the development and meaning of their work.

/en/course/2026/VGVB25PDT4.content:
Theory this semester consists of two assignments.
Context Essay
You theoretically research the ideas for your graduation project in the contexts and concepts of designers, thinkers and others. This helps you to ground the design dilemma you define for yourself.
You use your skills in finding sources, understanding them and sharing your own story.
You bring the findings of your design experiments and theoretical research together in a (visual) essay. In this essay, you contextualize your design dilemma, explaining your choices in an accountable way.
Your essay is 3000 words or 10 minutes listening/watching time.
Poster Pitch
In a short 5-minute pitch for which an A1 poster forms the base, you share your design dilemma and the plans you have for your graduation project. You use the findings of your Context Essay to explain your choices and use the feedback you get to make an updated version of your Poster Pitch.
NB  More detailed information on this content you can find on Brightspace > Design Graduation Year > 2627 Study Guide Design Graduation Year.
