/en/course/2026/SUVM23TPI.content:
Content of the module:
In this module the student will firstly acquire knowledge of physical aspects in relation to energy. Discussion of the fundamentals of fossil fuel and renewable energy technologies and energy carriers will follow. The student will also develop basic knowledge of the technical and economic issues relating to the planning and operation of power systems that use renewable energy sources. The influence of technology, cost and scale upon all items are discussed (e.g., after completing this module, the student must be able to judge the technical feasibility of wind energy and its contribution to the energy system and to make a rough cost/benefit analysis to evaluate the viability of such an idea). Gas and electricity grids are predominantly given separate consideration within this module.
The module content is divided in five main parts:
Energy Basics
Sustainable Technologies and Economics
Current Energy Systems (gas, electricity) and Economics
Transport & Distribution Technologies and Economics
Balancing and Energy Storage
Lab work provides 0.5 EC of the module.

metadata.Name: Energy Policy, Markets, Finance and Law
metadata.Assessments: Energy Policy, Markets, Finance and Law - Assignment

/en/course/2026/SUVM23MFL.outcomes:
Objective of the module:
After completion of this module the student is able to:
Understand how energy markets function and what types of market failures can occur.
Analyse the way energy markets could be regulated, using insights from micro-economics, finance, and international economics
Understand academic papers on the design of regulation of energy markets and how the effects of regulation could be evaluated.
Analyse potential business cases, by choosing and applying the correct scientific models (e.g. NCW, DCF, IRR, and WACC) and apply scenario analysis, sensitivity analysis and ratio analysis on the scientific models.
Evaluate the monetary value of Capex, Opex and revenues by collecting, assessing and analysing relevant data.
Analyse and advise on financing requirements (e.g. divided policy) based on predictions about the exploitation and cash flows.
Evaluate a financing proposal after considering various possible forms of financing, taking into account the requirements of potential capital providers.
Understand the functioning of different legal systems and apply different ways of finding legal documentation such as case law or legislation.
Analyse different developments in the energy markets from a legal perspective and identify legal bottlenecks.
/en/course/2026/SUVM23MFL.content:
Energy Markets, Policies and Regulation  (40 % content)
This module will provide the students with a thorough understanding of the functioning of energy markets, the underlying processes and stakeholder behaviour, and how energy markets interact with their policy, technology and societal context. The module will teach the student about the economic mechanisms that makes the various parts of the energy system to be aligned together. The module will discuss the concepts of liberalisation, regulation, restructuring and privatisation. Specific items to be addressed are: characteristics, role and functioning of different types of electricity and gas wholesale markets (forward, day-ahead, intraday and balancing markets), as well as energy retail markets. This module will also pay attention to the interaction between energy markets and environmental policies, such as the EU Emission Trading System (ETS) and policies to foster the supply by renewable energy sources, for instance by subsidies or green certificates Finally, the module will discuss the potential role of different technologies, as storage and power-to-gas, to deal with the impact of the growing supply from intermittent renewable energy sources on the stability of energy networks and markets.
Energy Finance (40% content)
The ‘Finance’ module is about the understanding that the innovations that are needed to realize the energy transition requires understanding of finance and how financial variables interplay with technical variables. Each of these financial variables may be closely related to technical variables, for instance the payback time of the project (the time needed to recover the investment) which is related to the total technical project costs, but also to energy prices and the costs of using the (existing) infrastructure. Investment opportunities are compared and assessed based on their expected capex and opex. Risk assessment and sensitivity analysis are also part of investment decisions.
In this module, the students will learn how to apply different valuation methods to evaluate an investment project. The main aim of the module is to acquire hand-on experience in this area. In this module, we will use basic finance knowledge / methods, such as NPV, DCF, IRR, and WACC. The students learn to use these methods and to perform sensitivity analysis and ratio analysis considering alternatives and dependencies.
This module aims at understanding and applying the basic finance concepts and furthermore the students can identify valuation issues by collecting and assessing relevant data, analyse the relevant data and using this to develop a valuation model.
Energy Law (20% content)
After the introductory course in the first course (introduction to law) students understand the functioning of different legal systems and are able to identify different legal disciplines. From this point, this course continues by explaining how law is used as an instrument to regulate the markets. The first class will go more in depth on the developments in the European gas market and how national markets were liberalized. In achieving one internal market, national markets needed to be liberalized. There are also legal challenges with regard to the upcoming market for (green) hydrogen and the (missing) legal framework. The second class will be on the electricity market, the role of aggregators and energy communities. In this class some legal aspects with regard to wind energy, smart grids, smart metering will be discussed. The last class will go in more depth on the legal challenges a DSO is facing in this changing energy market and regulated area.

Objective of the module:
The student has achieved the following learning outcomes:
After successfully completing this module, the student has achieved the following:

Apply modelling techniques to create transparent models on energy business ecosystems and use them to evaluate energy systems on efficiency, environmental impact and basic economics
Apply methods for the validation and verification of created models.
Apply the Material and Energy Flow Analysis (MEFA) methodology and energy flow diagrams (Sankey) to analyze the environmental impact of energy systems
Understand the basics of the Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) methodology for analysing the environmental impact of energy systems and integrate LCA data in energy modelling.
Evaluate the impact of the information and flexibility services on the viability of the business ecosystem, the related business processes and design workflows delivering such services
Create a basic business ecosystem from a techno economic perspective using technical modeling and buisinessmodel techniques
/en/course/2026/SUVM23MBEEFS.content:
Content of the module:
In this module, students acquire the fundamentals of modelling techniques and methods, applied to a real energy system. Furthermore, the role of flexibility services in optimizing decentralized energy systems will be introduced and tested in the assignment. The aim is to develop a business ecosystem, where a viable business model for all involved stakeholders needs to be designed.
The fundamentals of modeling will be explained using three methodologies namely, Material and Energy Flow Analysis (MEFA); Life Cycle Analysis (LCA); and validation and verification of models. The students apply the learned skills in Excel based models containing the aforementioned elements. The focus is on relationships between individual elements within energy systems, e.g. production, storage, conversion. The students program these relationships in a model and use the model to gain understanding and find optimal solutions, with respect to energy efficiency, environmental impacts, and basic economics (e.g. CAPEX and OPEX). Both theory and practice (building an actual model and a real life case) are integrated to give the students a fundamental understanding of energy systems and modelling thereof. The content of the module will be given as tutorials where the students will work on an assignment (e.g. building a model in excel) where the required theory is given to help them progress (just in time). On completion of this module the student will be able to construct a well-structured and transparent model, validate the model, run scenarios in the model, and draw conclusions from the model. The knowledge gained in this module forms a foundation on which the students can expand their modelling skills by using other specialized energy models while recalling the fundamentals of modelling.
The concept of flexibility will be introduced and the role of (smart) flexibility services will be explained.  Business modeling basics and the introduction of a tool for business modeling (e3value) will be introduced that can be used to design and optimize a business model for a real life neighbourhood.  With the introduction of decentral renewable resources advanced flexibility services will be needed to control and manage non-controllable generation, decentral demand-supply coordination, as well as the incorporation of advanced conversion and storage technologies. Energy-related services are crucial in this, but they cannot be deployed without adequate information support. A real life case will be modelled, where flexibility (e.g. storage, conversion) is needed. In order to deliver more advanced services, several stakeholders have to be lined up in a business value network, and various business processes need to be developed. Accordingly, students will be introduced to business process management and business process modelling.
To achieve the module learning outcomes the students attend lectures on modelling theory, perform a written exam, and make a modelling assignment. All components of the module will come together in a real-life case study that needs to be modelled and worked out into a viable energy eco-system. For this students will write an essay.

/en/course/2026/SUVM23RMS.content:
Reflective practitioner and transferable skills
A reflective practitioner is a professional with the ability to use transferable skills, see figure below.
Reflective practice is a way of improving individual and organizational effectiveness. Reflective practice consists of “mindful consideration of one’s actions” (Osterman, 1990 ) in which the reasons and assumptions that drive one’s behavior are thoughtfully reflected on in the interest of improving one’s professional effectiveness. Preferably, appropriate scientific theories are also part of the reflection. Thought and action are thus integrated through reflection. Osterman describes the process as a “challenging, focused, and critical assessment of one’s behavior as a means toward the development of one’s “craftsmanship”. The student will develop learning skills to allow autonomous learning and develop research skills to define and execute a small research project with the intention to act as a capstone assignment of the Core. The capstone assignment is focused on technical, economical, business and social aspects of the transition of a community to a sustainable community based on knowledge and understanding acquired in the previous modules of the CORE program.

/en/course/2026/SUVM23ESMA.content: In this 5 ECTS module the student will expand his/her knowledge of modelling (renewable) energy systems. The difference between simulation and optimisation, and deterministic and probabilistic models, are discussed, with typical applications. Sensitivity analysis and Monte Carlo techniques are explained and applied. A real life renewable energy system is modelled and optimised in an applicable modelling software environment. Modelling is done from a techno-economic-environmental perspective.

/en/course/2026/SUVM24SCBA.content:
Content of the module:
In this module the student will expand his/her knowledge of (renewable) energy technologies,  and the costs and benefits of their integration in energy systems. The focus will be on innovations in energy conversion technologies, and their implementation in stationary and mobile applications. This will enable the student to further develop knowledge, understanding, and systemic vision of the application of these technologies in energy system design. Also, the sustainability and reliability of future (renewable) energy systems are discussed.
This module is a continuation of the core modules Technologies, Plants and Integration at Different Scales, and Energy Policy, Markets, Finance, and Law. It places the core modules within a broader context. I.e., a systemic view on the interaction between energy carriers in the form of electrons and molecules is discussed, and business case development is expanded to social cost-benefit analysis in a case study. Students will study ways to transform the current energy system into one that is sustainable, without jeopardising the reliability and affordability of energy.

/en/course/2026/SUVM23SIP.content:
The ‘System Innovation Processes’ module is based on the understanding that developing new energy-related products, services and systems is a complex process with many interrelated variables. Each of these variables may be closely related to others, for instance when a new energy-efficient technology can only be implemented when new infrastructure is implemented. Or when new regulations are needed to be able to test new types of energy sources.
The objective of the ‘System Innovation Processes’ module is to work on the design of complex energy related systems, specifically looking at the multidisciplinary and multilevel aspects of this process. The module is not so much aimed at the design of the technological energy system as such, but aims to position the development of the physical or tangible energy system, in relationship to the related changes in the societal, organizational, and user context within which the technological system is functioning.
In this module, the student will get acquainted with the execution and management of such a complex design process and the related change processes. The main aim of the module is to acquire hand-on experience and ‘tacit knowledge’ in this area.
In the module, the basic design process will be applied. The student will learn to distinguish between the various design phases, and to structure an energy related design process according to those phases.
The module will aim at understanding and applying the basic concept of systems thinking, enabling students to separate energy related problems and solutions in smaller elements, among others by applying a work breakdown structure and a morphological analysis process.
The module is based on the Multilevel Design Model. This framework consists of a typical four-phase iterative design process (reflection, analysis, synthesis, experience), combined with a hierarchical system oriented perspective based on four system levels (product-technology system, product-service system, socio-technical system and societal system).
In the module, students will get acquainted with several design tools like Future Visioning, System Mapping, Story Boards, Scenario Building and Business Model Canvas

/en/course/2026/SUVM23BED.content: The Business Ecosystem Design (BED) module (10 EC) is the final module of the SIM specialisation, and builds upon the knowledge and skills of previous modules which paid attention to technology, modelling, innovation, and legal and economic aspects of the energy transition. In this module, business concepts are developed in such a way that several stakeholders collaborate to produce and exploit products and services. Such collaborations are also known as business ecosystems. When developing a business ecosystem a stakeholder analysis is necessary. In this module, an integrative business plan is developed, based on academic research and reflection: It includes adjacent factors in the proposed case, i.e. paying attention to the different PESTEL factors (PESTEL: Policy, Economy, Social, Technology, Ecology, Legal). E.g., it may include non-financial benefits or costs into the case. It is important that every stakeholder’s business is profitable.

/en/course/2026/SUVM23THP.outcomes:
The Master thesis project is the graduation programme in which the student shows that they possess the qualifications of a Sustainable Energy System Management Engineer as defined within the Programme learning Outcomes on master level:
The programme learning outcomes comprise:
Understanding of Techno-economical aspects
: The SESyM graduate is competent in analysing, assessing and applying techno-economical aspects of complex sustainable energy systems taking climate and resource issues into account
Using appropriate tools and methodologies:
The SESyM graduate is competent in analysing, assessing, and applying relevant technical, (socio)economical, environmental, legal and policy aspects of systems of sustainable energy while using appropriate tools and methodologies.
Specialism
: The SESyM graduate is competent in specific knowledge, insight and skills in at least one of the specialisation fields: system innovation management, sustainable energy management or sustainable energy and the digital transformation

/en/course/2026/FMVP23PEO.content:
In this series of classes, we focus on strategic analysis and organizational development from the perspectives of marketing, HRM and business administration. We begin by establishing objectives based on the organizational mission and strategy, examining the scope of activities, resource allocation and competitive advantages.
We further explore internal organizational aspects, such as structure, division of labor, motivation, tasks and coordination. We offer insights into organizational structures, models and systems.
In addition, we analyze the external environment, including the industries in which organizations operate and direct and indirect environmental factors. SWOT analysis and value chain analysis are covered as crucial tools for strategic decision-making.
This class series provides the concepts and tools necessary to understand effective strategic analysis and organizational development, with specific focus on marketing, HRM and business administration.

/en/course/2026/FMVB22PCM.outcomes:
The student:
Procurement
Explains the purchasing function and the phases of the (cyclical/linear) purchasing process in terms of their content and is capable of applying the elements from these phases (9);
Analyses the desired customer-supplier relationship on the basis of underlying purchasing theory to determine a suitable purchasing strategy (make, buy or ally) in which the sustainability of the solution is of prime importance (9).
Recognises the importance of supplier management for guaranteeing the quality of the service provision (SLA, KPI) for the customer (8, 9).
Legal
Explains the basics of procurement law and has knowledge of various European tendering procedures (9);
Identifies and explains the basic rules of the law of contracts (9);
Financial
6.    Quantifies and assesses the financial consequences of make, buy or ally decisions (9)
7.     Performs financial decision-supportive calculations (7,8).
/en/course/2026/FMVB22PCM.content:
Procurement:
Based on the sessions, you will gain an understanding of the role of purchasing, as it relates to facilities challenges and the rules for professional (European) tendering procedures. General key terms such as socially responsible or sustainable  procurement, purchasing process, (European) tendering procedures and purchasing strategy are explained and you will learn how to implement the various phases of the purchasing process, with a focus on contract management. The sessions support the central project and are evaluated in written form on the basis of case study questions.
Legal aspects:
In the Legal aspects sessions, you will gain knowledge about the legal aspects which arise in the process of purchasing and developing innovations. The focus will be on contract law and (European) procurement law. The sessions support the central project and are evaluated in written form on the basis of case study questions.
Managementaccounting:
The Financial aspects sessions will cover a wide variety of financial concepts that tie in with the subjects of purchasing and development of innovations. In so doing, the financial aspects of the Business Model Canvas will, for example, be covered. The sessions support the central project and are evaluated in written form on the basis of case study questions.

/en/course/2026/FMVB22DEV.outcomes:
Marketing
The student will analyse the market environment at the macro, meso and micro level and on that basis will develop a marketing strategy, with hospitality experience as the guiding principle (7)
The student will make use of the Business Model Canvas to give the marketing strategy concrete form and structure the service provision process (7,8)
Quality
The student will use various quality models and tools to implement and guarantee the future quality of service provision according to a front office/back office structure (7, 8, 9)
CSR
Identifies CSR developments and places these in a historical context(9)
Distinguishes and analyses conflicting CSR interests of the various stakeholders. (9)
Is capable of formulating ethical arguments in the area of sustainability, hospitality and health which play a role in CSR change processes in the context of facility services (9)
/en/course/2026/FMVB22DEV.content:
Marketing
The Marketing sessions provide the theoretical background to the Business Model Canvas in the context of Facility Management. In the seminars, the operation of the model, among other things, will be explained, and personas and hospitality concepts will be covered.
The sessions support the central project and are evaluated in written form on the basis of case study questions.
Quality of services
You will learn the basics of a quality mindset with the aid of quality models and standards. You will also learn how these models and norms can be applied in practice to guarantee the sustainability, healthfulness and hospitality of a service. The sessions support the central project and are evaluated in written form on the basis of case study questions.
Corporate Social Responsibility
Society is placing increasingly high demands on  organisations when it comes to their dealings with employees, customers and the environment.
Companies and organisations take this into consideration by means of Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR). In so doing, the organisation takes the 3 Ps of CSR into account in all of its activities: People, Planet, Profit. Attention will be paid to the reasons for CSR, to CSR and the market and to CSR reports. The sessions support the central project and are evaluated in written form on the basis of case study questions.

/en/course/2026/FMVB25PRJENT.outcomes:
The student:
4. Analyses the stakeholders of the ‘challenge’ issued by the client and identifies the client and stakeholder requirements (procurement and entrepreneurs role) (7, 8, 9)
5. Develops a scalable new service with the aid of the Business Model Canvas and based on the client and stakeholder requirements, making use of trends and developments at macro and meso level and innovation theories (entrepreneurs role) (7,9)
6. Identifies the consequences of implementation and management of the new service with the help of the completed Business Model Canvas and evaluates this as regards the feasibility of all model components (entrepreneurs role) (8)
/en/course/2026/FMVB25PRJENT.content:
In this semester, you will write a purchasing document for a service in which cooperation between the client and the contracted party plays a crucial role. You will do this based on a "challenge” (assignement from a client) as a member of a purchasing team. Next, you will also become a member of a development team and as a start-up, you will take on the "challenge” of a purchasing team and develop a new service using the purchasing document of that purchasing team. Whilst developing this new service, you will be a specialist in the area of sustainability, hospitality or health.
Both the purchasing process and the development process will be supported iteratively with the help of Scrum and Design Thinking.
For the entire semester, you will therefore have the role of purchaser and developer and you will put together a portfolio for both roles that contains (group)assignments and proof of your capabilities and development. The portfolios will also serve as input for the assessment meeting.

/en/course/2026/FMVB25ELC.outcomes: 4.1 Students shape their own development independently on the basis of their own learning wishes as future HBO professionals, substantiating and justifying choices made during the process, the learning result and further development as HBO professionals.
/en/course/2026/FMVB25ELC.content:
The 5 EC free space is intended as space for the student to shape what he/she wants to learn. This involves content that is not offered within the regular FM full-time curriculum. In addition to allowing the student to provide his/her own content, the aim is also to demonstrate and teach that the student can provide his/her own interpretation of free space, facilitate, monitor his/her own learning and challenge himself/herself to develop further as a professional.

/en/course/2026/FMVB23INT.outcomes:
- The student demonstrates his research skills by analyzing the current and desired situation in an organization regarding a (facility) issue and comes up with a problem solution that improves a facility product, service and/or process (derived from LO2).
- The student uses the PDCA cycle to demonstrate how he carries out the internship and emphasizes his own actions by reflecting on them (derived from LO2+12).
- The student works independently on his professional facility skills in a complex situation or social environment and reflects on his own professional attitude and learning skills (derived from LO 11+12).
- The student communicates in a proactive and clear way ideas and solutions to colleagues and client so that he thereby convinces and contributes to a professional cooperation within the organization/department (derived from LO 11+12).

/en/course/2026/FMVB24SED.outcomes:
1.            The student estimates the needs and motivations of users to achieve an optimal experience.
2.            The student justifies/explains the (strategic) added value when deploying facility services in the design.
3.            The student demonstrates how (desired) behaviour is stimulated by the (adapted) experience.
4.            The student performs a stakeholder analysis and uses it to increase the quality of the (process within the) project.
5.            The student delivers an innovative and/or inspiring result based on a clear vision of practice, including (strategic) follow-up steps.
6.            The student reflects, with explicit attention to the adjustment/optimisation of the process, on everyone's (including own) development, role and contribution.
/en/course/2026/FMVB24SED.content:
For a client, the student creates a new or improved experience by (re)designing a product, service or event. This design is in line with the organisational strategy. Measurability and quality control therefore play an important role. Attention is also paid to personal leadership, the individual journey that the student makes.
Guidance takes place in communities of learners. The assignment is developed into a prototype, on which the student receives feedback, as well as on his/her performance in the duo. The student presents the final design to the client and reflects on his/her personal journey.

/en/course/2026/IFVP26PRJVIW.outcomes:
The student:
- analyses the extent to which the office accommodation provided is suitable for the user (organisation), taking into account the organisational, technical, functional, financial, legal and information technology aspects relating to the accommodation.
- Collects, analyses (SPSS) and reports qualitative (including observation) and quantitative (big data) research data  relating to the use and performance of the completed premises, based on specific information requirements and accurate (sensor) data
- Advises on what information needs to be collected and which (technical) systems should be used to provide the organisation with the correct information, on the basis of which the performance of the accommodation can be optimised
- Under supervision, draws up a general operational overview, based on a methodical approach, for the property in question
- Investigates the perception and actual performance of facilities and their potential
- Advises on how facilities can make a positive contribution to reducing energy consumption, sustainable accommodation and healthy employees
The student explains how the (previously drawn up) Programme of Requirements has been translated into the delivered design for office accommodation. This explanation must, in any case, address the organisational, technical, financial, legal and IT aspects relating to the accommodation.
The student:
1.       Investigates and analyses the requirements regarding the spatial working, living and/or residential environment and provides advice on (new) spatial concepts
2.       Contributes, from a facilities management perspective, to the site selection, (re)design and layout of the built environment
3.       Identifies the criteria that influence the sustainability of the office environment and describes how sustainability has been incorporated into the design.
4.       Justifies all the choices made that have led to the final design and the associated fit-out.
5.       Under supervision, and based on a methodical approach, draws up a rough investment budget for the new office accommodation to be realised
6.       Identifies key points and highlights the contribution made by all individual project group members
7.       Articulates in a clear manner the choices made that have led to the final spatial and functional programme of requirements
8.       Is able to critically reflect on the process relating to the development of the final spatial and functional programme of requirements and identifies areas for improvement
/en/course/2026/IFVP26PRJVIW.content:
Each project group analyses a simple existing building to assess its suitability for its user (organisation). Information gathered during the assignments for Space Management & Technology and for Financial & Information Management is brought together in an analysis that focuses on the building’s added value for its users. This analysis covers, at a minimum: space utilisation; relationships between functions and spaces; functionality; legal aspects (e.g. ownership and liability); and financial aspects (particularly costs of ownership and use). A dashboard that clearly displays the building’s performance in these areas is a key outcome of this analysis.
This part of the semester focuses on designing an innovative office.
Following a practice assignment (model workshop), each project group will work on creating a new office environment for an organisation of their choice. Everything the student has already learnt and will learn during this period about offices (such as workstations, indoor environment, sustainability, safety, etc.) will come in handy here. First, a functional, spatial and relational Programme of Requirements is drawn up (separate component). Based on the Programme of Requirements, a design is then developed with floor plans and perspective drawings (3D visualisation) for both the building layout and interior design, accompanied by a clear justification of the design choices made (how the requirements have been translated into the design) and a rough estimate of the investment required to realise the design.
Finally, each student is able to answer questions individually regarding the new design. What are the highlights and key points? You explain the choices made for the spatial and functional programme. You critically reflect on the Programme of Requirements and identify areas for improvement.

/en/course/2026/IFVP21SPT.content:
Technology:
Whether a building is suitable for its intended use depends for an important part on how it performs in terms of indoor climate conditions, such as thermal comfort, air quality, daylight and artificial light, sound etc. The Buildings Physics course introduces students to the physiological aspects that influence personal comfort with regard to the indoor climate and to the function and operation of the various building installations and their components.
Space Management:
Whether a building is suitable for its intended use depends for an important part on how accommodation can add value to the primary process. The Space Management course introduces students to aspects of the changing demands of the building’s users and the built environment. They are also introduced to the key terms, concepts, trends and developments regarding office accommodation and workspace concepts. Knowledge of the above allows students to prepare a schedule of requirements and recommend a workspace concept.

/en/course/2026/IFVP21FIM.content:
Financial Management:
The focus in this course is on acquiring knowledge and developing skills with regard to the balance sheet, profit and loss account and liquidity statement of a business or organisation.
Aspects such as the distinction between various types of costs, the break-even point and the calculation of costs are also considered basic knowledge elements. The course is an introduction to the specialisation of financial management and management accounting and lays the foundations for students to be a competent discussion partner for stakeholders in the facility management industry.
Information Management:
The focus in this course is on acquiring knowledge with regard to the components and operation of information systems. The key aspect here is the general role that systems play in supporting operational processes and decisions at various levels within an organisation. The emphasis is on the role of building-related systems. Attention is also paid to the latest developments in the areas of ICT and buildings.

/en/course/2026/IFVP23PEO.content:
In this series of classes, we focus on strategic analysis and organizational development from the perspectives of marketing, HRM and business administration. We begin by establishing objectives based on the organizational mission and strategy, examining the scope of activities, resource allocation and competitive advantages.
We further explore internal organizational aspects, such as structure, division of labor, motivation, tasks and coordination. We offer insights into organizational structures, models and systems.
In addition, we analyze the external environment, including the industries in which organizations operate and direct and indirect environmental factors. SWOT analysis and value chain analysis are covered as crucial tools for strategic decision-making.
This class series provides the concepts and tools necessary to understand effective strategic analysis and organizational development, with specific focus on marketing, HRM and business administration.

Procurement

/en/course/2026/IFVB22PCM.content:
Procurement
Procurement:
Based on the sessions, you will gain an understanding of the role of purchasing, as it relates to facilities challenges and the rules for professional (European) tendering procedures. General key terms such as socially responsible or sustainable  procurement, purchasing process, (European) tendering procedures and purchasing strategy are explained and you will learn how to implement the various phases of the purchasing process, with a focus on contract management. The sessions support the central project and are evaluated in written form on the basis of case study questions.
Legal aspects:
In the Legal aspects sessions, you will gain knowledge about the legal aspects which arise in the process of purchasing and developing innovations. The focus will be on contract law and (European) procurement law. The sessions support the central project and are evaluated in written form on the basis of case study questions.
Managementaccounting:
The Financial aspects sessions will cover a wide variety of financial concepts that tie in with the subjects of purchasing and development of innovations. In so doing, the financial aspects of the Business Model Canvas will, for example, be covered. The sessions support the central project and are evaluated in written form on the basis of case study questions.

Learning outcomes:
The student:
Marketing
The student will analyse the market environment at the macro, meso and micro level and on that basis will develop a marketing strategy, with hospitality experience as the guiding principle (7)
The student will make use of the Business Model Canvas to give the marketing strategy concrete form and structure the service provision process (7,8)
Quality
The student will use various quality models and tools to implement and guarantee the future quality of service provision according to a front office/back office structure (7, 8, 9)
CSR
Identifies CSR developments and places these in a historical context(9)
Distinguishes and analyses conflicting CSR interests of the various stakeholders. (9)
Is capable of formulating ethical arguments in the area of sustainability, hospitality and health which play a role in CSR change processes in the context of facility services (9)
/en/course/2026/IFVB22DEV.content:
Development module
Marketing
The Marketing sessions provide the theoretical background to the Business Model Canvas in the context of Facility Management. In the seminars, the operation of the model, among other things, will be explained, and personas and hospitality concepts will be covered.
The sessions support the central project and are evaluated in written form on the basis of case study questions.
Quality of services
You will learn the basics of a quality mindset with the aid of quality models and standards. You will also learn how these models and norms can be applied in practice to guarantee the sustainability, healthfulness and hospitality of a service. The sessions support the central project and are evaluated in written form on the basis of case study questions.
Corporate Social Responsibility
Society is placing increasingly high demands on  organisations when it comes to their dealings with employees, customers and the environment.
Companies and organisations take this into consideration by means of Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR). In so doing, the organisation takes the 3 Ps of CSR into account in all of its activities: People, Planet, Profit. Attention will be paid to the reasons for CSR, to CSR and the market and to CSR reports. The sessions support the central project and are evaluated in written form on the basis of case study questions.

/en/course/2026/IFVB25PRJPCM.content:
In this semester, you will write a purchasing document for a service in which cooperation between the client and the contracted party plays a crucial role. You will do this based on a "challenge” (assignement from a client) as a member of a purchasing team. Next, you will also become a member of a development team and as a start-up, you will take on the "challenge” of a purchasing team and develop a new service using the purchasing document of that purchasing team. Whilst developing this new service, you will be a specialist in the area of sustainability, hospitality or health.
Both the purchasing process and the development process will be supported iteratively with the help of Scrum and Design Thinking.
For the entire semester, you will therefore have the role of purchaser and developer and you will put together a portfolio for both roles that contains (group)assignments and proof of your capabilities and development. The portfolios will also serve as input for the assessment meeting.

The student contributes, in line with the strategy of an organisation, to the (re)housing of the organisation, works this out from a hospitable, sustainable and healthy perspective, and acts as discussion partner for specialists in the field of building-related technological installations. The related learning outcomes are:
The student

(Healthy) outlines relevant concepts and trends in the field of health in relation to the built environment (and specifically building technology).
(Healthy) identifies how the health of users is influenced by the physical environment and describes how this environment can be made more healthy.
(Healthy) describes in their own words how different light, air, heat and water systems operate.
(Hospitable) can identify hospitality in the spatial environment and describes in their own words which factors can influence hospitality.
(Hospitable) indicates in which way the spatial environment can be influenced by means of  user behaviour and the physical environment in order to increase hospitality.
(Sustainable) outlines relevant concepts, trends and developments related to circularity in the field of space and technology.
(Sustainable) explains in their own words how a building and building systems can be managed circularly.
(Sustainable) explains in their own words which aspects in the field of circularity play a role in the creation of new housing.

The related learning outcomes are:
The student
:
(Finance) defines the concept of 'life cycle' of building-related installations and quantifies the associated life cycle costs.
(Finance) quantifies on the basis of a circular building both the benefits and burdens of this building and translates this into an investment budget and an operating budget'.
(Finance) calculates the added value of investments in a healthy, sustainable and hospitable building, assesses these and provides insight into the financial consequences for the operation.
(Management Information) analyses information collected by smart buildings (e.g. from building management systems and sensors) regarding the health of users, sustainability of the building and hospitality, and derives from this the actual building performance.
(Research) transforms theory about the topic to be researched (e.g. theory and literature about the project) into a feasible research question.
(Research) converts the research question into a measuring instrument with measurable survey or interview questions and collects and analyses data by means of the measuring instrument (10%).
(Research) evaluates at the end of a research project the measures that contribute to the five evaluation or quality criteria, construct validity, internal and external validity, reliability and usefulness.

2. Designs and justifies hospitality experiences that meet the needs of users and stakeholders.
The student translates research findings into a concrete, creative and feasible concept within the field of hospitality and facility management.
3. Demonstrates professional hospitality skills and communicates effectively in various professional situations.
The student demonstrates hospitable skills in interaction, collaboration and presentation, both verbally and non-verbally.
4. Adopts a professional, open and inclusive attitude in learning and practical situations.
The student demonstrates an awareness of diversity, ethical conduct and inclusivity, and applies these values in communication and decision-making.
5. Reflects critically on their own actions and demonstrates growth in personal leadership.
The student links reflections to behaviour in practical situations and develops their professional identity in a conscious and purposeful manner.
/en/course/2026/IFVB26PRO5.content:
Professional Skills focuses on strengthening professional hospitality skills and developing an inquisitive, design-oriented mindset. Students learn how to use design-led research to create meaningful and welcoming experiences within the field of Facility Management.
Through workshops, training sessions and practical assignments, students delve into hospitality skills, service design, communication, inclusivity and personal leadership. They apply theory and research methods directly in realistic situations, thereby developing a solid foundation for professional practice within the facilities sector.

/en/course/2026/IFVB24GRA1.content:
The student performs an analysis for an organisation and provides advice or a design for a complex facility issue. Supervision takes place in communities of learners in combination with workshops and organisational visits by the supervising lecturer. In the first phase of the programme, the assignment is developed into a graduation plan, on which the student receives feedback and which has to be approved.
The student presents the professional products to the client and collects feedback on his/her performance. The portfolio assessment covers the student's personal and professional development.

7. Pareto chart

/en/course/2026/ABVP26LAB1.outcomes:
Competences
Artistic Creation
Research & Reflection
Level 1: Orientation
A sufficient level is achieved when students demonstrate an insight into the nature of the profession, the significance of experimentation and research in acquiring the provided knowledge and skills and a potential for the ongoing acquisition of competencies.
Learning Outcomes
LO 2: Investigate
The student explores an artistic approach through a guided process of making, reflecting, and investigating given sources, references, and contexts, and formulates initial investigative artistic ideas.
LO 3: Materialise
As part of a guided process, the student explores material, form, intuition, reflection, and contemplation, and experiments with materials, techniques, and technologies, shaping an emerging understanding of their properties and effects.
/en/course/2026/ABVP26LAB1.content:
In Labs 1 and 2, students explore the role of materiality, technology and experimentation within artistic practice. Through hands-on assignments, they investigate a range of materials, techniques, tools and media, and learn how these shape artistic processes and outcomes.
The programme introduces students to different workshops and domains, fostering an open and inquisitive attitude towards making. Students experiment, test, and iterate, discovering how materials behave, how techniques can be applied, and how technological processes influence form and meaning.
Working closely with professional artists and workshop specialists, students become part of a make-and-learn community, where exchange, collaboration and shared experimentation are central. They produce multiple studies and outcomes, focusing on process as much as result.
The Theory component supports students in reflecting on material choices, technological developments and sustainability, and in understanding how these relate to contemporary artistic practices.
At this level, the emphasis lies on exploration and orientation: developing basic technical skills, material awareness and experimental working methods, while beginning to connect material processes to artistic intention and context.

metadata.Language: Dutch, with parts in English, English

/en/course/2026/ABVP26STU1.outcomes:
Competences
Connecting to the Environment
Research & Reflection
Artic Creation
Level 1: Orientation
A sufficient level is achieved when students demonstrate an insight into the nature of the profession, the significance of experimentation and research in acquiring the provided knowledge and skills and a potential for the ongoing acquisition of competencies.
Learning Outcomes
LO 1: Relate
The student notices and initially engages with sensations, perceptions, intuitions, environments, and social contexts, recognizing them as potential starting points for artistic work.
LO 2: Investigate
The student explores an artistic approach through a guided process of making, reflecting, and investigating given sources, references, and contexts, and formulates initial investigative artistic ideas.
LO 3: Materialise
As part of a guided process, the student explores material, form, intuition, reflection, and contemplation, and experiments with materials, techniques, and technologies, shaping an emerging understanding of their properties and effects.
/en/course/2026/ABVP26STU1.content:
In the first year, Studio introduces students to artistic practice as an exploratory, research-driven, and reflective process. Working in a studio-based environment, students develop fundamental skills in artistic creation, investigation, and positioning through making, experimenting, and reflecting. Students explore a wide range of contemporary artistic practices and learn to understand the studio as a flexible space: physical, social, and contextual.
In Studio 1, the emphasis is on orientation: initiating a work process, experimenting with approaches to making, and formulating initial artistic questions. Students begin to document their process and develop a study portfolio.
In Studio 2, students gradually take more ownership of their learning process. They work consistently with a Study Plan, learning to make choices, set directions, and reflect on their development.
The Theory component supports this process through practice-led research, critical reflection, and dialogue. Students learn to connect making with thinking, engage with multiple perspectives, and articulate their work in relation to artistic, social and ecological contexts. Participation in lectures, discussions, and public events introduces students to contemporary discourse and supports the development of an emerging artistic position.

/en/course/2026/ABVP26PPR1.outcomes:
Competences
Connecting to the Environment
Research & Reflection
Working in Practice
Level 1: Orientation
A sufficient level is achieved when students demonstrate an insight into the nature of the profession, the significance of experimentation and research in acquiring the provided knowledge and skills and a potential for the ongoing acquisition of competencies.
Learning Outcomes
LO 4: Position
The student recognises different artistic positions within artistic, cultural, social, and global contexts and, with guidance, identifies perspectives, differences, and sensitivities, beginning to relate their own work to these positions in a descriptive and exploratory way.
LO 5: Practice
The student participates in artistic processes and collaborative activities within guided contexts, shares work in supported settings, and begins to explore professional practice through basic presentations and introductory forms of collaboration and audience engagement.
/en/course/2026/ABVP26PPR1.content:
Professional Practice 1 and 2 introduce students to the foundations of working as an artist within a broader artistic and societal context. The course supports the development of study skills, professional attitudes and an awareness of artistic positioning.
Students learn to organise their work process, manage time, and develop effective working habits. Through guided assignments, they reflect on their strengths, interests and areas for growth, and learn to formulate and monitor their development through a Study Plan.
The programme emphasises communication, collaboration, and feedback. Students actively participate in discussions, learn to articulate their ideas, and develop skills in verbal, written, and visual presentation.
The Theory component provides a contextual framework by introducing key moments, perspectives and debates in art and cultural history. Students learn to analyse artworks, engage with different sources, and understand how artistic practices relate to historical, social, and contemporary contexts.
By connecting historical insight, reflection, and practice, students begin to position their own work in relation to others and to the world, forming a basis for developing a sustainable and self-directed artistic practice.

metadata.Language: Dutch, with parts in English, English

/en/course/2026/ABVB26LAB3.outcomes:
Competences
Artistic creation
Research & Reflection
Level 2:
Deepening & Enriching
A sufficient level is achieved when students deliberately choose their own solutions for problems or assignments with a divergent nature, and when they demonstrate the ability to employ relevant competences, skill, and knowledge in doing so, based on research and experiment.
Learning Outcomes
LO 2: Investigate
The student develops an artistic and conceptual approach through an increasingly independent and focused process of making, reflecting, and researching, in which relevant sources, references, and contexts are examined, and first artistic concepts and propositions are articulated.
LO 3: Materialise
As part of an increasingly independent artistic process, the student purposefully engages with material, form, intuition, reflection, and contemplation, and investigates the qualities and possibilities of different materials, techniques and technologies, showing a gradual awareness of how these shape the development and meaning of their work.
/en/course/2026/ABVB26LAB3.content:
In Labs 3 & 4, students further develop their understanding of materiality, media, and technology by making more focused and intentional choices within their artistic practice. Students select specific materials, techniques, or visual domains to investigate in depth, starting from their own learning questions. Through iterative experimentation, they test, combine, and transform materials and processes in relation to their artistic intentions.
The Labs programme functions as a catalyst for Studio, enabling students to expand and challenge their artistic questions through material and technical exploration. Students develop more individual working methods and gain insight into how material processes contribute to meaning, form and concept.
Working with workshop specialists and artists, students deepen their technical skills while maintaining an experimental and research-oriented approach. Exchange and collaboration contribute to a shared learning environment.
The Theory component addresses contemporary material practices, technological developments, and sustainability, supporting students in making informed and responsible choices within their work.
The Labs 3 & 4 programme is offered jointly with third-year students (Labs 5).

LO 2: Investigate

/en/course/2026/ABVB26STU3.content:
In the second year, the Studio programme deepens the student’s artistic practice through self-directed experimentation, practice-based research, and critical reflection. Students expand their working methods and begin to make deliberate artistic choices based on their own questions, interests, and emerging artistic position.
In Studio 3, students explore different approaches to making and research, testing directions and investigating the relationship between concept, material, and context. Through iterative processes of experimentation, analysis and reflection, they develop an emerging personal working method and begin to formulate their own criteria.
In Studio 4, students consolidate their direction by developing more coherent bodies of work. They take increased ownership of their process, articulate intentions, and make informed decisions regarding form, presentation and context.
The Theory component supports practice-based research, documentation and critical dialogue, enabling students to articulate their work in relation to conceptual, theoretical, and material perspectives.

LO 4: Position

LO 5: Practice
The student organises aspects of their artistic process and collaborates within a developing practice, shares work through targeted presentations and emerging networking, and makes initial choices in relation to audience, presentation formats, and professional development toward a more self-directed and sustainable practice.
/en/course/2026/ABVB26PPR3.content:
Professional Practice 3 and 4 support students in developing a more conscious and articulated artistic position within a broader professional and societal context. The focus is on self-directed development, contextual awareness, and communication. Students take increasing responsibility for organising their practice, formulating goals, and making strategic choices. They reflect on their development in relation to their artistic ambitions and begin to position themselves within the field.
The programme addresses different roles and positions of the artist, as well as the structures and stakeholders that shape the contemporary art world. Students engage with external contexts through activities such as field trips, exhibitions, and professional encounters.
They develop skills in presentation, communication, and contextual research, learning to articulate their work in written, verbal, and visual forms, and to engage in dialogue with diverse audiences.
The Theory component deepens students’ understanding of historical and contemporary discourses, enabling them to relate their work to broader cultural and societal perspectives, and to critically position themselves within these contexts

/en/course/2026/ABVB26LAB5.content:
In Labs 5, students further deepen their engagement with materiality, media, and technology by applying their knowledge and skills in a more independent and purposeful manner.
Starting from their own artistic questions, students select and investigate specific materials, techniques or domains in depth. Through iterative experimentation, they refine their ability to translate conceptual intentions into material and technical processes, and to critically evaluate the outcomes.
The Labs programme continues to function as a catalyst for Studio, supporting the development of a coherent artistic practice through material exploration. Students increasingly integrate technical decisions into their broader artistic strategies.
Working alongside students from different year levels, they engage in exchange and peer learning, contributing to a dynamic and collaborative workshop environment. Guidance by specialists supports both technical refinement and experimental approaches.
The Theory component addresses advanced material practices, technological developments and sustainability, enabling students to make informed, critical and responsible choices within contemporary artistic contexts.
The Labs 5 programme is offered jointly with second-year students (Labs 3).

/en/course/2026/ABVB26PPR5.content:
Professional Practice 5 focuses on strengthening students’ ability to position themselves and operate within the professional art field. The emphasis is on strategic development, contextual awareness, and public engagement. Students deepen their understanding of the structures, dynamics, and stakeholders of the art world, including the role of the art market and institutional contexts. They reflect on how these influence artistic practice and explore strategies for cultural entrepreneurship, both individually and collaboratively.
A central component of the course is the development, curation, and presentation of work in an external context, where students gain hands-on experience with professional presentation, collaboration, and audience engagement.
Students further refine their skills in communication and contextual research, learning to articulate their work and intentions in written, verbal, and visual forms, and to engage critically with diverse audiences.
The Theory component supports students in relating their work to historical and contemporary discourses, enabling them to take a more explicit and critical position within the artistic and societal field.

/en/course/2026/AMVB26PLEX1.outcomes:
Level Deepening (semester 3-7): The student shows insight into the importance of design and theoretical research and experiment for the acquisition of knowledge and skills and succeeds in giving shape to this.
3. CONNECTING WITH THE ENVIRONMENT
The student takes position as an artist/designer, both in terms of content and relation, in the (international) contexts in which he works.
The student's positioning is well-considered and is embodied in the work and working method. To this end, the student conducted research.
The student can make the value of this positioning clear in the context in which the student works. The student is able to deal with changing circumstances and different approaches to making and designing art in a resilient and agile way by being open to and acquiring new knowledge, insights and skills.
Artists/designers work in relation to and together with others. Collaboration, exchange and communication are crucial in the work process. The student actively seeks connections with others in order to advance their work. The student has insight into various forms of (collective) partnerships, both within and outside their own field.
In collaborations, the student can make an appropriate contribution and make their own voice heard, and deal inclusively with the different roles, relationships, motivations, responsibilities, interests, voices and specific qualities.
The student develops an understanding of the role that artists/designers can have in simple, interdependent systems. The student investigates one's own role as a maker in work and production processes and the implications of this for people, the environment and
society. In this way, the student sharpens the awareness that one's own work and work process are part of a larger, also international, whole: society, nature, history. In addition, the student relates to the world with work and working methods, in which ecological, technological, social and economic issues and transitions play a role.
4. WORKING IN A PRACTICE
The student is able to create conditions for his or her own work practice, in line with his/her own positioning. To this end, the student is able to organize and communicate with others.
In order to be able to work as an artist and designer in practice, the student organizes a suitable working environment. The student knows how to facilitate their own work processes and can create a safe working environment. The student deals with the physical and social working conditions in an agile way and adjusts the conditions of the working environment where necessary.
It takes self-confidence and courage to create the right working conditions, to claim time and artistic freedom, to negotiate finances, to be enterprising and to be enterprising, and to take a role in collaborations. The student has insight into this and develops confidence in their own positioning, qualities and ambitions.
It also requires empathy, inventiveness and imagination to see possibilities and opportunities in the field and to face them. The student takes initiatives to find work, for example by initiating and acquiring assignments and projects, but also by working together, exchanging knowledge and developing new forms of working practices.
/en/course/2026/AMVB26PLEX1.content:
Switchboard refers to a switching point in the study. You made preparations in semester 5 and formulated a learning question that is central for the choice you make in semester 6.
You can then choose from one of the options to go out into the world and encounter an aspect of the professional field. This gives you the space to develop a stronger profile. You have a switch board coach that guides you.

can choose from various options: internship, Major of choice, exchange, minor, research project at a research center within the Hanze, Out There and H.A.L. This course description is about the

/en/course/2026/ABVB26LAB7.content:
Research & Writing Lab supports students in developing a focused and independent research trajectory that is closely connected to their artistic practice and leads towards the Graduation Research.
Students identify and formulate relevant research questions arising from their work and conduct in-depth investigation into conceptual, theoretical, and contextual aspects of their artistic domain. They learn to select appropriate methodologies and sources, and to position their research within broader artistic and societal discourses.
Emphasis is placed on the integration of practice and reflection: students critically analyse their own work process and outcomes, and articulate the interrelation between concept, material, context and effect. The course develops advanced skills in writing, analysis, and presentation, including the formulation of an artist statement and the production of structured research texts. Students are guided in adopting appropriate writing styles and in communicating their ideas clearly and critically.
Through this process, students establish a solid foundation for their Graduation Research and further develop their ability to position themselves as reflective practitioners within the field.

/en/course/2026/MIVP24MOD11.content:
In this module, we focus on the (un)sustainability of the current healthcare system. The challenges in healthcare and social welfare are addressed through various themes. The themes are addressed through various teaching methods and assignments. You will become acquainted with the format and content of the higher professional education program, with the people who work there, and, of course, with each other; your fellow students who have also chosen the MiZ program. Collaborative learning is at the heart of the program, and a good relationship with your fellow students and the staff is crucial. The way the program is structured immediately demonstrates that you have to work together, yet you are assessed as an individual.
The professional themes central to this module are:
Leading oneself and others
Developing and connecting
Context/society

This module focuses on healthcare and welfare organizations in a changing society. A key message of this module is that when working with an individual, team, or organization, you always consider the context in your analysis. By context, we mean the environment that gives meaning to the individual, team, or organization. In module 2, you focused on "the organization," but now we'll zoom out and examine the societal context and developments within it. The professional themes central to this module are:
Leading oneself and others
Change and transformation
Context/society

/en/course/2026/MIVP22MOD14.content:
This module focuses on the importance of technological innovations (care technology) in the healthcare and social care sectors. Can care technology make a meaningful contribution and/or add value to the quality of care and social care? Is technology capable of reversing the ever-increasing cost of healthcare in the Dutch budget? And if the answer to one or both questions is "yes," how should we achieve this effectively? Can people, both care recipients and healthcare and social care workers, become accustomed to the technological possibilities available? How do you ensure that people become familiar with technology and begin to see and/or experience its value for themselves or their loved ones? And what about themes such as safety, ethics, and the perceived quality of care? The professional themes that are central to this module are:
Leading oneself and others
Innovation and entrepreneurship
Context/society

/en/course/2026/MIVB24MOD21.content:
This semester you will work together in a project group on an (innovation) issue/case of a healthcare and/or welfare organization. You will do this according to the Design Thinking method.
The phases of Design Thinking: empathize (empathy), define (understand), ideate (idea formation) and prototype will be central during the lessons. During this semester you will map users/stakeholders. You will get to know the organization and the user/client by observing, having conversations and analyzing documents. You will come up with ideas for the case and make prototypes in co-creation. You will also work on recognizing interaction patterns between people and systems. In the meantime, you work on your creative mindset and learn to deal with (your own) assumptions. With all these components, you will have formed your vision on innovation in healthcare and welfare at the end of this semester.
Professional themes this semester:
Entrepreneurship
Research

Leading self and others

/en/course/2026/MIVB24MODSTAGE.content:
A key principle of the Healthcare Management program is that the learning context is intertwined with the work context. Professional practices in healthcare, social services, and the societal domain are key and are incorporated into the program as much as possible through practical training.
During their studies, students are challenged to become acquainted with various organizations in addition to their own or future professional practice and to examine issues from different perspectives, including societal challenges (LOP, 2025). Therefore, practical training is a key component of the Healthcare Management program. In the third year, 20 weeks are dedicated to learning within the professional context of healthcare and social services. During these 20 weeks, students focus on achieving the above-mentioned PLUs and the learning objectives they have established.
The following professional themes are central:
Organizing

Leading Oneself and Others
Context of Healthcare and Social Services
Developing and Connecting
Innovating and Entrepreneuring

/en/course/2026/MIVB22MOD41IWW.content:
Besides simple problems, which can be easily defined and broken down into manageable pieces and solved, we also encounter complex issues. These are more difficult to grasp and not easy to solve. A key characteristic of complex problems is that they involve various stakeholders with different perspectives and interests. Complex issues can also be defined and interpreted in different ways, cannot be broken down into smaller problems, and can lead to very different solutions that, in turn, trigger subsequent problems. Complex problems develop unpredictably (Berkel and Manickam, 2019).
Existing problem-solving approaches and traditional change management approaches, which are suitable for simple problems, are insufficient for dealing with complex issues. A different approach is needed, one that allows us to embrace the complexity and persistence of complex problems. Consider a systems approach, which creates possibilities for new interventions. This offers a different perspective on policy formulation, strategy, change, planning, organization, leadership, and collaboration (Berkel and Manickam, 2019).
Because several complex issues are simultaneously at play in the world of healthcare and social work, this module was named "A Wicked World."
Students will gain a deeper understanding of the theory of complexity and systems thinking. Theory is alternated with practice, with attention also paid to their own role and professional identity as a future professional. On the one hand, we focus on themes that transcend organizations, with a focus on public health and the complex issues that come with it. In addition, students also demonstrate how to handle more straightforward organizational issues. This latter is demonstrated in an intensive master's thesis. Finally, the module concludes with a retrospective and reflection.

/en/course/2026/MIVB22MOD42PROND.outcomes:
Course content
This graduation module focuses on conducting practice-oriented research. Practice-oriented research aims to contribute to innovating and improving healthcare and prevention. Throughout the course, elements of research have been discussed that provide tools for the graduation research. In this phase of the training, research is continued and deepened. The focus is on further developing a critical and investigative attitude and learning research skills. To achieve this, two specialisations are offered: diagnostic and design research.
The graduation research is an integral assignment that brings together the knowledge and experience of recent years. With the graduation research we aim for the student to be demonstrably able to set up and carry out coherent practice-oriented research at the end of the course.
This module focuses on the following main theme:
Research
The student analyzes the complex practical issue within the domain of healthcare and welfare in co-creation with relevant stakeholders.
The student uses an appropriate research approach for the practical issue and substantiates it.
The student determines, with relevant stakeholders, new ideas in a methodical manner, planning products with regard to the complex practical issue.
The student contributes to creating impact in practice through practice-oriented research.
The student demonstrates a reflective attitude towards his or her own role as a novice professional and towards the research process.
/en/course/2026/MIVB22MOD42PROND.content:
After the preparation, the implementation of practice-oriented research starts.
In this phase of the graduation research you work in a methodical way on the following phases of the research cycle: data collection, data analysis, conclusions & recommendations and reporting & presentation.
The practice-oriented research is concluded with the writing of a research report and a presentation with defense of the graduation research.

/en/course/2026/MILB23KEUZEINTER.content:
Healthcare faces a number of challenges both in the Netherlands and internationally.
In the elective module internationalization, students can research themes from international healthcare in groups. It is clear that different countries make different choices. This can be related to financial possibilities, but also to culture and political choices. During this elective module, the situation in another country (or countries) can be compared with the Dutch one. This is done during this module by organizing a study trip. In recent years, students have been to Sweden, England, Germany and Belgium, Norway, for example. Visiting healthcare institutions and/or policy-making bodies on site provides a nuanced picture.
Own direction and responsibility.
The study trip is organized by the students themselves and you as a group are responsible for the success of the trip. This starts with establishing contacts and dividing up tasks. Making good agreements is essential here.
Additional costs
For the elective module internationalization, additional costs will often be incurred, many of which are not covered by regular financing. Take into account a personal contribution (possibly partly by the employer). The cost aspect (and financing) must be included in a planning/budget.

/en/course/2026/MILB23KEUZEZENT.outcomes:
The following learning outcomes are tested in the module Care & Technology:
Based on a practical issue in the field of care and technology, the student draws up a plan together with fellow students to investigate this further.
Based on the planning, the student plans, coordinates and monitors the progress with the aim of effective cooperation and feasibility of the activities.
The student collects and analyses information about the issue and can substantiate the usability for the research with the aim of coming up with a proposal that the client can use.
The student carries out the activities (work visits, etc.) for the purpose of further research and is able to connect the previously acquired information and new information with the aim of forming a complete picture of the theme.
Based on the information obtained, the student comes up with a substantiated proposal about the issue and the relevance for other organisations and their own work context.
In addition, the student submits a process report with an emphasis on their own/role contribution.
/en/course/2026/MILB23KEUZEZENT.content:
The student can choose activities from the range of electives that is determined each year. In recent years, this was for example:
Internationalization
Healthcare and Technology
It is also possible to develop activities yourself that fit within the theme of Management in Healthcare. The number of ECs will be determined per activity.
Content elective module Healthcare & Technology
In this elective module, students will work on practical issues in the field of Care and Technology. This is not about technological devising or developing, but about the question of how existing technology can be applied or deployed to support/solve issues in Care and Welfare. The reason can be diverse: from healthcare-related issues to solutions for staff shortages.
In addition to the technological innovation itself, there is always an implementation issue. Which lessons from change management can be included in the implementation of technological solutions? How can the innovative capacity with regard to technology be increased? What is needed to get the various relevant stakeholders on board, so that the innovation will actually be used, etc.
In this elective module, you will work together with other students on a practical issue in the field of Care and Technology. You will work as a group, which also means a focus on collaboration and organization among each other and coordination with the client. At the start of the elective module, stakeholders clarify the issue and there is room to ask additional questions. Students then work in groups on the issue based on question articulation.
