/en/course/2026/HRVH3TDY.outcomes:
In this course unit, the following learning-path-independent learning outcomes (LILs) will be achieved:
LIL 1: Professional Conduct
The starting HR professional demonstrates personal leadership and operates from a professional attitude. You demonstrate that you possess a professional attitude. This means your behavior shows that you are further developing in the following five facets: Professional Development, Personal Effectiveness, Ethical Conduct, Environmental and Organizational Sensitivity, and Communication and Collaboration. This implies that you possess the underlying knowledge required for this, allowing you to develop your professional identity.
LIL 4: Learning and Development
As a starting HR professional, you initiate and realize the desired development of individual employees, teams, and (departments of) the organization based on current and future needs in collaboration with stakeholders, ensuring that the continuous development of the organization as a whole is supported to enhance the agility of employees within the organization.
LIL 6: Research and Decision-making
As a starting HR professional, you prepare decisions regarding the deployment of HRM and/or organizational adjustments based on collected and analyzed data from practice and from current and recognized theory, ensuring that the proposed adjustments are well-founded and transparent.
/en/course/2026/HRVH3TDY.content:
Content
:
The HR profession is about people, work, and organizations. Work is often organized in teams. This means that an HR professional must not only have knowledge of individual psychology and business administration, but also of team dynamics.
In this course, you will delve into theories about teams. When do we call a group a team? What distinguishes successful teams from mediocre ones? What is the effect of diversity within a team? How do power, status, and leadership play a role? And, useful to know as an advisor: which levers can you pull when things aren't going well?
We will use this knowledge to analyze real-world situations. We do this through case studies, but also based on your own experiences working in groups and teams. By the end of this course, you will have developed the skills and knowledge needed to analyze and solve issues related to teamwork.

/en/course/2026/ITVP20INF.outcomes:
The student explains basic network architecture concepts and their components.
The student is able to describe both the TCP/IP protocol stack and the OSI model, and analyze the functions of each layer within these architectures.
The student identifies and compares important Internet protocols such as HTTP, SMTP, DHCP, DNS, TCP, UDP, and IP, and explains their use cases.
The student analyzes transport layer services and explains how applications utilize them in network communication.
The student is able to identify subnets and explain how a network can be divided into suitably sized subnets.
The student identifies basic network security threats and proposes appropriate mitigation techniques.
The student communicates and acts with knowledge of his own cultural background and culturally determined values ​​and norms within a pre-structured, international IT context.
The student expresses himself orally and in writing in English at level B2 in a pre-structured IT context.
The student is aware of ethical dilemmas and themes within ICT processes and takes this into account in his argumentation in a defined IT context.
/en/course/2026/ITVP20INF.content:
In the
Infrastructure and Security
course, we explore the fundamental question:
How does the Internet work, and how can we use it securely?
This course covers essential topics, including
Wi-Fi, Internet Protocol (IP), DHCP, HTTP, DNS, TCP, UDP, and Encapsulation.
The primary objective is to provide students with a foundational understanding of the
OSI and TCP/IP models,
focusing on their structures, functions, and associated protocol suites. Students will learn to distinguish between these models, comprehend how each layer contributes to network communication, and evaluate the security aspects of these layers.
The course is delivered using a
blended learning model
, with a strong emphasis on
practical sessions.
Note that there are
no traditional lectures
; instead, students will explore the theoretical concepts of this course through self-study.
Our journey through this course aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of the
how, what, and why
of computer networks. The weekly topics guide the roadmap for this learning experience:
Computer Networks and the Internet
Application Layer
Transport Layer
Network Layer
Link Layer
Network Security
Because you can also work with international clients and colleagues in the business world, this course focuses on your English language skills, which is combined with ethics. As a security expert, it is important to be aware of ethical dilemmas in the area of, for example, privacy. By discussing these types of themes, you work on developing a critical attitude.

/en/course/2026/BPVM26RIB1C.outcomes:
Students:
1. Define a theoretically grounded research problem on a selected topic.
2. Develop and justify research question(s).
3. Conduct critical and analytical literature review, synthesising and evaluating academic sources from multiple business disciplines.
4. Evaluate and select appropriate research designs and rigorous methods aligned with the research question(s).
5. Structure and develop a full academic research proposal using appropriate academic language and scholarly conventions.
Contribution to Programme Learning Outcomes (PLOs):
CLO1 contributes to PLO1 Research
CLO2 contributes to PLO1 Research
CLO3 contributes to PLO1 Research and PLO3 Interdisciplinary Approach
CLO4 contributes to PLO1 Research
CLO5 contributes to PLO5 Communication
/en/course/2026/BPVM26RIB1C.content:
Strategic Focus Areas:
Entrepreneurship, Global Mindset and Sustainability
To conduct rigorous applied research, a strong theoretical and methodological foundation is required, supported by critical engagement with academic literature. The course Research in Business (RIB) develops students’ ability to conduct applied research in an interdisciplinary context, through systematic analysis of scholarly articles and methodological reasoning. The course is the first component of the curriculum of the IBP master program. Students learn to use academic literature, build arguments, and engage with different research methods. The course places particular emphasis on the intervention cycle.
The outcome of the course is a full research proposal demonstrating students’ ability to design a rigorous research study based on sound methodological principles. This proposal forms the foundation for the Innovation Assignment (INA) in the first semester and supports students’ research preparation for the master’s thesis in the second semester.
This course contributes to SDGs 4, 8, 9, 11, 12, 16 and 17.

/en/course/2026/BPVM26INA1.outcomes:
Students:
1. Analyse a complex organisational or societal challenge using relevant data, research insights, and appropriate analytical tools to define a clear problem or opportunity.
2. Integrate perspectives, theories, and methods from multiple business disciplines to develop coherent insights and solution directions.
3. Design an innovative and sustainable solution that creates organisational and/or societal value, taking into account feasibility, risks, and stakeholder needs.
4. Work effectively in an interdisciplinary team and engage professionally with internal and external stakeholders throughout the project process.
5. Define and justify relevant impact indicators (economic, social, and environmental) to evaluate the proposed solution.
6. Communicate, critically reflect on, and defend the project approach, supporting evidence, proposed solution, and intended impact in a professional academic format.
CLO1 contributes to PLO1: Research
CLO2 contributes to PLO3: Interdisciplinary Approach
CLO3 contributes to PLO2: Innovation & Entrepreneurship
CLO4 contributes to PLO4: Professional Development & Leadership
CLO5 contributes to PLO1: Research and PLO2: Innovation & Entrepreneurship
CLO6 contributes to PLO4: Professional Development & Leadership and PLO5: Communication
/en/course/2026/BPVM26INA1.content:
Strategic Focus Areas:
Entrepreneurship, Global Mindset and Sustainability
The Innovation Assignment (INA) is a course in which students work in interdisciplinary teams on real-life complex challenges sourced from professional practice or research partners. Students apply and extend their research knowledge and skills acquired in Research in Business, integrating theory and practice to develop an evidence-based, innovative solution.
The course begins with a networking event where students engage with external stakeholders to acquire a project assignment. They then follow an applied innovation and research process structured around systems thinking, problem analysis, ideation, design thinking, stakeholder analysis, value creation, validation, and impact definition.
Students develop integrated solutions by combining disciplinary perspectives and collaborating across backgrounds, with emphasis on synthesising knowledge, analysing complexity, and creating coherent and actionable solutions with societal and/or organisational value.
The course culminates in a portfolio of assessed work, including a capstone research-based academic poster, pitch, and defense, in which students present and justify their research, approach, solution design, and impact.
This course contributes to SDGs 7, 8, 9, 11, 12, and 17.

/en/course/2026/BPVM26BKS1.outcomes:
Students:
1. Compare and critically evaluate theories, models and concepts from different disciplines
2. Demonstrate knowledge of the central BOKS themes.
3. Analyse a complex case study from a business perspective, integrating relevant fields relevant within the BOKS.
4. Interpret and critically analyze choices made within a business case, demonstrating corresponding knowledge of the literature.
5. Draw conclusions and formulate recommendations on a business case, supported by corresponding knowledge of the literature.

/en/course/2026/BPVM26BKS1.content:
Strategic Focus Areas: Entrepeneurship, Global Mindset and Sustainability
Body of Knowledge and Skilss (BKS) is a course in which students build an interdisciplinary frame of reference that supports their work across the MIBP programme. The course is organized around the Body of Knowledge and Skills (BOKS), which is structured into six themes: Transition Management, Sustainability, New Business & ICT, Globalisation & Localisation, Innovation & Entrepreneurship, and Organisational Design & Change.
Through workshops, guest lectures, guided reading, and case-based discussions, students engage with key theories, models, and concepts within each theme. They learn to move from broader perspectives toward the more specific lenses needed for their Innovation Assignment and master's Thesis. A central focus is the ability to compare and critically evaluate alternative theories, models, and conceptualizations rather than simply reproduce them.
Students apply these skills to a business case, analyzing the situation from a business perspective while drawing on relevant fields within the BOKS. They interpret choices made within the case in relation to the relevant literature and develop evidence-based conclusions and recommendations.
The course concludes with an individual oral exam in which students demonstrate their command of the BOKS themes and their ability to reason across disciplines.
This course contributes to SDGs 4, 7, 8, 9, 11, 12 and 13

/en/course/2026/BPVM26PSK1C.content:
Strategic Focus Areas: Entrepeneurship and Global Mindset.
In the Professional Skills Development & Leadership (PSKL) course, students develop their learning process towards becoming interdisciplinary business professionals.
This course focuses on continuous professional development through reflection on behaviour, values, personality, leadership style, diversity & inclusion, and conflict style in a social and professional context, leading to increased self-awareness of strengths and areas for development.
Based on this, students build their leadership toolkit and experiment with new behaviours in workshops and practice-based experiences, supported by feedback and reflection.
Progress and development are documented in a portfolio, which forms the basis for assessment through an interview in which students demonstrate achievement of the course learning outcomes and their development process.
This course links to SDG 4; 8 and 16

/en/course/2026/BPVM26THE1C.outcomes:
Students:
1. Formulate and justify a complex organizational or societal problem by critically analyzing relevant academic literature, data, and contextual factors, resulting in a clearly defined research objective and questions.
2. Critically integrate theories, concepts, and methods from multiple business disciplines (and, where relevant, adjacent fields) to develop a coherent analytical framework for addressing the research problem.
3. Design and execute an appropriate research methodology, demonstrating methodological justification, data integrity, and appropriate analytical skills in generating valid and reliable findings.
4. Develop and critically evaluate evidence-based, innovative, and sustainable solutions or insights that create organizational and/or societal value, explicitly considering feasibility, risks, stakeholder implications, and their economic, societal, and environmental impact. Translate findings into actionable, contextually appropriate recommendations for practice.
5. Demonstrate ethical awareness, professional responsibility, and critical reflection throughout the research process, including responsible stakeholder engagement and data handling, and justification of methodological choices, limitations, and implications.
6. Communicate and defend the research process, findings, and recommendations effectively across multiple formats, adapting content, argumentation, and style to the purpose and audience of each output in academic and professional contexts.
CLO1 contributes to PLO1: Research
CLO2 contributes to PLO3: Interdisciplinary Approach
CLO3 contributes to PLO1: Research
CLO4 contributes to PLO2: Innovation & Entrepreneurship
CLO5 contributes to PLO4: Professional Development & Leadership
CLO6 contributes to PLO5: Communication
/en/course/2026/BPVM26THE1C.content:
Strategic Focus Areas: Entrepeneurship, Global Mindset and Sustainability
The Master Thesis is the proof by which students demonstrate their ability to independently make a substantial contribution towards the solution of a complex problem in an interdisciplinary professional context. The thesis is written in the form of a Journal Article Style Thesis (JAST), meaning that students produce an academic paper in a journal article format. As Business Professional with an MSc title, students are able to conceive innovative solutions that are relevant for the profession and based on relevant academic insights.
​
The thesis is a commissioner-driven, supervised learning process. To the extent possible, it simulates a professional work environment, emphasizing deadlines and professional standards for deliverables, as well as the need to make decisions and recommendations based on imperfect information. It recognizes the importance of being responsive to:
professional stakeholders, interested in the solution;
academic advances and standards in the relevant field;
the interdisciplinary environment, which requires effective cooperation with others.
This course enables students to address one or more Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) through student defined, impact oriented research.

/en/course/2026/LBVP26DID1C.outcomes:
PLO1: International Business Opportunities
In this course, PLO1 is supported through Learning Line 1 by strengthening students’ capacity to work with evidence in international business contexts. Students develop skills to analyse and interpret data to inform managerial judgment. This enables them to identify and evaluate international business opportunities more effectively.
Specifically, in this course, students are expected to develop the following competencies:
Learning Line: Research & Data Analytics
CLO 1: Apply critical thinking and evidence-based reasoning to evaluate data, generate insights, and propose justified business decisions.
CLO 2: Conduct data analysis using digital tools to collect, interpret, and visualise information that supports informed and actionable managerial judgment.
PLO2: Business Transformation
This course positions students to engage with business transformation in a global and digitally mediated context. Learning Line 2 operationalises this focus by strengthening evidence-based business communication and professional development. It does so through structured quantitative reporting and the responsible use of digital and AI tools to support data-informed decisions.
Specifically, in this course, students are expected to develop the following competencies:
Learning Line: Global Mindset & Professional Development
CLO 1: Demonstrate digital and AI literacy to enhance the accuracy and ethical quality of data-informed decision-making.
PLO3: Relationship Management
In this course, students develop the ability to produce structured academic reports that present ideas in a coherent and logical manner, employ appropriate and precise professional language, incorporate source material effectively, and adhere to established academic conventions including formatting and accurate referencing.
Learning Line: Global Mindset & Professional Development
CLO 1: Produce a structured professional product that demonstrates quantitative and practical research skills in communicating data-driven business insights.
/en/course/2026/LBVP26DID1C.content:
This course equips students with the analytical and digital competencies to make data-informed business decisions in international contexts. By integrating critical thinking, digital literacy, ethical AI use, and professional English, students learn to analyse and communicate data-driven insights that guide responsible managerial action.
Aligned with SDG 8 (Decent Work and Economic Growth), the course prepares students to become future-oriented IB professionals who leverage digital and AI literacy to drive ethical, inclusive, and data-driven growth across international markets

/en/course/2026/LBVP26BES1C.outcomes:
PLO1: International Business Opportunities
In this course, students work in groups to make business decisions within a simulated environment, starting with business strategy, adapting to market changes, and making critical decisions across key business areas.

Personal and intercultural development sessions support the group's work process, while a business communication workshop equips students to effectively present their combined insights. Together, these elements foster responsible entrepreneurship and strategic thinking aligned with SDG 8: Decent Work and Economic Growth.

PLO1: International Business Opportunities
This course equips students with talent-management competencies that enable firms to identify and act on international business opportunities. Specifically, students will build HR and intercultural capabilities that support evidence-based people decisions across borders.

Learning Line 1:
Management
CLO1
: Students can develop an understanding of Human Resource (HR) processes in international contexts.
Learning Line 2:
Management + Global Mindset & Professional Development
CLO2
: Students can demonstrate knowledge and skills in the areas of cultural management and business communication, contributing to HR-related decisions.
PLO2: Business Transformation
This course focuses on talent management as a key factor of sustainable organisational change. Accordingly, students will build competencies that translate transformation principles into practice through the following learning lines and module learning outcomes:
Learning Line 1:
Management

: Students can put theory into practice and produce an actionable talent management plan for a fictional or actual company.​
Learning Line 2:
Management + Global Mindset & Professional Development

/en/course/2026/LBVP26GTM1C.content:
This course explores talent management in international business contexts, emphasising how organisations attract, develop, and retain talent across cultures to drive sustainable growth.
Students develop a global mindset through analysing HR processes, ensuring diversity and inclusion, integrating intercultural awareness, and creating strategic workforce planning in multinational settings.

/en/course/2026/LBVP26CPP1C.outcomes:
PLO1: International Business Opportunities
IB professionals thoroughly investigate the internal and external environment of the organisation on an international scale.
Learning line: Research and Data Analytics
CLO1: Students define and scope a consultancy problem using appropriate research approaches. They apply qualitative research methods (e.g. interviews, document analysis) and strategically use existing secondary and quantitative insights to support problem identification and analysis.
Learning line: Economics, Finance and Accounting
CLO2: Students apply financial and economic reasoning to evaluate trade-offs and assess cost implications within a dynamic macroeconomic and competitive environment.
Learning line: Management
CLO3: Students recognize and analyze relevant legal and regulatory frameworks, demonstrating awareness of compliance requirements and institutional constraints affecting business decisions.
PLO2: Business Transformation
IB professionals make recommendations as to how the organisation should be redesigned to successfully do business on an international scale in a responsible manner.
Learning line: Management
CLO1: Students design innovative, feasible, and sustainable business solutions, integrating financial, legal, and operational considerations, and translate them into a structured business development roadmap (implementation plan) suited to international and multicultural contexts.
PLO3:
Relationship Management
IB professionals build and maintain bridges and closely collaborate with stakeholders from diverse cultural and professional backgrounds using appropriate strategies.
Learning line: Management
CLO1: Communicate consultancy findings and recommendations structuring content logically and tailoring messages to different stakeholder audiences in a consultancy context.
PLO4: Self-Management
IB professionals manages themselves in complex surroundings and continuously develop their professionalism for the benefit of the organisation.
Learning line: Global mindset and professional development
CLO1: Students apply and demonstrate appropriate project management skills.
/en/course/2026/LBVP26CPP1C.content:
The Consultancy Plan Project (CPP) builds on the foundational knowledge students acquire in Semester 1, including organisational and consumer behaviour, human resource management, marketing, financial and managerial accounting, as well as secondary research and quantitative research methods (e.g., survey-based analysis). Students are also introduced to and expected to apply relevant legal concepts.
In Semester 2, CPP offers an integrative and applied learning experience in which students transfer and connect knowledge to a practical business consultancy context. Students work on a real‑world–inspired case that emphasises structured problem definition, analytical reasoning, and evidence‑based decision‑making.
The project incorporates key professional competencies such as B2B analysis, stakeholder management, and project management. Students apply qualitative research methods—including interviews and document analysis—and make purposeful use of secondary data and quantitative insights to support problem identification and root‑cause analysis.
Based on their findings, students develop a clear, realistic, and actionable implementation plan that outlines how the proposed solution can be effectively executed in a professional business environment.

/en/course/2026/LBVP26FAE1A.outcomes:

In this course, the student develops an intermediate understanding of financial and economic concepts to evaluate how firms create and sustain value through financial decisions.
Learning Line: Economics, Finance & Accounting:
CLO1: The student can use managerial finance concepts to assess the financial environment and firms’ financing choices in an international business context.
CLO2: The student can explain fundamental economic concepts, describe how markets operate, and analyse the effects of economic events on organisations and stakeholders.
PLO2: Business Transformation
In this course, the student learns to apply intermediate financial and economics insights to contribute to responsible, data-informed business transformation.
Learning Line:
Economics, Finance & Accounting:
CLO1: The student can apply financial analysis, working capital management and capital budgeting techniques to identify opportunities for improving sustainable business performance.
CLO2: The student can interpret economic trends and evaluate their implications for business operations and future opportunities.
/en/course/2026/LBVP26FAE1A.content: This course combines intermediate finance and economics to analyse how organisations create and sustain value through informed financial decision-making and an understanding of market dynamics. Students develop skills in working capital management, capital budgeting, and the interpretation of economic trends to assess business performance and future opportunities. The course supports entrepreneurship by strengthening data-driven evaluation of investment and growth options. It connects to sustainability and social impact through its focus on long-term performance and responsible resource allocation, aligning most strongly with SDG 8 (Decent Work and Economic Growth) and SDG 12 (Responsible Consumption and Production).

/en/course/2026/LBVP26GSC1C.outcomes:
PLO1: International Business Opportunities
In this course, the student develops an intermediate understanding of supply chain theory and related business functions to make informed, data-driven decisions in a complex simulated international business environment.
Learning Line:
Operations and Supply Chain:
CLO1: The student can analyse dynamic international supply chain environments and apply supply chain and logistics principles to make well-justified, data driven operational and strategic decisions in line with organisational goals.
Learning Line:
Management:
CLO2: The student can interpret and apply financial, marketing, supply chain and human resource information to support balanced, cross-functional decisions that align with the company’s overall strategy.
PLO2: Business Transformation
In this course, the student learns to integrate financial, operational, and human perspectives to improve organisational performance and work effectively in diverse, team-based business settings.
Learning Line:
Operations and Supply Chain:
CLO1: The student can monitor and evaluate supply chain and financial performance indicators to identify improvement opportunities and propose actions that strengthen operational efficiency and responsiveness.
Learning Line:
Management:
CLO2: The student can integrate insights from finance, marketing, and HRM to contribute to strategic alignment and responsible business transformation in an international context.
/en/course/2026/LBVP26GSC1C.content: This course combines Supply Chain Management theory and its application using a competitive simulation game to immerse students in managing supply chains across domestic and international markets. Teams make integrated decisions in supply chain management, finance, marketing, and HRM within a dynamic and uncertain environment. The international scope of the simulation strengthens a global mindset by developing intercultural awareness, collaboration, and communication in diverse teams. The course supports entrepreneurship by fostering strategic thinking and coordinated decision-making across business functions. Sustainability and social impact are addressed indirectly through responsible performance management in complex, resource-constrained business settings, with strongest relevance to SDG 8 (Decent Work and Economic Growth).

/en/course/2026/LBVP26IMS1C.outcomes:
PLO1: International Business Opportunities
The IB professional defines international business opportunities and recommends possible strategies for the organisation to create sustainable value for stakeholders.
To identify and capture international marketing opportunities (PLO1), students focus on the practical application of market intelligence and strategic planning for a real-world organization. This course bridges the gap between theoretical analysis and actionable growth strategies, teaching students how to evaluate a company's readiness for global expansion and formulate a data-driven path for foreign market entry.
Learning Line: Marketing
CLO 1: Apply marketing theories to evaluate business opportunities, analysing market fit, entry modes, and segmentation–targeting decisions.
CLO 2: Develop and justify a data-informed market entry plan that aligns company capabilities with target market dynamics and customer needs.
CLO 3: Generate innovative, feasible, and value-creating recommendations for international expansion.
PLO2: Business Transformation
Learning Line:
Economics, Finance & Accounting
CLO1: Students will be able to apply financial analysis and decision-making techniques to evaluate business opportunities, and assess the financial feasibility of business initiatives.
PLO3: Relationship Management
In this course, students further develop their ability to independently produce a structured and professionally written business report, communicating well-justified strategic insights in a clear, coherent, and audience-appropriate manner, while applying appropriate academic and professional conventions.
Learning Line: Global Mindset & Professional Development
CLO1: Students produce a structured and professional market entry report that communicates strategic recommendations in a clear and responsible manner to relevant stakeholders, integrating the conducted analysis.
PLO4: Self-Management
In this course, students analyse the legal context of an international market entry strategy for a real company, identifying potential risks and obligations, and develop a reasoned approach.
Learning line: Global mindset and professional development
CLO1: Students can apply international legal knowledge to address the legal risks and obligations involved in a real-world market entry scenario, demonstrating professional judgement and decision-making in complex business environments
/en/course/2026/LBVP26IMS1C.content:
This course teaches students how to conduct international market research for a real-world organization. The project integrates international marketing, finance, and law to create a comprehensive, actionable, and data-driven marketing plan.
Students analyse the strategic fit between an organization’s products and the international environment to justify their choice of market entry mode, positioning, and marketing mix. This planning process incorporates a deep understanding of underlying political and legal factors, specific regulatory requirements, and the management of legal liability.
Students consider the sustainable and ethical considerations of international expansion, which is linked to SDG 12: Responsible Consumption and Production.

/en/course/2026/LBVB26ABC1C.content:
This course provides students with an in‑depth understanding of advanced business consultancy practices and develops the practical competencies required to diagnose complex organisational challenges across diverse business domains. Students learn to design innovative, evidence‑based solutions suited to an international business environment. Throughout the course, strong emphasis is placed on critical thinking, applied business research, analytical problem‑solving, effective information management, collaborative teamwork, and professional communication with stakeholders.

It aligns particularly with SDG 12 (Responsible Consumption and Production) and SDG 8 (Decent Work and Economic Growth), encouraging students to consider the broader societal implications of consultancy recommendations.

/en/course/2026/LBVB26GBB1C.content:
This course focuses on developing essential skills for business professionals and enhancing international business awareness to achieve mutual business goals. /en/course/2026/LBVB26GPJ1C.outcomes:
After successful completion of the Graduation Project, students demonstrate the following integrated outcomes.
PLO 1 International Business Opportunities
The IB professional defines international business opportunities and recommends possible strategies for the organisation to create sustainable multi-sided value for stakeholders.
Learning line: Business domain relevant to project context (Economics, Finance & Accounting; Marketing; Management; Operations & Supply Chain; Entrepreneurship)
CLO1: Students can investigate the internal and external environment on an international scale and structure a complex organizational situation into a clear and bounded problem statement by integrating multiple perspectives, relevant evidence, and appropriate business theories into a coherent diagnostic framing.
Learning line: Research and Data Analytics
CLO2: Students can use disciplined research methods and diagnostic reasoning to collect, assess, and analyse relevant data in order to distinguish surface-level symptoms from underlying causes and generate reliable evidence for strategic decision-making.
PLO 2 Business Transformation
The IB professional contributes to business (systems) transitions and transformations in order to optimise sustainable international business practices.
Learning line: Management
CLO1: Students can synthesize research findings into coherent conclusions and formulate evidence-based recommendations that support sustainable business transformation within an international organizational context.
Learning line: Sustainability and Societal Impact
CLO2: Students can translate recommendations into an actionable implementation approach by considering execution, sustainability, and the impact of business transformation on internal and external stakeholders.
PLO 3 Relationship Management
The IB professional cultivates and manages internal and external relationships with culturally diverse stakeholders in a responsible manner in order to achieve (mutual) business goals.
Learning line: Management
CLO1: Students can effectively coordinate and manage relationships with diverse stakeholders by proactively engaging with the organization, aligning expectations, and building the necessary support to facilitate the project's progress.
Learning line: Global Mindset and Professional Development
CLO2: Students can communicate and defend complex business insights persuasively in English, demonstrating high levels of intercultural sensitivity by adapting their argumentation and style to the specific cultural and professional context of the audience.
PLO 4 Self-Management
The IB professional manages themselves in complex surroundings and continuously develop their professionalism for the benefit of the organisation, the field of international business and themselves.
Learning line: Entrepreneurship
CLO1: Students independently govern the full graduation process, demonstrating ownership of decisions, resilience in the face of uncertainty, and the ability to act as a self-starting professional who adapts to changing organizational contexts.
Learning line: Global Mindset and Professional Development
CLO2: Students can critically reflect on their professional identity, decision-making, and methodological choices, while consistently adhering to the ethical standards and professional accountability expected of an IB professional.
/en/course/2026/LBVB26GPJ1C.content:
The Graduation Project (GPJ) is an individual capstone assignment in which students address a complex international business problem or opportunity for a company or organisation. The objective is to deliver a professional business product based on rigorous research that provides actionable and feasible data driven recommendations aligned with the organisation’s strategic goals.
The GPJ requires students to:
Conduct structured and in-depth business research,
Integrate theory and practice (depth and combination of business domains depend on the specific project context)
Develop SMART and implementable recommendations,
Communicate professionally in written and oral formats,
Collaborate effectively with relevant stakeholders,
Demonstrate ownership, autonomy, and reflective professional development.
The GPJ emphasises international business awareness, critical thinking, analytical capability, responsible decision-making, and professional behaviour expected of an entry-level international business graduate.

The course contributes to IBS’s strategic focus areas by fostering a global mindset through international opportunity evaluation, strengthening entrepreneurial competences, and embedding sustainability aligned with SDG 12 (Responsible Consumption and Production).
The module concludes with a professional individual defence.
And as an extra: some selected teams present their business concepts to external stakeholders in a “Dragon’s Den” simulation to reflect real-world entrepreneurial conditions.

PLO2: Business Transformation

Learning Line: Global mindset and professional development

/en/course/2026/LBVP26IBC1C.content:
Business Report writing:
Students will know how to organise sources, using APA, and how to integrate these in business reports. In addition, students will learn how business reports are built up and structured and written, using formal business English. Report writing can contribute to strategic themes of sustainability, global mindset, and entrepreneurship. Integrating with the business consulting project, students research and describe innovative solutions to sustainability challenges (SDG7). Overall, this can promote critical thinking, effective communication, collaboration, and creativity, and allow students to apply these skills to real-world challenges.
Presenting:
Students present, as an independent entrepreneur, (a niche) product and its expected sales projection and can present this professionally to potential investors. Students use professional business English and apply the presentation style and structure addressed, while using appropriate (audio) visual material. Students who learn to present their ideas in a clear and concise manner can effectively communicate with diverse audiences and work collaboratively with people from different backgrounds and cultures. This can enhance their global mindset and facilitate their ability to work in international contexts.

metadata.Name: Financial Statement Analysis of a Multinational Enterprise

/en/course/2026/LBVB26FSA1C.outcomes:
PLO1: International Business Opportunities
In this course, the student learns to apply an intermediate understanding of finance, accounting, and supply chain management to analyse how firms create value through financial performance, capital structure, and operational efficiency.
Learning Line: Economics, Finance & Accounting:
CLO1: The student can interpret financial statements and ratio analyses to assess a company’s financial health, capital structure, and potential for long-term value creation.
Learning Line: Operations and Supply Chain:
CLO2: The student can evaluate how inbound logistics influence performance and propose straightforward improvements to enhance value creation.
PLO2: Business Transformation
In this course, the student learns to apply intermediate financial, operational, and sustainability insights to identify improvement opportunities and provide responsible, evidence-based recommendations for business transformation.
Learning Line: Economic, Finance & Accounting:
CLO1: The student can analyse financial data and external business information to draw conclusions about a company’s future financial performance and formulate realistic, data-driven recommendations for improvement.
Learning Line: Operations and Supply Chain:
CLO2: The student can use financial and operational information to propose actions that optimise the cash conversion cycle and strengthen sustainable supply chain performance.
Learning Line: Sustainability and Societal Impact:
CLO3: The student can evaluate a company’s sustainability developments and apply the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) framework to formulate value-adding recommendations for responsible business transformation.
/en/course/2026/LBVB26FSA1C.content: This course focuses on the financial and operational analysis of a multinational enterprise. Working in teams, students assess financial performance, capital structure, and the cash conversion cycle, and develop improvement proposals that integrate inbound logistics. The international company context supports a global mindset by strengthening analytical skills in cross-border business environments. The course connects to sustainability and social impact through the evaluation of corporate sustainability strategies and their financial implications, with strongest alignment to SDG 12 (Responsible Consumption and Production) and SDG 8 (Decent Work and Economic Growth).

Learning Line: Operations and Supply Chain:
CLO2: The student can explain and evaluate how inbound logistics and procurement decisions affect the efficiency, responsiveness, and financial health of an organisation.

PLO1: International Business Opportunities
In this course, the student develops an intermediate understanding of supply chain and related business functions to make informed, data-driven decisions in a complex international business environment.

CLO1: The student can analyse dynamic international supply chain environments and apply supply chain and logistics principles to make well-justified operational and strategic decisions in line with organisational goals.
Learning Line: Management:
CLO2: The student can interpret and apply financial, marketing, and human resource information to support balanced, cross-functional decisions that align with the company’s overall strategy.
PLO2: Business Transformation

Teams make integrated decisions in supply chain management, finance, marketing, and HRM within a dynamic and uncertain environment. The international scope of the simulation strengthens a global mindset by developing intercultural awareness, collaboration, and communication in diverse teams. The course supports entrepreneurship by fostering strategic thinking and coordinated decision-making across business functions. Sustainability and social impact are addressed indirectly through responsible performance management in complex, resource-constrained business settings, with strongest relevance to SDG 8 (Decent Work and Economic Growth).

/en/course/2026/LBVB26MES1C.content:

CLO1
: Students can design an integrated talent management framework that aligns workforce planning, recruitment and selection, development, and performance management with organizational objectives.
CLO2
: Students can justify proposed talent management interventions based on organizational analysis and identified development needs.

: Students can contribute effectively to a team-based project by fulfilling assigned roles and responsibilities in the development of a talent management plan.
/en/course/2026/LBVB26ITM1C.content:
This course focuses on developing an international talent management plan within a project-based learning environment. Working in teams, students design a coherent framework integrating workforce planning, recruitment and selection, development, and performance management. They translate HRM theory into structured and feasible talent management solutions, with emphasis on system coherence, organizational alignment, and practical implementation.
This course supports the SDG8 (Decent Work and Economic Growth) by promoting strategic talent development, productive employment practices, and sustainable organizational performance in international contexts.

/en/course/2026/LBVB26IPM1A.outcomes:
PLO1: International Business Opportunities
In this course, students learn to understand how human resource management systems contribute to organizational performance and strategic alignment in international contexts.
Learning line: Management
CLO1
: Students can explain how strategic human resource management supports organizational goals and performance.
CLO2
: Students can analyze how workforce planning, recruitment and selection, training and development, and performance management operate within diverse organizational environments.
PLO 3: Relationship Management
In this course, students learn to apply intercultural and human resource management theories to analyze managerial and organizational processes in culturally diverse settings.
Learning line: Management
CLO1
: Students can apply cultural frameworks (e.g., national culture dimensions and intercultural communication models) to analyze differences in managerial practices.
CLO2
: Students can explain how cultural values influence leadership, communication, HR policies, and organizational behavior in international organizations.
PLO 4: Self-Management
In this course, students develop awareness of cultural assumptions and their implications for managerial practice.
Learning line: Global Mindset and Professional Development
CLO1
: Students can critically reflect on cultural assumptions and their influence on managerial perception and decision-making.
CLO2

/en/course/2026/LBVB26IPM1A.content:
This course examines people management in culturally diverse organizational contexts by integrating human resource management and intercultural management theory. Students explore how organizations design core HR processes and how cultural differences shape leadership, communication, and organizational behavior. Through lectures and seminars, they apply theoretical frameworks to contemporary international business situations.
This course supports the SDG 8 (Decent Work and Economic Growth) by promoting inclusive HR practices, culturally responsive leadership, and responsible people management that enhance productive employment and sustainable organizational performance.

In this course, students deliver a service for the community. Students will apply knowledge of business etiquette and interpersonal skills to secure a community service role and complete the service while collaborating effectively with individuals from diverse roles, disciplines, and cultures.
Learning Line: Global mindset and professional development
CLO1: Students can reflect on their collaboration with people from different backgrounds and reflect on their personal growth.
PLO4: Self-Management
In this course, while completing the community service role, students apply their planning and organization skills, and self-motivation skills, to go through the process of job solicitation, task execution and acquisition of feedback in a protected environment with a reflection moment at the end of the service. Students will also work on their personal branding by creating products for personal presentation in the job market.
Learning Line: Global mindset and professional development
CLO1: Students can create professional products for personal presentations in the job market.
CLO2: Students can communicate professionally, digitally and live, verbal and non-verbal and reflect on their professional development.
/en/course/2026/LBVB26CDC1C.content: This course allows students to continue working on their professional skills development. The students engage in community service and build a professional presence in a global business environment with the aim of securing a suitable internship. The course aligns with SDG4 (Quality Education) by facilitating skills for personal growth and employability.

metadata.Name: Intercultural and Professional Skills in Business 2

/en/course/2026/LBVB26IPS2C.outcomes:
PLO3: Relationship Management
In this course, students critically analyse intercultural business situations and apply their learning by designing and facilitating interactive workshops, focusing on mitigating cultural misunderstandings and managing professional relationships responsibly.
Learning Line: Global mindset and professional development
CLO1: Students can analyze and mitigate the pitfalls of cultural differences in business and social contexts to cultivate and manage relationships responsibly with culturally diverse stakeholders.
PLO4: Self-Management
In this course, students critically reflect on their personal development and apply intercultural insights through interactive and reflective activities, developing a structured personal learning plan to enhance self-management and professionalism.
Learning Line: Global mindset and professional development
CLO1: Students can critically reflect on their personal development and apply intercultural insights to a personal learning plan, enhancing self-management and professionalism.
/en/course/2026/LBVB26IPS2C.content:
Intercultural and Professional Skills in Business (IPS2) aims to develop students’ competencies of relationship management and self-management through two paths of the learning journey.
During the first path of the IPS2 learning journey, students work in teams to develop and deliver a professional workshop to train peers. The workshop is planned and organized based on students’ different training needs related to intercultural competence. During the second path of the IPS2 learning journey, students work individually to develop a personal intercultural learning plan for either their year-abroad or exchange to IBS.
IPS2 is related to SDG 4 (Quality education) and Global Mindset. During this module, students embrace SDG target 4.5 (Eliminate all discrimination in education) and develop a global mindset by enhancing intercultural competence and sensitivity, facilitating diversity and inclusion, addressing discrimination and stereotypes, and providing intercultural competence training to peers.

/en/course/2026/UTVM25FMA1C.content:

The course provides students at graduate levels with knowledge, skills and insights in contemporary topics and issues regarding corporate finance, financial controlling systems, ethical accounting and finance and financial management. Following items are of particular interest:

Measuring and Controlling Assets Employed, Structure of the Analysis, EVA vs. ROI, Additional Considerations in Evaluating Managers, Managing risks
Evaluating the Economic Performance of the Entity
New economic realities and emerging trends in the financial sector
Decentralization and outsourcing, profitability vs. corporate social responsibility
The course focus on the role of the manager:
to assess and monitor the (global) organization
act as a successful financial consultant
link cultural differences with strategic decisions
promote a holistic vision that aside profitability considerers environmental and social impact of an organization

/en/course/2026/UTVM25IMA1C.outcomes:
The course learning outcomes are:
IMA1: Analyze and apply advanced knowledge of marketing-related problems and critically evaluate current challenges, trends and new insights which are at the forefront of international business and management research and practice.
[Refers to PLO1]
IMA2: Apply knowledge and skills related to marketing environment, and its core aspects linked to product, price, place and promotion decisions (accordingly, linked to the value creation, vale capture, value delivery and value communication), together with a practical understanding of how established techniques of market research are used to gather and interpret data about international business and management.
[Refers to PLO2]

/en/course/2026/UTVM25IMA1C.content:
Strategic Focus Area:
Entrepreneurship
This course provides an advanced approach to the fundamentals of International Marketing Management and is based on a combination of lectures and discussions, business cases, videos, outside speakers, and country snapshots. Students will learn the scope and challenge of international marketing; the dynamic environment of international trade; the influence of the culture once doing business at the international level; political, legal, and business systems of international markets; the global market opportunities; and the ways to develop international marketing strategies.
The course covers the following topics:
Introduction to innovative marketing in modern organisations.
Marketing environment and market analysis.
Market Research.
Buyer Behaviour (both on a consumer and organisational level).
Segmentation, Targeting and Positioning.
Product (value creation).
Price (value capture).
Place (value delivery).
Promotion (value communication).
Final Project Review Session.
The module contributes to the Sustainable Development Goals as set by the UN, and in particular to the SDG12 (Responsible Production and Consumption) and engages the participants to get involved in Hanze activities on SDG’s.

/en/course/2026/UTVM25SDB1C.outcomes:
After completing the course, the student is able to:
assess the theoretical importance and practical applicability of major theories of decision-making and their application in complex and uncertain international politico-economic environments (Contributes to PLOs 1,3)
evaluate the emotional, moral and cognitive dimensions of the executive exercise of governance  (Contributes to PLOs 3,4)
analyse and appraise the institutional environment and the incentives of decision-making in a large multi-national corporation against the backdrop of Sustainability and Circular Economy norms and values (Contributes to PLOs 6, 7, 8)
create appropriate approaches to address stakeholder problems and exercise ethical judgment (Contributes to PLOs 5, 7, 8)
/en/course/2026/UTVM25SDB1C.content:
This module consists of a series of lectures/seminars, in which advanced theoretical knowledge will be provided about decision-making in complex and uncertain environments, and more specifically about the emotional, cognitive and moral dimensions of the exercise of corporate governance, boardroom roles, and the group dynamics of boards. Next to that, the institutional environment and incentives determining decision-making in a large corporation, and the associated ethical issues as well as normative paradigms like Sustainability and the Circular Economy are analyzed.
A key part of the module involves an extensive as well as intensive two-day boardroom simulation game. Participation in this game has students apply the above mentioned theoretical knowledge of decision-making in the context of executive team meetings. It has them face and deal with major problems, respond to unexpected challenges, and reflect on the experience gained.
Students will be introduced to the case beforehand during a preparation phase.
There are two assignments in the module: a group memorandum produced after the two executive team meetings, and a reflection paper referring to the theories and concepts covered and evaluating the experiences during the meetings.
Directly and indirectly, the module refers to Sustainable Development Goals 7 (affordable and clean energy), 8 (decent work and economic opportunity), 9 (industry, innovation and infrastructure) and 11 (sustainable cities and communities)

/en/course/2026/UTVM25STM1.content:
Strategic Focus Areas: Global Mindset & Sustainability
The course International Strategic Management covers all three dimensions of strategic management (process, content and context) and deals with a wide range of issues on each dimension.
As the course aims to go beyond understanding and applying basic tools and concepts, students are challenged to understand more complex phenomena and to critically reflect upon them. This is reinforced by not shielding students from the uncertainties, inconsistencies and disputes within the field of strategic management.
This course contributes to the following SDG’s: 1, 8, 9 & 12.

/en/course/2026/UTVM25ISB1C.outcomes:
Upon a successful completion of the course ISB, participants will be able to:
• ISB1: Learn on working in an international team of upcoming professionals from multiple universities in both on- and off-line setting (contributes to PLO 7 & 8)
• ISB2: To analyze and apply on the impact on the latest insights on sustainability e.g. circular economy, sufficiency and de-growth theories, models and concepts on contemporary business practices (contributes to PLO 1, 2, 3, 4 & 6)
• ISB3: To identify sustainable and actionable strategies for businesses to enhance their sustainable and competitive advantage (contributes to PLO 1, 3 & 6)
• ISN4: To evaluate and decide on strategies on solving their (international) business challenge on sustainability and competitiveness (contributes to PLO 1,3 & 6)
• ISB5: To develop realistic and grounded recommendations that supports the business to enhance both their sustainable and competitive position (contributes to PLO 3, 4, 5 & 6)
/en/course/2026/UTVM25ISB1C.content:
Strategic Focus Areas: Global Mindset and Sustainability
The course ISB is a BIP (EU Erasmus+ program) where students will develop an advice for a real-life company on how to start or enhance their competitive position using sustainable concepts like e.g. circular economy, sustainability or de-growth. Teams will be a mix from all the participating universities and the main research question: “How can contemporary durable concepts contribute to <company>  to become a more sustainable business whilst enhancing their (sustainable) competitive position?”
Students must of underpin their results:
• using the theories, models and concepts of the selected concepts,
• collecting relevant data
• finalizing with tailored analysis
• and building actionable recommendations for business
This course actively contribute to instill the development on knowledge, skills and attitude of participants on the following SDG’s: 8, 9, 11 & 12

metadata.Name: European Business in a Global Context

/en/course/2026/UTVM25EBG1C.outcomes:
After completing the course the student is able to:
EBG1 analyze and assess the function, structure, and dynamics of the EU (PLO 1)
EBG2 examine the role(s) of EU politics and economic policy making (PLO1, PLO3)
EBG3 appraise industries’ capabilities and environments in terms of EU related opportunities and constraints (PLO1, PLO2, PLO3, PLO4, PLO5, PLO7)
EBG4 propose corporate / business strategies based on evaluation of EU related opportunities and constraints (PLO1, PLO2, PLO3, PLO4, PLO5, PLO6, PLO7)
/en/course/2026/UTVM25EBG1C.content:
The course covers following topics:
1. Introduction to the European Business in the Global Context:
1.1. A Portrait of Europe: key features.
1.2. European Business: structure and performance.
1.3. Europe in the lead for sustainability.
2. The EU strategies for resilient and sustainable future & international business.
2.1. The Six European Commission’s priorities for 2019-1024.
2.2. Recovery plan for Europe: opportunities for business.
2.3. A European Green Deal: opportunities for business.
2.4. Overall targets and reporting: what does it mean for business?
3. EU Energy, Climate Change, and Environment Policies: main features and implications for business organisations in the EU.
3.1. Implementation of EU Energy, Climate Change, and Environment Policies in EU countries: implications for business.
3.2. EU standards, tools and labels: implications for business.
4. EU international cooperation on climate, energy and environment and contribution to SDGs: main features and implications for international business.
4.1. EU international cooperation on climate, energy, and environment: what does it mean for international business? International Climate Finance.
4.2. EU contribution to international sustainable development goals: what does it mean for business?
5. EU digital economy, EU social economy and reforms in the EU financial sector:
5.1. A Europe fit for the digital age: what does It mean for international business?
5.2. An economy that works for people.
5.3. Reform support for the financial sector
6. EU in the world economy: opportunities and challenges for international business.
6.1. EU engagement within the European Space – relations with candidate countries and European Neighbourhood Policy: economic aspects, opportunities and challenges for businesses
6.2. EU trade relations with developed countries.
6.3. European and the BRICs: opportunities for businesses
6.4. Europe and the Least Developed Countries - trade, aid and the ACP states. Opportunities for businesses.

/en/course/2026/UTVM25PRA1C.outcomes:

/en/course/2026/UTVM25PRA1C.content:
Strategic Focus Areas: Entrepeneurship and Global Mindset
International business encounters political and security factors that create risks as well as opportunities for them in volatile, complex and uncertain conditions.   This course teaches students to understand the theoretical body in political risk analysis, and to apply such knowledge, in order to assess challenges and to generate options for the company executives in managing these challenges.
This course contributes to
SDG 7, 8, 9, 11

/en/course/2026/UTVM25EWP1C.outcomes:
1. Understanding Well-Being and Performance Theories:
Explain and critically analyze contemporary theories related to employee well-being and performance, including the Job Demands-Resources (JD-R) Theory, Self-Determination Theory, and Conservation of Resources (COR) Theory
(Contributes to PLO 1 & 2).
2.  Analyzing Organizational and Personal Factors:
Evaluate how organizational factors (e.g., leadership, HR practices, work characteristics) and personal factors (e.g., job crafting, playful work design, vitality management) influence employee well-being and job performance.
(Contributes to PLO 1 & 4)
3. Developing and Implementing Well-Being Strategies:
Apply theoretical insights to design, implement, and assess well-being initiatives that enhance employee performance and organizational effectiveness for an organization
(Contributes to PLO 2 & 5).
/en/course/2026/UTVM25EWP1C.content:
trategic Focus Area: Sustainability
This course offers a hands-on approach to understanding employee well-being and job performance in today’s workplaces. Students will delve into key theoretical frameworks and apply them through engaging workshops, case studies, and real-world examples. The course equips students with the skills to design and assess employee well-being programs that drive both individual and organizational performance.

/en/course/2026/UTVM25ITX1C.outcomes:
Upon completion of this course students will understand:
How to communicate effectively with tax consultants and accountants in order to recognise and understand international tax items.
the principles of international tax legislation, avoidance of double taxation and international tax planning schemes.
Issues as transfer pricing, international mergers & acquisitions, withholding taxes, tax-avoiding schemes.
PLO’s: 1, 2, 4, 6, 8
/en/course/2026/UTVM25ITX1C.content:
Strategic Focus Areas: Entrepreneurship & Global Mindset & Sustainability
Cross border business activities imply (by definition) the application of international tax regulations in order to avoid double taxation. To this end guidelines are provided by the OECD and the European Community. These result among other things in unilateral and bilateral tax treaties and EC legislation. Prospective managers to be involved with cross border activities should recognise the international tax framework and its possibilities and limitations.
The successful student acquires and understands a range of international tax issues in headlines. The student recognises (international) tax aspects arising from cross border business activities. This module focuses on the role and meaning of tax treaties for the avoidance of double taxation, OECD Guidelines, EC Directives and jurisprudence and tax planning schemes
SDG’s: 4, 5, 7, 8, 9, 12, 14, 16

/en/course/2026/UTVM25CBO1D.outcomes:
CBO1: demonstrate and apply knowledge about the major theories and perspectives concerning entrepreneurship, business opportunities and innovation in an international environment. (PLO1, PLO2)
CBO2: Identify and specify business opportunities in complex environments under conditions of uncertainty and unpredictability. (PLO3, PLO5)
CBO3: present him/herself professionally as a member of a multidisciplinary and multicultural teams and develop relations with important stakeholders. (PLO3, PLO7, PLO8)
/en/course/2026/UTVM25CBO1D.content:
Strategic Focus Area
:
Global Mindset and Entrepeneurship
The Creating Business Opportunities course is designed to equip Master-level students with conceptual frameworks and an understanding of identifying and creating business opportunities in complex environments under conditions of uncertainty. Through an entrepreneurial lens, the course delves into the theory and practice of creative destruction and disruptive innovation and their role in economic growth and sustainable economies.
The course contributes to SDGs 8, 9 and 12.

/en/course/2026/UTVM25CBT1C.outcomes:
The course learning outcomes are:
By the end of this course, students should be able to:
CBT1: Understand key contemporary business trends and their implications for marketing strategy and examine how global shifts, such as digital transformation and consumer behavior changes, are reshaping marketing tactics and creating new opportunities for businesses.
[Refers to PLO1]
CBT2: Analyze real-world case studies and emerging business models and investigate how organizations successfully adapt to market disruptions by evaluating practical examples and identifying innovative approaches to business challenges.
[Refers to PLO4]
CBT3: Evaluate the role of technology, sustainability, and innovation in business and assess how emerging technologies, sustainable practices, and a culture of innovation are driving competitive advantage and influencing long-term business success.
[Refers to PLO1]
CBT4: Develop strategic approaches to managing change in a rapidly evolving environment and formulate actionable strategies for organizations to remain adaptable, resilient, and forward-thinking while responding to shifting market dynamics and industry trends.
[Refers to PLO4]
/en/course/2026/UTVM25CBT1C.content:
Strategic Focus Area: Global Mindset
This course explores emerging and contemporary trends in business, examining their impact on industries, organizations, and global markets. Topics include digital transformation, sustainability, globalization, innovation, and leadership in a dynamic, unpredictable, and rapidly changing business environment. The course combines theoretical insights with real-world applications, fostering critical thinking and strategic decision-making skills.
The course covers the following topics:
Week1: Introduction to Contemporary Business Trends: Overview of the contemporary business landscape, forces shaping the modern business environment, and the  role of technology, globalization, and policy changes
Week 2: Digital Transformation & Emerging Technologies: Impact of AI, Big Data, and automation on business, digital business models and platform economy, and blockchain and cybersecurity concerns
Week 3: Sustainability and Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR): The role of ESG (Environmental, Social, Governance) in business strategy, circular economy and sustainable business practices, and ethical leadership and corporate governance
Week 4: Globalization and International Business Trends: Trade policies, global supply chains, and geopolitics, the impact of emerging markets on global business, cross-cultural management and international leadership
Week 5: Innovation and Business Model Disruption: Disruptive innovation and market dynamics, the role of startups and venture capital in business evolution, and case studies of innovative companies (e.g., Tesla, Uber, Airbnb)
Week 6: Leadership and Organizational Change: Managing change in turbulent business environments, leadership styles for contemporary business challenges, and organizational agility and resilience
Week 7: Future Business Trends and Course Wrap-Up: The future of work: Remote work, gig economy, and workforce trends, AI and human collaboration in business decision-making, and reflection and final discussions on emerging business paradigms.

The personal development is to be made quantifiably and measurable by a section of the proposal (Personal Development section).
The student’s proposal need to be thorough, rigorous and well organized and involve undertaking systematic activities. /en/course/2026/UTVM25ARU1.content:
The Master in International Business & Management (MIBM) programme offers students the opportunity to spend their second semester studying at Anglia Ruskin University (ARU) in Cambridge, United Kingdom. Please note there are limited places available for outgoing MIBM students.
This is a unique opportunity to achieve a truly international experience while studying, and to obtain two officially recognised international degrees within an 18 month period: Master of Business Administration (MBA) from Hanze University UAS and Master of Science in International Business (MSc) from ARU in Cambridge. The tuition fee for the Dual Degree Programme is the same as for the regular MIBM programme.

/en/course/2026/UTVM25THE1C.outcomes:
By developing and writing the Master thesis the student will show the ability to:
CLO1: Conduct applied research into business issues in the international business context through appropriate use of research and business/management resources and methodologies to deliver practical solutions (PLO2, PLO3).
CLO2: Analyses critically, primary and secondary data to provide adequate recommendations to improve practice of a specific context (PLO2, PLO3, PLO4).
CLO3: Reflects on the results and relevance of the research to situations other than those researched (PLO8).
CLO4: Innovate and improve professional practice, based on critical appraisal of published research on business theories and practices (PLO5).
CLO5: Deal with complex and dynamic business contexts by making substantiated choices evidence-based on business theories and models (PLO2, PLO3).
CLO6: Recognize and address changes of strategic importance for the organizations due to new economic realities and propose strategies to enhance and transform business processes and articulate the implications of the progress of the proposed changes (PLO1, PLO4).
CLO7: Reflect on environmental, social, cultural and ethical aspects within business strategy, for implementation of sustainable improvement of practice (PLO6, PLO7).
CLO8: Communicate effectively to an academic and professional business community about strategic goals and potential changes in the business environment (PLO7).
CLO9: Write a research report in a scientific, clear and systematic format (PLO2, PLO7).
CLO10: Reflect on the research performance within the thesis project (PLO8).
/en/course/2026/UTVM25THE1C.content:
Strategic Focus Areas: Entrepeneurship, Global Mindset and Sustainability
The MIBM thesis will give students the opportunity to explore and integrate in length aspects of theory or methods, knowledge and skills, given along the first year of the MIBM programme.
The combination of that specific content with research approaches and professional practice questions, will create the relevant content and educational process of the thesis course.
The thesis project is an individual assignment that is linked to a practical issue in an existing organisation, or type of organisation or to the start-up of a new organisation. The thesis research should be carried out as an assignment given by an organisation (profit or non-profit) or a professorship linked to the business issue (e.g. IBS is linked to the Knowledge Centre Entrepreneurship: KCO). Students are expected to acquire the assignment, define the problem, and formulate the research objectives and research questions themselves.
Students need to describe the theoretical framework, design a suitable methodology, gather and analyse information, draw logical conclusions and recommend realistic solutions or courses of action and /or further research.
The project should involve primary data collection by the student and should relate to the field of Marketing, Finance and Accounting, Human Resource Management, Operations Management, or Strategic Management.
The student’s investigations need to be thorough, rigorous and well organised and involve undertaking systematic research in the context of applied research. Therefore, students have to use appropriate methods to systematically collect and analyse data, argue why the results obtained are meaningful, and explain any limitations that are associated with them (Saunders, Lewis & Thornhill, 2007). MIBM students will present their Master Thesis report during a defence session.
The thesis should contribute to knowledge on the application of business theories in a real situation of practice, or to theory formation in the business field.
The MIBM thesis is an individual thesis that requires an individual assessment.
This course contributes to
SDG 7, 8, 9, 11, 12

During this project, the student will be working in peer groups of international students, and learn more about the role of a communication professional within an organisation. They will interview different communication professionals. The research will result in a clear view on what it is like to be a communication professional. The visualisation of these result will be presented during the event #ComPro. The target audience of this event consists of the student’s own international peer group, as well as alumni students. During this event, the role of a communication professional will be approached and highlighted from different angles by various guests, and through different ‘meet & greet’ sessions with professionals in the field. To conclude, the student will be giving a media presentation for an international audience in which the role of a communication professional within an organisation is clearly highlighted.
In order to achieve all of this, the student will need to obtain good knowledge of different visions within the field of communication, hence the student will be taking a proactive role in contacting communication experts who can help the student in this respect and who can maybe play a role at the conference as well. In other words: the student will have to network in a target driven manner in order to yield him/her the necessary results.
Furthermore, the student should be aware of different forms of communication, and able to research different types of organisations which have communication professionals working for them, and understand how economical, organisational, national and international factors influence such an organisation.  In

/en/course/2026/ICVP21CIB1.content:
In today’s complex information age, forward thinking communication professionals are continuously challenged to master the most demanding communication frontiers in creating engaging, strategic, and relevant content and information valued by their most important target groups, as well as making their client company stand out from the crowd. To this end, online marketing mix tools have an overwhelming impact on today’s society and businesses.
The student finds out how online marketing communications can be instrumental in achieving organisational objectives in a relatively complex business context from a client’s perspective. Students work in project groups and assume the role of a marketing communication advisor for a real (inter)national client company. Their task is to scan and monitor existing online content related to one of the client’s brands. Students carry out research to identify the most important market segments and the competitors. Subsequently, students develop target group profiles and brand positioning that is consistent with the core values of the client. In the final stage, students create content, making use of creative texts and visuals, and present their advice and content to the client.
In

/en/course/2026/ICVP26MEE.content:
An
entrepreneurial mindset
is a set of knowledge and skills that enables people to identify and make the most of opportunities, learn from setbacks, and succeed in a variety of contexts.
In this project, students (individually or in small groups) select or create an opportunity they want to execute within
7 weeks
. The opportunity can be aimed at generating financial profit or creating a positive impact for a chosen target audience.
The project emphasizes a
growth mindset
, supporting the development of professional reflective and collaboration skills. Students progress through the steps of idea generation, opportunity recognition, opportunity screening, and action plan development, including a promotional plan (which includes video formats). To strengthen their plans, students gather insights through interviews with experts or their target audience.
The
entrepreneurial mindset
framework guiding this project is built around the following key concepts: fixed and growth mindset, developing an entrepreneurial mindset, idea generation strategies, the four pathways for opportunity recognition, opportunity screening analysis (including context analysis, market feasibility, competitive positioning, and organizational feasibility), the action mindset and action plan, as well as creative and contemporary promotion formats for the promotional plan.
During this block students learn how to create a video for their project’s promotional plan and are introduced to the fundamentals of visual storytelling, including mise-en-scène, decoupage, visual rhetoric, Gestalt principles, semiotics, and the use of the third dimension to enhance meaning and impact. Students also learn practical skills for crafting engaging video content, such as shot selection, composition, structuring a three-act storyline, storyboarding, and hands-on camera training. Together, these classes equip students to translate their ideas into clear, compelling, and visually engaging promotional material.
The professional skills
supporting the project assignments include creative thinking, pitching ideas for different purposes, and writing media products tailored to specific target groups.

Public and private organizations constantly seek to engage their audiences and communicate effectively to influence behaviours. Whether promoting sustainability, ethical consumption, workplace safety, or social responsibility, designing impactful communication campaigns is key to driving behavioural change.
In this course, students take on the role of communication consultants, working on a project for a client facing a communication challenge. Collaboration is at the heart of the course. Students work in teams, inspire each other, apply diverse expertise, and use Design Thinking techniques to develop innovative campaign solutions.
