Building on insights from Project 1, students work in teams to design behaviour change communication campaigns. Each team develops a comprehensive Communication Plan, starting with strategic communication objectives and outlining targeted interventions aligned with the client’s current strategy. Using the Design Thinking process—particularly Ideation and Prototyping—students create and test their campaign concepts to ensure alignment with the intended audiences.
The Campaign Plan also includes an implementation plan covering pre-launch preparations, a campaign timeline, and suggestions for post-campaign evaluation based on the agreed-upon key performance indicators.
Collaboration with the client is central to the process. Students engage the client during the ideation phase, co-create the campaign concept, and refine the prototype through feedback from both the client and target audience. The final campaign, along with all associated media products, is delivered in an agreed format, equipping the client with a ready-to-use communication strategy
Visual Communication 6:
Students create animations using After Effects.

In the project students create a communication campaign. To create it and different media products, they need a theoretical basis.
Communication theory is about different topics related to creating a communication campaign, such as integrated marketing communications, customer journey, objectives, budget, content and media strategies, testing and measuring, GDPR and ethics.
Media theory
addresses the role played by the visual elements in any type of media-related communication, from photography to time-based media. Students pay attention to the composition of images, the colours used, the contrast, the point of view, the typographic choice and many other characteristics, with a critical eye on the immediate meaning (denotation) and additional meanings (connotations) that might occur. It is of great importance for communication professionals to have insight into organizational changes and communicative processes within organizations.
The student acquires knowledge and insight into the communicative processes of organizations, especially in an international context. The student learns to analyze changes with the help of concepts from corporate communication theory and internal communication theory (mission, vision, organizational identity, reputation and image). Transition and Communication - Project:
Change communication contributes to the creation of value for an organization in change, and for its stakeholders. This includes well-founded means of communication to foster the organizational culture needed to embrace the change.
Students establish a communication strategy, make appropriate recommendations about the use of communication interventions, choose appropriate themes and formulate core messages. The block focuses on creativity and knowledge of what kind of communication works and how. The student justifies the use of communication means with professional arguments.

Learning outcome:
After completing the course, the participant will have basic knowledge of the Dutch language and culture and will have developed skills to engage in simple conversations, understand short texts, and express themselves in everyday situations.
https://www.coe.int/en/web/common-european-framework-reference-languages/level-descriptions
/en/course/2026/LCK25DUTA1.content:
Content
During this course the student specializes in the Dutch language and the culture of the Dutch language area (The Netherlands, Belgium, Suriname).
Topics of language skills:
Introduce yourself, asking for information, greet and say goodbye, spelling, describing people, asking what time it is, ordering and paying, thanking, asking and telling how you are, making an appointment, make a proposal, respond positively/negatively, asking/saying what you want to buy, the price and paying, asking how someone feels about something, judging positively/negatively, giving a tip, trying on and buying clothes, looking for a place to live, describing complaints, responding to doctor's questions, giving responses.
Grammar topics:
Personal pronouns (subject forms), possessive pronouns, structure of main sentences and subordinate clauses, structure of question sentences, use of definite and indefinite articles, diminutives, structure of main sentences with inversion, the use of the verb “zullen” (will, part I),  forming the plural of nouns and adjectives, imperative mood, modal verbs degrees of comparison (comparative and superlative) demonstrative pronoun (adjective use), personal pronouns (direct object forms), negation, prepositions,  the forms and use of the present perfect, the use of the indefinite pronouns “iets” and “niets”.

We expect a minimum of 80% attendance and full (100%) preparation for each lesson.

/en/course/2026/ICVB24GRA.content:
This year focuses on your growth from student to entry-level communication professional. You’ll show that you’re ready to enter the professional world and that you’ve mastered seven key competencies at end level (level 3). You will do this by working on various assignments and projects. We don’t assess separate tasks, instead, we look at your overall performance and development, which you will demonstrate in your portfolio. If everything meets the required standard, you will receive 60 credits (EC) for the entire year in one go.
Throughout the graduation year, you’ll follow different types of learning and receive support. Some activities you’ll do with all students, like training in writing, research, and concept development. In addition, you choose elective modules that match your interests and ambitions. You will apply what you learn straight away in projects. This helps you specialize and shape your professional profile.
Your personal and professional development is also part of your final assessment. During the year, you’ll work on learning goals that you set yourself. You will do this in a Community of Learners (CoL), supported by a mentor. You are in charge of your own learning. Feedback plays an important role in this: you’ll receive regular feedback from your mentor, clients, subject experts, and coaches. You’ll also reflect regularly on your progress.

PLO A1:
Creates communication strategies that convey organizational values, strategic directions, and priorities, while addressing the interests of diverse stakeholders.
PLO B3:
Designs, conducts, and critically reviews (online) communication research to underpin communication strategies and tactics, as part of decision-making and with relevance to professional practice.
PLO C5:

/en/course/2026/LCVM21MIC01.content:
In this 15 EC Module, students explore the dynamic role of a corporate communication consultant, serving as a strategic partner, providing fresh perspectives to engage diverse stakeholders, and delivering measurable impact in competitive, often global, environments.
Students will:
Advise companies on the new realities of strategic corporate communication.
Design strategies that build stakeholder trust across all platforms, internally and externally.
Use cultural insights to align corporate vision with diverse stakeholder expectations.
Develop a leadership toolkit that supports continuous professional growth.
The module is supported by applied research methodology, corporate communication theory, intercultural communication, personal leadership, and relevant workshops. Deliverables can include, but are not limited to, a professional advice report, a presentation, a research memo, a case study, and a leadership toolkit. The deliverables are assessed in a portfolio to determine how well the program learning outcomes have been achieved.
Capstone project
In a team-based capstone, students work in international groups to apply advanced knowledge of corporate communication, critical thinking, and problem-solving skills to develop a strategy that enables a brand to communicate authentically, consistently, and effectively worldwide.
Applied Research Methodology

Professional Skills
The student develops his Professional Identity (PI) by being aware of his own knowledge, skills and qualities in relation to his education and his future profession and accounts for them orally and in writing. He knows what he can do and knows his development points.
The student shows his own professional identity by:
Showing professional craftsmanship by reflecting on his own knowledge and skills, ICT literacy, sustainability, oral and written communication and on their own future profession also in relation to society and social expectations

collaborating effectively with fellow students in a project group/class on assignments focused on the financial economic field. The collaboration is aimed at on quality improvement of the final result.
/en/course/2026/FOVP26TCEB.content:
The
OutLook
project is a research based project in which the theory and practice of research will play a central role. The application of research will be closely related to the content of both courses in 1.4. Goal of the project is to deliver a research report together with a presentation of this report.
During this project the students work in small groups of approximately four persons on a self-defined topic. The project outline will describe the preconditions for the topic to be chosen.
The project
In recent years a shift in society’s mindset has been taking place. This focusses on a growing awareness on sustainable development of the world. With as ultimate goals a circular economy. Multiple new business ideas have been created and many of these business innovations prove to be successful. E.g. Tesla with its electric cars. The production capacity of its factories cannot even catch up with the demand in the market. Multiple other car manufacturers announced their new vision on transport and also switch to more sustainable power resources as a source of power for their future vehicles.
Within this project the students come up with a sustainable business idea (sustainable as defined by the Brundtland report and it can be an existing idea in the market). During this project the students will conduct an exploration of the market for this product in two self-defined countries. Precondition is that one of these countries should be within Europe and one of these countries should be located outside of Europe.
Students should integrate the knowledge which they develop during the courses International Finance & Economics 1 and Quantitative Data Analysis into their report to create a decent level of quantitative research output.
The research will be developed as a diagnostic research in which the exploration of the market will be central.

/en/course/2026/IFCP18IFE1A.outcomes:
1. The student explains and interprets data relating to the business cycle and structure of the economy and its impact on different industries.
2. The student defines and explains the interrelationship between macroeconomic variables and the influence of government on the economy, in particular with a Keynesian model.
3. The student describes and explains structure characteristics and pricing and profit maximizing behavior within different market forms and industries.
4. The student defines and explains the role of financial institutions and the basic principles of monetary policy.
/en/course/2026/IFCP18IFE1A.content:
Enterprises do not operate isolated, but within an constantly changing environment, also known as the external or operating environment. Developments in that external environment influence the company result. The enterprises need to align their decisions to the current and future environmental developments at a strategic level.
Insight in macroeconomic developments, like the development of the business cycle, inflation, interest and the growth of world Trade is of great importance for the business management of an enterprise. Besides that it is also very important to have an insight in the changing competitive relations in their markets; which tools are used to compete, are there entry barriers, is the market cyclically sensitive, in which phase of the product life cycle is the market? When it comes to this kind of questions we talk about meso-economic analyses. The international and financial markets and institutes are also a big component of the entire financial system, which is carried by the central banks and the monetary policy.
The course International Finance & Economics 1 offers, next to a theoretical insight in the efficiency of the economy at a both macro as meso level, also an insight in the current economic developments. These are relevant for the (inter)national operating companies and in functioning of the financial markets and the role of financial institutions.

/en/course/2026/IFCB19ILA3.content:
At Hanze University researchers, education and the professional field work together in so-called Innovation Labs, where research power and field knowledge are combined to solve problems that businesses and institutions experience. In this block the students work on an assignment for a professional client participating in such an Innovation lab. The assignment will be done in groups, and supervised by a coach from the Hanze bachelor programme. Students can consult professionals from the field in the Innovation Lab. Although all the assignments have a financial and economic context, each group will receive different tasks.
At the end of the semester the research report will be graded group-wise. In addition students will be assessed on the development of their personal and professional skills, as demonstrated in a development portfolio that is individually composed. In this portfolio the student proves that s/he has met the learning outcomes by using examples from blocks 1 up to and including 4. Furthermore, the student reflects on the experience from the practical assignment during this block.
The student passes this course when the research report is graded sufficient and if s/he has proven his/her development in the area of professional skills in a criterion based interview with the coach.
This course is offered in semester 2B.

/en/course/2026/IFCB19IFE2A.content:
In this course the theory and working of central banks and financial markets will be teached and discussed.

Central Bank policies
Money supply
Measurement of financial risks
Analyse the impact of these risks
Useful financial tools
International currency market

/en/course/2026/IFCB19IA21.outcomes:
The students knows different business models and can motivate and apply the right model for a company.
The student identifies and analyses the risks that come with the chosen strategy, designs appropriate processes and finds new solutions.
The student can consider alternative trade possibilities based on a chosen strategy and in combination with the environmental influences and the financial situation.
The student recognizes risks that are caused by interest and exchange rates and covers them with financial instruments.
The student communicates in English in writing in a financial economic context. The communication is aimed at advice and forming an opinion: the student delivers an advisory report.

The student demonstrates the research skills of a financial professional, and can motivate and argue solutions chosen from a helicopter perspective and with an objective view of practical issues.
/en/course/2026/IFCB19IA21.content:
During this assignment you will draw up an export strategy for an existing organization. During 10 weeks you work in groups with fellow students and via the scrum methodology.
You will apply the knowledge you have gained in the courses Strategic Management and International Finance and Economics 2. Various topics are discussed, such as internal and external analysis, the translation of a strategy into goals, interest and currency risks. The purpose of the Integral Assignment is that you gain insight into relationships between the two different fields.
To find out what the company is asking for related to an export strategy you will conduct a semi-structured interview. You demonstrate research skills of a financial professional, the outcomes of the research will has to be written in an advisory report for the organization.

/en/course/2026/IFCB19IA22.outcomes:
The student evaluates the management control system in relation to organization structure, responsibility centers & management style.
The student describes and explains the budget process and develops, partially, the budget using sensitivity analysis.
The student evaluates performance measurement regarding the alignment with the business strategy, the use of financial and nonfinancial performance measures and the balance between different perspectives.
The student understands and carries out the appropriate journal entries for the budget.
The student understands and carries out the appropriate journal entries for plant assets, natural resources or intangible assets.
The student can discuss, identify, explain and/or describe financial statements analysis with the ratios.
The student demonstrates IT-literacy and skills in a broad financial economic context.
The student demonstrates the research skills of a financial professional, and can motivate and argue solutions chosen from a helicopter perspective and with an objective view of practical issues.
The student individually presents (part of) the professional product and related advice to the project client in a simulated classroom setting.  The student answers client questions in a professional and well-argued manner in order to defend the professional product and the advice.
/en/course/2026/IFCB19IA22.content:
How do you get to achieve organizational goals? For this purpose, many organizations use a Planning & Control system, amongst other means. This implies that the strategy systematically is translated in plans and budgets and that performance is evaluated frequently. In this context, “Control” means that you try to manage the organization by making the right decisions based on valuable information. Valuable information, that in particular comes from a well-designed accounting system.
During this course you will use the knowledge you gained at Business Administration 2 and Management Accounting & Control 2. The assignments you will be working on apply to a company in the field. Several subjects will be covered, such as budgeting, performance measurement, journal entries and ratio analysis. The goal of the integrated assignment is that you understand relations between both fields.
You will also develop several skills during this course. To get the necessary information you will conduct an interview, taking validity and reliability into account. You will use Excel to generate useful information. When your research is done, you will persuasively hand the company your results and advice through a presentation.

/en/course/2026/IFCB19MAC2A.outcomes:
The student describes and explains the basic framework for management control systems.
The student explains the role of budgets in overall organization plans.
The student explains the role of performance measures within an organisation and computes and interprets financial performance measures such as return on investment, residual income and economic value added.
The student computes the cost of products, taking work-in-process to account, using a relevant cost accounting system and explains the consequences of choices made.
The student computes and interprets sales variances, variable cost variances and fixed cost variances. Cost variances will include (amongst others) variabel overhead (price and efficiency) variances and fixed price variances.
/en/course/2026/IFCB19MAC2A.content:
This course focusses on Performance Management. It is a follow-up to Management Accounting & Control 1.
The following subjects are covered:
Management Control
Planning and budgetting
Performance measurement
Cost accounting
Variance analysis
Using the strategy as a starting point, an organization needs to decide on which activities it should carry out. Subjects such as planning, budgeting and cost accounting are then relevant. Subsequently it is important to measure performance to find out whether the organization is on course or if it is necessary to make adjustments. In doing so, management control, performance measurement and variance analysis play an important role.
Because an organization cannot afford to focus on numbers only, the subjects will also be highlighted from the perspective of soft controls and ethics.

/en/course/2026/IFCB19BAD2A.outcomes:
The student understands and makes the appropriate journal entries for plant assets, natural resources and intangible assets.
The student understands and makes the appropriate journal entries for liabilities and the methods for the presentation and analysis.
The student understands and can record the following items related to the equity of corporations: share transactions, dividends and retained earnings.
The student understands and makes the appropriate journal entries for investments and the consolidated financial statements.
The student can prepare and analyze cash flows and a statement of cash flows.
The student can discuss, identify, explain and/or describe financial statement analyses with means of ratios.
/en/course/2026/IFCB19BAD2A.content:
In this course the focus lies on recording / administrating the firm’s business transactions and monitoring how the financial position is evolving. This will be done for several subjects like plant assets, natural resources, intangible assets, liabilities, share transactions, dividends, retained earnings and investments. Next, financial reporting is subject of this course. In the first year you learned about the balance sheet, profit and loss statement and cash flow statement as the most important financial reporting instruments. In this course we will build further on this by introducing the consolidated financial statements and a statement of cash flows. Last subject is about analysing the financial statements with using financial ratios. This is all done for drafting financial statements necessary for correctly monitoring the financial position and reporting this to management and the external stakeholders. The financial reporting is in line with the IFRS guidelines.
The course is build on the textbook 'Financial Accounting with International Financial Reporting Standards' (4th edition) by Weygandt, Kimmel and Kieso.

/en/course/2026/IFCB19SM1C.outcomes:
The student can make an internal and external analysis for an international organization.
The student can apply strategic management models in a given case or problem for a client
The student can translate global strategic statements to concrete steps which has to be taken to reach strategic goals.
The student is able to recognize the theory on strategic management and apply it in a given case
The student is able to analyze a given case and come up with recommendations.
/en/course/2026/IFCB19SM1C.content: During this course you will learn about strategic decisions within a company. You will learn different strategic models and how to analyse and apply them to an organiztion. During a simulation you will bring the theory into practice. After the course you can translate global strategic statements to concrete steps which has to be taken to reach the strategic goals.

/en/course/2026/IFCB19CF2A.outcomes:
1. The student can use financial arithmetic to assess the extent to which an investment is financially profitable according to various selection methods (including the NCW method)
2. The student can describe the strategy of an organization and investment selection under uncertainty by means of sensitivity and scenario analysis.
3. The student can assess and advise on financing requirements, repayment capacity and dividend policy on the basis of predictions about exploitation and cash flows.
4. The student can prepare a financing plan with various possible forms of financing, taking into account the requirements of potential capital providers.
5. For valuation issues, the student can calculate the future free cash flows and the relevant cost of capital using the CAPM and WACC method.
6. The student can assess the financial position of a company by means of ratio analysis.
7. The student can describe or assess working capital management and advise on this.
8. The student is able to outline the main points of how irrational behaviour can influence prices and financial decisions (behavioural finance).
/en/course/2026/IFCB19CF2A.content:
The module Corporate Finance 2 elaborates on the fundamentals of financial management (COF1). Drafting and understanding financial statements at market values, interpreting various valuation models and comparing values with book values. Calculating and interpreting financial ratios. Drafting and understanding financial planning and investments. Investment decisions and other financial computations. Working capital planning and cash management. Funding for investments, the capital structure of a company and the influence of leverage. Break-even analysis and general indifference computations. All is provided within an applied form with the help of Excel.
Summary of subjects:
Financial arithmetic
Financial instruments
Valuation methods
Investment analysis
Asset management
Risk and capital costs
Ratio analysis

/en/course/2026/IFCB19CLT1A.content:
This course provides a concise introduction to, and overview of, the fundamental concepts of the law of corporations and corporate tax law, both at an (inter)national and European level.
The course centers on the international company will familiarize students with common legal and tax problems that an international company encounters.
In doing so, this course provides a broad theoretical insight into the area of corporate law and tax law.  Students will learn to recognize and understand key differences in corporate regimes, gain insight into and evaluate international contracts as well as identify and analyze tax opportunities and liabilities. The course will enable students to provide basic corporate advice on issues of risk and compliance within the area of corporate governance. Students will be able to analyze and evaluate various (inter)national legal issues and provide case-by-case recommendations. The course will encourage and require students to apply critical thinking and problem-solving skills e.g. to the taxation of individuals and corporations.
Overall, the course will provide students with a broad understanding of the legal and tax risks that an international company faces. Insight into such risks as well as a proper understanding of the internal structure of a company is indispensable to the modern corporate advisor or financial professional.

/en/course/2026/IFCB19MIS2C.outcomes:
The student analyses and determines which information and data is required to control, govern and improve the organization.
The student designs and develops a database based on functional demands and standardized techniques.
The student advises on the choice for a relevant IT system which is focused on both financial as non- financial information as well as international regulations and compliance. The student also advises on the internal design of the system.
The student performs an analysis on the required management information (both recurring as well as specific) and is able to store, create and present this information in a visualization tool which incorporates geographical segregation.
The student understands the functioning of computerized algorithms, is able to apply machine learning techniques on a dataset and give an advise based on the outcomes.
The student creates a mixed integer linear programming solution that creates an optimal solution for a given case.
/en/course/2026/IFCB19MIS2C.content:
In this course students will develop the essential skills to leverage their data analytics skills. The course starts with how to collect data and how to design a database to store various sources of relational data. After this students will learn how to select IT systems for international organization and what factors are involved in selecting the right program.
Students will also learn how to visualize data in a dashboarding tool while creating a smart impact. At the same time they will also get a basic understanding of predictive analytics and machine learning. Students will learn what algorithms are and how they can use algorithms for decision making. Lastly, basic skills in optimization will be learned to solve tasks in the most cost effective manner. This means that students go through a cycle of collecting and storing data, visualizing information and predicting and optimizing organizations based on data.

/en/course/2026/IFCB19OM1A.content: Operations Management is about organizing resources in organisations to get to succesful servcies and products. Operations Management is relevant for many aspects and levels of the company and in this course we aim to provide a broad perspective on the subject. Furthermore, the cours will teach concepts and calculations for solving pratical problems within the field of operations.

Through various assignments, the student prepares to visit another country. He or she is expected to be challenged to know the country, explore and eventually evaluate the culture of another country.

/en/course/2026/IFCB20BC1C.outcomes:
The student understands and formulates his own vision on tasks and responsibilities of a business controller and links the various areas of expertise such as business strategy, management accounting, management control and internal control and accounting information systems (ICAIS)
For an organization the student defines the need for information necessary for managing and controlling, appropriate for the internal and external context. It specifically concerns the need for information stemming from the need for management accounting and management control activities as mentioned in learning outcomes 2 and 3. The student uses standard models.
The student evaluates and designs the management control system, keeping business strategies and accountability centres into account.
As a business controller the student evaluates and designs a system of performance measurements with the aim to advise on efficiency and effectiveness of business processes.
The student  makes analyses belonging to the area of Management Accounting, including (for instance) budgetting, cost accounting, scenario analyses, gap/disparity analyses and investment calculations and het advises management on the basis of them.
The student evaluates and designs a system of risk management aimed at efficient and effective operations management, reliability of internal and external reporting and complying with laws and regulations. With these aspects in mind he describes relevant internal control risks for the organization, using valid models and theories
The student sets up administrative processes including internal control systems.
/en/course/2026/IFCB20BC1C.content:
In this block you will take on the role of a business controller who advises the owner of a company (Spar Appel supermarket) on managerial accounting, control, business risks and management information systems. The occasion is that the company wants to expand their business (and after expansion) maintain a firm grip on the company’s financial situation now and in the future.
The course of Business Control goes deeper into the function of a business controller. The course is related to the course of Business Strategy and Risk (BSR), which goes deeper into the role of strategic partner in business as a part of the controller’s function. Led by weekly assignments in the case the student learns to perform analyses for the company to be able to make decisions. The student will advise on decisions that need to be taken. These decisions will lead to a need for information within an organization. The student will therefore set up a planning and control system based on accepted models and theories and will advise management on efficiency, effectivity and risk management. The student will make a final report on the tasks and responsibilities of the business controller and will make the link between the different aspects of the job. This report is an individual product

Strategic Control Model
Responsibility/accounting model
Pricing model
Investment analysis
Budgeting model
Performance management model
Planning & Control Cycle in Service companies
Risk Management

MIS reliability
MIS relevance

/en/course/2026/IFCB20BSR1C.outcomes:
LeveL 3
PLO1: Strategic Management
The student provides insight into an organization's national and international external environment and advises management on sustainable decisions for the organization.
The student uses various strategic models to describe the external context of an organization.
The student considers several trends, describes the effects on the external context of a company and  incorporates this into the strategy of the organization.
The student describes and  applies a theoretical framework using theories on risk management and current affairs to come up with a strategy for managing the risks of the company.
The student knows different aspects of change in an organization differentiating between transitions in design and development
PLO4: 4: Governance, Risk & Compliance
The student advises on establishing information and business processes aimed at sustainably managing risks in an organization
The student describes and assesses the risk management process and the way in which the risk management process is set up within an organization. He advises about this. This involves both the process itself and the way it is embedded in the organization.
In a case study the student manages a risk management process on a strategic level, consisting of a description and an evaluation of risks and identifying risk management measures, whereby a risk-control matrix is drawn up. He gives recommendations/advice to the organization.
The student understands the role of the strategic partner in business as part of the responsibilities and tasks of a business controller. He can formulate his own vision on this role. In a personal reflection the student describes what the importance is of a strategic partner in business for the processes of designing strategy, strategic risk management and change management in the organization.
/en/course/2026/IFCB20BSR1C.content:
The course Business Strategy & Risk (BSR) comprises determining business strategy and concomitant risks and formulating them at an operational level.
It entails studying current theories and applying these on real case assignments in groups, mainly in accordance to the graduation research framework.
Students conduct an internal and external research of the organization based on correct methodological principles, evaluate the existing corporate strategies and risks, and subsequently formulate substantiated recommendations related to business strategy and measures for strategic risk management, based on pertinent theories.
This time we shall move from the abstract towards the concrete, by operationalizing business strategies and describing execution and tangible outcomes.
The module is related to the Business Control module coming up in the following period.
Both these modules highlight the pivoting role of a business/financial controller in an organization.
After this course you can:
Research and explore the external environment of an organization and distinguish the determining factors and trends needed to realize the firm's business strategy while controlling strategic risk.
Describe the main theories related to strategic and risk management.
Recommend measures and organizational changes in the management of business strategy and risk.

Learning Outcomes

/en/course/2026/PIVP23PC1PH.content:
PT-care 1 consists of 2 courses of 5 EC that are interwoven with each other. Course 1: Physiology & Health and course 2: Anatomy & skills.
This course concerns covers the more theoretical part of PT-care 1.
Prevention plays an increasing significant role in our society – especially when it comes to prevention in the context of ADL, work and sports. Physiotherapists are expected to have the professional skills to design training programmes for clients aimed at improving strength and endurance, and to guide the clients during the execution of these programmes. In the daily practice of physiotherapy, setting up a solid training programme is a common activity. To set up such a training programme and evaluate it, you need basic knowledge of physiology/exertion physiology, anatomy and training theory. To this end, every week, students will elaborate on a simple and single -problemcase study about a healthy person  to various health risks. The study tasks are about osteology, syndesmology, myology, kinesiology, physiology/exertion physiology, training theory, testing, measuring and training, and giving information, health information, instruction and feedback. Basic anatomy and physiology in relation to the heart and lungs and the corresponding measurements will also be discussed, as well as the behavioural side of health and exercise. Important: This casuistry is a means to get to know the didactic materials really well, but does not cover the entirety of materials that will be tested at the end of the training programme. Independent study, especially of the required literature, is absolutely necessary.

/en/course/2026/PIVP25PC1AS.content:
PT-care 1
consists of 2 courses of 5 EC that are interwoven with each other. Course 1: Physiology & Health and course 2: Anatomy & skills.

PT-care 4 consists of 2 courses of 5 EC that are interwoven with each other. Course 1: Neurology & Rehabilitation 1 and course 2: Skills & integration.
This course concerns Neurology rehabilitation 1 and covers the more theoretical part of PT-care 4.
With knowledge and insight into the client’s problems, the physiotherapist can provide high-standard qualitative care. The variation in symptoms among patients with neurological problems is considerable. Patients with similar diagnoses can display very different clinical pictures. To  provide assessment and treatment adequately and in a patient-specific fashion during professional practice, it is indispensable for physiotherapists to have comprehensive knowledge of neurology. The quality of the clinical reasoning will follow the degree to which a skilled practitioner is knowledgeable about the client’s problems.
By gearing the instruction towards knowledge of and insight into aspects of central and peripheral neurological problems, we aim for the professional growth of physiotherapists-in-training. This theoretical background is examined during an oral exam.
Anatomy 4 is a course where theorectical background is being tested. It comprises identifying, localising bony structures, as well as origin and attachment of muscles, ligaments, tendons and nerves, skin areas and dermatomes. In this course we will discuss and test the basic anatomic knowledge and skills that we use as physiotherapists. This course delves deeper into the materials and expands on Anatomy 1 to 3, and is being examined in a written test.

Learning Outcomes
The student identifies and analyzes modifiable lifestyle factors and explores potential collaborative partners within the field of preventive care with the aim of promoting healthy (physical activity) behavior. The student is able to describe these findings in a written report. Professional role: HP-1
The student demonstrates mastery of the fundamental principles and basic knowledge (the Body of Knowledge) required to successfully perform the professional role of health promoter — including ethics, rights, laws, and regulations — at proficiency level 1 (primarily factual knowledge, understanding, and reproduction). /en/course/2026/PIVP23LP.content:
Prevention aims to promote physical, mental, and social well-being. A physiotherapist who focuses on prevention is concerned with behavioral change and focuses on people's ability to adapt and control life's social, physical, and emotional challenges.
In this course, prevention focuses on a healthy lifestyle in which aspects such as eating habits, exercise, and dealing with stress are treated. In this course, students work in small groups on various assignments. The student is given the assignment to map out the offer in the field of prevention and the wishes and needs in the field of health and well-being for a specific group of people. Physiotherapeutically relevant questions are formulated and answered. In this course, the student thus learns important preventive measures for a healthy lifestyle and the roles of various care providers, trainers, and volunteers within this range. The course is concluded with a group presentation and a group report.
This course also includes the IPE Cluster Project Health, Care & Vitality Year 1 (1 EC).
In this project, students are introduced to interprofessional collaboration in an active way by working together with various degree programs within the Health, Care & Vitality cluster. Through a shared assignment, they get to know each other better, both socially and professionally. Central to this is discovering role clarity and making use of complementary differences in perspectives and expertise.
The Meta-Model of Interprofessional Development (Reinders, 2018; Reinders & Pesut, 2022; Reinders et al., 2023) helps them understand how these different contributions come together to create effective collaboration.

/en/course/2026/PIVP23RI1.outcomes:
Learning Outcomes
1. The student can translate a specific information need of a patient or practice into an answerable research question (PICO). IP-1
2. The student is able to conduct a systematic search to identify relevant English-language research articles on a health-related problem. IP-1
3. The student is familiar with various information sources, including books, websites, AI, and research articles, and can critically appraise them. IP-1
4. The student can determine the level of evidence of (English-language) research articles and assess the validity and usefulness of research articles using an appropriate assessment tool. IP-1
5. The student has knowledge of basic methodological and statistical aspects of a research article (including research design, measures of central tendency and dispersion, significance, correlation, and the interpretation of graphs and figures). IP-1
6. The student can, in collaboration with fellow students, explain findings from scientific literature through a presentation and share them professionally with others. COM,COL-1
/en/course/2026/PIVP23RI1.content:
Society places high demands on professional conduct. Physiotherapists must demonstrate to clients and health insurers that their physiotherapeutic interventions are well substantiated from a scientific point of view. Physiotherapists are expected to examine and treat their patients in the best possible way. The physiotherapist's actions are based on the norms and values of the patient(s) concerned, the physiotherapist's clinical expertise, and the best available scientific evidence. Therefore, working according to these principles of evidence-based practice (EBP) is a must for every physiotherapist.
Research & Innovation 1 deals with the basic principles of applied scientific research. In this course, the investigative ability of students is stimulated: the student becomes acquainted with the EBP cycle and applies this method to a physiotherapeutic case. During the course, small groups will work on formulating research questions; searching scientific literature; assessing and interpreting this literature; organizing, summarizing, and displaying results in a fact sheet. The student will also gain knowledge about research designs and basic statistics. The course is concluded with a group assignment and an individual knowledge test. At the end of this course, the student has acquired basic knowledge about applied scientific research and gained experience with the EBP cycle. As a result of the course, the student can broadly understand and interpret research on physiotherapeutic treatment effects.

/en/course/2026/PIVP26PD1JI1.content:
This course consists of Professional Development 1 and Junior Internship 1.
The student career trajectory is part of the physiotherapy studies; the student learns to establish a connection between his studies and the profession of physiotherapist. This requires a learning process in which he learns to organise and plan, take responsibility for the choices he makes, and give shape to the ensuing actions. In this way he learns to give a sense of direction to the physiotherapy studies. In our programme a student has primary responsibility for his studies and career.
A professional identity emerges through an interaction between the student, their education, and their immediate environment. It gives the student their own identity as a starting physiotherapist at the end of their studies. A professional identity is formed gradually through (work) experiences. Professional and personal development are closely related. Personal development influences, colors, and shapes professional development, and vice versa. This course mainly focuses on developing the competences of the 'Reflective Professional' of the Physiotherapist's professional profile.
In professional development 1 following themes will be addressed during the first year: getting acquainted with the education, the role of the reflective professional, and the profession of physiotherapist.
Junior Internship 1 has a group- and an individual component. Gaining practical experience through internships at an early stage is essential. Early exposure allows students to become familiar with the profession beyond the classroom, working with real patients, bridging the gap between theory, case studies and practice. By working directly with patients and observing experienced physiotherapists, students develop a clearer understanding of professional roles of a physiotherapist. During the internships, the student will not only interact with patients but also gain firsthand experience of working within a healthcare institution. This will enable them to develop an understanding of the overall functioning and organization of healthcare.
Portfolio Assessment 1 and 2 will include critical reflections on both Professional Development 1 and Junior Internship 1.

/en/course/2026/PIVB25EHP.content:
In the section of the curriculum dedicated to entrepreneurship, the focus is on innovation in physiotherapy. Within the competence profile of the physiotherapist, the ability to organize and innovate becomes increasingly crucial. The dynamics in healthcare are changing, as are the needs of patients. This calls for flexibility and an expanded skill set for new healthcare providers.
At Hanze University of Applied Sciences, entrepreneurship is considered a key focal point, but it does not mean that every physiotherapist must start their own business. However, every University of Applied Sciences (HBO) student is expected to possess entrepreneurial qualities by the end of their studies.
Entrepreneurial qualities are also important in existing organizations. These qualities are necessary to continually innovate and develop new ideas to enhance physiotherapeutic care.
As an entrepreneurial physiotherapist, it is crucial to respond to the needs of the environment. To understand these needs effectively, various research methods are employed. Only when the needs are clear we contemplate possible solutions. Different techniques and methodologies are applied for this purpose, such as design thinking, moonshot thinking, and the business model canvas.
By practising and working with these methods, students are able, by the end of this module, to make an innovative contribution to the organization of healthcare.
This course includes the
IPE Cluster Project Health, Care & Vitality – Year 2
Collaboration in healthcare contributes to the quality of care for patients and clients, but it is not always self‑evident. Healthcare professionals act from a strong professional identity, which guides their choices and decisions. Effective collaboration requires insight into each other’s roles, perspectives, and areas of expertise, so that role clarity can develop and more can be achieved together.
In this project, students use the Meta-Model of Interprofessional Development (Reinders, 2018; Reinders & Pesut, 2022; Reinders et al., 2023). They work through: Phase 0 (professional identity), Phase 1 (shared problem domain), and Phase 2 (combining priorities and alternatives), with the aim of strengthening collaboration and making use of the added value of each other’s differences.

The education focuses on the Study and Professional Development of students. Throughout the entire physiotherapy program, the student develops their own professional identity. Professional identity is about who you are, what is distinct about you, making you recognizable to others, and enabling you to stand firm in challenging situations. Professional identity develops through interaction between the student, the program, and the immediate environment. Professional identity forms gradually. Personal and professional development are closely interconnected, with personal development influencing, colouring, and shaping professional development, and vice versa.
Directly linked to the Professional Development curriculum is Junior Internship 2.

/en/course/2026/PIVB25PC9PE.content:
The course Pediatric Physiotherapy consists of 2 parts.
Part 1:
Theoretical and practical instruction will be given in the field of physiotherapy for children. The main focus of this module is the development (motoric and social-emotional) and locomotor learning of children (ages 0 to 18 years). We will discuss specific pediatric physiotherapeutic clinimetric tools and observational skills. Observational skills will be tested by means of a presentation. When relevant, we will work with patient demonstrations. The module will end with a practical test in which skills and clinical reasoning are tested by means of case study.
Part 2:
A number of specific conditions will be discussed in this module. Attention will be paid to the development of these conditions and the role of a pediatric physiotherapist. The module will end with a practical test in which skills and clinical reasoning are tested by means of case study.

/en/course/2026/PIVB25PC9AD.content:
Employees have to work longer and experiencing more and more work pressure. The physiotherapist is important in analyzing and reducing mental and physical stress factors that are related to work. In addition, the physiotherapist is competent in different mental and physical stress-reducing techniques. During various previous courses, the student has gained experience in reduced participation by means of written cases. Within this course the student performs a work analysis at a person who works with complaints.
Also physiotherapeutic methods that can be applied to nonspecific musculoskeletal problems such as back pain, neck pain and shoulder pain, which often are workrelated, will be discussed.
Complex work-related health problems are also addressed. This enables the student to better respond to complex work-related complaints that put the sustainable employability of workers under pressure. Attention is paid to both acute complaints and care in the post-rehabilitation phase, in collaboration with other healthcare professionals

/en/course/2026/BOVP23RINTROLAB.content:
In this module, you will correctly learn the basic operations of working in a biological laboratory (weighing, dissolving, pipetting with micropipettes) taking into account safety and environmental aspects. You need knowledge of chemistry to estimate the properties of a substance and its correct name and formula. With the Periodic Table of Elements and knowledge of modern atomic theory, you learn about the chemical properties of atoms to know what type of compounds they prefer to form.
In Biology classes, you will learn about the diversity of life from the theory of evolution and discover the different domains of life (prokaryotes, archaea, eukaryotes). In the tutorials, you will complete assignments to practise the material, learn to use English terms and acquire general study skills.
To prepare for module 3's basic maths skills, 4x maths lessons (fractions/calculus rules/scientific notation/solving first- and second-degree equations) are given to refresh your knowledge.

/en/course/2026/BOVP23RVISUAL.content:
Microscopy is an important technique in medical and biological laboratory research. There are many different types of microscopes, each with its own field of application and associated techniques. In this module, you will use a light microscope in the practical. A light microscope is not a 'plug-and-play' instrument. To perform microscopy properly, it is important to understand the properties of the instrument. For this, you will receive applied theory lessons in geometrical and physical optics. In addition, in biology lessons you will learn more about the different cells, tissues and organs of the animal and plant kingdom.
When working in the laboratory, you must always document exactly what you did and how you worked out the results of your experiments. To do this, you learn to use a digital logbook (e-labjournal).

You independently perform simple chemical calculations (mol, gram, reaction equations, molarity, dilutions) using a scientific calculator according to current scientific knowledge;

/en/course/2026/BOVP23RANALIST.content: Many different model organisms are used in the field of biological and medical research, such as Escherichia coli, Hansenula polymorpha, Drosophila melanogaster, Caenorhabditis elegans, Arabidopsis thaliana, etc. In this module, you will get to know some of these organisms in the lab, giving you a good overview of your future profession. In a project group, you find out how they grow and for which research questions they are used in the work field of the research analyst. You present the results of your research to your fellow classmates. Chemical calculation is an essential part of the research analyst's work, necessary for making the right growth media, among other things. To this end, we make a start with chemical arithmetic (mole calculations and dilutions). You are also taught mathematics in order to be able to calculate correctly with scientific notations, second-degree equations and logarithms. Because this module already gives you a very good idea of your future profession, we let you reflect extensively on the past module. This conscious self-evaluation will enable you to assess whether you have made the right study choice.

This module covers some basic aspects of microbiology. First, you will learn how to work under VMT (Safe Microbiological Techniques) conditions in practice. This 3-day VMT course concludes with a test in which laws and regulations are also interpreted. After satisfactory completion of the course in terms of test, actions and logbook, you will receive the nationally recognised VMT certificate. The data from the course is used to get acquainted with descriptive statistics. You make assignments with types of errors, normal distribution and concepts such as mean, standard deviation, variance, error in the mean and confidence intervals, among others.
You will also delve into how the metabolism of bacteria works and how you can use it to identify different bacteria. Together with your project group, you will practically identify a bacterium from the Enterobacteriaceae family and make a presentation about the organism for your fellow students. You will be supported with background information and exercises in presentation and collaboration.

These macromolecules are covered in detail chemically and biologically. This includes the following aspects: DNA as an information carrier, DNA replication, transcription and translation. In addition, the principles of various molecular techniques are covered so that the student understands the background of the techniques during lab practical.

/en/course/2026/BOVP23RPRJMOLBIO.content: In this module, students will apply the home-made molecular techniques from the module "Molecular lab techniques" during a project that ties in with the theory of the module "The central dogma". Examples include "Expressing GFP in an E. coli and demonstrating it on SDS-PAGE" and "Determining rhesus factors in blood using PCR". Techniques used include SDS-PAGE and PCR and the project will deal with at least one of the macromolecules and/or with the central dogma. During the project, the student will receive instruction from a supervisor and will then work in groups to develop a plan of action that includes the associated theory and a clear schedule of how to approach the experiment in the lab. With the help of a supervisor, the group must come up with this planning themselves and sign up for practical days (4 x half-day sessions) to carry out the experiment. After the execution, the results are presented to each other via a scientific poster at a mini-symposium.

/en/course/2026/BOVH24RMICROBIO.content: In this module, the basics of microbiology are covered. You delve into the structure, metabolism, and growth of prokaryotic microorganisms. Attention is also given to the interaction between humans and microorganisms and the function of antibiotics. The acquired knowledge is assessed through written exams. During the practical component, you learn various methods to (selectively) culture, isolate, and identify microorganisms. With this knowledge, you design your own isolation method for a microorganism in a project and execute your plan. The practical component is supported by lessons on microbiological techniques and project work. You process and discuss the results in a digital logbook and a scientific report.

/en/course/2026/BOVH24RMOLMICRO.content: This module provides a molecular microbiological foundation for research students. The theoretical part of the module extensively covers the regulation of gene expression in bacteria and the structure and functioning of viruses. The acquired knowledge is assessed through written exams. The practical component consists of a computer lab session combined with a laboratory session. During the computer lab session, you use bioinformatics software to analyze in silico DNA sequences, design primers, and simulate cloning experiments. During the laboratory session, you conduct a cloning experiment in Escherichia coli. You process and discuss the results in a digital logbook.

/en/course/2026/BOVH24RIMMUNO.content:
This module provides an introduction to immunology. The immune system is involved in the defense against pathogens, including certain bacteria, viruses, fungi, yeasts and parasites. Under certain circumstances, the immune system can also target its own body, resulting in  autoimmune diseases. In this module you will gain knowledge of the immune system, including the development of T and B cells, the humoral and cellular immune response, the structure and function of lymphoid organs, the Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC), pattern recognition and anti-microbial proteins. A number of immunological techniques that are frequently used in the laboratory will also be discussed.
During the practical course we will conduct research in the field of Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD). COPD is characterized by chronic inflammation of the airways, leading to airway obstruction, tissue destruction and pulmonary emphysema. Tobacco smoking accounts by far the leading cause of COPD in high-income countries. During the practical course you will investigate the effect of cigarette smoke on human cells and the consequences for the immune system. Various immunological techniques are used for this.
An international project week also takes place in this module. During this week, students from a number of different countries are exchanged and attention is paid to intercultural communication, collaborating on a project in the laboratory and the English language. This week ends with a reflection paper and active participation is expected.

/en/course/2026/BOVH24RGENETICA.content:
Growing older is unfortunately still accompanied by unnecessary risks, such as a higher chance of chronic diseases. If this is also combined with an unhealthy lifestyle, such risks may increase even further. It is therefore important to research what a healthy lifestyle is and how you can age more healthily, ie. "healthy ageing."
Within genetics, "healthy ageing" is an important topic, because certain risk factors in the aging process are genetically determined.
During the Genetics lectures,you will learn what processes are responsible for aging in eukaryotic organisms, what aberrations are involved and what possible solutions for "healthy aging" could be.
This acquired knowledge can then be applied by the students during the practical course in which they work with a eukaryotic model organism, namely C. elegans, which is often used in the field to study genetic mutations to gain the necessary insights in the field of "healthy ageing."
Moreover, it is important to elaborate and present the data obtained from the practical C. elegans experiment in scientific English using a poster. The poster is one of the most widely used forms in the international biomedical field, therefore it is required to provide the necessary training.
At the conclusion of this module, you will orient to a possible internship and/or graduate position by interviewing a trainee or graduate and write a report about this.

metadata.Name: Plant Physiology & Biotechnology
metadata.Modes of delivery: Guest lecture International excursion Lecture Practical / Training Project-based learning Tutorial
metadata.Assessments: Plantenfysiologie Theorie - Computer, organised by STAD examinations Practicum & Project Planten - Other assessment

/en/course/2026/BOVH24RPLANTBIO.content:
Due to climate change and the loss of biodiversity, global food production is under increasing pressure. Issues such as "How can we make agriculture future-proof?" are more important than ever. Plants form the basis for food production. To grow crops sustainably, productively, and with high nutritional value, knowledge of plant physiology is crucial. This course covers how plants are structured, how they respond to light, nutrients, and other environmental factors, and how these responses are related to the plant's chemical composition.
The module consists of several components. Various plant physiological concepts and analytical methods are covered in lectures. This knowledge is applied during several practical experiments with plants. In these experiments analytical techniques such as TLC, HPLC, and spectrometry are applied. Focus is also given to growing plants under sterile conditions and isolating plant constituents using setups like a Soxhlet apparatus. Statistical analyses are performed on the obtained data to examine its value.
In addition to experiments with pre-designed protocols, students work in project groups on setting up their own experiment. Within the given framework of the project, the project group conducts research on growth, development, and/or constituents of plants under defined conditions. Based on this project, each student authors a scientific report individually.
To gain more insight into how companies working with plants operate, a group excursion is organized to a plant-related company. Here, the connection is made with the Sustainable Development Goals and how the company contributes to these goals. Reflection on this is done through a report.
The module concludes with self-reflection on the professional development of the student so far and their own ideas about future professional development are presented.

metadata.Name: Project Genetic Engineering
metadata.Assessments: Molecular Biology Theory - Computer, organised by STAD examinations Project CRISPR - Other assessment

/en/course/2026/BOVH25RPJGENETIC.outcomes:
You have an overview of various molecular biology methods and techniques used in biomedical and biotechnological research.
You can simulate and perform various molecular genetic techniques in silico and in practice, such as DNA cloning and PCR.
You can plan, simulate, and apply CRISPR-Cas9 technology or CRISPR interference techniques in a laboratory setting to modify specific genes and analyze the effects on the target organism.
You are able to analyze research data from the experiment in a scientifically responsible manner and discuss the data based on literature and draw a conclusion.
You can create an English report about the performed experiment according to established guidelines.
/en/course/2026/BOVH25RPJGENETIC.content:
In this module, the emphasis will be placed on several general molecular genetic techniques, such as restriction analysis, DNA cloning (ligation and transformation of bacterial cells), and PCR.
During the theory lessons, you will gain knowledge of the various molecular biological techniques. In addition, you will learn to perform simulations on the computer before you carry out the techniques in the lab.
In the project, the CRISPR-Cas9 technique, specifically CRISPR interference, is used as a tool for genetic modification of
Bacillus subtilis
. CRISPR interference (CRISPRi) is a method used to downregulate specific genes in an organism. In the case of
Bacillus subtilis
, the
amyE
and
sunI
genes can be targeted with CRISPRi to reduce their expression levels. This technology utilizes the CRISPR-Cas9 system to bind to the promoter region of target genes and prevent transcription, leading to decreased gene expression. By downregulating the
amyE
and
sunI
genes in
Bacillus subtilis
, you will be able to study the function of these genes and potential applications in biotechnology. You will complete this project by writing a report in English, in which the research results are presented and discussed in an organized manner and according to established guidelines. You will receive support for this by following a series of writing skills lessons.

metadata.Name: Data Analysis & Data Visualisation
metadata.Assessments: Data Analysis using R - Other assessment Introduction data & Data Analysis using Excel - Other assessment

/en/course/2026/BOVH25RDATAVISUA.outcomes:
You can explain the fundamental concepts of data, including data types, data structures, and the importance of data quality, and you can apply these concepts in the context of both Excel and R.
You can import data from various sources (such as CSV, TXT, Excel files) into both Excel and R, and you are able to select the appropriate methods and functions for different data formats and structures. You can clean and prepare data for analysis in both Excel and R by applying techniques for identifying and handling missing values, outliers, inconsistencies, and duplicates.
You can apply and interpret various data analysis functions in both Excel and R, including determining minimum and maximum values, calculating percentiles, selecting specific data based on criteria, applying conditional formatting to visually identify patterns, and sorting data to gain insights.
You can create effective data visualizations in both Excel and R (such as bar charts, line charts, pie charts, and box plots) to communicate patterns, trends, and relationships in data, and you can customize the visualizations for a clear and purpose-driven presentation.
/en/course/2026/BOVH25RDATAVISUA.content:
Health and biological sciences are transforming due to vast data from sources like genomics, proteomics pharmacological data and clinical trials. Researchers use data analysis and visualization to gain insights. Analysis involves processing data to find patterns. Visualization transforms data into charts, aiding understanding, pattern identification, and communication. These tools are crucial for unlocking health data's potential.
This module teaches data analysis and visualization using Excel and R (Tidyverse). You'll learn to analyze and visualize different data types for reports. R is a key programming language in this field. Assignments will be completed with Excel and R. The module concludes with an independent portfolio assignment.

metadata.Name: Project Cell Biology & Oncology
metadata.Assessments: Ethics, Data Security and Scientific Integrity - Other assessment Project Oncology - Other assessment

/en/course/2026/BOVH25RPRJCELL.outcomes:
You can apply cell biological techniques individually as well as part of a team, for the purpose of diagnostic and scientific research on cancer within a biomedical laboratory setting.
You will implement an experimental design and research strategy, independently and as part of a team, in which you will be considering the specific safety, environmental, and hygiene aspects.
You can analyze, interpret, and evaluate self-obtained research results, which you will report and present through work meetings, presentations, and a scientific report.
You can manage data according to the FAIR data principles and ensure that the data is properly disclosed.
You have processed the data according to the following ethical, integral, and scientific principles: honesty, care, transparency, independence and responsibility.
You demonstrate that you can actively participate in career-enhancing activities, such as visiting and evaluating poster presentations, attending a job application training including the creation of a CV and cover letter, and participating in a Meet and Greet with professionals. You reflect on these experiences and can clearly explain how these developments contribute to your professional growth and preparation for the job market during a mentoring session. Additionally, you will acquire knowledge of international awareness within your professional context and reflect upon its significance.
/en/course/2026/BOVH25RPRJCELL.content:
During this project assignment, students develop independence and creativity by planning and executing a research project in pairs and groups. The projects are related to oncology and, in addition to conventional 2D cell culture, sometimes also include 3D cell culture techniques and trans-differentiation techniques. They go through the entire process, from literature research and protocol selection to experimental execution and data analysis. They present their progress and results in work meetings, where they also receive feedback from lecturers and fellow students. The project, spread over 9 practical days, requires thorough preparation in the first weeks, followed by experimental execution and reporting.
In addition to their development of practical research skills, this project also places a strong emphasis on the principles of good data management and scientific integrity. The students learn to manage their data according to the FAIR principles (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable), which is essential for the transparency and reproducibility of scientific research.
Furthermore, students are expected to adhere to the ethical standards and values that apply within science. This includes honesty (not falsifying or fabricating data), diligence (handling data and methods accurately and critically), transparency (openly sharing data and methods so that research is verifiable), independence (avoiding conflicts of interest and conducting research objectively), and responsibility (taking responsibility for the integrity of the research and the ethical implications of the work).
By integrating these principles into the project, students are not only trained in research methods, but also in the essential values of scientific integrity.
The possibilities of generative AI will also be explored, and students will learn to work with generative AI in a transparent and responsible manner.
Finally, you participate in career-enhancing activities that help with your professional development. You visit and evaluate poster presentations by fellow students. Additionally, you attend a job application training where you work on your CV and cover letter. During a Meet and Greet, you get to know professionals from the field. By reflecting on these experiences and discussing them during a mentoring session, you gain insight into your own growth and preparation for the job market.
The field of biological research analysis is highly international, making 'International Awareness' an indispensable professional skill. You will not only learn to recognize inter- and intracultural differences but also develop the ability to collaborate effectively within international research teams. By critically integrating your practical experiences into a reflection, you will substantiate how these cultural competencies enhance the quality of your future professional practice.

metadata.Name: Human Genetics & Cell Biology
metadata.Assessments: Human Genetics & Cell Biology - Computer, organised by STAD examinations Scientific literature - Other assessment

/en/course/2026/BOVH25RHUMANGENS.outcomes:
You can name different DNA mutation and repair mechanisms and understand their contribution to the development of diseases such as cancer.
You can describe how cells replicate, how the cell cycle works, and know which proteins are involved, and you can explain the role of specific proteins in the different phases of the cell cycle.
You can describe how communication takes place at different levels between eukaryotic cells and within cells in a multicellular organism, and you can name how to intervene in this, for example for the treatment of cancer.
You can describe the molecular mechanisms that underlie the development of neurodegenerative protein folding diseases such as Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, and Huntington's disease.
You are able to read, understand, summarize, and present the main points of scientific literature on cell biology and genetics to fellow students.
/en/course/2026/BOVH25RHUMANGENS.content: This module delves into the fundamental processes of life at the cellular and molecular level. Students explore the complexity of DNA mutations and repair mechanisms, and how these contribute to the development of diseases such as cancer. The module covers the cell cycle and cell replication in detail, highlighting the role of essential proteins. Additionally, it addresses communication between and within cells in multicellular organisms, and how these processes can be influenced for therapeutic purposes, particularly in the context of cancer treatment. The molecular mechanisms behind neurodegenerative protein folding diseases such as Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, and Huntington's disease are also covered. Students learn to critically analyze, summarize, and present scientific literature in a flip-the-classroom setting.

/en/course/2026/BOVP23MDANALIST.outcomes:
You have an understanding of the curriculum of the study of medical diagnostics and on the professional duties of the medical analyst for the purpose of professional orientation.
You have mastered the general laboratory skills of a medical analyst, including laboratory rules and safety, correctly setting up and using a microscope and drawing according to drawing rules with the aim of learning to work safely and responsibly in the laboratory.
You will name the structure and function of the various organ systems in mammals, correctly dissect the rat and point out organs to learn mammalian anatomy and physiology.
You and a project group will present a self-test as an introduction to a diagnostic method, explaining how the self-test works and explaining the concepts of sensitivity and specificity.
You will create, track and evaluate a realistic weekly schedule leading to timely completion of tasks and assignments to master study skills.

/en/course/2026/BOVP23MDANALIST.content:
You are going to explore the profession of medical analyst and how it fits into the curriculum of the Biology and Medical Laboratory Research - Medical Diagnostics programme.
You will delve into the work field of the medical analyst using various sources (e.g. the programme description, the curriculum overview, job banks, media articles, the internship/graduation archive, research publications, interviews with trainees/analysts and possibly your own sources).
During the practicals, you will learn basic laboratory skills and safety aspects related to them.
In addition, you will investigate the use and principle of a self-test within a group and present this via a multimedia product. You will study the theory of organ systems and present it to each other. To conclude, you will examine, name and draw the different organs and organ systems of an organism in the laboratory.
Finally, you will reflect on the professional content by presenting your experiences together with fellow students at the end of the module.

metadata.Assessments: Cells and Cell Division - Other assessment Central Dogma and Biomolecules - Computer, organised by STAD examinations

/en/course/2026/BOVP23MDCEL.outcomes:
You name and describe the anatomy and physiology of the cell and the different cell organelles and you distinguish under a microscope between pro- and eukaryotic cells as the basis of general cell biology.
You explain the successive steps of the central dogma as the basis of molecular biology in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes and you recognize and illustrate the different phases of mitosis by visualizing these phases in the cells of onions with a fellow student during the practical.
You know the structure of different macromolecules (sugars, proteins, DNA/RNA) and you explain their function in a cell/organism as the basis of biochemistry.
You name the function and construction of neurons, the action of neurotransmitters such as acetylcholine and the action of sodium/potassium pumps of the cell.
You collaborate effectively and record agreements verifiably for social, communication and information skills to produce a multimedia group product on cells or cell division.

/en/course/2026/BOVP23MDCEL.content:
During this module, you will study the structure of the prokaryotic and eukaryotic cell in both theory and practice. In the process, you will learn about the functions of different cell organelles and macromolecules.
You study the cell organelles in a group and present them to classmates. With the same fellow student, you visualize the different phases of mitosis during the practical. You work out classwork in a logbook during a tutorial under the guidance of a teacher.
The central dogma and macromolecules are tested at the end of the module by means of a digital test.
