/en/course/2026/CIVB25OCM2.outcomes:
Learning Outcomes
After completing this course the student is able to:
demonstrate the ability to analyze key components of integrated marketing communications (IMC)
demonstrate the ability to analyze marketing campaign effectiveness
audit the digital marketing activities of a company or brand based on a relevant customer segment and their journey
provide relevant advice by creating suitable content and visualizations for different digital marketing channels
understand how to calculate costs and impact of a proposed digital marketing strategy
find and refer to relevant sources to substantiate choices and calculations
/en/course/2026/CIVB25OCM2.content:
Content
The course uses two main topics to provide an inclusive view on omnichannel marketing:
Marketing Communication
In recent decades, the number of communication channels has grown exponentially. There are many ways to communicate with potential customers, and competition for attention is high. You will learn how to investigate the target audience, decide which media to use, and identify criteria for an effective communication plan within an integrated marketing communications (IMC) approach. You will learn how to analyze and evaluate marketing campaign effectiveness using relevant performance indicators.
Digital Marketing
Understanding digital marketing starts with understanding the customer and their journey. You will learn how the customer journey is the foundation for composing SMART goals, defining target audiences, segments, and personas. Topics include paid, owned, and earned media, possibilities of main digital marketing channels, and content creation and visualisation for different channels. You learn to estimate costs, set budgets, and assess the financial impact of digital marketing strategies.
These theories and developments are put into practice by you through applied written assignments that combine Marketing Communication and Digital Marketing, involving the analysis of marketing communication and digital marketing activities, the development of recommendations, and the use of relevant sources to substantiate choices and calculations.
Literature/study materials
See Brightspace.

/en/course/2026/CIVB20IPA6.content:
Content
In this course, you work in a team on a real-world marketing communication project based on a Request for Proposal (RFP) or research brief. You analyse client goals, customer needs, and market insights to define a clear strategic direction for the project. Based on this analysis, you design targeted communication strategies that use appropriate mix of tools and touchpoints to reach the intended audience.
You prototype visually appealing digital and non-digital communication solutions and test them with real users to gather feedback. You use this feedback to refine and optimise your concepts, paying attention to both effectiveness and visual clarity. Throughout the project, you apply the design thinking process and document both the process and the resulting marketing communication campaign in a written proposal.
Together with your group, you develop and deliver a professional and engaging pitch that clearly communicates the campaign’s vision, potential impact, and financial feasibility. You also respond to client questions and demonstrate a clear, well-supported, and persuasive understanding of your proposal.
Literature/study materials
See Brightspace.

metadata.Name: Professional Identity 5
metadata.Assessments: Sales Training - Other assessment Storytelling - Other assessment

/en/course/2026/CIVB26PI5.content:
Level
Intermediate
Content
The course uses two main topics (Sales and Storytelling) to develop the skills needed for IPA 6 as part of the student’s professional identity. In IPA 6 you will develop a marketing communication campaign and pitch it to a client in a convincing way.
Sales Training
Selling is a profession in which, to be successful, you need knowledge of your product or service, the (prospective) client, the goals you aim to achieve, as well as effective sales conversation and negotiation techniques. Since the sales professional represents the company, it is also important that you understand how you come across to others, the image you convey, and how you can influence others effectively.
The training sessions consist of role play, giving feedback, and learning from each other. You learn the skills needed for an effective sales conversation and the phases it consists of. You learn how to identify customer needs and tailor your offer accordingly in order to sell your solution in a convincing and successful way.
Storytelling
Imagine this story:
Your business is in shambles. A marketing campaign has failed, you are short on budget, and your most valuable client has left. Your dream to start a successful business no longer seems realistic.
And then… something changes:
You find a way to clearly explain your value. Your message connects with customers, restores trust, and helps your business move forward. You feel relieved and confident again. Your story works!
This course focuses on storytelling as a professional marketing skill. You will learn how to apply storytelling structures and key components to craft clear and compelling business stories. You will practice delivering business narratives that communicate ideas and strategies effectively to stakeholders in a specific business context. These skills are essential for your future role as a marketing professional.
Literature/study materials
See Brightspace.

metadata.Name: Marketing Analysis
metadata.Assessments: Corporate Social Responsibilty - Assignment - Other assessment Finance - Assignment - Computer, organised by STAD examinations Marketing Analysis - Assignment - Other assessment

/en/course/2026/CIVB22MKA.outcomes:
Learning Outcomes
After successfully completing this course, the student is able to:
analyse a company’s brand mission and recommend improvements in line with Marketing 3.0 principles
assess marketing project-related decisions based on period profit, cash flows, and net present value
assess marketing campaign-related decisions based on relevant financial metrics
apply and justify suitable marketing models from theory in external and internal analyses in a case situation
use a systematic route to solve marketing challenges
/en/course/2026/CIVB22MKA.content:
Content
This course uses three topics to provide a comprehensive view on market analysis.
Marketing, Sales & Communication
You will learn the theory for conducting internal and external analyses in preparation for a strategic marketing plan. Internal analysis includes a marketing audit to assess the company’s marketing effectiveness. External analysis covers customer, industry, and competitor analysis. By using a structured system and tools based on marketing theory, you will understand the benefits of a systematic approach in solving marketing challenges.
Financial Management
You will learn which metrics evaluate digital marketing campaigns, marketing channels, and (capital) marketing projects. Metrics include conversion rates, customer acquisition cost, sales by channel, return on investment, payback period, and net present value. You will create a dashboard in Excel to transform inputs into actionable outputs.
Organisation & Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR)
Building on previous CSR knowledge, you will explore sustainability from a strategic perspective. You will understand how integrating sustainability and Marketing 3.0 principles into a company’s mission, vision, and values affects stakeholders, including customers, employees, and shareholders. The course covers the evolution of marketing to address deeper social, cultural, and environmental needs and demonstrates how brands can impact poverty, sociocultural changes, and environmental sustainability.
Literature/study materials
See Brightspace or intranet.

/en/course/2026/CIVB20IPA7.content:
Content
In this course, you will work on a real-life strategic marketing problem. You follow a systematic approach to analyse the current situation.
You start by designing the research plan and then conduct both secondary and primary research to capture the full external and internal environment. Based on this research, you perform a thorough analysis, draw conclusions, and report the findings regarding possible strategies or an unchanged policy.
All research, analysis, and conclusions are documented in a structured research report. During the course, you are expected to apply marketing theories and models correctly and reflect critically on your findings. This approach enhances your analytical, strategic, and problem-solving skills.
Literature/study materials
See Brightspace or intranet.

metadata.Name: Professional Identity 6
metadata.Assessments: Career Development Skills 2 - Other assessment Research Tooling 2 - Other assessment

/en/course/2026/CIVB26PI6.content:
Content
This course combines two topics to provide a comprehensive perspective on the professional skills required in IPA 7 and as part of the student’s overall professional identity.
Career Development Skills
The goal of this component is to help students recognize their strengths and knowledge, which will assist in securing a suitable internship or job placement. You will work on self-promotion skills, creating application documents that clearly demonstrate your interest in a specific job and what you can contribute to the company. You will also receive guidance on preparing for professional interviews and demonstrate your self-presentation skills in a simulated interview setting.
Research Tooling 2
This component focuses on core topics that determine the quality of applied research. It complements IPA 7 research by addressing research design, execution, and evaluation. The emphasis is on execution and evaluation, using a pragmatic approach that includes qualitative tools (e.g., interviewing) and analysis methods (e.g., coding and Atlas.TI). You will apply these methods to strengthen your research practice in IPA 7.
Literature/study materials
See Brightspace or intranet.

metadata.Name: Strategic Marketing
metadata.Assessments: Strategic Marketing - Assignment - Other assessment Strategic Marketing - Theory - Computer, organised by STAD examinations

/en/course/2026/CIVB20STM.outcomes:
Learning Outcomes
After successfully completing this course, the student is able to:
Marketing decisions:
compare international marketing strategies for different types of markets to justify companies’ choices
appraise market entry strategies chosen by various types of firms
question and integrate perspectives on international marketing strategy
analyse how competitive advantage may be achieved or sustained
Branding:
explain the role of brands, the advantages of creating strong brands and the sources of brand equity
explain the four components of brand positioning according to Lane Keller and the guidelines for brand positioning (including the brand mantra) and apply this knowledge by analysing existing brands
explain and identify the four steps in brand building resonance (CBBE model) and the stages in the Brand value chain
apply the CBBE model for the analysis and evaluation of existing brands
explain the guidelines and criteria for implementing the brand strategy in marketing program choices (brand elements and leveraging secondary associations)
identify different approaches to measuring brand equity
explain and evaluate the key components of brand architecture strategy and brand portfolios
explain the different types of brand extensions and analyse the main advantages and disadvantages of brand extensions
Digital Marketing:
choose and build campaign templates within digital marketing platforms based on the characteristics of a company
/en/course/2026/CIVB20STM.content:
Content
Marketing decisions:
In this course, you learn how to apply and execute the second part of the marketing planning process: the decisions. This includes market entry decisions and other marketing decisions at strategic (organizational and marketing), tactical, and operational levels. For each level, you learn to use different models.
Branding:
Increased competition, fast-changing markets, media transformation, and savvy consumers have made it more difficult for organisations to gain a distinctive, positive, and unique position in the minds of consumers. Implementing a clear and effective brand strategy can expand business opportunities because creating and nurturing a strong brand or brand portfolio can be one of the most valuable assets for a company. This applies to manufacturers, service providers, non-profit organisations, cities, or even persons. You will learn the meaning of brand equity for companies and consumers and the components for building strong brands. Steps and guidelines for designing and implementing a brand strategy will be explained and evaluated through theory, practical examples, and case studies. Students will also analyse competing brands using the presented theory.
Digital Marketing:
You will gain hands-on experience creating digital marketing campaigns on platforms such as Google Ads, Facebook, and LinkedIn. Tutorials cover the ins and outs of each platform and how to utilize them effectively for a company.
Literature/study materials
See Brightspace or intranet.

/en/course/2026/CIVB20IPA8.outcomes:
Learning Outcomes
After successfully completing this course, the student is able to:
formulate strategic organizational and marketing decisions for a company and support these decisions with data from the external and internal environment.
formulate tactical and operational marketing decisions for a company and substantiate these decisions using research and analysis;
present and defend the final advice to the CEO and/or management of a company;
reflect on their own behaviour, performance, and role in the project team
.
/en/course/2026/CIVB20IPA8.content:
Content
In this course, you build on the results and conclusions from the marketing analysis conducted in the previous block. You provide a comprehensive set of marketing recommendations for the company at strategic, tactical and operational level.
All recommendations are supported by research findings, analysis, and relevant marketing models and theories. You will also integrate knowledge from brand management and online marketing. In addition, you analyse the internal and financial consequences of your advice.
After completing the report, you present and defend your recommendations to the company’s management. You also reflect on the quality of your work, the team collaboration process, and your own contribution to the project.
Literature/study materials
See Brightspace or intranet.

metadata.Name: Professional Identity 7
metadata.Assessments: Business Communication English 5 - Other assessment Marketing & Culture skills - Other assessment

/en/course/2026/CIVB26PI7.outcomes:
Learning Outcomes
After completing this course the student is able to:
BCE 5:
write and pitch Marketing Advice keeping in mind the intercultural aspects of the company students collaborate with as part of the Integrated Project Assignment
give and receive constructive peer feedback
write marketing materials used in corporate communication
ICC 3:
focus on effective cooperation and the use of intercultural knowledge in the marketing field
identify the effects of cultural differences on strategic choices
make cultural transitions while working in an intercultural team
reflect on their own performance
/en/course/2026/CIVB26PI7.content:
Content
The course uses two topics to provide an inclusive view on which professional skills are needed in IPA 8 and as part of the student’s professional identity.
BCE 5
This course helps you write a formal business report in APA style. Additionally, you practise pitching your IPA marketing advice with integrated cultural elements. Collaboration and presentation skills are improved through constructive peer feedback on assignments.
ICC 3
As a student in Marketing Management, you are part of an intercultural working environment. Intercultural Communication (ICC) is an integrated part of the program. This ICC course explores the impact of cultural differences on corporate life, including the performance of international teams, saying 'no' and saving face while doing business, and cultural decisions in international marketing.
Literature/study materials
See Brightspace or intranet.

/en/course/2026/CIVB24INL.outcomes:
Learning Outcomes
After completing this course the student is able to:
behave professionally within a project group and demonstrate professional attitude and behavior toward clients
develop a professional marketing solution, including strategic, tactical, or operational product elements depending on the client assignment
create and manage a project planning in consultation with the Innovation Lab client, aligned with the chosen marketing solution
/en/course/2026/CIVB24INL.content:
Content:
In one intensive week, you will work in a group on solving a marketing issue for a real life client from the north of the Netherlands. You will meet the client at the beginning of the week, visit the company and at the end of the week present your groups solution to the client.
Leading in this project is the need of the client. If your client is happy, with your solution, then your had a successful Innovation Lab week
The intensive week takes place in P3. In P4, you will report on the development you have made on a self-chosen professional skill.
Literature/study materials
See Brightspace or intranet.

/en/course/2026/CIVB20CHM.content:
Content:
This course teaches you how to effectively manage change within organisations. You will learn that creating strong marketing plans is only the first step; implementing them requires collaboration with people who have different goals, perspectives and expertise.
In Block 1, you participate in an intensive week in collaboration with a partner University of Applied Sciences. You work in teams of up to five students as a Junior Change Consultant. Lecturers act as Senior Change Consultants to guide you in a virtual simulation game focused on change management and decision-making.
In Block 2, you complete individual and group assignments that deepen your understanding of the experiences from the simulation game. You apply theory, reflect on personal and team performance, and explore the human and organisational factors that influence successful change processes.
Literature/study materials:
See Brightspace or intranet.

metadata.Modes of delivery: Action learning Assignment Individual supervision International work placement Practical / Training Problem-based learning Project-based learning Work placement

/en/course/2026/CIVB26DOC.outcomes:
Upon successful completion of this course, the student is able to:
Describe and analyse the internal organisation, products/services, customers and competitors of the work placement company  applying marketing theories and models
Describe their daily duties and connecting these with professional competences
Set up a research proposal including the description of the marketing issue of your company assignment using the SMART model, MQ, MRQ, RQs
/en/course/2026/CIVB26DOC.content: By the end of the course, you will have an understanding of the company in which you are carrying out the internship, be able to explain its context, explain the marketing issue and set up a fitting research proposal with the goal of gaining insight to solve the marketing issue.

metadata.Name: Report Company Assignment
metadata.Modes of delivery: Action learning Assignment Individual supervision International work placement Practical / Training Problem-based learning Project-based learning Work placement

/en/course/2026/CIVB26ASS.outcomes:
Upon successful completion of this course, the student is able to:
Implement and conduct primary and secondary research
Based on research produce an analysis, extract conclusions and substantiate advice
Implement a marketing activity derived from research conclusions and evaluate the results according to the PDCA cycle
/en/course/2026/CIVB26ASS.content: By the end of this course you will have conducted primary and secondary research, carry out a marketing activity derived from research conclusions and evaluate the results according to the PDCA cycle.

metadata.Modes of delivery: Action learning Assignment International work placement Practical / Training Problem-based learning Work placement
metadata.Assessments: Professional Identity Work Placement - Other assessment

/en/course/2026/CIVB26PIWP.outcomes:
Upon completion student is able to:
Report on the progress of his activities and intercultural experiences
Reflect on their personal and professional development
Take ownership and effectively collaborate with various stakeholders
/en/course/2026/CIVB26PIWP.content: By the end of this course you will be able to manage different projects, collaborate with different stakeholders and reflect on your personal and professional development by using different reflection methods.

/en/course/2026/CIVB22PIA.outcomes:
Learning Outcomes
After completing this course the student is able to:
reflect on their professional identity by comparing their starting and current position
critically assess their professional development during the programme
formulate short-term learning and professional development goals
brand themselves as a young professional in a format of their choice
/en/course/2026/CIVB22PIA.content:
Content
This course prepares you for the labour market by supporting reflection on your professional skills and identity, and by developing these skills further. Lectures and workshops cover relevant theories and models. You will collect peer feedback from fellow students and use various tests and tools to guide your development.
To support preparation for the Graduation Project and career readiness, workshops and presentations by business professionals are part of the course.
Literature/study materials
See Brightspace or intranet.

/en/course/2026/CIVB22CAV.outcomes:
Learning Outcomes
After successfully completing this course, the student is able to:
based on a business or social challenge, identify the target audience, define the communication objective, and choose an applicable communication format
individually prepare and execute the chosen communication format(s)
demonstrate significant growth in the selected communication and/or visualisation skills compared to entry-level at the beginning of the course
reflect on and evaluate their own development and progress in desired communication and/or visualisation skills
evaluate the effectiveness and impact of other students' communication and/or visualisation skills
/en/course/2026/CIVB22CAV.content:
Content
Effective communication is essential for influencing people’s behavior or attitudes. Communication can take many forms, such as posters, videos, written opinion pieces, speeches, or performance art. A modern marketing professional should be able to explore beyond traditional presentations. You will be challenged to develop skills in a new, and innovative communication formats.
Starting from a business or social challenge, you will determine what needs to be communicated to change the attitudes and behavior of the target audience. You will define the message, identify the audience, and select the most appropriate communication format, which may be oral, textual, visual, or other. The quality and effectiveness of the execution will be assessed by the target group, fellow students, and the assessors.
Literature/study materials
See Brightspace or intranet.

metadata.Name: Dot, dot, dot Marketing
metadata.Assessments: Dot, dot, dot Marketing - Other assessment

/en/course/2026/CIVB24DDD.outcomes:
Learning Outcomes
After completing this course the student is able to:
deepen knowledge in a specific marketing domain
produce academic content on the chosen marketing topic
present and communicate insights to peers in an engaging and structured way
reflect on and evaluate personal learnings from the course
/en/course/2026/CIVB24DDD.content:
Content
In this course, you focus on a self-selected area of marketing to deepen your understanding and develop expertise. The first week introduces various topics to spark creativity. Afterwards, you choose a topic (“fill in the dots…”) and conduct independent research, including finding an expert on the chosen topic and interviewing them. You will produce an insightful output and share key findings with the class through a presentation or other suitable communication format. The format of the course combines workshop moments with individual consultations.
Literature/study materials
See Brightspace or intranet.

/en/course/2026/CIVB22SAL.outcomes:
Learning Outcomes
After completing this course the student is able to:
apply business development theory in a commercial B-to-B environment
distinguish between and adjust to the various roles and interests of the Decision Making Unit
build and maintain an effective long-term relationship with the client
negotiate a favourable deal for both parties aligned with the strategy of the company
/en/course/2026/CIVB22SAL.content:
Content
In this course, you will learn how to achieve high performance in business development through a combination of knowledge, skill, and discipline. The course combines theory, case studies, and role-play exercises to simulate real-life B-to-B commercial sales situations. You will:
understand business development in a commercial B-to-B context
apply theoretical insights in practical exercises, including simulations and role-plays
gain experience in managing authentic client interactions and negotiation processes
develop negotiation and relationship-building skills applicable to a commercial career or other professional contexts
Literature/study materials
See Brightspace or intranet.

/en/course/2026/CIVB22PFP.outcomes:
Learning Outcomes
After completing this course the student is able to:
criticise management questions, research questions, conceptual models, and methodologies
independently construct management questions, research questions, and a conceptual model based on a company issue
independently select an appropriate methodology to examine research questions
independently create a research proposal that functions as an educational tool to start the Graduation Project
/en/course/2026/CIVB22PFP.content:
Content
This course serves as a stepping stone for the Graduation Project.
You will initially review essential elements of a research proposal using teacher-provided material. In the second half of the course, you construct your own research proposal based on the company selected and approved for your Graduation Project. All decisions and elements are substantiated by the theory and methodology covered in the course. The assessment is individual and based on the research proposal, which also serves as the entry requirement for the Graduation Project.
Literature/study materials
See Brightspace or intranet.

/en/course/2026/CIVB22SSG.outcomes:
Learning Outcomes
After completing this course the student is able to:
Formulate a long term company goal and derived short term goal and select, justify and plan tasks that align with these goals and the company’s situation.
Execute a coherent set of interrelated tasks, based on one’s own analysis, that contribute to the creation or growth of a company, and adapt these tasks based on progressive insight.
Use networking and research skills to gather and interpret information for decision-making and expert validation.
Use networking and research skills to gather and interpret information for decision-making and expert validation.
Deliver a tailored business pitch or presentation to an audience relevant to the company’s current development stage (e.g., investors, clients, partners).
Reflect critically on key factors influencing business success, including one’s own role and responsibility.
/en/course/2026/CIVB22SSG.content:
Content
In this course, you take control of your entrepreneurial journey, whether you are starting a new business or scaling an existing one. You will work on your own business idea or growth plan, from the first concept to market testing, first sales, and initial steps toward scaling or attracting investors.
Course activities include:
Guest lectures providing insights into entrepreneurial practices
Community of learners sessions where students and teachers discuss and apply relevant theory and frameworks
Coaching sessions where teachers guide students in formulating actionable advice or strategies for a specific business context
Literature/study materials
Suggested literature and study material material will be shared in class and/or via Brightspace.

/en/course/2026/CIVB22SMM.outcomes:
Learning Outcomes
After completing this course the student is able to:
understand the relationship between business goals and campaign marketing goals
develop campaign marketing goals
identify metric and KPI selection options within different marketing channels and relate these to campaign marketing goals
analyse marketing impact using tools such as Google Analytics
/en/course/2026/CIVB22SMM.content:
Content
In this course, you deepen your understanding of marketing goals and their implications for campaign planning and evaluation. You will learn to:
connect business objectives with specific marketing campaign goals
select appropriate KPIs and metrics for different marketing channels
measure marketing impact through practical analytics tools, including Google Analytics
apply goal-setting, monitoring, and evaluation techniques to real-life marketing scenarios
The course emphasizes hands-on application to ensure you can integrate campaign goals with business strategy and assess marketing performance effectively.
Literature/study materials
See Brightspace or intranet.

/en/course/2026/CIVB22CPB.outcomes:
Learning Outcomes
After successfully completing this course, the student is able to:
create an intervention for a specific consumer behaviour challenge an organisation is facing, making use of psychological theories and models
critically evaluate and analyse consumer behaviour studies and apply the results of these studies to solve marketing problems related to products and services
consider psychological, personal, social, and cultural factors while finding solutions to marketing problems of products and services
apply various theoretical models of consumer psychology to solve marketing problems related to products and services
apply findings from neuromarketing and consumer neuroscience to solve marketing problems related to products and services
/en/course/2026/CIVB22CPB.content:
Content
During this course, you will deepen your knowledge of consumer psychology and apply it in a practical marketing context. You will develop the skills to analyse marketing problems and design strategies based on a thorough understanding of consumer behaviour and psychological concepts. Topics covered include consumer psychology, neuromarketing, and consumer neuroscience. The course combines theoretical frameworks with practical learning activities, in which you will design behavioural interventions and analyse real purchasing decisions from both a consumer and a marketer perspective.
Literature/study materials
See Brightspace.

/en/course/2026/CIVB19AO.content:
Content:
In this graduation course, you work independently on a clearly defined marketing, marketing communication or sales-related issue for an external organisation. You produce a professional advisory report (graduation thesis) supported by primary research and, where needed, literature or desk research.
You apply the full research cycle: analysing the problem, designing and conducting research, interpreting results and formulating actionable recommendations for the client. Your written work demonstrates analytical ability, methodological justification and clear communication of findings.
For the oral component, you defend your research approach and recommendations. You place your advice in a broader organisational and market context and answer questions professionally.
Written component:
Advisory report based on a defined marketing problem, supported by primary and secondary research.
Oral component:
Oral defence of research process, conclusions and advice.
Literature/study materials:
See Brightspace or intranet.
Prerequisites:
For credit prerequisites please check TER or Brightspace

/en/course/2026/BFVM23PREPDATSC1.outcomes:
You interpret mathematical notation.
You apply basic equations analytically, including linear, rational, quadratic, trigonometric, exp/log equations in one variable.
You execute differentiation and integration of standard functions in simple forms.
You understand basic matrices operations.
/en/course/2026/BFVM23PREPDATSC1.content: In this course, you will revise basic mathematical skills and knowledge in the fields of calculus. This is one of the three optional modules of the Preparatory course. It’s intended for students without a sound background in mathematics. The basic mathematical skills are a required level for the data sciences subjects.

/en/course/2026/BFVM23PREPPROGR1.outcomes:
By the end of the course
You use diverse suitable data types.
You employ appropriate Python flow control logic.
You implement and use functions, classes, and modules.
You translate a given problem into a robust and flexible object-oriented software product.
You can use the Linux shell to navigate and execute commands to do basic file operations.
/en/course/2026/BFVM23PREPPROGR1.content:
Overview
The course will start with introducing the basic programming concepts, code organization, data types, structures, and functions/standard libraries. Followed by more advanced technologies like the concepts of object-oriented programming.
Context learning line
In this course, you will revise the basics of programming in preparation for the Programming 1 course needed for the DS for personal health project assignment. This is one of the three optional modules of the Preparatory course. It's intended for students without a sound background in programming.

metadata.Name: Preparatory Course Omics 1
metadata.Assessments: Preparatory Course Omics 1 - Written, organised by School

/en/course/2026/BFVM23PREPOMICS.outcomes:
You can understand basic physiological processes.
You know the core components of both prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells and knows your role in the context of cell biology.
You know all the actors and components of the Central Dogma of Genetics and can describe what these are and what their role is.
You know the types of biological sequences, their characteristics, and their relationships.
You can understand basic concepts of laboratory "omics" techniques.
You know about the main methods used to analyse sequences.
/en/course/2026/BFVM23PREPOMICS.content:
Overview
You will be introduced to basic (animal) physiology, cell biology, and molecular genetics – primarily the Central Dogma. Also, the different types of biological sequences will be introduced; their properties, and ways of analyzing them (alignment, mapping, Blast).
Context learning line
This is one of the three optional modules of the Preparatory course. It’s intended for students without a background in (molecular) life science (e.g. ICT students). The content provides a base for annotating and understanding biological data.

metadata.Name: Data Science 2
metadata.Assessments: Bayesian Statistics - Computer, organised by School Numerical Analysis - Computer, organised by School

/en/course/2026/BFVM23DATASCNC2.outcomes:
You assess the quality of life science data and perform data clean-up.
You apply frequentist and Bayesian methods to estimate parameters with standard errors and confidence intervals.
You implement and apply numerical methods for analysis of data, including differentiation, integration and finding roots and extrema.
You explain how discretization, round-off and error propagation may affect the results of outcomes.
/en/course/2026/BFVM23DATASCNC2.content:
This course is designed to provide students with the practical implementation of Bayesian Statistics and Numerical Analysis using Python.
The first subject, Bayesian Statistics, covers topics such as constructing histograms, calculating sample moments, estimating parameters using the Method of Moment and Maximum Likelihood methods, evaluating various distributions, using null hypothesis significance tests, assessing normality, calculating standard errors and confidence intervals, and interpreting effect sizes. Students will learn how to use Bayes' theorem/law to calculate conditional probabilities and evaluate Bayesian estimators for parameters of various distributions using conjugated priors.
The second subject, Numerical Analysis, is focused on the application of numerical methods to solve mathematical problems. The course will provide an overview of numerical differentiation, numerical integration, root finding, optimization, and differential equations, and characterize their propagated errors.
By the end of the course, students will have an understanding of Bayesian Statistics and Numerical Analysis, and the ability to apply these concepts in their research.

/en/course/2026/BFVM23PROGRAM2.outcomes:
Apply Python, Numpy and pandas to effectively clean, transform, and structure raw data into a format suitable for analysis, demonstrating.
Evaluate and choose appropriate data exploration, processing, analysing and visualization methods. Critically assess trade-offs between different strategies and justify the chosen approach.
Design and develop functional and visually appealing data visualizations that effectively communicate insights and finding of categorical and non-time related data. Create interactive and informative visualizations.
Demonstrate the ability to create a well-organized and well-documented codebase, with clear separation of concerns and modular components, all managed through a Git repository.
/en/course/2026/BFVM23PROGRAM2.content:
This course is designed to provide practical skills for processing and analyzing data, preparing it for modeling and visualization. You will learn to work with data science tools such as Jupyter Notebooks, NumPy, Pandas, Matplotlib, and Bokeh.
Each week, you will practice programming techniques for loading, cleaning, analyzing, and visualizing different types of data, mostly focused on numerical and categorical data.
You will explore best practices for organizing and documenting to ensure that it remains readable, understandable, and reusable over time.
By the end of this course, you will have a solid understanding of the data processing pipeline and be able to use these tools and techniques to handle diverse datasets, conduct exploratory data analysis, and create effective visualizations.

metadata.Name: Research & Professional Skills
metadata.Assessments: Research & Professional Skills 1 - Other assessment Research & Professional Skills 2 - Other assessment

/en/course/2026/BFVM25RPS.outcomes:
You demonstrate effective communication and collaboration skills using different communication styles.
You demonstrate taking initiative and acting autonomously in the face of challenges, while also being a team player.
You develop a simple business case for a new product or methodology and supervise the execution of a project plan to deliver projects on-time and within prescribed conditions.
You create a stimulating environment to facilitate and enhance the performance of a project team by recognizing and utilizing individual team members' strengths and personal qualities.
You evaluate the relevance and significance of scientific literature in relation to your research.
You evaluate the design and outcomes of scientific research in data sciences and/or life sciences, considering the key elements of the scientific process, applied to own work, work of others, and the relation between them.
You evaluate the reliability, validity, and reproducibility of data analysis methods and results, both of own research and that of others, before and/or after the research is conducted.
You evaluate and address possible ethical, legal, and societal implications of a research project.
You evaluate your own learning process and use this to make well-founded choices concerning your personal and professional development.
/en/course/2026/BFVM25RPS.content: This course is designed to enhance your abilities to function as critical, independent, and effective scientific researchers. The course consists of several activities, including a personal assessment (DISC report) to identify preferred communication styles and develop effective communication and collaboration skills. Workshops will cover topics such as code management, version control, business case, IP patenting, and the scrum methodology to teach youto work in a professional environment. Project management lectures will train you to structure project plans, make realistic plans, and integrate effective communication and collaboration skills. The course will also include workshops on lateral thinking, scientific reading and writing, critical thinking, and ethical, legal, and societal implications. All these learning outcomes will be developed and trained throughout the entire master program.

metadata.Name: Data Science 3
metadata.Assessments: Linear Algebra - Written, organised by STAD examinations Signal Analysis - Computer, organised by School

/en/course/2026/BFVM23DATASCNC3.outcomes:
You manipulate mathematical expressions involving real and complex numbers, scalars, vectors and matrices.
You invert and decompose matrices, manually or assisted by computer, and diagnose and solve rank-deficient or ill-conditioned problems.
You process time-series data, including resampling, interpolation, and curve fitting by linear regression.
You apply linear filters and other data transformations in both the time- and frequency domains.
/en/course/2026/BFVM23DATASCNC3.content:
This course introduces the fundamental concepts and techniques of linear algebra and their applications in solving problems in different areas. The course comprises an introduction to complex numbers, vectors and matrices and how to operate on these. It includes topics such as matrix determinants and trace, matrix inversion and decomposition, and characterization of matrix rank.
In parallel, the course covers signal analysis. Topics covered in this section include interpolation and curve fitting, windowing, filtering and convolution, Fourier transformation, and the design of elementary discrete filters. Overall students learn to analyze and manipulate a wide range of time series data to identify patterns, remove noise and artifacts, and enhance signals.

/en/course/2026/BFVM23PROGRAM3.outcomes:
Apply Python to effectively clean, transform, and structure raw signal data into a format suitable for analysis or machine learning tasks, demonstrating proficiency in pandas, Numpy, and other relevant libraries.
Develop a maintainable and effective preprocessing and evaluation pipeline for time series and streaming data. Critically assess trade-offs between different strategies and justify the chosen approach.
Implement mathematical algorithms in Python, applying vectorization and other performance optimizations when appropriate. Validate the correctness and accuracy of the implemented algorithm through testing.
Design and develop functional and visually appealing data visualizations that effectively communicate insights and findings. Use best practices and relevant libraries to create interactive and informative visualizations.
Deliver an organized solution that complies with FAIR principles.
/en/course/2026/BFVM23PROGRAM3.content: This course teaches practical skills for processing and analyzing time-series, streaming, and signal data using popular data science tools such as Jupyter Notebooks, NumPy, Pandas, and Bokeh. Throughout the course, you will practice programming techniques for loading, cleaning, analyzing, and visualizing streaming data, with an emphasis on creating maintainable solutions. By the end of the course, you will have a solid understanding of the data processing pipeline and be able to handle diverse streaming data, conduct exploratory data analysis, and create effective visualizations. The course is designed to equip you with the skills needed to work with complex data and provide new insights as a foundation for future research and exploration.

metadata.Name: Data Science for Personal Health
metadata.Assessments: Data Science for Personal Health 1 - Professional product

/en/course/2026/BFVM23DSPH.outcomes:
After completing the course, you can:
Pose an exact and answerable research question (hypothesis).
Translate a research question into an experiment and carry out the necessary measurements to answer the research question.
Design a useable interface (web-based dashboard) to disclose research data and answer a research question.
Implement appropriate data(base) technologies given data sources.
Collaborate with team members to organize the project and carry out the practical work.
Write a scientific article about the research
/en/course/2026/BFVM23DSPH.content:
The objective of this research project is to enhance your comprehension of the Data Science domain, particularly in relation to personal health. To achieve this, health-related data will be visualized to answer health-related research questions. You will apply fundamental data transformation and munging techniques to pre-process the data for visualization. Additionally, the project aims to reinforce the programming concepts taught in the preparatory course while teaching you the principles of good UI design.
The project's secondary objective is to reinforce the concepts of the Scientific Method (hypothesis-experiment-analysis-conclusion/iteration) and scientific writing and reasoning. You're going to identify a personal health related domain you are interested in, study the state of the scientific literature in the field, pose a realistic research question and hypothesis and design and carry out an experiment.

metadata.Name: Data Science 4
metadata.Assessments: Graph Theory - Computer, organised by STAD examinations Multivariate Analysis - Assignment

/en/course/2026/BFVM23DATASCNC4.outcomes:
You can design a graph or multivariate model to represent a dataset within the life sciences domain and defend their choice based on the relational nature of the data.
You can choose appropriate existing algorithms to answer questions in the life sciences domain and justify this choice.
You can develop working code for an existing algorithm, given the relevant pseudocode and supporting libraries, such as NumPy and NetworkX.
You can interpret and explain mathematical set builder notation in the context of graph theory.
You can calculate complex attributes of abstract graphs, for example, the radius of a path graph of size n.
You can interpret the results from multivariate models in terms of relations within and between coupled datasets.
You can interpret the results from multivariate models in the context of the life sciences domain.
/en/course/2026/BFVM23DATASCNC4.content:
This course introduces you to
relational models of data
, with a focus on graphs and multilinear models. The course begins with an overview of
graph theory
, including the concepts of graphs, trees, adjacency matrix, directed acyclic graphs, paths and cycles, tree search, shortest path, random walks, Markov chains, sorting, and algorithmic complexity. The course then delves into the analysis of complex datasets using
multivariate linear models
, including multiple linear regression, partial least squares, canonical correlations, singular value decomposition, and principal component analysis.
Throughout the course, you will learn various methods for investigating and assessing relational features and complex datasets using graphs and multilinear models, with applications to the life sciences. You will also gain practical experience through programming assignments and data analysis projects.

/en/course/2026/BFVM24PROGRAM4OO.outcomes:
Design parallel solutions for computational problems.
Apply SOLID principles to software design.
Manage object life-cycle and multiple class interaction.
Use list comprehensions, generators, and map-reduce to design efficient parallel solutions.
Apply the Divide and Conquer mindset and algorithm to develop effective parallel solutions.
Deliver organized and responsible solutions to computational problems.
/en/course/2026/BFVM24PROGRAM4OO.content:
In this module, we look some more into object life-cycle and multiple class interaction
s
. After this, we look into the Divide and Conquer and Map Reduce algorithms, which provides us with the mindset of separating our unit of work into several sub-problems, that can be easily distributed over several machines.

/en/course/2026/BFVM24PROGRAM4R.outcomes:
You demonstrate proficiency in utilizing the R programming language, showcasing mastery in handling data types, functions, and flow control elements.
You display the ability to identify, assess, and choose packages tailored to your workflow requirements. You preferentially make use of the tidyverse packages, or packages built on top of these.
You construct workflows for data cleaning, pre-processing, and exploration on multivariate tabular data, with a keen focus on the data's purpose, especially the outcome variable.
You create and implement scientifically accurate data visualizations using ggplot2 or related packages that extend its capabilities.
You utilize RMarkdown for generating comprehensive exploratory data analyses (EDAs), reports, and presentations.
You use the shiny library to develop interactive documents and independent reactive data dashboards or analysis applications.
You publish your R code in a documented package structure, employing devtools and roxygen, on a git-managed platform following GitHub standards (Readme, license, etc.).
/en/course/2026/BFVM24PROGRAM4R.content: Tailored for master's students in Data Science for Life Sciences, this elective course enhances proficiency in R programming, offering a robust foundation for applied data science tasks within the life science domain, emphasizing crucial skills for data exploration, analysis, and dissemination in professional settings, specifically in the omics fields. Key topics covered include the development of efficient workflows for data cleaning and exploration, utilizing tidyverse packages, and creating impactful data visualizations with ggplot2. Participants will also gain hands-on experience in using RMarkdown to generate customized reports. Furthermore, you will learn to deliver well-organized solutions through the development of a professional documented package structure.

metadata.Name: Data Science 5
metadata.Assessments: Data Science 5 - Computer, organised by School

/en/course/2026/BFVM25DATASCNC5.outcomes:
You utilize an argumentative approach to select and apply appropriate supervised machine learning techniques and algorithms for a given problem in life science.
You implement predictive machine learning algorithms for regression and classification in Python and evaluate their validity and effectiveness.
You execute the general steps of the machine learning lifecycle, including data engineering, model selection, hyperparameter tuning, and model deployment, and apply them effectively to life science problems.
You demonstrate knowledge and understanding of the challenges and limitations of supervised machine learning in the context of the life science problem at hand.
/en/course/2026/BFVM25DATASCNC5.content: This course introduces the fundamental concepts and techniques of classical supervised Machine Learning and their applications in solving problems in different areas. The course begins with a repetition of linear regression, extending it to more general regression models. Subsequently, various classification methods are introduced, some of which are implemented extensively (e.g. Logistic regression, Naive Bayes, Decision trees) and some of which are covered more succinctly (e.g. k-Nearest Neighbor, Discriminant Analysis, Support Vector Machines). Finally some general topics and best practices are covered (e.g. ensemble learning, model evaluation metrics, feature selection, cross-validation, learning curve, and more).

/en/course/2026/BFVM25PROGRAM5.outcomes:
Following this course you will;
Understand the principles of parallel programming on large clusters.
Be able to use the Apache Spark framework to process large datasets, larger than fit on one computer.
Understand the performance of your program, and structure data and operations in such a way that you maximize throughput.
/en/course/2026/BFVM25PROGRAM5.content:
This course introduces you to parallel programming on large clusters, using the Apache Spark framework. Spark is a good example of a big-data processing framework, which gives you a set of tools to operate on very large datasets on multiple computers transparently. In other words, you don't program any differently than you would, using the same abstraction (dataframes) on a single node; the framework takes care of all network programming overhead.
There are a couple of extra tools that we will use, which are not directly part of the Spark eco-system, but which are both essential knowledge for Data Scientists, and which will help you in your work with Spark.
These are:
Structured Query Language (SQL), the standard programming language for interacting with relational databases.
SLURM, a workload manager, which allows you to run programs on a cluster of computers in a controlled way.
Cassandra, a distributed database, which is a good example of a NoSQL database, and which is often used in combination with Spark.
This is a 7-week practical research course, meaning you will be graded on programs that you submit, and that those programs are dealing with biological or biomedical research data. The course is taught in Python, and you are expected to have a good understanding of Python programming before you start this course; otherwise you will not be able to complete it.

/en/course/2026/BFVM23PRJOMICS.outcomes:
Formulate a clear, verifiable hypothesis on the basis of a client’s research question; identify and understand possible Omics techniques necessary for answering a research question and hypothesis.
Evaluate datasets for utility in answering a client’s hypothesis.
Pre-process datasets in order to be able to do inter-dataset analysis.
Apply and validate data science techniques in pre-processing data and meta-analysis across datasets.
Identify business and economics factors applicable to the research question and integrate them with the final conclusion (where applicable).
Present findings in a clear and scientific manner to the target audience (client, researchers, peers).
/en/course/2026/BFVM23PRJOMICS.content:
This course introduces the integration of various "omics" techniques that are used to address research questions that cannot be answered by a single analysis. These techniques are both quantitative and high throughput, generating large datasets that can be analysed using advanced statistical and machine learning methods. The course begins by introducing state-of-the-art lab techniques in areas such as (meta)genomics, transcriptomics, metabolomics, proteomics, epigenomics, foodomics, imaging, and epidemiology. You will have the opportunity to select a research project from partner research centres such as UMCG, AVEBE, KCBBE, and the Digital Society Hub that provide multiple datasets, and formulate and test hypotheses using appropriate data science techniques (Statistcs/Machine Learnng/Artificial Intelligence). A key aspect of this course is effectively communicating the methods and findings to peers and clients.
This course builds upon the technologies mastered in the first research project, and when appropriate, visualizations and web techniques from the first project will be utilized to report and clarify findings.

metadata.Name: Data Science 6
metadata.Assessments: Deep Learning - Computer, organised by School Unsupervised Learning - Assignment

/en/course/2026/BFVM25DATASCNC6.outcomes:
You utilize an argumentative approach to select and apply appropriate unsupervised machine learning techniques and algorithms for a given problem in life science, while also being able to evaluate their effectiveness.
You demonstrate knowledge and understanding of the challenges and limitations of unsupervised machine learning and deep learning in the context of the life science problem at hand.
You explain concepts related to neural networks in appropriate terminology, reason about their properties, and diagnose problems with chosen network designs.
You choose, design and implement a fully-connected feed-forward neural network, or a convolutional or recurrent neural network to perform classification or regression of tabular, image, or time series data.
/en/course/2026/BFVM25DATASCNC6.content: This course is designed to provide both foundational and in-depth knowledge of unsupervised and deep learning machine learning techniques, focusing on their application in life sciences. You will explore various data-driven approaches, enhance your analytical skills, and develop a comprehensive portfolio that includes practical assignments. The course emphasizes critical thinking and problem-solving, enabling you to interpret results thoughtfully and consider your biological implications. The course is structured to build expertise progressively, from introductory concepts to advanced topics like deep learning and neural networks. You will gain practical experience implementing these techniques in Python.

/en/course/2026/BFVM25PROGRAM6.outcomes:
You design, implement, and optimize scalable data processing and or ML pipelines using Snakemake, ensuring efficient resource usage, high performance, and reproducibility for practical big data applications.
You create a comprehensive model card for an ML model that documents its intended use, data provenance, performance metrics, limitations, and ethical considerations, and you critically evaluate how this artifact supports transparency, responsible deployment, and effective stakeholder communication throughout the ML lifecycle.
You design and implement an automated documentation system, integrated into a pipeline, that systematically captures installation procedures, usage instructions, and model versioning, and you critically justify how this documentation ensures traceability, reproducibility, and auditability of ML models across the entire operational lifecycle.
/en/course/2026/BFVM25PROGRAM6.content:
This course builds on foundational concepts of distributed computing frameworks, such as Spark, job schedulers like SLURM, and distributed storage and batch processing systems like Hadoop.
In this course, you will explore additional essential tools for big data and distributed computing, such as Snakemake. You will gain hands-on experience in using these tools to design and implement efficient, scalable solutions for big data and high-performance computing challenges. The course will also cover best practices for integrating machine learning into operational workflows (ML-OPS), ensuring robust and optimized performance.
To enroll in and be evaluated for this subject, completion and or granted exemptions of 3 preparatory courses is required.

/en/course/2026/BFVM23GRADUATION.outcomes: The purpose of the graduation program is to ensure that you can function as a Master of Science in the Life Sciences in a research or development organization like an institute, company, or professorship.
/en/course/2026/BFVM23GRADUATION.content:
To graduate from the master DSLS, you must write a scientific master thesis based on research that you have carried out in a graduation project in the fourth semester.
The graduation project is a means of showing that you can work autonomously and independently on a complex project and that you are able to evaluate, challenge, modify and develop theory and practice. You are expected to demonstrate an ability to isolate and focus on the significant features of the problem you choose to work on and to offer coherent solutions. You are producing original and innovative work that is generally applicable within the field of the Life Sciences, and therefore worthy of publication, public usage, or display.
You will disseminate your graduation work in a thesis in a timely, accurate, and clear manner. In addition, you will submit and defend your research by means of a presentation and discussion in which you orally explain your work, present supporting arguments, and answer questions.

/en/course/2026/MUVM26AD1.outcomes:
1.1 Students create and produce artistic concepts at a high professional level.
2.1 Students independently develop musical products at a high professional level based on their own artistic concept and/or put together programmes on the basis of that concept.
2.4 Students express a musically artistic personality.
/en/course/2026/MUVM26AD1.content:
The Artistic Development course is all about exploring and developing your own artistic voice in creating and producing musical/artistic concepts. For this, you receive practice orientated coaching from the technical, creative, and artistic perspective, as well as the perspective of engagement. Coaches use an innovative approach designed to train flexible and professional musicians, who are able to connect their artistic skills to changing environments and situations.
The aims of the Artistic Development course are:
• To build a wide range of approaches for creating and shaping musical concepts.
• To strengthen your performance and production skills to realise your ideas
• To develop your own artistic voice and identity as a music professional
To do this, you learn:
• How to explore and apply a range of approaches to developing musical ideas, and to shape your own creative process.
• How to innovate your practice, critically reflect on your creative process, and evaluate how your work relates to listeners and its broader context.
• How to identify and further develop the musical and technical skills that best support your artistic direction.
Students from all directions have individual and/or group lessons on their instrument. In addition, the course contains activities that are related to the direction of choice. \
Classical students
can form chamber music ensembles and receive coaching on request.
Jazz students
work within a ‘lab band’ and a master’s ensemble.
NAIP students
will partake in a series of LAB sessions, the content of which feeds directly into our three intensive context-based-learning projects.
The course also offers Master classes by various international professionals that are open for all students.
All Master students
take part in the project
Artistic Synthesis
. In this project, students create a cross-genre, interdisciplinary performance by working together in groups, sharing their ideas, expertise and learning from one another. This fosters innovation, cross-pollination, and results in unique and unexpected performances. Expert instrumentalists and interdisciplinary artists coach the groups as they develop their performance. The first semester focuses on building co-creative skills and ideas through workshops and group sessions.

metadata.Name: Practice Based Research 1
metadata.Modes of delivery: Individual supervision Teaching method 1 Teaching method 2

/en/course/2026/MUVM26PBR1.outcomes:
3.1 Students are aware of developments in their specialist field, the wider professional music world and society at large. Students demonstrate how they integrate that awareness into their professional abilities and use it to enhance their own career and to serve the community.
4.3 Students reflect on their own working methods, and understand the implications of choices and decisions, which they can explain retrospectively both to colleagues and to individuals working outside the field.
4.6 Students conduct research in a structured manner on issues that are connected to their professional practice.
/en/course/2026/MUVM26PBR1.content:
The aim of the Practice-based Research (PBR) course is to foster your curiosity and inquisitive attitude, and to learn basic research skills that help you to develop your professional practice. When working towards your goals several questions may emerge. These might be artistic questions, entrepreneurial questions or questions related to psychological or social issues. The PBR course helps to explore such questions in a systematic way, and to reflect on the relevance of various sources for practice and research.
Therefore, the aims of the PBR course are:
To develop an appropriate method of following developments in the professional field and society in a structured way
To develop a reflective attitude and research skills as tools for the development of practice
To develop (your) professional practice using a research-informed approach
To do this, you learn:
How to form useful research questions
How to conduct a literature search that informs your research project
How to conduct your research in a systematic way using an appropriate methodology
How to analyse the information that you find in your research
How to share your research findings with others in writing and speaking.
During semester 1, you develop several research skills, for instance: How to look for reliable sources, how to compile an annotated bibliography, how to construct a research design, how to communicate plans visually and how to write a Research Proposal.

/en/course/2026/MUVM26ENT1.outcomes:
3.2 Students identify opportunities in the community, turning these into concrete actions. They are not afraid to take risks and positions themselves with their products or activities.
5.1 Students present themselves and their work, individually and/or collectively, in a way that is suited to the work presented and the intended audience.
6.5 Students respond to changing situations and circumstances and contribute to solving complex context-specific problems and issues.
/en/course/2026/MUVM26ENT1.content:
Entrepreneurship is part of your professional practice. It is important to learn how to position yourself as an artist and to formulate strategies that resonate with your audience, customers and other stakeholders. This course is designed to develop an entrepreneurial mindset, enabling you to adeptly manage organizational and operational responsibilities while also maintaining the integrity of your artistic products or services.
Throughout the first semester, you follow seminars that cover relevant entrepreneurial subjects such as networking, business modelling, strategic planning and analysis, project planning, persona development, and effective pitching techniques. In addition, you participate in group meetings in which students share and discuss their plans and peer learning takes place. During the seminars and group meetings, you receive coaching and constructive feedback from our teachers and peers to effectively evaluate your plans. The outcome of the course is outlined in an entrepreneurial plan concerning your professional practice.

/en/course/2026/DGVM23DUURZAAM.content:
To identify and improve the sustainability of commodities, products and chains, certain insights are needed on issues such as: What do food systems look like (global and regional)? What initiatives can you use to make the chain more sustainable? What is the impact of sustainability on the organization and the environment?
The Food Chain Sustainability Module focuses on the sustainability and innovation of food systems and their impact, and focuses on the first part of the food chain, starting from agriculture and other commodities. This module particularly addresses the first part of the food chain.
The module consists of an Integrated Assignment and three supporting units of study: Sustainability and Business, Regional and Global Food Systems and Commodities and Adaptation.
The integral assignment involves working with a client from the field to map their food system. Where can sustainability take place and what is the impact of this change including assessing this impact. A professional product is delivered in the form of an advisory report.
The three supporting units of study all contribute to the theme of this module and support the integrated assignment. Throughout the module, work is done to develop research and professional skills in addition to gaining new insights and in-depth knowledge of the food chain and food systems.
The Sustainability and Business unit of study contributes to the module by defining, exploring, studying and applying with you the components of sustainable business models and business cases in the analysis of business models of existing organizations and the creation and analysis of business cases focused on sustainability.
For sustainable and healthy food, it is important that food systems become (more) sustainable. In order to be able to examine a food system at a company for sustainability, it is important to be able to identify the different components of the food system in question and systematically make them more sustainable. The global nature of food systems is also addressed in this process. In the study component Regional and Global Food Systems, you will learn about and analyze regional and global food systems in various ways. The sustainability of food systems will be examined through various analyses.
The study component Commodities and Adaptation contributes to the integrated assignment in several ways. The focus of this unit of study is on the beginning of the food chain: raw materials. Knowledge about sustainability of a crucial link in the food system, the land row is addressed in this study component.

/en/course/2026/DGVM23VOEDING.content:
This module focuses on healthy eating for humans. What exactly is healthy food, and for whom is it healthy? How can we continue to feed everyone healthily and sustainably. And do health and sustainability always go hand in hand?
In the second module of the Masters in Sustainable and Healthy Nutrition, you use the knowledge, skills and abilities acquired in module 1 to develop further as a professional in the domain of food, nutrition and health. Whereas Module 1 focuses on the beginning of the food chain, Module 2 focuses on the latter part of the food chain (see Figure 1). The theme of this module is Healthy Nutrition.
Together you will work on an integral assignment from the field in which these different aspects of healthy nutrition come together. The integral assignment will be introduced in the first week of the module and you will work under supervision on the integral assignment in a Community of Learners (CoL).
The integral assignment concerns the development of an innovative concept/program of requirements for a client from the field, culminating in a professional product: an advisory report for the client aimed at an innovative, healthy and sustainable food concept.
The module consists of four parts:
Integral Assignment
Supporting study components:
Customized Nutrition
Market and consumer
Nutrition of the future
The research and professional skills learning line is reflected in all components.
The supported study units Food by Measure, Market and Consumer and Food of the Future all have a connection to the integral assignment. At the start of the semester, the focus is more on the supported study units, which provide content and skills to be well equipped to work on the integral assignment. Customized Nutrition explores scientific and practice-based insight which is translated by the student into the innovation in the integral assignment. In addition, regional, national and international social developments are identified, valued and integrated into practical applications. You will learn about the topics of nutritional needs of specific target groups or individuals, nutrigenomics, healthy versus happy lifestyle and human health.
The Market and Consumer study section focuses on sustainability and health. And it covers managing the chain production of raw materials, producing for business (B2B) or consumer (B2C). You will investigate for which appropriate target group the innovation will be developed, you will get to know the target group and you will involve the target group in the development. In addition, you will map all stakeholders and examine everyone's interest in the innovation. This is done using the method Design Thinking, an iterative process to solve and methodically address complex problems (wicked problems). The study component Food of the Future, focuses on connecting the different domains in the field of food, nutrition and health (the chain) both horizontally and vertically within companies and organizations. Students investigate how future-proof the innovation is, taking into account sustainability, and current transitions for the sake of food production regionally and globally. The future is uncertain, how do you deal with it? Instead of learning to predict the future, you are taught to deal with uncertainties using the Future Literacy method, and to make wise decisions now for the future.

/en/course/2026/DGVM23TOEKOMST.content:
“The main societal challenge in the field of nutrition is to achieve healthier and more sustainable diets. Therefore, it is important not only to map out the composition of our food, what and how much we eat, and how much of which nutrients we take in (nutritional status), but also to evaluate and make opportunities to make food and food consumption healthier and less environmentally damaging (RIVM1).”
Most Dutch people do not eat according to the guidelines for good nutrition established by the Health Council. For example, only 5 to 10 percent of the population eat enough fruits and vegetables, 90 percent ingest too much saturated fat, and our salt consumption is far too high. Moreover, half the population is overweight. The current diet causes many diseases and premature death in the Netherlands.
The production and consumption of food is also harmful to the environment. Worldwide, food is responsible for 20 to 30 percent of greenhouse gas emissions. A more sustainable diet would not only be better for the environment, it is also often healthier. For example, if we ate less meat, or replaced soft drinks with tap water.
The module The sustainable and healthy product of the future focuses mainly on the production of healthier (plant-based) foods or their ingredients. The goal of this module is to produce a healthy ingredient or food product that is less harmful to the environment and contributes to consumer health.
In this third module of the Master of Sustainable and Healthy Nutrition, the middle part of the journey from raw materials (farmer) to product/consumer of the food chain. Module 1 covered the beginning of the food chain, and Module 2 the end of the chain.
You work in Module 3 on assignments, leading to innovative food products and production processes focused on health, sustainability, and the future. The proposals made in module 2 can be the input for these assignments.

/en/course/2026/DGVM23MEESTER.content:
The graduation program of the Master of Sustainable and Healthy Nutrition is the master's thesis (30 EC). The purpose of the master's thesis is to ensure that you can function as a master professional in an organization focused on sustainable nutrition and health, in which change processes play an important role. The role your student fills here is focused on design & innovation, focused on connecting and/or focused on business and involves the entire food chain or a large part of it.
The master's thesis will be carried out in the field (of partners involved) in the Agri & Food or Life Sciences & Health sector, with a focus on sustainable transitions of food and nutrition focused on health, whether or not in collaboration with relevant professorships of Hanze University. The master's thesis builds on your personal development plan in the previous modules. In the master's thesis, you demonstrate that you have achieved the final level of the master's degree on the basis of the competencies, translated into program learning outcomes, including his development in terms of interprofessional action.
It is important that you, in collaboration with the organization where the master's thesis is conducted, define a number of professional products with which all intended program learning outcomes can be achieved. Depending on the roles you take on during the master's thesis (and their focus), the professional products may vary by topic. The research assignment is always linked to a complex practical problem, to which different professional products can be linked, such as an advice, a design, a physical (or digital) product, a series of actions or a research report.
Importantly, the Innovation and Strategy competency is particularly demonstrated through the professional products to be delivered.
The research and professional skills, as offered and developed in the three previous modules, are applied during the creation of the professional products of the master's thesis.  You justify the research and professional skills in the master's thesis with a master's thesis, which provides evidence for the delivered professional products. For some professional products, such as a consulting report or research report, the justification may be an integral part of the professional product. For a design, physical product, or action, you document the accountability in a separate report (the master's thesis).
The research activities (project activities) are always supervised by an appointed person within the organization where the research assignment is carried out (company supervisor). The project activities are evaluated in consultation with the company supervisor by means of a Company Assessment Form. You are also required to justify your research with a presentation, explaining the research question with the chosen research methodology, the results and conclusions, linked to the creation of the professional products. Following the presentation, the master pouf will be concluded with a criterion-based Interview (CGI) in which it will be determined whether you have actually achieved the final level (the program learning outcomes).
You carry out a research project independently/autonomously, but embedded in a multidisciplinary environment of an organization in the field. A large and complex research project may involve multiple students. Each student is required to have a clear individual research assignment defined, reflected in their own problem definition with associated professional products. You will individually write a justifying master's thesis and present the project individually, which will be concluded in an individual CGI.
