metadata.Assessments: AVZ - N2 - Critical dialogue - Oral AVZ - N2 - Research process and final project - Portfolio assessment

/en/course/2026/HVXB26AVZN2.outcomes:
Area of Expertise and Learning Outcome(s)
5. Analysing and improving care – Level 2
LOL 5.1 – AVZ – N2
The novice practitioner formulates an objective and a research question based on an existing practical problem, in line with the problem analysis, and interprets the results obtained to generate knowledge.
LOL 5.2 – AVZ – N2
The novice practitioner makes an impact within professional practice to improve the quality of care.
Indicators
Description
5.1 Substantiates the practical problem with relevant scientific and professional literature (BN2030).
5.2 Formulates, based on the practical problem, an objective and a research question appropriate to the problem analysis and the needs of professional practice (BN2030)
5.3 Methodically designs a well-founded and consistent research study appropriate to the objective and research question (BN2030).
5.4 Carries out the research, reports on it and formulates a conclusion based on a critical review of the research results (BN2030)
5.5 Formulates recommendations based on the research that contribute to high-quality care and supports these, where necessary, with relevant literature (BN2030).
5.6 Communicates the recommendations through a professional output appropriate to the needs of professional practice in order to make an impact (BN2030).
5.7 Demonstrates an inquisitive attitude throughout the research process (BN2030).
/en/course/2026/HVXB26AVZN2.content:
The ‘Analysing and Improving Care’ (AVZ) course focuses on research skills, with the aim of improving a specific professional situation in healthcare practice. During the course, early-career professionals learn to work through the various phases of the research cycle and, based on the results, to formulate recommendations for professional practice. The necessary knowledge is provided through recommended (scientific) literature, knowledge clips and feedback sessions held throughout the research period. Within the course, early-career professionals learn with and from one another by discussing research designs, presenting progress and providing each other with feedback. During the implementation phase, the early-career professional works on data collection in practice and the analysis of the results. Based on this, recommendations are drawn up that contribute to high-quality care. These recommendations are presented in a professional product aimed at achieving an impact within professional practice.
During the sessions, the student gains insight into their own learning process and the steps they need to take to achieve the learning outcome. This is achieved, amongst other things, by giving and receiving feedback.
Topics that may be covered:
General themes comprising:
Stages of a research cycle
Ethical aspects of practice-based research
Research population/stakeholders
Research quality assurance
Communicating recommendations (professional output)
Research methodologies comprising:
Design-oriented and action research: phases of design thinking, participatory action research and the intervention cycle
Quantitative research: descriptive and inferential statistics, use of SPSS
Qualitative research: interview techniques, transcription and coding, use of Atlas.TI
Competence Proficiency Level 2 (CBN, 2022)
At the second level, the context is highly complex, with the focus on acting methodically in unpredictable, complex situations. The nature of the task is complex and unstructured. The focus is on student-led learning, with supervision provided primarily on request. Actions are carried out as independently as possible, with justification provided retrospectively. The novice professional is encouraged to apply (strategic) planning, self-efficacy, motivation and reflection independently. Reflection on one’s actions centres on daring, willing and being, with the focus on sustainable development.
Assessment:
In this course, students’ competences are assessed on the basis of specific learning outcomes, with the indicators serving as a guide and support for the assessment. Two assessments take place within this course:
Critical dialogue –
oral (individual)
During the design phase of the research, an individual oral presentation of the research design takes place, in which the trainee demonstrates an understanding of the subject and context of the practical research, and can justify the choices made in the design of the methodology.
The critical dialogue must be assessed as at least a pass (mark > 5.5) in order to be permitted to carry out the research in practice.
Process report –
written (individually or in pairs)
At the end of the course, the process report is assessed and awarded a mark. The process report consists of a description of the research process and the professional product.
Both assessments are marked using a rubric and must be passed.
TEST 01 – AVZ – N2 – Critical dialogue
TEST 02 – AVZ – N2 – Research process and final project
Evidence for the assessment
Description of the research process
Individual or pair project
The description of the research process sets out all the stages of a research cycle and justifies the choices made: from the formulation of the practical problem, the objective and research question, through to the analysis of the results, the critical reflection in the discussion, the conclusion and, finally, the recommendations for the client.
Professional output
Individual or pair project
A presentation and justification of the professional output in which the recommendations are communicated in an appropriate manner to make an impact within professional practice.

/en/course/2026/HVMB26PPO.outcomes:
Area of Expertise and Learning Outcome(s)
6. Personal and Professional Development (PPO) – Levels 1 and 2
LOL 6.1 – PPO – L1 and L2
The novice practitioner reflects on meaningful situations relating to the development of personal and professional leadership.
Indicators
Description
6.1 The student reflects on meaningful situations that contribute to the development of personal and professional identity (BN2030).
6.2 The student explores the significance of nursing leadership (in practice) and reflects on the role he or she can play in this (BN2030).
6.3 The student actively examines their own behaviour, habits and workload in relation to healthy functioning (professional vitality) within professional practice (BN2030).
6.4 The early-career practitioner reflects on meaningful situations that contribute to personal and professional development at the micro and meso levels (BN2030).
6.5 The early-career practitioner reflects on a personally formulated vision of nursing leadership (BN2030).
6.6 In their reflection, the early-career professional demonstrates an understanding of the choices made to promote their own professional vitality (BN2030).
/en/course/2026/HVMB26PPO.content:
In this course, students and new entrants to the profession learn that they themselves are the most important tool in nursing practice. Students and new entrants to the profession develop an understanding of how personal and professional development shape their performance as nurses. In doing so, they reflect on their own self-image, their behaviour and the effect this has on the person receiving care. The student/newly qualified nurse learns to take control of their own development and career and explores how nursing leadership takes shape in practice. Addressing these questions and applying reflection form an essential part of the programme.
Topics covered:
- Methodical reflection
- Nursing leadership
These topics are integrated into the curriculum as follows:
Full-time standard and MBO intake
For full-time students, learning to reflect and writing a reflection will take place in the core groups. During these lessons, students will learn the theory behind reflection and how to apply it. The application of reflection and its formative assessment take place during lessons in other modules.
Throughout the programme, students will collect various pieces of evidence in their portfolio to demonstrate their development.
Part-time standard, FastSwitch and Part-time transition programme
During lessons in other modules, students are challenged to continually set learning objectives, gather feedback from relevant parties and reflect. Based on the insights gained, students set new learning objectives.
Throughout the programme, students collect various pieces of evidence in their portfolio to demonstrate their development.
Competence Mastery Level 1 (CBN, 2022)
The first level involves a moderately complex context in which the focus is on the methodical application of knowledge and skills in accordance with guidelines and protocols in varying but similar situations. The nature of the task is structured, with familiar methods being applied.
The student learns to direct their own learning (self-direction) in terms of planning, motivation and reflection. Reflection is aimed at knowledge and understanding, with a focus on innovation. The guidance provided here is aimed at increasing self-direction
Competence Proficiency Level 2 (CBN, 2022)
At the second level, the context is highly complex, with the focus on acting methodically in unpredictable, complex situations. The nature of the task is complex and unstructured. The focus is on student-led learning, with guidance provided more on an on-demand basis. Actions are carried out as independently as possible, with justification provided afterwards. Students are encouraged to independently apply (strategic) planning, self-efficacy, motivation and reflection. Reflection on actions centres on daring, willing and being, with the focus on sustainable development.
Assessment:
In this course, the competences of the student/novice professional are assessed on the basis of specific learning outcomes, with behaviours (indicators) serving as a guide. The assessment consists of a portfolio assessment, which is marked using a rubric. A student is entitled to two assessment opportunities per year.
Exemptions may be granted on the basis of previously achieved results elsewhere and/or work experience.
TEST 01 – Midterm plea
TEST 02 – Nursing plea
Evidence for the assessment
Reflections
Individual project
The student collects reflections to consciously reflect on experiences, behaviour or actions in order to make sense of them and learn from them.
Feedback collected that supports personal and professional development
Throughout the programme, the student collects feedback in the portfolio to demonstrate their development, through evidence gathered from 360-degree feedback sessions and short practical assessments.
Development scan
The student includes a fully completed development scan in the portfolio
Curriculum Vitae
The student includes an up-to-date curriculum vitae in the portfolio.
Outline of the professional the student has (already) become up to that point
The student includes in the portfolio an outline of the professional they have (already) become at that point. The format is open.

/en/course/2026/HVVP26BVZT1.outcomes:
Area of Expertise and Learning Outcome(s)
Clinical reasoning and arguing - Level 1
LOL 1.1 - BVZ - N1 - Simulated (VT & VT MBO bridging programme)
The student justifies and provides care, partly under supervision, in moderately complex simulated care situations, in accordance with the prevailing nursing philosophy and based on clinical reasoning within the nursing process. This is carried out in accordance with the methods, guidelines, (legal) frameworks and evidence-based practice provided, whilst encouraging the care recipient’s self-management in a manner appropriate to the situation.
LOL 1.2 - BVZ - N1 - Simulated (VT & VT MBO bridging programme)
The student, partly under supervision, uses the communication tools provided to communicate in a person-centred and professional manner with the care recipient, their relatives and other healthcare professionals within a moderately complex simulated situation, in order to encourage self-management.
Indicators
Description
1.1 Determines the nursing process based on provided theories and classifications relating to clinical reasoning, and makes decisions based on the steps of Evidence-Based Practice (EBP) and relevant legislation and regulations (BN2030).
1.2 Works in accordance with standards, guidelines and protocols (BN2030).
1.3 Supports care recipients in vulnerable situations in promoting self-management, drawing on provided models, theories and tools (BN2030).
1.5 Applies provided models and methodologies to communication within the nursing process (BN2030).
1.4 Provides care based on a provided nursing philosophy (BN2030).
1.6 Communicates during conversations at both the content level and the relational level (BN2030).
1.7 Assesses the effects of their own verbal and non-verbal expressions during conversations (BN2030).
/en/course/2026/HVVP26BVZT1.content:
The course begins with an introduction to the nursing profession. Key themes include: the nursing code of practice, the nursing philosophy, the nursing professional profile, relevant legislation and regulations, and collaboration with other disciplines. The aim is for students to understand what nursing entails, how the nursing profession differs from other disciplines, and what this means for their own development as nurses.
Students then develop clinical reasoning skills to underpin the nursing process for a fictional care recipient. Particular emphasis is placed on encouraging and strengthening self-management among care recipients and their loved ones.
Students work with methodologies and classifications such as NANDA-1 and the Omaha system, learning to use these to establish nursing diagnoses, goals and interventions through data collection. Care plans are drawn up in collaboration with the teaching team, underpinned by theories, classifications, protocols, standards and legislation. The course focuses on evidence-based practice (EBP) to underpin nursing interventions, including the evaluation of scientific literature.
Communication skills are taught through simulated conversations, with an emphasis on person-centred communication, person- and family-centred care, and the use of ICT. Various models and basic skills are provided for this purpose. Students learn to communicate at different levels, such as the content and relational levels, and are able to assess the impact of their own communication.
In the learning group, students explore – drawing on the principles of person-centred care and their own vision of nursing – how end-of-life care aligns with the wishes and needs of the care recipient and what this requires of the nurse.
During the sessions, students gain insight into their own learning process and the steps they need to take to achieve the learning outcome. This is achieved, amongst other things, through giving and receiving feedback.
Topics covered:
Perceptions of hospital care and community care
Code of practice, professional profile, vision on nursing
Nursing care process and classifications (clinical reasoning)
Self-management
E-health
Person-centred and family care
Various communication scenarios such as taking a medical history, evaluation, delivering bad news, and professional resilience
Electronic client records
Legislation
Interprofessional practice
Competence Mastery Level 1 (CBN, 2022)
The first level involves a moderately complex context in which the focus is on the methodical application of knowledge and skills in accordance with guidelines and protocols in varying but similar situations. The nature of the task is structured, with known methods being applied.
The student learns to manage their own learning (self-direction) in terms of planning, motivation and reflection. Reflection is aimed at knowledge and understanding, with a focus on innovation.
Supervision in this regard is geared towards increasing self-direction.
Assessment:
In this course, the student’s competences are assessed on the basis of specific learning outcomes. For each learning outcome, indicators are provided against which assessment is carried out.
Assessment consists of a portfolio assessment and an assignment. Feedback is provided on the individual pieces of evidence for the portfolio or the assignment. The portfolio assessment and the assignment are assessed using a rubric with a mark and must be passed.
The final mark for this course is the average of these two assessments, with the portfolio accounting for two-thirds (2/3) and the assignment for one-third (1/3).
TEST 01 – BVZ – N1 – Nursing Process
TEST 02 – BVZ – N1 – Nursing Communication
Evidence for the assessment
Care plan
Group project
Together with the learning team, the nursing process is described for a fictitious care recipient and translated into a care plan. Appropriate classifications are used for this purpose.
The care plan addresses the care recipient’s support network.
Topic:clinical lesson on appropriate care
Group project
Students, working in learning teams, deliver a clinical lesson on appropriate care for a care recipient in the final (palliative) phase of their life and the role of the nurse in this context.
The format of this clinical lesson is flexible.
Oral account of the nursing process
Individual assignment
The student gives an oral account of the nursing process, demonstrating an understanding of the choices made within the care plan(s) and substantiating these with the methodologies learnt. The student substantiates this account in a written self-assessment. In addition, the student briefly explains her vision of nursing practice and how this is reflected in her choices and working methods.
Evidence-Based Practice
Group assignment
Students, together with their learning team, produce and present a poster which, amongst other things, explains the steps of the EBP process and makes a recommendation for a fictional care recipient.
Professional (care) consultation
Individual assignment
The student conducts a professional care consultation with a simulation patient, applying basic communication skills. The student substantiates the communication skills used in a written self-assessment.

/en/course/2026/HVVP26SLO1.outcomes:
Area of Expertise and Learning Outcome(s)
8. Skills lab education  – Level 1
LOL 8.1 – SLO – N1
The student works safely in accordance with professional standards and guidelines, and is able to deviate from these in a reasoned manner in order to provide integrated care.
LOL 8.2 – SLO – N1
The student works in accordance with applicable legislation and regulations and uses materials and resources responsibly.

Description
8.1 Provides personal care tailored to the needs of the care recipient (BN2030)
8.2 Works in the field of hygiene and basic care in accordance with standards, guidelines and protocols associated with their functional responsibilities, and can deviate from these in a responsible manner (BN2030).
8.3 Identifies the objectives, (contra)indications and complications of procedures within the context of hygiene and basic care (BN2030).

/en/course/2026/HVVP26SLO1.content:
In skills lab education, the emphasis is on learning and mastering various nursing skills from a holistic and person-centred perspective, underpinned by theoretical principles. Students work in accordance with protocols, guidelines and quality standards, and develop the ability to deviate from these, where necessary, in a conscious and reasoned manner, based on the context and the wishes of the care recipient.
This course covers the fundamentals of nursing practice, such as maintaining hygiene, providing basic care and ensuring the comfort, safety and wellbeing of the care recipient. Through e-learning modules, instructional sessions and scenario-based training, students work specifically on their own professional development. Students receive feedback on their attitude, communication and technical procedures as part of their training, either in a simulated setting or during workplace-based learning.
Topics that may be covered:
Hygiene
Basic care (ADL, oral care, elimination, compression therapy, repositioning techniques)
Vital signs
Nursing documentation (EPD)
Oral medication, nebuliser therapy and oxygen administration
Competence Mastery Level 1 (CBN, 2022)
At the first level, the context is of medium complexity, with the focus on the methodical application of knowledge and skills in accordance with guidelines and protocols in varying but similar situations. The nature of the task is structured, involving the application of familiar methods.
The student learns to manage their own learning (self-direction) in terms of planning, motivation and reflection. Reflection is aimed at knowledge and understanding, with a focus on innovation.
The guidance provided is aimed at fostering increasing self-direction.
Assessment:
At the end of the course, there is a skills assessment in which knowledge, attitude and competence are demonstrated. The assessment is graded and must be a pass (5.5 or higher).

2.5 Carries out an environmental analysis at target group level using a provided model and draws up a prevention plan (BN2030).
2.6 Identifies and monitors health risks within a specific target group (BN2030).
2.7 Assumes a supporting role in promoting a healthy living environment within an interdisciplinary team (BN2030).
/en/course/2026/HVVP26WAGT1.content:
This course reinforces the nursing role in prevention and health promotion. The focus is on positive health, early detection, self-management, the use of interprofessional interventions and eHealth in healthcare. Students will learn, through various methods, how health can be promoted in a systematic way and how to carry out a neighbourhood and target group analysis. Students will learn how to analyse risky behaviour and self-management in a care recipient and their loved ones (case studies) and how these can be influenced. Working with a learning team, this will be incorporated, substantiated and justified in a health promotion plan.
Students will apply the conversation techniques they have learnt in a simulated context. Attention will be paid to person-centred communication, person-centred care, behavioural change and the application of motivational interviewing techniques.
During the sessions, students will gain insight into their own learning process and the steps they need to take to achieve the learning outcome. This is achieved, amongst other things, through giving and receiving feedback.
Competence Proficiency Level 1 (CBN, 2022)
At the first level, the context is of medium complexity, with the focus on the methodical application of knowledge and skills in accordance with guidelines and protocols in varying but similar situations. The nature of the task is structured, involving the application of familiar methods.
The student learns to manage their own learning (self-direction) in terms of planning, motivation and reflection. Reflection is aimed at knowledge and understanding, with a focus on innovation.
The guidance provided here is aimed at increasing self-direction.
Assessment:
In this course, the student’s competences are assessed on the basis of specific learning outcomes. For each learning outcome, indicators are provided against which the assessment is made.
Assessment consists of a portfolio assessment and an assignment. Feedback is provided on the individual pieces of evidence for the portfolio or the assignment. The portfolio assessment and the assignment are assessed using a rubric with a mark and must be passed. The final mark for this course is the average of these two assessments, with the portfolio accounting for two-thirds (2/3) and the assignment for one-third (1/3).
TEST 01 – WAG – N1 – Prevention
TEST 02 – WAG – N1 – Behavioural Analysis
Evidence for the assessment
Health promotion plan for the care recipient
Group project
Students work with their learning team to explain how the health of an individual care recipient can be promoted. Based on an analysis, the students formulate goals and interprofessional (eHealth) interventions aimed at improving a healthy lifestyle suited to the care recipient and their loved ones. The level of self-management of the care recipient and their loved ones is assessed and reinforced through interventions.
Professional (care) consultation
Individual assignment
A simulated consultation with a care recipient (simulant) on the topic of a healthy lifestyle, in which basic communication skills and the principles of motivational interviewing are applied. The student justifies the communication skills used, drawing on theories of conversational techniques and levels of communication, either orally or in writing.
Neighbourhood and target group analysis
Group project
The learning team carries out a neighbourhood analysis focusing on health issues affecting that neighbourhood and develops a target group analysis on one specific health issue within that neighbourhood, using this as a basis to devise appropriate preventive group interventions. The student applies relevant theories and models in this process.

/en/course/2026/HVVB25BVZ1.content:
As a healthcare provider, nurses focus on strengthening people's self-management in their social context wherever possible. The need for nursing care is determined through clinical reasoning by the nurse. Clinical reasoning is a continuous process of data collection and analysis focused on the questions and problems of the care recipient and their loved ones.
Nursing thinking and acting, or clinical reasoning, can be methodically structured in different ways in different fields of work. The nurse demonstrates a critical, inquisitive and reflective (basic) attitude and justifies their actions based on various sources of knowledge (EBP). In this process, the nurse focuses on risk assessment, early detection, problem recognition, intervention and monitoring (LOOV, 2016).
In this module, students demonstrate skills in the nursing process in an authentic context to support self-management among care recipients and their loved ones. The student applies the previously learned methodologies and classifications, such as Nanda and Omaha classification, in an authentic context. He/she learns to systematically collect information in an authentic context from a care recipient. He/she combines this information and draws up a care plan, substantiated with theories, classifications and legislation, and justifies this care plan in the portfolio assessment.
In the nursing process, students apply the communication skills they have learned, with a focus on person-centred communication, person- and family-centred care and the use of ICT. In this module, EBP plays an important role in substantiating an intervention and its application in practice. The student presents this intervention with supporting evidence to colleagues in practice and discusses its application.
This module also focuses on personal and professional (identity) development in a cyclical process, aimed at learning objectives, self-evaluation and reflection. These reflections must be carried out using a reflection method that has been taught.
The module is linked to a 20-week practical learning period, during which the student will complete two other modules. Within the supportive education, the student will be guided by the teacher supervisor. Formative action is one of the basic principles of supportive education. Supportive education takes place in groups in learning communities and through individual conversations.
Topics covered:
EBP in practice
Nursing process and classifications
Application of the nursing process in practice
Clinical reasoning and electronic client files
Person- and family-centred care
Cultural sensitivity
Asking for and receiving feedback
Formulating learning objectives
Competence mastery level (CBN, 2022)
The first level involves a moderately complex authentic context in which the focus is on the methodical application of knowledge and skills based on guidelines and protocols in varying but similar situations. The nature of the task is structured, with known methods being applied.
You learn to guide your own learning (self-management) in terms of planning, motivation and reflection. Reflection is aimed at knowledge and understanding, with a focus on innovation.
The guidance provided is aimed at increasing self-management.
Assessment
In this module, competencies are assessed on the basis of specific learning outcomes. For each learning outcome, various pieces of evidence are collected in a portfolio. Each piece of evidence is included in the portfolio once. The completed portfolio is used as input for the portfolio assessment (which also assesses the other modules belonging to the PLP1).
During the portfolio assessment, the student demonstrates that they have mastered the learning outcomes. The input from the portfolio and the assessment together form the assessment.
The assessment takes place individually at the internship location with the teacher supervisor and the work supervisor. The module is assessed on all learning outcomes with a grade.
All learning outcomes must be at least satisfactory. If a module is assessed as unsatisfactory during the regular assessment, the student may retake the module during the same practical learning period. In consultation with the teacher supervisor and work supervisor, it will be determined what the retake will entail and how it will be organised.
Resit
There are various reasons for taking a resit, namely:
Missed opportunity (MO) due to failure to complete the entire practical learning period; no portfolio assessment will take place. The student will try again to pass the modules in a subsequent practical learning period. The student, work supervisor and teacher supervisor will schedule a final meeting.
Missed opportunity (MO) due to the absence of MAZ criteria in the elaboration of the modules; the assessment will take place at the agreed time. The student has the opportunity to make up for the gap in a resit of the module in the same learning period.
Insufficient; If one or more modules are assessed as insufficient during the portfolio assessment, the module(s) in question will be marked as insufficient. The student is entitled to retake the module during the same learning period. It is not possible to extend an internship period.
In order to progress to PLP2/3, students must pass the three modules belonging to PLP1 (Arguing for care, Working on health and Directing care). If one module is not completed satisfactorily, it is possible, in consultation with the teacher supervisor, to restart PLP 2 within the resit semester. This procedure and conditions are explained in more detail in the PLP1 course.
Feedback from the work supervisor, other colleagues and professionals in the field, fellow students and lecturers prior to the assessment is part of the learning process.
(Exemptions may be granted on the basis of previous results obtained elsewhere and/or work experience).

/en/course/2026/HVVB25WAG1.content:
Nurses operate in a society and healthcare sector in which thinking in terms of care and illness is shifting towards thinking in terms of behaviour and health. As a result, there is an increasing focus on the prevention of health problems and early detection. To support this, decisions are increasingly being made about whether and which appropriate ICT options can be used.
Where possible, nurses influence the lifestyle and healthy behaviour of citizens and care recipients, with a view to promoting and protecting health, preventing illness and detecting possible complications at an early stage. In doing so, they also focus on supporting self-management.
Nurses actively approach people at high risk of health problems and their environment. Where this is lacking, nurses establish contact with or initiate a social network around the care recipient. This takes into account the physical (living) environment, social relationships, culture and lifestyle. The nurse's work therefore focuses on individual care recipients, their environment and their loved ones, groups of care recipients and other professionals or agencies, or local authorities.
How prevention in the broad sense of the word can be applied in practice, and therefore also during the internship, depends of course on the context. For example, the student will not be able to focus on the behaviour of the care recipient in all target groups in order to work towards lifestyle changes. However, this does not mean that preventive care cannot be provided. The student will have to demonstrate appropriate interventions in this regard. Where lifestyle influence is not (or no longer) possible, the student will look for ways to apply preventive care in the context (environment and own attitude/behaviour).
During the theoretical module WaG, the student has studied the nursing role in prevention and health promotion. Topics covered included:
Perceptions of youth health care, elderly care
Positive health
Neighbourhood analysis methods
Self-management and use of e-health
Behavioural change and motivational interviewing
Relevant legislation
Ethics
Person- and family-centred care
Gerontology
Assessment
Depending on their internship placement, students will be able to apply some of these topics in practice during their internship, and the above areas of focus will be covered to a greater or lesser extent. However, how prevention in the broadest sense of the word can be applied in practice will of course depend on the context. For example, it is not possible to work towards lifestyle changes in all target groups. However, students will always be able to provide preventive care.
Within this Working on Health module, students will also work integrally on their personal and professional (identity) development in a cyclical process focused on learning objectives, self-evaluation and reflection. These reflections must be carried out using a reflection method that has been taught.
The module is linked to a 20-week practical training period, during which the student will complete two other modules (Directing Care and Arguing Care). Within the supporting education, the student will be supervised by the teacher-supervisor. Formative action is one of the basic principles of supportive education. Supportive education takes place in groups in learning communities and through individual conversations.
Competence mastery level (CBN, 2022)
The first level involves a moderately complex authentic context in which the focus is on the methodical application of knowledge and skills based on guidelines and protocols in varying but similar situations. The nature of the task is structured, with familiar methods being applied.
You learn to guide your own learning (self-management) in terms of planning, motivation and reflection. Reflection is aimed at knowledge and understanding, with a focus on innovation.
The guidance provided is aimed at increasing self-management.
Assessment

Each piece of evidence is included in the portfolio once. The completed portfolio is used as input for the portfolio assessment (which also assesses the other modules belonging to the PLP1).
During the portfolio assessment, the student demonstrates that they have mastered the learning outcomes. The input from the portfolio and the assessment together form the assessment.
The assessment takes place individually at the internship location with the teacher supervisor and the work supervisor. The module is assessed (on all learning outcomes) with a grade.
All learning outcomes must be at least satisfactory. If a module is assessed as unsatisfactory during the regular assessment, the student may retake the module during the same practical learning period. The teacher supervisor and work supervisor will determine the nature and format of any retake.
Resit
There are various reasons for taking a resit, namely:
-Missed opportunity (MO) due to failure to complete the entire practical learning period; no portfolio assessment will take place. The student will try again to pass the modules in a subsequent practical learning period. The student, work supervisor and teacher will schedule a final meeting.
-Missed opportunity (MO) due to the absence of MAZ criteria in the elaboration of the modules; the assessment will take place at the agreed time. The student has the opportunity to make up for the gap in a resit of the module in the same learning period.

/en/course/2026/HVVB25RVZ1.content:
The nurse directs the care process in consultation with the care recipient, their loved ones and other care providers in order to arrive at a well-considered, interprofessional and coherent range of services that meets the needs of (groups of) care recipients.
In their coordinating role, nurses take the initiative, coordinate and organise the deployment of informal carers and/or other care providers in consultation with the care recipient. With their knowledge of chain processes and (potential) partners, nurses can ensure that care is provided effectively and efficiently and monitor this.
The nurse reports on the care provided through accurate reporting and transfer using modern digital techniques, within the relevant legislation and regulations. The nurse also records information efficiently and effectively and transfers care meticulously to fellow professionals, even beyond the boundaries of their own organisation (LOOV, 2016).
Within this module, students apply what they have learned in the theory of year 1 (module Directing Care) in an authentic, moderately complex situation. Students look for meaningful situations with regard to directing care and collect evidence focused on their own performance in practice.
The emphasis here is on stimulating self-management and the associated communication skills, contributing nursing insights within an interprofessional collaboration, transferring relevant information and recognising one's own role and that of the various participants within the care chain.
This module also focuses on personal and professional (identity) development in a cyclical process, aimed at learning objectives, self-evaluation and reflection. These reflections must be carried out using a learned reflection method and serve as input for the PIO portfolio.
The module is linked to a 20-week practical training period, during which the student will complete two other modules. Within the supportive education programme, the student will be supervised by the teacher-supervisor. Formative assessment is one of the basic principles of supportive education. Supportive education takes place in groups in learning communities and through individual conversations.
Topics covered include:
Shared decision making
Person-centred and family-centred care
Nursing leadership
Reporting, transfer and documentation
Relevant legislation
Chain care and care pathways
The nursing professional profile
Competence mastery level (CBN, 2022)
The first level involves a moderately complex authentic context in which the focus is on the methodical application of knowledge and skills based on guidelines and protocols in varying but similar situations. The nature of the task is structured, with known methods being applied.
You learn to guide your own learning (self-management) in the areas of planning, motivation and reflection. Reflection is aimed at knowledge and understanding, with a focus on innovation.
The guidance provided is aimed at increasing self-management.
Assessment
In this module, the competencies are assessed on the basis of the specific learning outcomes. For each learning outcome, various pieces of evidence are collected in a portfolio. Each piece of evidence is included in the portfolio once. The completed portfolio is input for the portfolio assessment (in which the other modules belonging to the PLP1 are also assessed).
During the portfolio assessment, the student demonstrates that they have mastered the learning outcomes. The input from the portfolio and the assessment together form the assessment.
The assessment takes place individually at the internship location with the teacher supervisor and the work supervisor. The module is assessed on all learning outcomes with a grade.
All learning outcomes must be at least satisfactory. If a module is assessed as unsatisfactory during the regular assessment, the student may retake the module during the same practical learning period. In consultation with the teacher supervisor and work supervisor, it will be determined what the retake will entail and how it will be organised.
Resit
There are various reasons for taking a resit, namely:
Missed opportunity (MO) due to failure to complete the entire practical learning period; no portfolio assessment will take place. The student will try again to pass the modules in a subsequent practical learning period. The student, work supervisor and teacher supervisor will schedule a final meeting.
Missed opportunity (MO) due to the absence of MAZ criteria in the elaboration of the modules; the assessment will take place at the agreed time. The student has the opportunity to make up for the gap in a resit of the module in the same learning period.
Insufficient; If one or more modules are assessed as insufficient during the portfolio assessment, the module(s) in question will be marked as insufficient. The student is entitled to retake the module during the same learning period. It is not possible to extend an internship period.
In order to progress to PLP2/3, students must pass the three modules belonging to PLP1 (Arguing for care, Working on health and Directing care). If one module is not completed satisfactorily, it is possible, in consultation with the teacher supervisor, to restart PLP 2 within the resit semester. This procedure and the conditions are explained in more detail in the PLP1 course.
Feedback from the work supervisor, other colleagues and professionals in the field, fellow students and lecturers prior to the assessment is part of the learning process.
(Exemptions may be granted on the basis of previous results obtained elsewhere and/or work experience).

Students learn to proactively identify bottlenecks in the quality and sustainability of care. Together with the study group, students develop an improvement and implementation proposal for a relevant problem, based on a substantiated problem analysis. The maths test is also linked to this module. Medical maths is an essential skill for the safe and correct dispensing and administration of medication.
The 15-week module comprises an average of 7 hours per week of teaching sessions, supplemented by self-study, assignment work and learning team consultations.

/en/course/2026/HVVB25MKE3.content:

In Medical Knowledge 3, students will deepen their knowledge by studying a number of complex clinical pictures associated with the organ systems discussed in Medical Knowledge 1 and 2. In addition, the subjects of genetics, human development, laboratory research and fluid balance will be covered.
The organ systems that are the focus of this semester are the circulatory system, respiratory system, urinary system, digestive system, immune system, reproductive system and central nervous system.

Learning outcomes independent of learning pathway:
The novice professional knows, identifies and works safely in accordance with professional standards, guidelines and protocols (applicable laws and regulations) concerning (high-risk and reserved) procedures aimed at patients whose lives are in danger and is able to deviate from these in a reasoned manner, if possible in consultation with the care recipient, in order to provide comprehensive care.
The novice professional collects and analyses data in a systematic manner, such as the purpose, (contra)indications, complications, anatomy, physiology, psychology, pathology and pharmacology relating to the performance of high-risk and reserved procedures.
The novice professional applies methods for risk assessment, problem recognition and intervention while performing nursing skills on patients in a life-threatening condition and is then able to report and transfer this information efficiently, effectively and methodically.
Indicators level 1:
Performs (reserved and high-risk) procedures aimed at patients in life-threatening situations in various settings, such as palliative care, first aid and intensive care, taking into account their own authority and competence.
Works according to standards, guidelines and protocols (in accordance with legislation and regulations) aimed at patients whose lives are at risk, which are part of their functional responsibility, and is able to deviate from these responsibly if the wishes of the care recipient or their own professional or moral considerations give cause to do so
Takes into account the wishes and needs of the vitally endangered care recipient in their actions, after consultation with the care recipient and their relatives about the care required
Is familiar with the underlying basic principles of, among other things, anatomy, physiology, psychology, pathology and pharmacology as they relate to vitally endangered patients
Identifies the purpose, (contra)indications and complications of the nursing procedures performed on the vitally endangered patient
Applies methods for risk assessment, early detection, problem recognition, intervention and monitoring in the care of vitally endangered patients
Can efficiently and effectively report, consult and transfer information regarding the critically ill patient
Can provide feedback to fellow students on their actions and professional behaviour in relation to the care of critically ill patients
Demonstrates an understanding of the consequences of their own actions in relation to the creation of unsafe situations in the care of critically ill patients
Works in the care of critically ill patients in accordance with the guidelines of safety policy and infection prevention, privacy, ergonomics, economics and ecology
CanMeds role:
Care provider, collaborative partner, reflective EBP professional, organiser
The learning outcomes contribute to the areas of expertise ‘Justifying care’ and ‘Working on health’.
Key concepts from the BN2020 training profile
Clinical reasoning: The continuous, process-based collection and analysis of data aimed at identifying the questions and problems of the care recipient and selecting appropriate care outcomes and interventions.
Care delivery: Providing integrated care by independently performing all nursing tasks (including reserved and high-risk tasks) in low-complexity care situations, in compliance with applicable laws and regulations and from a holistic perspective.
Continuity of care: Sharing knowledge and information aimed at ensuring the uninterrupted involvement of the necessary care providers in the care process of the care recipient and their loved ones over time.
Promoting expertise: Demonstrating active and critical behaviour in order to maintain and improve one's own nursing expertise and that of others, and actively contributing to the search for, development and sharing of new (forms of) knowledge.
Promoting safety: Continuously and methodically contributing to promoting and safeguarding the safety of care recipients, their loved ones and employees.
Competence mastery level (CBN, 2022)
The first level involves a moderately complex context in which the focus is on the methodical application of knowledge and skills based on guidelines and protocols in varying but similar situations. The nature of the task is structured, with known methods being applied. There is a build-up of self-management, leading to partly guided, partly unguided supervision. Supervision is provided during preparation and implementation, with a focus on learning (strategic) planning, self-efficacy, motivation and reflection. Reflection on actions is aimed at knowledge and understanding, with a focus on innovation.
/en/course/2026/HVVB25SLO3.content:
As a nurse, you will receive broad training so that you can work in various fields, where you will play an important role in the integrated care of patients and their loved ones. Regardless of the setting in which you work, nursing procedures (including reserved and high-risk procedures) will be part of your work.
During this module, the emphasis is on learning and mastering various nursing skills from a holistic, reflective, care recipient-oriented basic attitude with a theoretical foundation. You will learn to work according to protocols, guidelines and standards and to deviate from them in a reasoned manner. In a moderately complex simulated setting, you will learn to perform skills, give and receive feedback, and communicate with care recipients based on various case studies, in collaboration with fellow students. You will use various working methods, such as e-learning, instruction lessons, and scenario training.
Assessment:
Within this module, you will work on achieving the learning outcomes by submitting various pieces of evidence at an individual level. 1. Clinical reasoning and arguing– Level 2
LOL 1.1 – BVZ – N2
The novice practitioner, through clinical reasoning based on evidence-based practice, assesses the need for nursing care in consultation with the care recipient and their relatives, and provides this care in authentic, complex situations.
LOL 1.2 – BVZ – N2
In an authentic setting, the novice practitioner encourages the self-management of the care recipient and their relatives in a culturally sensitive manner, whilst responding to their needs.
LOL 1.3 - BVZ - N2
The novice practitioner communicates, in an authentic setting, in a person-centred and interprofessional manner with the care recipient, their loved ones and the relevant healthcare professionals, ensuring that the needs of the care recipient and their loved ones are met.
Indicators
Description
1.5 Combines and determines the nursing process in a systematic, valid and reliable manner, makes reasoned choices based on the steps of EBP, and utilises the best available evidence from scientific research (BN2020).
1.6 Provides nursing care, appropriate to the moment and circumstances, from a holistic perspective encompassing living, wellbeing, care, meaning, social context and culture (BN2020).
1.7 Applies appropriately substantiated information and communication technologies to complement personal contact with the care recipient and their loved ones, with the aim of strengthening the self-management of the care recipient and their loved ones (BN2020).
/en/course/2026/HVVB26BVZ2.content:
In this course, the novice practitioner demonstrates skills in the nursing process within a highly complex, real-world context, with a view to supporting self-management amongst service users and their loved ones. The novice practitioner applies the methodologies and classifications learnt within this highly complex, real-world context.
The novice practitioner combines this information and determines the nursing care required on the basis of relevant theories and models. Evidence-based practice (EBP) plays a key role throughout the entire nursing process. In doing so, the novice practitioner combines scientific insights, the wishes and needs of the care recipient and their loved ones with clinical expertise. All of this culminates in a case discussion, which the novice practitioner organises on two occasions to gather feedback. One session takes place in a clinical setting and the other in front of a supervising tutor and a second examiner. During the case discussion, emphasis is placed on encouraging the care recipient’s self-management.
Within the nursing process, the novice practitioner applies the communication skills they have learnt, with a focus on person-centred communication, person- and family-centred care, and the use of ICT.
This course also focuses on personal and professional (identity) development through a cyclical process, centred on learning objectives, self-evaluation and reflection. These reflections must be carried out using a taught reflection methodology.
Formative assessment is one of the basic principles of supportive education.
Competence Mastery Level 2 (CBN, 2022)
At the second level, the context is highly complex, with the focus on acting methodically in unpredictable, complex situations. The nature of the task is complex and unstructured. The focus is on student-led learning, with guidance provided more on an ad hoc basis. Actions are carried out as independently as possible, with justification provided retrospectively. The novice professional is encouraged to apply (strategic) planning, self-efficacy, motivation and reflection independently. Reflection on one’s actions centres on daring, willing and being, with the emphasis on sustainable development.
Assessment
In this course, the required competences are assessed on the basis of the specific learning outcomes. The learning outcomes must be demonstrated at CBN Level 2 through a portfolio assessment.
During the work placement, the trainee professional collects various supporting documents for the portfolio. Feedback from the work supervisor, fellow students and the supervising lecturer prior to the assessment forms part of the learning process and also serves as input for the final assessment. The fully completed portfolio serves as the basis for the portfolio assessment interview (during which the other course associated with PLP 3 – RVZ – is also assessed).
Together, the portfolio and the portfolio assessment interview lead to the assessment of the course’s learning outcomes. In this way, the novice professional demonstrates mastery of the learning outcomes.
The assessor reviews the portfolio prior to the portfolio assessment interview to identify any questions, uncertainties or areas requiring further exploration. During the portfolio assessment interview, the novice professional can then provide additional explanations. The assessment takes place at the placement site in the presence of the academic supervisor and the workplace supervisor, with the workplace supervisor able to provide additional input and the academic supervisor ultimately responsible for the assessment.
The course is assessed against all learning outcomes. All learning outcomes must achieve at least a pass mark. If a course is assessed as a fail during the regular assessment opportunity, the trainee may take a resit during the same practical training period. The nature and format of any resit will be determined in consultation with the academic supervisor and the workplace supervisor.
Exemptions may be granted on the basis of results previously achieved elsewhere and/or work experience.
Retake
There are various reasons for taking a resit, namely:
Failure to complete the practical training period; no portfolio assessment will take place. The trainee will attempt to pass the course again during a subsequent practical training period. The student, workplace supervisor and academic supervisor will schedule a final review meeting.
Missed opportunity (GK) due to the absence of MAZ criteria in the module’s implementation; the assessment of the content will still take place at the agreed time. The trainee professional has the opportunity to rectify this shortcoming during a resit of the course within the same learning period.
Fail; If one or more modules are marked as a fail during the portfolio assessment, the module(s) in question will be classified as a fail. In this case, the trainee professional is entitled to retake the course within the same study period.
Procedures and conditions are explained in more detail on the PLP2/3 course.

/en/course/2026/HVVB26BKV2.content:
In this course, the trainee professional draws up a proposal for improvement based on a quality aspect within an authentic context, and takes the initiative to implement and embed the innovation.

Following the analysis, the novice professional works methodically to establish the conditions for the innovation. The diverse interests and objectives of stakeholders, formal and informal structures, and professional standards within the healthcare context are taken into account. The final improvement proposal is aimed at a sustainable innovation, utilising healthcare technology where possible.
A quality-oriented approach is demonstrated through the use of systems and measurement tools, and the ability to analyse, monitor, evaluate and ensure quality at all levels of care (micro, meso and macro levels). In addition, attention is paid to nurses’ entrepreneurial attitude and patient safety. In many situations, healthcare technology can make a valuable contribution.

/en/course/2026/HVVB24AVZ2.outcomes:
The novice professional methodically designs, from an issue in professional practice, a substantiated and consistent research based on a problem analysis.
The novice professional conducts the research, reports and formulates a conclusion based on critical consideration of the research results.
The novice professional makes recommendations based on the results of the research and shares them appropriately to improve the specific professional situation.
Indicators level 2
Analyses a nursing relevant practice problem and substantiates it with the latest scientific and professional literature
Formulates an objective based on a professional product and a question appropriate to the problem analysis and the needs of the practice from the practice problem described
Designs a method to answer the research question and justifies the choices made
Applies aspects of research ethics and laws and regulations to his/her own research and justifies the choices made
Analyses the data collected and describes the results
Discusses the results, interprets and compares them with existing research and/or theories
Reflects critically on the chosen methodology and execution of own research
Formulates a conclusion in the light of the discussion
Formulates recommendations appropriate to professional practice based on the conclusion
Presents the recommendations using a product appropriate to the needs of professional practice
Displays a critical inquisitive and reflective basic attitude
CanMeds role
: Reflective EBP professional, Organiser, The professional and quality promoter.
Core concepts from BN2020 programme profile
Investigative ability
: Demonstrating a critically inquisitive and reflective (basic) attitude in care situations and care and organisational issues, justifying one's actions from (different) sources of knowledge, adopting a methodical approach with a thorough problem analysis and completing a research cycle aimed at improving a specific professional situation.
Use Evidence-based practice (EBP)
: in consultation with the care recipient (and/or his network), colleagues and other disciplines, weighing up (1) actively sought recent (nursing) knowledge from (scientific) literature, guidelines or protocols, (2) professional expertise and (3) personal knowledge, wishes and preferences of the care recipient and/or his network.
Expertise development
: demonstrating active and critical behaviour to bring and maintain nursing expertise of self and others, and actively contributing to the search, development and sharing of new (forms) of knowledge.
Professional reflection
: critically considering one's own nursing behaviour in relation to the professional code and professional values and in (mono and multidisciplinary) discussions oer care recipients involved and carefully arguing, taking into account the emotions and interests of the care recipient from the awareness that care involves a moral-ethical practice.
Nursing leadership:
taking the initiative in directing one's own profession from an entrepreneurial, coaching and results-oriented attitude.
Participating in quality assurance:
making a proactive contribution to the quality assurance of the healthcare organisation.
Competency mastery level (CBN, 2022)
Within the second level, there is a highly-complex context where the focus is on acting methodically in unpredictable, complex situations. The nature of the task is complex and unstructured. The focus is on student-driven teaching where there will be more on-demand supervision. Acting takes place independently as much as possible with argumentation afterwards. Students are encouraged in the independent application of (strategic) planning, self-efficacy, motivation and reflection. Reflection on action is aimed at daring, wanting and being, with a focus on sustainable development.
/en/course/2026/HVVB24AVZ2.content:
The module Analysing and Improving Care (AVZ) focuses on conducting a practice-oriented research with the aim of improving a specific professional situation in the professional practice. During the module, you learn to methodically write a research design in the form of an analysis, advice or design, carry it out and make recommendations to professional practice based on the results. You formulate the practice problem, objective and question and a professional product fitting the need of the practice. You gain the knowledge you need for this from the recommended (scientific) literature, knowledge clips on Blackboard and response lectures offered during the research period.
You learn within a learning community with weekly physical and online meetings. In the learning community, you will learn from and with each other by reading each other's research designs, presenting the progress of your research and collecting feedback from both fellow students and lecturers. In the implementation phase of your research, you work on data collection in practice and analysis of the results. You write a critical review of the results in the discussion, a conclusion and then recommendations. As the final product of the module, you hand in the research report and present the research results to the client and other interested parties.
The 20-week module involves an average of 32 hours per week of self-study, research elaboration and consultation.
Teaching themes
Research methodologies consisting of;
Design-oriented/action research
Stages of design thinking/ intervention cycle
Quantitative research
Descriptive and test statistics
Use of SPSS
Qualitative research
Interview techniques
Transcribing and coding
Use of Atlas
General topics consisting of;
Phases of research
Ethical aspects for practice-based research
Sampling
Inclusion/exclusion criteria
Validity and reliability
Data analysis
Description of research results
Assessment
In the module, your research competencies are assessed based on specific learning outcomes and associated indicators. You will collect several pieces of evidence in each pair during the research period, which will be formatively assessed on a 'below level', 'at level' or 'above level' scale. The pieces of evidence do not all have to be 'at level' at the time of assessment. Through the assessment and feedback, you gain insight into your own learning process and know what steps you still need to take to eventually achieve the learning outcomes and complete the module. Formative evidence including feedback is collected in a feedback log and included in the assessment of the research report.
Two assessment moments take place in the module. In the design phase of the research, there is an oral individual critical dialogue where you justify the choices made of your research design. The critical dialogue is assessed on a 'sufficient' or 'insufficient' scale, and must be assessed with 'sufficient' to be allowed to carry out the research in practice. In case of an 'insufficient' on the critical dialogue, you will receive specific feedback and the opportunity to retake the dialogue once.
At the end of the module, the research report, consisting of a description and substantiation of the research process and the feedback log, is assessed with a mark. In case of a failing grade on the research report, you will receive specific feedback and the opportunity to resit it once.

Critical dialogue, oral (individual)

Area of Expertise and Learning Outcome(s)
6. Professional Identity Development – Levels 1 and 2
LOL 6.1 – PIO – N1 and N2
The novice practitioner demonstrates nursing leadership, professional conduct, an inquisitive attitude and moral sensitivity within nursing practice in order to strengthen personal and professional (identity) development (and positioning within the organisation).
LOL 6.2 – PIO – N1 and N2
The novice practicioner reflects on significant situations relating to personal and professional (identity) development.
Indicators
Description
6.1 Takes the initiative in coordinating care provision for the care recipient and their loved ones, drawing on professional expertise, and collaborates interprofessionally in this regard (BN2020).
6.2 Acts in accordance with professional standards, legislation and regulations, and the professional code of conduct, and takes responsibility for their own actions (BN2020).
6.3 Demonstrates a critical, inquisitive and reflective (basic attitude) and acts responsibly, drawing on various (scientific) sources of knowledge (BN2020).
6.4 Demonstrates compassion for the wishes, needs and associated emotions of the care recipient and their loved ones, and is able to relate these to the moral and ethical context of care provision (BN2020).
6.5A VT Methodically reflects on meaningful situations in which actions are directed towards knowing and understanding, with a focus on innovation (BN2020).
6.5B VT Methodically reflects on meaningful situations in which actions are directed towards daring, willing and being, with a focus on sustainable development (BN2020).
/en/course/2026/HVVB25PIO.content:
Description
Support for personal and professional (identity) development takes place within core groups, which are supervised by the student counsellor throughout the programme. These core groups consist of a maximum of 15 students and are formed in the first year. The core group is an important space where students (1) become aware of their own personal and professional (identity) development, (2) learn to take control of this themselves, (3) forge bonds with fellow students and, by extension, with the programme, and (4) thereby achieve a positive impact on student wellbeing and academic success.
Within the core groups, various themes take centre stage, linked to the key concepts of nursing leadership, moral sensitivity, professional conduct and an inquisitive attitude. In addition, attention is given to student guidance through a programme covering related topics such as study and career choices, study skills and personalised study advice (PSA), as well as themes focused on student wellbeing.
During the core group meetings, students set their own learning objectives and present these during the module they are currently undertaking.
Professional reflection is taught through a continuous reflection process, which is incorporated into the modules. During each semester, students submit two reflections on situations that have been meaningful to them and contribute to their personal and professional identity development.
These reflections are assessed by the module tutor. All reflection pieces, including the assessment and feedback received, are included in the portfolio, and the learning outcomes from these reflections serve as input for the mid-term assessment and the nursing case presentation.
Competence Proficiency Level 1 (CBN, 2022)
At the first level, the context is of medium complexity, with the focus on the methodical application of knowledge and skills in accordance with guidelines and protocols in varying but similar situations. The nature of the task is structured, involving the application of familiar methods.
The student learns to direct their own learning (self-direction) in terms of planning, motivation and reflection. Reflection is aimed at knowledge and understanding, with a focus on innovation. Guidance in this regard is aimed at increasing self-direction
Competence Mastery Level 2 (CBN, 2022)
At the second level, the context is highly complex, with the focus on acting methodically in unpredictable, complex situations. The nature of the task is complex and unstructured. The focus is on student-led learning, with guidance provided more on an on-demand basis. Actions are carried out as independently as possible, with justification provided afterwards. Students are encouraged to independently apply (strategic) planning, self-efficacy, motivation and reflection. Reflection on actions centres on daring, willing and being, with the focus on sustainable development.
Assessment
In this module, competences are assessed on the basis of the two learning outcomes. Assessment takes place on two occasions: at the end of Level 1 through a mid-term presentation, and at the end of Level 2 through a nursing presentation. The presentation is based on a compiled portfolio.
During the mid-term presentation, progress in relation to both learning outcomes is discussed. The student reflects on the personal and professional development they have undergone up to that point. They also look ahead to the development they wish to undergo in order to ultimately graduate as a higher professional education (HBO) nurse.
During the nursing presentation, the student outlines the personal and professional development they have undergone during the programme and how this has shaped them into a novice higher professional education (HBO) nurse. Credits are awarded once the portfolio containing the supporting documents has been submitted on time for both the mid-term and nursing presentation, and after both interviews have taken place. The mid-term and the presentation are assessed by a qualified examiner. A resit must be assessed by an examiner other than the student’s own supervisor.
Explanatory notes
For both the mid-term presentation and the nursing presentation, the student must submit a portfolio containing the supporting documents listed below.
As described in the overview below under ‘Assessment’, 2 ECs are awarded as a partial mark for the successful completion of the mid-term presentation, and 3 ECs are awarded as a partial mark for the successful completion of the nursing presentation. Upon awarding these final 3 ECs, the full 5 ECs are credited in Osiris.
TEST-01 - Midterm plea
TEST-02 - Nursing plea
Evidence for the assessment
Development scan
Individual assignment
The student completes a development scan each semester. This scan is based on the higher professional education (HBO) competences, ICOMs and the following key concepts: nursing leadership, professional conduct, professional reflection, moral sensitivity and an inquisitive attitude. The development in relation to these core concepts is discussed in the case presentation. This ensures compliance with indicators 6.1, 6.2, 6.3 and 6.4.
Assessed reflections
Individual assignment
The student has submitted reflections on situations that are meaningful to them and which contribute to their personal and professional identity development. These reflections are assessed by the module tutor using the rubric formulated for this purpose. At level 1, the reflection focuses on knowledge and understanding, with an emphasis on innovation. At level 2, the reflection on practice focuses on daring, willing and being, with the emphasis on sustainable development. In order to participate in both the mid-term and the nursing case presentation, at least two of all assessed reflections must have been assessed as satisfactory. In the plea, the student also provides insight into at least two meaningful situations and what they have learnt from them during the programme. This ensures compliance with the two indicators relating to reflection: 6.5A and 6.5B.
Personal learning objectives
Individual assignment
Based on the development scan, 360-degree feedback and the reflections, the student sets personal learning objectives which they work towards during the semester and on which they gather feedback.
360-degree feedback
Individual assignment
During the semester, the student seeks 360-degree feedback on their personal learning objectives. This feedback comes from fellow students, work supervisors, colleagues and/or experts from the field.

/en/course/2026/PHLM25BH.content:
In this course, common endocrinological and hematological patient problems are central. These patient problems serve as the starting point for learning medical diagnostic skills and the (pharmaco)therapeutic process. Through lectures, practical sessions, and working groups, students learn to reason and act clinically, with attention to both curative and preventive aspects. This includes being able to logically compose and implement a (pharmacotherapeutic) treatment plan.
The actions of the Physician Assistant (PA) are preferably evidence-based, meaning they are partly grounded in data from scientific research. Therefore, it is important that students are able to assess the quality, outcome, and relevance of research results and conclusions. To this end, the key methodological and statistical aspects are covered.

/en/course/2026/PHLM25HKO.content:
This course centers on common dermatological, ENT (ear, nose, and throat), and ophthalmological patient problems. These clinical issues serve as the foundation for developing medical diagnostic skills and understanding the (pharmaco)therapeutic process. Through lectures, practical sessions, and small-group discussions, students learn clinical reasoning and decision-making, with a focus on both curative and preventive aspects—including the ability to logically construct and carry out a (pharmacotherapeutic) treatment plan.
The actions of the Physician Assistant (PA) should preferably be evidence-based, meaning they are informed by findings from scientific research. Therefore, students must learn to evaluate the quality, outcome, and relevance of research findings and conclusions. At the end of the first academic year, students write a research proposal that serves as a go/no-go moment for conducting practice-oriented research.
As part of the Communication & Professional Development module, students work on competencies such as communication, collaboration, and (professional) personal leadership.
Additionally, there is emphasis on efficient, structured (medical) consultations, communicative skills, and reflection on one’s own (professional) actions.

/en/course/2026/PHLM25SPL1.content: Specialist practice learning is organized through Specialist Entrustable Professional Activities (SEPAs). The students acquire specialist competencies (SEPAs) at their own practical learning place. A medical specialist as a preceptor is a necessary condition for monitoring the learning process and for providing medical education in practice. Daily supervision can be delegated to a mentor (i.e. fellow medical doctor or certified Physician Assistant). For the requirements of assigning such a mentor role, reference is made to the apprenticeship agreement. The own practical learning place is a powerful learning environment in which knowledge is applied and skills are practiced. Specific skills are acquired in one's own work situation, with the SEPAs being formulated by the preceptor. As an extension of this, students write the learning work plans that describe how the SEPAs in specialist practice are achieved. This competence development and the supporting documents are carefully kept in the portfolio. At the end of each semester it will be assessed whether the goals set by the student in his learning and working plans have been achieved. The portfolio must show, among other things, that the student is able to complete the determined SEPAs at level 4, after which a declaration of competence (Statement of Awarded Responsibility) by the preceptor and at least 1 other committed staff member or colleague GP is signed. The duties and responsibilities of the student, the preceptor, the employer and the coach from the study program are described in the "Learning in practice" manual.

In this course, common endocrinological and hematological patient problems are central. /en/course/2026/PHLM19KGFT8-P.content: During the course Clinical Medicine & Pharmacotherapy 8 "Complex Care Issues" in academic year 3 attention is paid to patient problems in all life phases from pre-conception to end of life. Healthy Ageing forms the theoretical framework by means of which various complex health issues are addressed. Central theme is the question of how medical care can connect to these issues in an integrated manner. Students are thus stimulated to act as Master-trained healthcare professionals, also in situations when standard interventions fail. All this after careful consideration and intercollegiate consultation regarding the medical-ethical and legal aspects that play a role in complex care problems. In a case study all these aspects of complex care are illustrated based on a patient for whom the candidate was responsible for the most part of the coaching and/or treatment.

/en/course/2026/PHLM24CZ.content:
In the course Complex care issues the topics for Clinical Medicine & Pharmacotherapy 8 “Complex care questions” and Behavior & Communication-* are integrated. In the 3rd study year, attention is paid to patient problems in the life phases from preconception to life-long learning. Within the context of Healthy Ageing, various complex health issues are addressed. Pivotal during this block of education is the question how medical care can address these questions in an integrated manner. Students are encouraged to act as master's degree care professionals, especially at the moment when standard interventions do not suffice any longer. All this after a careful assessment of an intercollegiate discussion on the medical, ethical and legal aspects that can play a role in complex care issues.
Students are encouraged to develop a vision of how they can contribute to positive health and self-management of the patient as healthcare professionals. Attention is paid to communication skills through discussion and conversation linked to specific complex care questions: sexuality, problematic parenting situations, Atypical Somatic complaints, and palliative care. Through role-play, interdisciplinary consultation with the neighborhood team, and directing theatre concerning discussions with family, attention is paid to discussing and practicing dealing with specific and complex care questions.
