/en/course/2026/PHLM19SEPA-SEM5.content:
Specialist practice learning is organized through Specialist Entrustable Professional Activities (SEPAs). The students acquire specialist competencies (SEPAs) at their own practical learning place. A medical specialist as a preceptor is a necessary condition for monitoring the learning process and for providing medical education in practice. Daily supervision can be delegated to a mentor (i.e. fellow medical doctor or certified Physician Assistant). For the requirements of assigning such a mentor role, reference is made to the apprenticeship agreement. The own practical learning place is a powerful learning environment in which knowledge is applied and skills are practiced. Specific skills are acquired in one's own work situation, with the SEPAs being formulated by the preceptor. As an extension of this, students write the learning work plans that describe how the SEPAs in specialist practice are achieved. This competence development and the supporting documents are carefully kept in the portfolio. At the end of each semester it will be assessed whether the goals set by the student in his learning and working plans have been achieved.  The duties and responsibilities of the student, the preceptor, the employer and the coach from the study program are described in the "Learning in practice" manual.
The portfolio shows besides the products also the proces of development.

/en/course/2026/PHLM21LDS.content:
The Master Physician Assistant program works with a step-by-step approach to the theme of leadership during the training. In the first year, the focus is on developing Personal Leadership, in which the students question themselves on how to position themselves as a new professional in the medical domain. During the second year, the development of Professional Leadership is the central focus. Then it is about how the student positions and profiles himself within his organization and associated partner institutions as a versatile professional (both in the medical and scientific domain and in the field of collaboration within the organization). Finally, in the third year, the focus is on Public Leadership; the following topics are discussed: how can the student contribute to the "Bigger Picture" of his profession as a PA, nationally and internationally? Think of participating in working groups, giving presentations, contributing to societal issues, and increasing social awareness of your profession. In short: "The 3 P's of PA Leadership in Education and Practice". In academic years 1, 2, and 3 of the Physician Assistant program, themes are related to leadership and medical professionalism during the Behaviour and Communication lectures/working groups. In the so-called Masterlabs Leadership, the Canmeds model and Framework Plan for Medical Training 2020) and specific topics from medical professionalism offer in-depth knowledge from which the student can develop a vision of the practice of the profession in the context of the bigger picture. The topics covered in the Master labs are Personal motives, qualities/values and norms, ethics, patient safety/quality care, vision development and positive health and change management.
In academic year 3, students write a 'position paper PA Leadership' in which the development of 'novice to expert' is described, and the students are challenged to describe their dream image concerning professional practice in 5-10 years from now. Central to this is the question of which leadership qualities they need to achieve the goal.

/en/course/2026/PHLM21MP-CGI.content:
At the end of the Master's track Physician Assistant, the student demonstrates through a Criterion-Oriented Interview (COI) during this Master Aptitude Test that he has acquired those competencies that define a Master Physician Assistant and can integrate and critically consider them. A professional master's student can deal with complex matters in a broader context related to the field and analyze them from different theoretical, organizational, scientific, and managerial perspectives.
During the COI, the student demonstrates the acquired competencies and convinces why he is ready to start a career in medicine as a PA professional. During the Master Aptitude Test, reflection on the professional roles/competencies is requested explicitly at the level of the intended learning outcomes. Supported with the help of the STARRT methodology, addressing: situations, tasks, activities, results, reflection, and transfer, students bring all of the aspects into the limelight for the present examiners. Admission to the exam is only possible after meeting the entry requirements: the Specialist Case Study, the Master Thesis, the Position Paper Leadership, and the portfolio Learning in Practice.

/en/course/2026/FYVP23FZ1FG.content:
PT-care 1.consists of 2 courses of 5 EC that are interwoven with each other. Course 1: Physiology & Health and course 2: Anatomy & skills.
This course concerns covers the more theoretical part of PT-care 1.
Prevention plays an increasing significant role in our society – certainly when it comes to prevention in the context of ADL, work and sports. Physiotherapists are expected to have the professional skills to design training programmes for clients aimed at improving strength and endurance, and to guide the clients during the execution of these programmes. In the daily practice of physiotherapy, setting up a solid training programme is a common activity. To set up such a training programme and evaluate it, you need basic knowledge of physiology/exertion physiology, anatomy and training theory. To this end, every week, students will elaborate on a simple and single -problemcase study about a healthy person  to various health risks. The study tasks are about osteology, syndesmology, myology, kinesiology, physiology/exertion physiology, training theory, testing, measuring and training, and giving information, health information, instruction and feedback. Basic anatomy and physiology in relation to the heart and lungs and the corresponding measurements will also be discussed, as well as the behavioural side of health and exercise. Important: This casuistry is a means to get to know the didactic materials really well, but does not cover the entirety of materials that will be tested at the end of the training programme. Independent study, especially of the required literature, is absolutely necessary.

PT-care 4 consists of 2 courses of 5 EC that are interwoven with each other. Course 1: Neurology & Rehabilitation 1 and course 2: Skills & integration.
This course concerns Neurology rehabilitation 1 and covers the more theoretical part of PT-care 4.
With knowledge and insight into the client’s problems, the physiotherapist can provide high-standard qualitative care. The variation in symptoms among patients with neurological problems is considerable. Patients with similar diagnoses can display very different clinical pictures. To  provide assessment and treatment adequately and in a patient-specific fashion during professional practice, it is indispensable for physiotherapists to have comprehensive knowledge of neurology. The quality of the clinical reasoning will follow the degree to which a skilled practitioner is knowledgeable about the client’s problems.
By gearing the instruction towards knowledge of and insight into aspects of central and peripheral neurological problems, we aim for the professional growth of physiotherapists-in-training. This theoretical background is examined during an oral exam.
Anatomy 4 is a course where theorectical background is being tested. It comprises identifying, localising bony structures, as well as origin and attachment of muscles, ligaments, tendons and nerves, skin areas and dermatomes. In this course we will discuss and test the basic anatomic knowledge and skills that we use as physiotherapists. This course delves deeper into the materials and expands on Anatomy 1 to 3, and is being examined in a written test.

Learning Outcomes

The student is able to describe these findings in a written report. Professional role: HP-1
The student demonstrates mastery of the fundamental principles and basic knowledge (the Body of Knowledge) required to successfully perform the professional role of health promoter — including ethics, rights, laws, and regulations — at proficiency level 1 (primarily factual knowledge, understanding, and reproduction). /en/course/2026/FYVP23LP.content:
Prevention aims to promote physical, mental, and social well-being. A physiotherapist who focuses on prevention is concerned with behavioral change and focuses on people's ability to adapt and control life's social, physical, and emotional challenges.
In this course, prevention focuses on a healthy lifestyle in which aspects such as eating habits, exercise, and dealing with stress are treated. In this course, students work in small groups on various assignments. The student is given the assignment to map out the offer in the field of prevention and the wishes and needs in the field of health and well-being for a specific group of people. Physiotherapeutically relevant questions are formulated and answered. In this course, the student thus learns important preventive measures for a healthy lifestyle and the roles of various care providers, trainers, and volunteers within this range. The course is concluded with a group presentation and a group report.
This course also includes the IPE Cluster Project Health, Care & Vitality Year 1 (1 EC).
In this project, students are introduced to interprofessional collaboration in an active way by working together with various degree programs within the Health, Care & Vitality cluster. Through a shared assignment, they get to know each other better, both socially and professionally. Central to this is discovering role clarity and making use of complementary differences in perspectives and expertise.
The Meta-Model of Interprofessional Development (Reinders, 2018; Reinders & Pesut, 2022; Reinders et al., 2023) helps them understand how these different contributions come together to create effective collaboration.

/en/course/2026/FYVP23OI1.outcomes:
Learning Outcomes
1. The student can translate a specific information need of a patient or practice into an answerable research question (PICO). IP-1
2. The student is able to conduct a systematic search to identify relevant English-language research articles on a health-related problem. IP-1
3. The student is familiar with various information sources, including books, websites, AI, and research articles, and can critically appraise them. IP-1
4. The student can determine the level of evidence of (English-language) research articles and assess the validity and usefulness of research articles using an appropriate assessment tool. IP-1
5. The student has knowledge of basic methodological and statistical aspects of a research article (including research design, measures of central tendency and dispersion, significance, correlation, and the interpretation of graphs and figures). IP-1
6. The student can, in collaboration with fellow students, explain findings from scientific literature through a presentation and share them professionally with others. COM,COL-1
/en/course/2026/FYVP23OI1.content:
Society places high demands on professional conduct. Physiotherapists must demonstrate to clients and health insurers that their physiotherapeutic interventions are well substantiated from a scientific point of view. Physiotherapists are expected to examine and treat their patients in the best possible way. The physiotherapist's actions are based on the norms and values of the patient(s) concerned, the physiotherapist's clinical expertise, and the best available scientific evidence. Therefore, working according to these principles of evidence-based practice (EBP) is a must for every physiotherapist.
Research & Innovation 1 deals with the basic principles of applied scientific research. In this course, the investigative ability of students is stimulated: the student becomes acquainted with the EBP cycle and applies this method to a physiotherapeutic case. During the course, small groups will work on formulating research questions; searching scientific literature; assessing and interpreting this literature; organizing, summarizing, and displaying results in a fact sheet. The student will also gain knowledge about research designs and basic statistics. The course is concluded with a group assignment and an individual knowledge test. At the end of this course, the student has acquired basic knowledge about applied scientific research and gained experience with the EBP cycle. As a result of the course, the student can broadly understand and interpret research on physiotherapeutic treatment effects.

/en/course/2026/FYVP26PO1JS1.content:
This course consists of Professional Development 1 and Junior Internship 1.
The student career trajectory is part of the physiotherapy studies; the student learns to establish a connection between his studies and the profession of physiotherapist. This requires a learning process in which he learns to organise and plan, take responsibility for the choices he makes, and give shape to the ensuing actions. In this way he learns to give a sense of direction to the physiotherapy studies. In our programme a student has primary responsibility for his studies and career.
A professional identity emerges through an interaction between the student, their education, and their immediate environment. It gives the student their own identity as a starting physiotherapist at the end of their studies. A professional identity is formed gradually through (work) experiences. Professional and personal development are closely related. Personal development influences, colors, and shapes professional development, and vice versa. This course mainly focuses on developing the competences of the 'Reflective Professional' of the Physiotherapist's professional profile.
In professional development 1 following themes will be addressed during the first year: getting acquainted with the education, the role of the reflective professional, and the profession of physiotherapist.
Junior Internship 1 has a group- and an individual component. Gaining practical experience through internships at an early stage is essential. Early exposure allows students to become familiar with the profession beyond the classroom, working with real patients, bridging the gap between theory, case studies and practice. By working directly with patients and observing experienced physiotherapists, students develop a clearer understanding of professional roles of a physiotherapist. During the internships, the student will not only interact with patients but also gain firsthand experience of working within a healthcare institution. This will enable them to develop an understanding of the overall functioning and organization of healthcare.
Portfolio Assessment 1 and 2 will include critical reflections on both Professional Development 1 and Junior Internship 1.

/en/course/2026/FYVB25OZP.content:
In the section of the curriculum dedicated to entrepreneurship, the focus is on innovation in physiotherapy. Within the competence profile of the physiotherapist, the ability to organize and innovate becomes increasingly crucial. The dynamics in healthcare are changing, as are the needs of patients. This calls for flexibility and an expanded skill set for new healthcare providers.
At Hanze University of Applied Sciences, entrepreneurship is considered a key focal point, but it does not mean that every physiotherapist must start their own business. However, every University of Applied Sciences (HBO) student is expected to possess entrepreneurial qualities by the end of their studies.
Entrepreneurial qualities are also important in existing organizations. These qualities are necessary to continually innovate and develop new ideas to enhance physiotherapeutic care.
As an entrepreneurial physiotherapist, it is crucial to respond to the needs of the environment. To understand these needs effectively, various research methods are employed. Only when the needs are clear we contemplate possible solutions. Different techniques and methodologies are applied for this purpose, such as design thinking, moonshot thinking, and the business model canvas.
By practising and working with these methods, students are able, by the end of this module, to make an innovative contribution to the organization of healthcare.
This course includes the
IPE Cluster Project Health, Care & Vitality – Year 2
Collaboration in healthcare contributes to the quality of care for patients and clients, but it is not always self‑evident. Healthcare professionals act from a strong professional identity, which guides their choices and decisions. Effective collaboration requires insight into each other’s roles, perspectives, and areas of expertise, so that role clarity can develop and more can be achieved together.
In this project, students use the Meta-Model of Interprofessional Development (Reinders, 2018; Reinders & Pesut, 2022; Reinders et al., 2023). They work through: Phase 0 (professional identity), Phase 1 (shared problem domain), and Phase 2 (combining priorities and alternatives), with the aim of strengthening collaboration and making use of the added value of each other’s differences.

/en/course/2026/FYVB24OI2.outcomes:
The student is able to formulate an answerable research question (PICO) and conduct a systematic search to identify relevant English-language research articles on a health-related problem. Professional Role IP, Level 2.
The student can assess the validity and usability of (English-language) research articles using a suitable assessment instrument. Professional Role IP, Level 2.
The student can interpret and explain methodological and statistical aspects of a research article (research design, central tendency and dispersion measures, significance, correlation, and the interpretation of graphs and figures) to others. Professional Role IP, Level 2.
The student can apply Shared Decision Making (SDM) to a patient problem. Professional Role IP, ZV, Level 2.
The student can, in collaboration with fellow students, develop an evidence-based treatment plan based on the three pillars of EBP to address a patient problem. Professional Role IP, SWP, Level 2.
The student can, in collaboration with fellow students, professionally share research findings based on the three pillars of EBP with third parties through a presentation. Professional Role COM, Level 2.
/en/course/2026/FYVB24OI2.content:
Clients and health insurers expect physiotherapists to provide optimal care. The Royal Dutch Society for Physical Therapy (KNGF) defines optimal care as care based on the best available evidence from three pillars of Evidence Based Practice (EBP): Scientific literature; Patient expectations, and Provider experience.
Through Shared Decision Making (SDM), the physiotherapist can bring together these 3 pillars and collaboratively develop a treatment plan with a patient. SDM is a method of communication where mutual information exchange is essential.
In Research and Innovation 2, students will apply SDM, based on the 3 pillars of EBP. The scientific literature pillar is addressed by writing a review article on physiotherapeutic treatment, systematically searching the scientific literature, and working on accurately interpreting scientific articles. Patient expectations are determined through qualitative research. For the last pillar, the experience gained from physiotherapy education and practice is utilised. At the end of the semester, students conclude with an SDM conversation and a presentation in which they explain and justify their SDM process and the ultimate treatment plan they have arrived at.

A number of specific conditions will be discussed in this module. Attention will be paid to the development of these conditions and the role of a pediatric physiotherapist. The module will end with a practical test in which skills and clinical reasoning are tested by means of case study.

In collaboration with fellow students, the student can explain all phases and components of a research project through a presentation and share it professionally with third parties. Professional Role: IP, COM, Level 2.
/en/course/2026/FYVB25OI3.content:
To provide the best possible care, it is important that physiotherapists keep their knowledge up to date and are able to substantiate their treatments. Physiotherapists must demonstrate to both clients and health insurers that their physiotherapeutic interventions are scientifically well-founded. Being able to interpret and critically assess the scientific value of research and literature is therefore an essential skill.
In O&I 3, students will work in a ‘journal club’ during the first few weeks to gain insight into the differences between qualitative and quantitative research and to develop a deeper understanding of the reliability of quantitative research and statistical testing. After that, students are introduced to conducting research using both quantitative and qualitative research designs. Each student, in collaboration with fellow students and under the supervision of their tutor, will design and conduct both a quantitative and a qualitative study. For the quantitative study, they will formulate a research question, select an appropriate method and statistical test, and carry out data collection and analysis. For the qualitative study, students will also formulate a research question, and each student will conduct at least two in-depth interviews, transcribe and code these interviews. Students will learn how to process and interpret the collected data and draw appropriate conclusions. The results will be presented in a research article (for the quantitative study) and in an oral presentation (for the qualitative study).
During sessions with the supervising lecturer, the progress of the research is discussed and there is room for (peer) feedback on intermediate products. In addition, supporting education is offered, such as an SPSS practical and a scientific presentation lesson.
This module builds on the O&I modules from years 1 and 2 and prepares the student for the final research project. After completing this module, the student will have acquired knowledge, understanding, and experience with both qualitative and quantitative research

The student demonstrates adequate knowledge and application of the Body of Knowledge, Skills and Attitudes. Professional role: IP, level 3.

As a communicator, the student can communicate in English and takes cultural, social, and religious differences into account. The student demonstrates adequate knowledge and application of the Body of Knowledge, Skills and Attitudes. Professional role: Com, level 3.
/en/course/2026/FYVB26SST1.content:
The internships within the physiotherapy programme are aimed at developing, in practice, the professional roles characteristic of a beginning physiotherapist. The senior internships and the graduation internship together form a learning process in which the student deepens and broadens their professional role.
During the senior internships, the student learns to take responsibility for their own actions and works under supervision to strengthen the professional roles, with emphasis on the roles of healthcare provider and collaborator.
In the graduation internship, the focus shifts to functioning at final‑qualification level. Here, the student is expected to act independently and professionally, integrating all roles. The student demonstrates the ability to analyse complex problems, select appropriate interventions, and carry them out responsibly.
The programme includes two senior internships and one graduation internship.
Throughout the senior internships and the graduation internship, the student works towards level 3 in all seven professional roles of the physiotherapist within the context of professional practice. The final level of the graduation internship is level 3, the level of a beginning practitioner.
During the first senior internship, which lasts 10 weeks, the student works on several professional products alongside the internship itself. This includes writing a CAT, a CASE (and presenting the CASE at the internship site as part of an Intercollegial Consultation – Case Presentation), and submitting various patient documentation assignments.
During Senior Internship 2, the student works on the graduation assignment alongside the internship.
During the graduation internship, the student works towards a high degree of independence and complexity.

/en/course/2026/FYVB25ASO.outcomes:
Under the supervision of a lecturer, the student can develop a research plan to answer a physiotherapy-relevant research question. Professional role IP, level 3.
Under the supervision of a lecturer and in collaboration with third parties, the student can design and conduct a practice-based research project or literature review. Professional roles IP, ORG, SWP, level 3.
Under the supervision of a lecturer, the student can write a Bachelor thesis. Professional role IP, level 3.

/en/course/2026/FYVB25ASO.content:
During this course, students work on a graduation assignment that requires applied scientific/practice-oriented research. The graduation assignment is related to the physiotherapy domain and the aim is to have students work on an assignment from the field. Knowledge and skills acquired in R&I courses are applied at the final level while working on the graduation assignment.
In the first half of the course, students work on a research plan. This is submitted for feedback halfway through the trajectory. In the second half of the course, students carry out the research and the results are recorded in the form of a Bachelor's thesis. The course is concluded with an individual final presentation followed by a criterion-based interview.
Admission requirements:
To be admitted to the Graduation Assignment, students must have completed all educational units from the first and second year of study. In addition, O&I from year three must have been successfully completed. Finally, internship 1 must have been completed.

/en/course/2026/SEVM19SSE.outcomes:
At the end of this module the student is able to:
manipulate matrices to solve a linear system of equations.
analyse a dynamical system using determinants to find eigenvalues and eigenvectors.
solve least squares problems.
apply singular value decomposition to problems in data analysis and signal Processing.
manipulate and visualize numerical data using typical Python packages, such as Numpy and MatPlotlib.
calculate and apply discrete Fourier transform.
apply sampling theorem of Shannon, the Nyquist frequency, the concepts of aliasing and windowing.
/en/course/2026/SEVM19SSE.content:
The course covers the following topics:
the aim of this course is to introduce or refresh your knowledge on digital signal processing, basic software development and linear algebra. This should prepare you for the technical courses taught throughout the rest of the master.

/en/course/2026/SEVM25IP.outcomes:
At the end of this module the student is able to:
expected to show the following knowledge and skills:
research and analyse a given straightforward engineering problem and design a solution for it .
based on the problem analysis, select, read and process sensor data .
program a (control) system to perform smart reactions to the sensor data/signals.
report on the research, design, implementation, and testing in a technical report or paper.
define the areas in which the student needs to strengthen in order to achieve the above mentioned skills. Depending on their prior education and knowledge, students are expected to set their own learning goals, discuss these with a tutor, explain them, and evaluate them.
/en/course/2026/SEVM25IP.content:
The course covers the following topics:
The students have different educational  backgrounds when entering the Smart Systems Engineering master. The goal of this project is to bring all students to a common level on a variety of topics. The idea is that students that are lacking in certain areas will improve their skills in those and will be helped by the ones that have already skills in those areas. The students will select those areas beforehand together with the project supervisor, who will monitor the student’s progress.

/en/course/2026/SEVM19AML.outcomes:
At the end of this module the student:
the student can analyse a data analysis task and compare features to evaluate their fitness for the machine learning task at hand.
the student can evaluate whether a data analysis task requires dimensionality reduction, blind source separation, cluster analysis or classification.
the student can interpret high dimensional data using dimensionality reduction techniques such as principal component analysis.
the student can interpret multi-sensor data:
using blind source separation techniques like independent component analysis.
using cluster analysis techniques like hierarchical agglomerative clustering and k-means.
using classification algorithms like support vector machines.
the student can apply anomaly detection on a stream of sensor data.
/en/course/2026/SEVM19AML.content:
The course covers the following topics:
machine learning overview, dimensionality reduction, blind source separation, cluster analysis or classification, coverage plot, confusion matrix, cost functions.

/en/course/2026/SEVM21DFA.outcomes:
At the end of this module the student:
create data processing software for a sensor system which combines multi-sensor data into correct interpretations.
analyse system requirements to identify applicable sensor fusion architectures.
analyse data acquisition by a sensor system to construct a common representational format.
adapt sensor system design to create correct temporal and spatial alignment and normalization of multi-sensor data.
design interfaces for sensor system management.
design and implement a system architecture using data stream management systems.
design and implement mathematical data fusion models.
/en/course/2026/SEVM21DFA.content:
The course covers the following topics:
sensor fusion architectures, common representational format, temporal and spatial alignment, error propagation analysis and device virtualization.

/en/course/2026/SEVM21AF.outcomes:
At the end of this module the student is able to:
understand the link between Fourier analysis and the Z-transform.
create and understand how a digital filter (FIR/IIR) works.
clean data using advanced filtering techniques, including the Wiener filter, (normalized) Least-Mean-Square (LMS) adaptive filters, Recursive Least Squares (RLS) adaptive filters, and Kalman filtering.
describe systems in the time-domain and/or frequency domain using stationary discrete-time stochastic processes and models, such as autoregressive (AR) and moving-average (MA) models.
/en/course/2026/SEVM21AF.content:
The course covers the following topics:
Z-transform, FIR and IIR filters, stati
onary discrete-time stochastic processes and models, (normalized) Least-Mean-Square adaptive filters, Recursive Least Squares Adaptive Filters and Kalman filtering, model simulation tools, model-based reasoning.

/en/course/2026/SEVM19PSD.outcomes:
At the end of this module the student:
Demonstrates their ability and understanding by delivering:
a design debrief: a methodical and systematical analyses of a case/assignment, context and/or market and stakeholders.
a methodical approach for a design of a product or service, from case to concept.
a systematic description of the case as a Cyber Physical Human System.
a relevant, useful, verifiable, list of hierarchically structured requirements.
purposeful and convincingly presented pitch(es) and posters.
/en/course/2026/SEVM19PSD.content:
The course covers the following topics:
Engineering is about discovering and formulating rules and consequently designing according to those rules. In the end it is always about meeting expectations: of clients, of markets, of other -connected- systems.
Smart-System Engineers design Cyber-Physical-Human system (CPHS). The “H” puts the human in the loop and that is where expectations are always present but often implicit: hidden, unknown, unrecognized, subjective.
Every engineering project starts with agreeing upon a list of requirements. Unambiguous, highly specific, and verifiable requirements enable clear communication between you and your stakeholders. Only clear communication will lead to successful solutions.
You as Smart System Engineer should be able to clearly answer, and communicate, the three questions:
Why is there a need to create a solution?
How will we get from need to concept?
What valid tangible solutions meet the why?
In this course you will go through the process of defining the why, how and what for your project and purposefully communicating those to stakeholders and peers.

/en/course/2026/SEVM26ICPS.outcomes:
At the end of this module the student:
Identifies each parameter necessary for the models.
Describes the physical system using linear and nonlinear dynamical system models.
Designs the communication framework between the cyber- and physical world.
Designs and builds a digital twin and optimizes the accompanying models.
Controls the physical system with the digital twin.
/en/course/2026/SEVM26ICPS.content:
The course covers the following topics:
linear and non-linear dynamical system models, model simulation tools, and knowledge-based systems (expert systems). In this course, the student learns how to design and build a digital twin to control a physical system with the digital twin.

/en/course/2026/SEVM19DCA.outcomes:
At the end of this module the student is able to:
design and/or implement a Digital Signal Processing Architecture considering fixed point core, floating point core, PLD, FPGA, GPU and mixed signal systems.
implement algorithms by means of the most suitable programming model (i.e., sequential/linear, functional, parallel).
design an IoT system considering edge, fog, cloud or mist computing  IoT architectures.
design IoT system  connectivity considering wireless and wired communication technologies, such as for example: Wifi, mobile G4/G5,  LoRa, ethernet, etc.
evaluate the impact of system design choices on resource usage considering at least energy consumption and usage of rare materials.
/en/course/2026/SEVM19DCA.content:
The course covers the following topics:
The student is trained in architectural design at two conceptual levels. At the level of System Architectures for “big data” applications they learn about top-level trade-offs, e.g. between measured data rates and required processing power.
The student get introduced to high-performance computing and streaming database technology. At the level of Digital Signal Processing Architectures, the student learns key concepts (fixed point, floating point) and technologies (FPGA, GPU, Mixed signal chips).
Linear and Functional programming as well as Parallel processing are covered.

/en/course/2026/SEVM26NNDL.outcomes:
At the end of this module the student:
utilizes the fundamental principles of neural networks and deep learning, including architectural components, training procedures, and objective functions to implement, train, and evaluate neural network models using a modern deep learning framework such as PyTorch.
designs and justifies neural network architectures appropriate to a given problem, considering data characteristics and task requirements.
assesses and improves model performance using appropriate evaluation metrics, hyperparameter tuning, and systematic troubleshooting.
applies deep learning techniques to different data modalities, such as structured, image-based, or sequential data, using architectures such as convolutional or recurrent networks.
designs and executes an end-to-end deep learning project, including data preparation, model development, validation, and communication of results, for tasks such as classification, prediction, or anomaly detection.
/en/course/2026/SEVM26NNDL.content:
The module covers the following topics:
neural network fundamentals, deep learning workflows & implementation, model architectures (e.g. feedforward, convolutional, recurrent), training and optimization strategies, hyperparameter tuning, evaluation metrics and performance analysis, feature and representation learning, and project-based application to tasks such as classification, prediction, or anomaly detection.

/en/course/2026/SEVM26RS.outcomes:
At the end of this module the student:
independently gathers, selects and analyses relevant new information in a responsible way by using scientific databases, correct search terms, and evaluating the source of the information.
formulates and critically verifies a research question with sub-questions through a logical line of reasoning from the practical problem to the specified research question.
designs a research methodology that delivers relevant and reliable results and communicates this methodology in a way that is easy to replicate by others.
communicates the knowledge, gained by critically judging insights originating from the forefront of smart system design, in a logical line of reasoning to a public of experts by writing a research paper, including a clear context and research goal, detailed methods, a structured presentation and discussion of the results, and sound conclusions that lead to answering the research question and giving advice to the client.
presents their research in a presentation in the format of a scientific conference, in an effective and clear fashion, with high information density and leaving no gaps.
optimizes the advice or design of an advanced smart sensor system application through critical reflection on the impact on society, environment, and end-user implications, based on ethical aspects, risk analysis and any other relevant information.
considers the ethical implications when designing an advanced smart system by reflecting on the impacts on society, environment, and end-user implications, based on ethical aspects, risk analysis and any other relevant information.
/en/course/2026/SEVM26RS.content:
The course covers the following topics:
Research and innovation in engineering have a multitude of impacts on society and on the world. The study unit Sustainable Research Skills allows the student to improve (some of) their research skills, such as addressing a practical problem, investigating that problem in scientific literature, and finding possible solutions that lead to proposing a research question with sub questions. The student is expected to be critical of his/her research as well as that of others, while also being called to reflect on the relevance of ethics in the engineering field in general by taking part in a series of discussions on different ethical issues relevant for engineering and preparing themselves discussions on specific ethical problems.

metadata.Name: Professional Skills & Community Contribution
metadata.Assessments: Professional Skills and Community Contri - Assignment

/en/course/2026/SEVM19PSCC.outcomes:
At the end of this module the student is able to:
show understanding of the differences between distributive and integrative bargaining and identify them in an applied setting.
describe and analyze the main factors that affect intercultural negotiations in own country and compare them with a second country of his/her own choice.
design and evaluate a negotiation plan based on feedback received after a role-modelling exercise.
design a questioning strategy and evaluate its suitability on a given negotiation situation.
explain the arguments that constitute the business case for Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR).
/en/course/2026/SEVM19PSCC.content:
Negotiation skills
– the student will learn about the different types of negotiation styles the student can use and practice developing effective arguments. We will also see how questions should and should not be used in a negotiation context and the type of conventions that apply in intercultural negotiations.
Sustainability
- the student will be introduced to concepts like Green Engineering and Cradle to Cradle, as well as Corporate Social Responsibility.

/en/course/2026/SEVM25S2P.outcomes:
At the end of this module the student is able to:
methodically design and implement a detailed smart-system proof of concept that leads to a specific solution.
critically validate the answer to the research question/goal and sub-questions/goals through a logical line of reasoning that connects the research question to the specific solution.
critically reflect on the investigation and results, recognizing strengths and weaknesses and indicating possible improvements to achieve a specific solution based on a smart system design.
communicate the new insights, obtained by critically performing research, in a logical line of reasoning to a public of experts via a research paper and presentation, with high information density.
/en/course/2026/SEVM25S2P.content:
The course covers the following topics:
The student undertakes an assignment originating from the professional field, either at a company in Smart Systems or within one of the professorships affiliated with the SSE master’s programme. The project serves as preparation for the working methods and expectations associated with the graduation project.

/en/course/2026/SEVM21MT.outcomes:
At the end of this module the student:
Shows that he/she possess the end level qualifications of a Smart Systems Engineer as defined within the Programme learning Outcomes:
SSE1 – Giving meaning to Sensor Data
SSE2 – Building Intelligent Architectures
SSE3 – Creating Reliable Services
SSE4 – Professional Skills
SSE5 – Performing Applied Research for System Design
SSE6 – Contributing to Sustainable Innovation
/en/course/2026/SEVM21MT.content: The Master thesis project is part of the graduation programme in which the student shows that he/she possess the end level qualifications of a Smart Systems Engineer.

LILO 1:
Professionalism of the sports professional

/en/course/2026/SKVP24IEM.content:
Content of the course component:
The complex world of today consists of an enormous number of challenges and wicked problems. These complex problems are problems that are beyond the scope of any single organisation, both in terms of understanding and response. Additionally, there is often disagreement about the cause of the problems and how to address them. Wicked problems lack clarity in both their aims and solutions and are subject to real-world constraints. This means that risk-free attempts to find a solution are highly unlikely. Within the sport studies program, students will work on challenges and wicked problems and will try to solve a part of the complex issues that exist.
During this course, students will be introduced to the structure and method of working in a specific challenge and they will gain experience when it comes to working in a complex situation with many different stakeholders and target groups.
In this introductory challenge, the students will work in multidisciplinary teams on developing, organising, executing and evaluating a unique (innovative) sports experience for a specific target group. The team works according to the principles of project management, in which skills in marketing, communication, research, organisation and supervision are indispensable.
The event must be based on one of the intersections of the values ​​of sport (economic, social or health). In order to set up a successful event, the students will be guided by both a client and a supervisor of Sports studies. Focus points of this assessment include:
Pre-event:
- Research;
- Marketing/promotion;
- Finance;
- Sponsorship.
During event:
- Coordination;
- Guiding;
- Supervision;
- Leading volunteers.
post event:
- Evaluation;
- Aftercare.
To further enhance their professional development, students will participate in an outdoor week in the Belgian Ardennes. During this week, students will have a unique experience that includes several challenges around the topics of personal leadership and development and team building whilst participating in different outdoor activities.
Course structure:
The course consists of guest lectures, regular lectures, and tutorials led by your instructor.
Assessment structure:
Portfolio assessment.

By the end of this course, students will have developed a comprehensive understanding of the historical and contemporary landscape of sports, including its diverse manifestations and social implications. They will be able to critically analyze the evolution and current trends in sports, identify and articulate their professional identity within the sports industry, and effectively engage in professional practices through debates, dialogues, and presentations. This will prepare them to navigate and contribute to various sports organizations and communities, fostering their growth as informed and adaptable sports professionals.

/en/course/2026/SKVP24SWO.content:
Content of the course component
: Sport world and Identity allows students to gain insight into the world of sport by considering the past and the ongoing challenges. Based on this knowledge they will develop themselves as sport professionals and find their orientation and identity within the world of sport.
Literature and digital knowledge sources will allow students to prepare for the seminars and the included active teaching methods such as debate, dialogue and presentation.
Central key points in this course are:
· the sport community (the broad and diverse character of sport & exercise);
· the dual nature of sport (specificity of different manifestations of sport versus the social embedding of sport);
· the issue of what is the meaning and form of expression of sport depending on the participant's motives;
· (sub)cultural differences between (groups of) participants;
· how sports originated over the years and have continued to evolve on many fronts.
The student will also learn about the processes and developments that were behind these changes and which, among other things, led to the popularisation, differentiation, (partial) informalisation, professionalisation and commercialisation of participation in sport, the experience and organisation.
This results in an understanding of traditionally organised practice of sports (in sports clubs), commercially organised practice of sports (in fitness centres) and ‘other organised practice of sports’ (e.g. organised by oneself).
In addition to this the students learn to orientate themselves, to create and develop a professional identity regarding sport and exercise. Therefore the central key points connected to this development are:
· To understand the organization behind sports
· Orientate in the professional world of sports
· Personal preferences and development of who the student would like to be as a sports professional

/en/course/2026/SKVP25SPD.content:
Content of the course component
: According to Vohs and Baumeister (2016), self-regulation is a process in which human beings do something they would not normally do in order to reach a desired state or outcome; that is, individuals go out of their comfort zone to positively change their behavior and/or learn something. Self-regulation of learning (SRL) is a more specific form of self-regulation which is defined as the manner in which individuals take charge of their learning process (Zimmerman, 2006). SRL consists of metacognition (thinking about your own thinking, such as planning and reflection), motivation (wanting to learn something) and behavior (take action to enable learning). An important misconception about self-regulation is that it is a purely individual process; on the contrary, it always takes place within a context, meaning that it always happens in relationship with others. This in turn means that it is important to pay attention to emotions and skills such as dealing with frustration and adversity.
The motivational climate as well as the physical environment greatly influence the self-regulation process. As an example, more self-regulation takes place in a motivational climate that allows for intrinsic motivation (motivation stems from doing an activity in itself; Deci & Ryan, 2000) compared to a situation in which extrinsic motivation is elicited (motivation stems from external sources such as rewards; Deci & Ryan, 2000). In addition, the design of the physical environment automatically influences our decisions. Relevant in this regard is the concept of nudging (Thaler & Sunstein, 2009). The concepts mentioned will be put in light of current complex societal challenges we face (e.g., mental health decrease, sedentary lifestyle, sustainability in sport) and together we’ll define relevant transition skills to tackle these issues as a sport professional.
During the course, you will work on assignments in which you can research and challenge yourself when it comes to your personal and professional self-regulation. We will make use of the intercultural context found in your Sport Studies class, design and test small interventions, and define and apply some transition skills.
Sources:
Deci, E. L., & Ryan, R. M. (2000). The" what" and" why" of goal pursuits: Human needs and the self-determination of behavior.
Psychological inquiry, 11(4),
227-268.
Thaler, R. H., & Sunstein, C. R. (2009).
Nudge: Improving Decisions About Health, Wealth and Happiness.
Pengiun Books.
Vohs, K. D., & Baumeister, R. F. (Eds.). (2016
). Handbook of self-regulation: Research, theory, and applications.
Guilford Publications.
Zimmerman, B. J. (2006). Development and adaptation of expertise: The role of self-regulatory processes and beliefs.
The Cambridge handbook of expertise and expert performance,
186, 705-722.
Course structure:
The course consists of lectures, weekly assignments, a module assignment and work field visits.
Assessment structure:
Students will complete weekly assignments and the module assignment, and these will be presented at the end of the course.

/en/course/2026/SKVP24EMA.content:
Content of the course component:
The Event Management course requires the student to independently study literature and digital knowledge sources related to the international event management landscape (e.g. podcasts, webinars, and official reports of respective events). This is in preparation for seminars in which the student gives substance to the knowledge they have gained through instructional modes such as lectures, dialogue and presentations throughout the overall program of Event Management. The topic of Human Resource Management (HRM) is also part of this course. A basic understanding of the overall HR process will be presented covering aspects including recruitment and selection, retention, diversity and equality, pay and reward and volunteer management. Students will then be expected to apply these key concepts to various sporting scenarios and events in order to enhance their knowledge and understanding. Pine and Gilmore in their book: 'Experience Economy' (1999) argue that businesses must orchestrate memorable events for their customers, and that memory itself becomes the product: the "experience". More advanced experience businesses can begin charging for the value of the "transformation" that an experience offers, e.g., as education offerings might do if they were able to participate in the value that is created by the educated individual. This, they argue, is a natural progression in the value added by the business over and above its inputs. Although the concept of the experience economy was initially focused on business, it has crossed into other fields. The Experience Economy is also considered to be the main underpinning for customer experience management and will therefore be addressed as a key aspect of this course, alongside other theoretical models, in order to provide students with a solid knowledge base regarding the many facets of Event Management.
The complete body of knowledge is required to fulfil the challenges and assignments during the West Ham United (WHU) international game. The game participants are students from the Sport Studies as well as students from partner universities in Europe. West Ham United is a professional football club in London, England. The international game WHU is a time management game in order to develop skills in the application of current sport, health and management theories to a practical situation.
Aims of the Event:
* develop skills of teamwork through the execution of an applied sport, health and management exercise
* critically appraise event management issues including volunteering, promotion, marketing, branding and organising
* analyse and evaluate the importance and power of a sport event and event management
Objectives of the event: at the end of the game successful students will be able to recognise and respond to the demands of a (simulated) management experience and to:
* develop an understanding of diversity management and cultural differences within sport event management
* develop personal competencies associated with working in a team, making decisions, taking responsibilities and applying sound principles to the effective execution of a sports event
Course structure:
The course consists of guest lectures, regular lectures, and tutorials led by your instructor.
Assessment structure:
Written exam

/en/course/2026/SKVP22IVC1.content:
Content of the course component:
The complex world of today consists of an enormous amount of challenges and wicked problems. These complex problems are problems that are beyond the scope of any single organisation, both in terms of understanding and response. Additionally, there is often disagreement about the cause of the problems and how to address them. Wicked problems lack clarity in both their aims and solutions and are subject to real-world constraints. This means that risk-free attempts to find a solution are highly unlikely. Within the sport studies program, students will work on challenges and wicked problems and will try to solve a part of the complex issues that exist.This course will be separated into two parts. Part 1 will consist of the use and collection of conceptual and empirical data. Part 2 consists of developing the sport/health intervention.
The European Vital City – part 1 is a challenge where students will work from a multidisciplinary perspective. The students acquire usable knowledge in the field of strategy formation to allow them to analyse the degree of vitality of the international city and apply this knowledge by conducting analyses of various policy fields and themes that are of importance in the city and which interface with sport and exercise (diagnostic research). The future is explored, developing various scenarios (Nekkers 2011), after which an inspirational vision and city strategy are developed.
The following questions need to be answered. How is the city currently set up to optimally use sport to create the greatest possible positive effect on the health of the urban population, quality of life and the economy of the international city? What strategic planning is needed to influence the vitality of the city in the future? Which scenarios could enhance and develop the city to be ready for future?
The European Vital City – part 2 also requires students to work from a multidisciplinary perspective where the student builds further on the discoveries and knowledge from the European Vital City – part 1. The creative vision and city strategy can now be further researched and elaborated into an actual sport/health intervention. The team of students must execute and coordinate sport/health and exercise programmes and projects in consultation with relevant stakeholders and collaborate with other disciplines. The intervention is of an innovative nature. The student team is responsible for costs related to traveling, accommodation etc, concerning the sport/health intervention.

The course consists of guest lectures, regular lectures, and tutorials led by your instructor.
Assessment structure:

Portflow will be used for the portfolio, containing formative assessments and a final video.

/en/course/2026/SKVP25BOK2.content:
Content of the course component:
The body of knowledge of Sport Marketing will be introduced in the weeks prior to the international West Ham United Game.
The Body of Knowledge of Sport Marketing is presented in this module. The Sport Marketing Framework is the leading model in this, providing a clear overview of the different steps in the (Sport) Marketing process and all theory that is to be discussed. Important topics include: the sports market, challenges and controversial issues of Sport Marketing, opportunities and strategies and the Marketing mix: price, product, distribution and promotion. These topics are then supplemented with digital marketing, social media and ethics. In addition to the theory provided, much work is conducted across assignments in which the theory is tested in a practical form.
New technology, different forms of organisation, emerging sports and changes of values - the world is in transition, and this means that the future of many (sports) organizations is uncertain. Although every organization must periodically consider its raison d'être and strategic course, this certainly also applies to organizations that are active in the context of sports and exercise. Using theory and an entrepreneurial and investigative attitude, the student learns how to support and advise organizations in a change process, while the world around the student is also changing.
The complete body of knowledge is required to fulfil the challenges and assignments during the Great Run (GR) international game. The game participants are students from the Dutch and English stream of Sport Studies as well as students from partner universities in Europe. The GR is a half marathon with its origin in Newcastle, England. The international game GR is a team-based simulation in order to develop skills in the application of current sport, health and management theories to a practical situation in the context of a real-life event.
Through the game, the students will:
* develop skills of teamwork through the execution of an applied sport, health and management exercise
* achieve an integrated view in which the following components are recognised: planning, sports marketing, management & organization
Objectives at the end of the game successful students will be able to recognise and respond to the demands of a (simulated) management experience and to:
* develop an understanding of diversity management and cultural differences within sport, health and management
* develop an understanding of ethical issues in sport management and marketing
* develop personal competencies associated with working in a team, making decisions, taking responsibilities and applying sound principles to the effective execution of a sports/health event
* strategy and policy activities and practical communication skills in association with a group exercise.
After the intensive period of 5 full days and the GR game, the course is concluded with a written exam/case study
Course structure:
The course consists of guest lectures, regular lectures, and tutorials led by your instructor.
Assessment structure:
Written exam – case study

/en/course/2026/SKVP23CK.content:
Content of the course component:
Challenge dedicated knowledge 1 is directly linked to the challenge chosen: "International Event" and "Blue zones and healthy lifestyle" and European Vital City”.  The complex world of today consists of an enormous amount of challenges and wicked problems. These complex problems are problems that are beyond the scope of any single organisation, both in terms of understanding and response. Additionally, there is often disagreement about the cause of the problems and how to address them. Wicked problems lack clarity in both their aims and solutions and are subject to real-world constraints. This means that risk-free attempts to find a solution are highly unlikely. Within the sport studies program, students will work on challenges and wicked problems and will try to solve a part of the complex issues that exist.
All existing challenges require, alongside the general body of knowledge, specific information (challenge dedicated knowledge) focussed on the specific part of the challenge that needs to be solved. Through dialogue, learning by doing and field work, students will gain information from different areas in and outside the domain of sport and health, enabling them to combine information to solve part of the challenges. Sources therefore can be experts from different fields but also literature etc.. Students can also follow other modules within the Hanze university and at partner universities. If a student chooses to follow other modules, approval of the study coach is required.
The level of complexity therefore depends on the level of available knowledge, the amount of multi-disciplinarity, the existing knowledge of people involved and the need for adaptivity, the number of stakeholders and interests involved, the fast changing and developing context, the end-user being part of the design cycle, an unclear end-result, the design process to be concentric and non-linear, and the unique process  that is non-repeatable. The challenge dedicated knowledge therefore requires a personalised approach as each student will be involved in different parts of the challenge and will bring an individual level of personalised knowledge and experience.
The challenge dedicated knowledge is part of the Knowledge Management (KM) of each challenge. KM concerns the collection of methods relating to creating, sharing, using and managing the knowledge and information of the organisations involved with the challenge. It refers to a multidisciplinary approach to achieve organisational objectives by making the best use of that knowledge.
Knowledge management efforts typically focus on organisational objectives such as improved performance, competitive advantage, innovation, the sharing of lessons learned, integration and continuous improvement of the organisation. These efforts overlap with organisational learning and may be distinguished from that by a greater focus on the management of knowledge as a strategic asset and on encouraging the sharing of knowledge. KM is an enabler of organisational learning and learning within the challenge specifically.
Various frameworks that address different 'types of' knowledge already exist. One proposed framework for categorising the dimensions of knowledge is the Knowledge Spiral (as shown below) which distinguishes tacit knowledge from explicit knowledge. Tacit knowledge represents internalised knowledge that an individual may not be consciously aware of, such as the knowledge required to accomplish particular tasks. Conversely, explicit knowledge represents knowledge that the individual holds consciously in mental focus, in a form that can easily be communicated to others.
The Knowledge Spiral (1995) as described by Nonaka & Takeuchi.

/en/course/2026/SKVP22INC.content:
Content of the course component:
Working in an intercultural environment – in The Netherlands or abroad – provides a unique dynamic to teamwork, causing multicultural teams to either excel or underperform. Differences can help creativity blossom but may also be a source of uncertainty. This can create tension or even feel threatening to some, as power balances start to shift. Effective leadership, efficient management and organising therefore will be needed. Alongside the ability to use the English language at a proficient level and to communicate empathically, respectfulness and working constructively with people from different fields of language and culture in both national and international contexts is then required. As a group leader, how do you control these cultural dynamics?
The intercultural competency matrix is a systematic tool that can help us gain insight into our views on interculturalism. It identifies our cultural patterns by means of flexible comparisons, confrontation with others and adjustment to unfamiliar cultures. As professionals, our intercultural identity is determined by: 'what we know', 'our views on both our own and other cultures', 'the way we communicate on these issues' and 'how we establish relationships with others' - aspects which will be further explored throughout this module.

Ad 2: The Team part: The festival will take place in the Willem Alexander Sports Building (canteen and surrounding). This festival will be organised by the teams of SpSt1. Each team consists of max. 4 students. The theme of the festival is:
Diversity in Sports, your concern!?

/en/course/2026/SKVP22VWO.content:
Content of the course component:
Vital organizations are attractive organizations where people enjoy working. They are able to adapt well to circumstances, the work is being done with active engagement and enthusiasm and the employees work together to create a pleasant organizational culture. The employees are energetic, the customers are satisfied, and absenteeism is low. A vital organizational culture arises when employees take responsibility for their own health and employability (bottom-up approach) but can certainly be facilitated or supported by management and policy (top-down approach). Vital organizations arise from interventions on multiple levels: the (HRM) policy, the way of working (together) in teams and at an individual level.
In this course, students will develop a project which aims to make an organization (company, government, non-profit) more vital and to increase the sustainable employability of employees. Based on a diagnosis of the current situation, work is being done on the design of an approach to improve the vitality of the employees. Challenges at the various levels to create an active lifestyle at and around work are examined and innovative solutions based on existing knowledge are used to remove any barriers. Knowledge of behavioural change, active and healthy lifestyle and HRM are important here. Based on the performed research, the designed approach and the implementation of (part of) this approach is tested by means of an evaluation study, project report and a final presentation.

/en/course/2026/SKVH22GAM.content:
Content of the course component:
Sport and physical activity are growing social and economic phenomena that make an important contribution to the European Union's strategic objectives of solidarity and prosperity. This is of course adapted to national and local level.
Sport and physical activity attract European citizens, with a majority of people taking part in sporting activities and active leisure on a regular basis. It generates important values such as team spirit, solidarity, tolerance and fair play, contributing to an active lifestyle, personal development and fulfilment. It promotes the active contribution of citizens to society and thereby helps to foster active citizenship.
The important role of sport and physical activity in European local communities and its specific nature were recognised in December 2000 in the European Council’s Declaration on the specific characteristics of sport and physical activity and their social function in Europe, which should be considered when implementing common policies (the "Nice Declaration"). In addition, sport and physical activity are increasingly recognised for their contribution to active (and in doing so; healthy) lifestyles.
In this module, students will be challenged to develop innovative policies on a local level towards active lifestyles for citizens, taking into account knowledge of policymaking and population management that will be discussed in this course. A key question will be: ‘how can local policymakers and municipality governmental bodies influence populations on this matter in a positive way?’
This module comprises two short phases:
Phase 1: training for understanding local policymaking on different governmental levels. Knowledge, insights and skills will be acquired during intensive seminars and by autonomous thorough study of literature and web sources. This phase will be concluded with an analysis of EU, national and local policy. This analysis will also be presented in a so called ‘Pechua Kucha’
Phase 2: Game on! Students will be submerged in a dynamic and intensive simulation game. In this game, students will have to react to real time events and tasks that are part of the policy context that they will be part of. This phase will be concluded with a policy report that results in presented advice for policymakers and politicians such as the alderman and members of the city council. During this semester, the student participates in Urban Sports. This provides students with first-hand physical experiences and understanding concerning new urban sports that are best suited to urban culture in big cities and that relate to the latest trends and developments in society.
Students will receive formative feedback for all in between reports delivered and receive 1 grade (summative assessment) at the end.

Content of the course component:
The Body of Knowledge (BOK) of sport and exercise psychology will cover central theories and concepts related to sport performance and well-being (Weinberg & Gould, 2023), such as motivation, mindset, and stress. In addition, a range of mental skills will be discussed, such as coping with adversity and stress management. Students will be expected to apply their knowledge and skills in several contexts relevant to sport, society, health and entrepreneurship to enhance their understanding of how psychological processes can play a role in these contexts. Specific attention will be given to how the environment in which we act can influence our behavior. A well-known concept in this regard is nudging (Thaler & Sunstein, 2009). This BOK also focuses on students' professional development through self-reflection skills.
During the course, you’ll work on weekly assignments related to mental skills and how they influence athletes’ performance and well-being. In addition, there will be assignments in which you can research yourself when it comes to concepts and skills relevant to your professional development. The module assignment will entail the application of sport psychological concepts to contribute to solutions of a complex societal issue in the domain of sport (e.g., mental health decrease, social inclusion and diversity, sedentary lifestyle).

Content of the course component:
Sport can be considered as a social phenomenon that can create a diversity of values. As far as the entrepreneurial process is concerned, creating value is also a central theme. Sport entrepreneurship is shaped by new initiatives relating to products/services, markets, transactions, and systems in the world of sports. One of these entrepreneurial initiatives is the collaboration between an (elite) sports organization and its business partners that engages start-up companies to create value together.
This module therefore focuses on the entrepreneurial process in the context of the world of sports for which a diversity of values can be created through the combination of sport and the entrepreneurial process.
The students must analyse the context and positioning of new innovative sport and exercise concepts within the following three areas: “public”, “commerce” and “civil society”. The student therefore must show leadership skills in developing communities and networking by having an impact on the intersections of the economic, health and social value(s) of sport.
Course structure:
Sport can be considered as a social phenomenon that can create a diversity of values. As far as the entrepreneurial process is concerned, creating value is also a central theme.
The entrepreneurial process consists of the following three phases:
- recognizing or creating an opportunity for value creation;
- converting this opportunity into an executable concept;
- putting the concept into operation in a (growing) organization.
This module focuses on the first two phases of the entrepreneurial process in the context of the world of sports for which a diversity of values can be created through the combination of sport and the entrepreneurial process.
First part of the module consists of lectures / workshops about theories related to business eco systems / sustainability / business models / multiple value creation / innovation paradigms and business concepting. The lectures / workshops include individual assignments. During this module the student takes the perspective of an analytical and creative professional being a team player that values each individual contribution to the joint assignment. Context of the final team assignment concerns the sport and tourism sector.
To provide more in-depth information, at least two in-depth interviews are conducted with an expert from the sport and tourism field. The interview should ensure that you discover the vision of the expert and process this vision in a meaningful way. To make a comparison possible the interview is provided by Hanze and therefore standardized. The interview must be conducted face-to-face (or Skype), must be recorded and takes at least 20 minutes. Both recorded data and processed interviews must be handed in.
During the last weeks of the module, students have to apply the gained knowledge in a group business case called Sunset Waters. The group of students will be divided into smaller teams (marketing, HRD, facility, finances) responsible for creating and implementing new strategies, based on multiple value creation and embedded innovation paradigm and analysis of the context and its stakeholders.

/en/course/2026/SKVH22LSP.content:
Content of the course component:
Although leadership studies are relatively new as an academic discipline, leadership as a topic has been studied for thousands of years (Bolden, Hawkins, Gosling & Taylor, 2011). Starting in the early – to mid – twentieth century, initial research in the field of leadership endeavoured to explain leadership as a property of leaders. However, the presence of any or all of these traits does and did not make someone a leader, nor did the absence exclude that person from being the leader. In the following years, several theories were developed and various approaches to leadership can now be identified with varying degrees of focus on either the leader or follower, the interactive process between them, and/or the influence of the context. Recent leadership theory shifted the focus from the leader to leadership, emphasising the shared social process to which many people contribute (Pearce & Conger, 2003).
Leadership, both as a research area and as a practical skill, encompasses the ability of an individual, group or
organization
to "lead", influence or guide other individuals,
teams
, or entire
organizations
. The word "leadership" often gets viewed as a contested term (Grint, 2005).
This module has two main objectives. On one hand it provides a common understanding about theories and concepts of leadership with an emphasis on individual - and team leadership. On the other hand, it provides (practical) insights into the question: “who are you as a leader?”.

/en/course/2026/SKVH22BHL3.content:
Content of the course component:
The complex world of today consists of an enormous number of challenges and wicked problems. These complex problems are problems that are beyond the scope of any single organization, both in terms of understanding and response. Additionally, there is often disagreement about the cause of the problems and how to address them. Wicked problems lack clarity in both their aims and solutions and are subject to real-world constraints. This means that risk-free attempts to find a solution are highly unlikely. Within the sport studies program, students will work on challenges and wicked problems and will try to solve a part of the complex issues that exist. The current course will be separated into two parts. Part 1 will consist of the use and collection of conceptual and empirical data. Part 2 consists of developing the sport/health concept/Blue zone.
In part 1 of the Blue Zone/Healthy Lifestyle (BZ/HL) challenge students will work from a multidisciplinary perspective. The students acquire knowledge of and about the field of Healthy Ageing by taking part in a (international) Blue Zone/Healthy lifestyle project. The focus lies on prerequisites and different variables that influence the adoption of a healthy lifestyle (diagnostic research). These will be based on an ecological approach (Sallis 2006) and derived from evidence-informed models, such as the model of Positive Health (Huber 2011).
The following questions need to be answered in Part 1: What are key determinants influencing healthy behaviour? What is the role of sport and movement in healthy behaviour? How does this relate to other determinants? How could healthy behaviour be stimulated using sport and movement? Which target groups can be distinguished and what proven and possible strategies exist to activate these people? After answering these questions, advice is given to enhance and develop the field.
In part 2 of the Blue Zone/Healthy Lifestyle Part 2 students will work from a multidisciplinary perspective. The student builds further on knowledge and discoveries from BZ/HL part 1; that is, the student takes part in the development and execution of health interventions in Blue Zones, using the knowledge gained in part 1 to innovate the field. Emphasis will be placed on critical thinking, with the aim of creating impact while working together with different stakeholders from several disciplines.
Course structure:
The course consists of guest lectures, regular lectures, and tutorials led by your instructor.
Assessment structure:
Students will receive formative feedback for all in between reports delivered and receive 1 grade (summative assessment) at the end.
Level 2 consists of: program-based, applying new technology, intervention/program: long-term legacy

/en/course/2026/SKVH23BOK6.outcomes:
By the end of this course, students will have developed a thorough understanding of change management principles and practices. They will learn how to prepare, support, and guide individuals, teams, and organizations through significant organizational changes. This includes methods for reallocating resources, redefining business processes, and adjusting budget allocations. Students will explore the multidisciplinary nature of change management, encompassing behavioral and social sciences, information technology, and business solutions. They will also gain insights into organizational change management (OCM) and its impact on overall organizational performance. This course will equip students with the skills to effectively manage and implement change, ensuring sustainable growth and financial stability for organizations.
